                   Dedication

With hopes and dreams of a better life, they left their homelands and journeyed
into the unknown. With courage and strong faith, they faced the adversities of
the Prairie. With fortitude and persistence, they formed our land and community,
leaving us with a legacy of which we are proud. It is to these gallant pioneers
that we, with gratitude, dedicate this Centennial Book.


                   Song of remembrance

Where are the old-timers gone,
That robust race of pioneers?
Where are their memories flown
Of joy and grief in by-gone years?

Where are the tales they used to tell
Of life and love when they were young?
Where are the songs they sang so well,
The hearty sounds of the mother-tongue?

Where are the sayings wise and true
From tradition's ample store?
Where are the customs old and new
That graced the lives of rich and poor?

Shall their history turn to dust,
Windswept from short-lived memory?
Will it be saved in sacred trust
As a living heirloom for posterity?

                        Joseph S. Height


                   FOREWORD

This publication is a collection of memories throughout a century of hardships
endured, family strength, laughter and tears. It is filled with stories of the
perseverance and community effort that brought us from a townsite to a village,
which became, and has remained, our town of Java.

We hope that the culmination of the many hours of preparation, sleepless nights
and worries involved in creating this Centennial Book give you, the reader, many
enjoyable moments of discovering who you are, where you have been, and where you
are going. This book is about you, your community and your roots.

In these pages, we have tried to include every history and story submitted to
us. We have chosen to present the family histories by generation whenever
possible, giving an idea of the resilience of the pioneers who made this 100th
Anniversary a reality.

The Centennial Book Committee gratefully acknowledges all who participated in
submitting histories, stories and photographs. We also extend our gratitude to
our advertisers who have helped defray publishing expense.

Although we have had to edit material, we have done our best to portray the
chronicle of Java. We admit that this book is not free of error and we apologize
to those who find mistakes or omissions. We cannot claim infallibility. We can,
however, claim appreciation for the opportunity given us to bring about such a
book. We hope that you will treasure the memories you find among the pages.

                                 Executive Proclamation
                                  State of South Dakota
                                 Office of the Governor

Whereas, The village of Java sprung up at the site where Chicago, Milwaukee &
St. Paul Railway Line employees, traveling between Bowdle and Glenham, stopped
for refreshments and great coffee; and the Dedication Plat of the original town
of Java was recorded by the Milwaukee Land Company on October 23, 1900; and

Whereas, In the three years that followed, Java grew into a bustling town of 280
souls who built a school, a church, five general stores, a bank, a newspaper,
two liveries, four implement warehouses, three grain elevators, a grist mill,
and two lumber yards; and,

Whereas, Just ten years later, the community was home to a Catholic; a
Presbyterian, a German Lutheran, and a German Congregational Church, another
bank, a hotel, an opera house, another grain elevator, another newspaper, and a
food mill to accommodate the commercial, spiritual, and entertainment needs of
Java's 473 citizens; and,

Whereas, Java has endured for one hundred years, and its founders of German,
Russian, Dutch, English, and Hungarian ancestry would be proud of their
descendants and the 200 citizens who continue to make Java their home; and

Whereas, Java will be commenmorating its centennial with a big celebration June
15-18, 2000, and it is fitting and proper for the Governor to join the former
and current citizens of Java in paying tribute to the little town named for a
great cup of coffee:

Now, Therefore, I, William J. Janklow, Governor of the State of South Dakota, do
hereby proclaim June 15-18, 2000, as

                             Java Centennial Days

in South Dakota.

In Witness Whereof, I have herunto set my hand and caused
to be affixed the Great Seal of the State of South Dakota, in
Pierre, the Capital City, this Nineteenth Day of January in the
Year of Our Lord, Two Thousand.

William J. Janklow, Governor
Attest:
Joyce Hazeltine, Secretary of State

Dear Friends:

Congratulations to Java on your centennial,  I want to share my greetings and
best wishes with community residents and friends celebrating Java's first 100
years. As you will learn from reading the Java Centennial History Book, the
community has seen its share of challenges, opportunities, tragedies and
triumphs.  Through it all, Java has maintained its strong German heritage and
traditions.

I enjoyed the opportunity to learn more about the community from one of its own,
Alice Kundert.  From the early days, when the Russian German immigrants came to
Java from the southern part of the state, to present day, the first things that
come to mind are the delicious kuchen and the coffee, after which the community
was named.  Java also has a rich sports tradition, dating back to the fantastic
basketball teams coached by Roy Stewart and the outstanding baseball teams and
players, including Floyd Biel, who was inducted into the South Dakota Baseball
Hall of Fame in 1992.

I would like to recognize those from the area who gave their lives for our great
country, so that we can continue to enjoy our freedom and democracy.  We must
never forget those who made the ultimate sacrifice.

The hard working, never say die attitudes of the town's founding fathers is
still evident today.  This trait has been passed on through generations of proud
people.  America is a getter place thanks to the extraordinary caliber of people
like those found in Java.

Congratulations again on your centennial.  I wish Java all the best during the
next 100 years.

Very truly yours,
John Thune
Member of Congress

JAVA by Hazel Zeller

Java -- nestled among trees.
Long ago the plan was started,
And trees became part of the plan.
Java -- the crew named it
While laying the railroad tracks.
Each day they stopped for coffee.
From lands near and far, the people came
Bringing their treasures to their new home,
Including their recipes from the Old Country --
Kuchen, strudles and all.
Women bringing seeds sewed into the hems
Of their skirts -- to plant in their new gardens.
The fortunate ones brought steamer trunks
With a "keepsake quilt" -- a pattern for years ahead.
They came from various places -- thus a community was formed.
Graduates went forth from the school they built,
Became doctors, ministers, lawyers, teachers,
And all manner of leaders in an ever widening circle.
Churches were built in gratitude to God.
Gardens were planted and orchards and trees
To grow tall over the years.
Wars were declared and our youth
Responded to the call of duty.
When the war had ended,
Gratefully, most returned to the "home front".
By their war efforts they were bonded
Thus the Legion was formed and its Auxiliary.
As we round out the Century, we look back and ahead.
With care, gardens still flourish.
At the annual flower show for the past
Forty-five years many display their produce,
The quilters still fashion quilts,
And for the last decade the Kuchen Festival
Tempts with delicacies of the kitchen.
There is pride in our town -- a Community Store,
A Community Cafe, the Nutrition Site
And a beautiful church built to serve all who come.
The roads lead out in each direction
To farms surrounding Java and lead back as well.
What would we be without our farmers and our Co-op?
What would we be without all these and friendliness?
Java -- a century has passed
And all roads lead home to Java.


                   Homesteaders

An astonishing law: the Homestead Act, decreed that anyone at all could have 160
acres of land free just by agreeing to work it and produce a going crop within
five years.

The immigrant stream flowed out of Scandinavia, Germany, Ireland, England, and
Canada. Following them came the mass migration of so-called Roosians. Emigrant
trains, mostly linked box cars, had started deep inside Russia to the ports of
embarkation. At these ports, the people with dreams of a better life were
checked to see if they had the required passports to America: an exit paper, the
price of the passage, and an extra $25. In an enclosure outside their point of
embarkation, they would be bathed, de-loused, and fed, and their baggage and
clothes fumigated. They were then ferried out to the big ship and stowed aboard,
sometimes as many as 900 in steerage.

Crowded in the ships, and with no privacy, they kept occupied by playing cards,
singing, and continually checking their exit papers. As America came nearer,
some of them worried about how they got here in the first place. The younger
ones purposely failed school exams to prove unfitness for military service;
older ones had masked illness with massive doses of medicine.

Once on the docks, the babble of languages could be heard, while the new
arrivals sorted their baggage. They crowded into the main building, were given
numbers and herded into groups of 30, where they were assembled in a large hall
to begin the clearance procedure. The doctor in charge of examining them would
look at the hands, hair, and faces, and ask questions. Those suspected of heart
disease would receive a chalk mark of "H" on their back; an "F" would note a
facial rash, an "L" for a limp. The most dreaded mark was a circle with a cross
in the middle, indicating, "feeble minded." If anyone had trachoma, a common
disease at that time in southern and eastern Europe, an "E" was chalked on the
back and deportation became the fate. About eight in ten survived this scrutiny
and moved to the final leg of examinations, that of being questioned before an
immigrant inspector with an interpreter. Finally, the name was checked against
the ship's manifest. Many were fortunate to begin their new life with their old
name.

Why would the Russians, or more correctly, Germans, for their forefathers had
migrated to the Volga basin, at the invitation of Catherine the Great, to
improve the farming, settle 1500 miles inland, in the empty center of the U.S.?

They had an instinct for the familiar land and would go where the soil was ready
for the crop that had been their staple, wheat. Each of them brought to America
seed of their native strain, Turkey Red wheat.

The homesteaders were the first true inhabitants of the plains. They introduced
the stable element of Family, and began a raw life with raw materials. The
prairie was treeless, so their houses were made of sod. Doctors were rare, and
there was sickness and death. Many otherwise healthy women went mad, from the
scrimping, droughts, burning summers and freezing winters, the loneliness, and
the never-ending wind.

Three things made it possible for the homesteader to make a life: the windmill,
a special plow, and barbed wire. The iron plow simply could not cut through the
heavy matted prairie sod. It was left to John Deere, a man from Vermont who had
moved to Illinois, to invent a plow with a revolving blade and a steel
moldboard. It cut the sod and then turned it over. The homesteaders arrived,
settled, and endured; and hence began, on a part of the vast prairie, a new life
and dreams fulfilled.


Before Java was a Town
By Herbert Geigle

Writing a complete history of the pre-Java Community is an impossibility.
However, with what we have, a nearly accurate account can be given.

On June 1861 President James Buchanan signed the Organic Act creating "Dakota
Territory". Eight years later, in 1869, the Sioux nation signed a treaty with
the U.S. government, giving up territory, which included what are now Java and
the Java Community. Not until after the Civil War was the nations' attention
turned to settlement of Dakota Territory. The advent of the Chicago, Milwaukee
and St. Paul railroad, which was pushing westward through Dakota Territory to
the Pacific Ocean to establish markets, was directly important in establishing
Java and its community. The period of growth in Dakota Territory from 1877 to
1885 has been called the "Dakota Boom". The official survey and establishment of
townships in the Java area began on May 12, 1882, and was completed October 21,
1884. Now the area was ready for homesteaders.

Promoters and adventurers, but also a large class of honest but inexperienced
persons, attracted by the free government land, came to establish claims, first
the pre-emption, tree claim, and eventually, the homestead. These people
preceded the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul railroad by about fifteen years. By
1884 the railroad had reached Ispwich, and not until 1900 did the railroad
arrive at the Missouri River and thus, Java was born in the summer of 1900.

As early as 1883 settlers filed claims on what is now the Java trading area. The
Java trading area consists of Blessing, Thompson and the eastern half of Valley
Townships located in the SE portion of Campbell County, and in Walworth County,
the townships of Adam, Highland, eastern Hiddenwood, Spring Lake, Spring Valley,
Theodore and Glenn. The first group of people who filed claims were mostly
Americans from OH, PA, WI, IA and MN. They selected their claims by following
the freight trail, which ran from Ipswich to approximately the present-day site
of Bowdle. The trail split here with one going towards the NW to Mound City in
Campbell County, and the other trail straight west to Bangor in central Walworth
County. Of interest is that records reveal that women made many of the claims,
but it is not known whether they were wives or sisters. Most of the claims were
filed where the ground water was shallow, or near a lake or creek, so they would
have access to water for drinking and for their livestock. In the years 1883 and
1884, the majority of claims filed were in Spring Lake, Spring Valley and Bangor
Townships. This followed the freight trail from Ispwich to Bangor. Also, the
land in these townships is level and somewhat free of rocks. In the Highland
Township, the claims filed were located in the NW corner and in the area that
borders Spring Valley Township. Adams, eastern Highland and northern Spring Lake
Townships were less favorable as much of this area is hilly and has many rocks,
leaning toward raising livestock rather than cultivating crops. The north fork
of the freight trail from Bowdle to Mound City passes thru Sutley Valley, which
is comprised of Thompson, Blessing and Valley Townships. In 1883 the first
claims were filed in Thompson Township and in 1884, in Blessing and Valley.

HIGHLAND TOWNSHIP
Highland Township lies directly north of Java. Records reveal that the people
who filed claims in 1883 and 1884 were Americans. They were John C. and Mankin
Bosch, Henry Cook, Edward Davis, Willis Hayes, Horace & Harmon Mallory, Aaron
Gilley, William, Amy, Frank, and Sarah Winkley, P.E. Cummins, James L. Buns,
George E. Hoffman, William McLean, Hannibal Hughes, Thurman Corson, Charles
Scott; Samuel Rein, John Derr, Frank Clark Benley, M. Pettit, Robert Maas, John
W. Ryan, John Barker, John C. Davidson, Ella Donovan, Nancy Whitlock and William
Vary. At the same time, many claims were filed in Spring Valley and Spring Lake
Townships in Walworth County, and in Campbell County near Sand Lake and Renz
Lake near Mound City. The reason was that the Bangor trail had been promoted
more than Mound City. By the year 1885, a number of original settlers turned
their claims back to the government or sold them to newly arrived settlers. The
role of pioneer in Dakota Territory proved to be too much for less hardy
settlers. However, the hardiest pioneers stayed. Those families who stayed were
Sief, Hofmeyer, Consolver, Schwartz Brothers, Corson, Stowell, Payne, Noble,
Erbe and Campbell. By 1884 a fairly large group of people from Holland, and
Hollanders from the east, with the names of Kosters, Noble, Lakeman and Dyk
settled in Spring Valley Township, and those who settled in Highland were the
Cornelius Nobel, John Vander Vorm, Martin Poorkaliib and Peter de Knief
families. Southeast of Java, a group of families from Austria filed their claims
in Spring Lake and Spring Valley Townships. They were the Erbe, Stangl, Theilen,
Mueller, Bruckner and Meyer families. The Raba and Kormendy familes arrived from
Hungary several years later and also settled in this area.

THOMPSON TOWNSHIP
The first family to file a claim in Thompson Township was an American by the
name of Frederick Mayer, who filed in 1883. The next year, I.C. Barnes, John D.
Gillette, Peter C. Thompson, Joseph C. Thompson, Katie M. Thomas, Richard
Eustine, Osborne Dotto, Henry H. Goodwin, Richard D. Smith, Ferdinand L. Bloise,
James Flynn, Walter Ernest, Willis M. Goodwin, Peter Smith, William C. Chadle
and Sue L. Sim filed their claims.

The first Germans from Russia, who played a major role in the development of
this area, started arriving in 1884 and settled in Thompson Township NE of Java
in Campbell County. These people had migrated from central Europe, mostly from
Wurttemberg, to Russia in the early 1800's, and in 1872, started their migration
to the U.S. and settled in the area of Yankton, then Dakota Territory. As there
was a shortage of free land around Yankton and Menno, the first group of Germans
from Russia families shipped their goods to Ipswich in 1884 and filed their
claims in Thompson Township. They were Gottlieb and Jacob Oswald, Andreas and
Lorenz Buckenberger, Michael Schenkenberger, Johann Kerner and the widow
Christine nee Oswald Kunz and family. The next year, 1885, additional families
from the East and from Russia, filed their claims in Thompson Township. They
were Thomas H. Hutchinson, Thomas Crisman, Theodore Grunhagen, Christian Strand,
John A Johnson, George Stout, Omer Clery, Jim Soreson, Lowell Ford, Charles P.
Cooper, John W. Markin, Cullie Rouneville, John Abraham, Irvin Austin, Emery F.
Ethridge, William Munroe, Sam N. Midgood, Phillip Morrison, Katie Peterson,
Julius Forensen, Maggie W. Cadmore, and Andrew Olson. The immigrants from
Russia, who found the countryside similar to the steppes in Russia, came to this
area in great numbers after 1885. They were Edward Xylander, Andreas Weixel,
Jacob Axt, Johannes Bauer, Henry Krebs, Gottlieb, Fred, and Christof Banek,
Johann Seefried, Gottlieb Zimmermann, Andreas and Jacob Delker, Henry & John
Eider, John, George and Jacob Bender, Johann Bauer, Simon Hirsch, Jacob Hirning,
Andrew Weixel, Andrew C. Berreth, Heinrich Krebs, Valentine Weisenberger and
Jacob Aichele.

BLESSING TOWNSHIP
Blessing Township lies on the west side of Thompson and no claims were filed in
1883. However, five claims were filed in 1884 and they were Asa & Clara Jones,
Elisabeth Wellsay, Kate Hupa, Samuel Coats, John Walsh, and T.R. Tollefson. In
1885 another sizeable group of Germans from Russia came and settled north of
Salt Lake in Blessing Township. They were Jakob Geigle, Adam, Philip, and Kaspar
Sieler and Philip's sons Henry, Peter and Adam, and the Wilhelm Ottmer, Konrad
Vollmer, Jacob Schaeffer, Adam Leno and Frederick Klemmer families. We call this
group the Sieler Clan.

From 1886 to 1895, the following families from Russia came to Blessing Township:
the Jakob Ackerman family with his sons Heinrich and John, daughters Margaretta
(Mrs Johannes Ackerman) and Katharine (Mrs Efrim Stepinenko), and Jacob's
mother-in-law Mrs. Korb; John, Mathias, Johann, Gottlieb, Anton, and Christina
Knodel; Peter and Jacob Schneider, Christian Rau, Paul, Heinrich and Christian
Huether; Johann Hezel, Wilhelm Martin, Jacob Doremaier, Ernst Freimark, Heinrick
and Paul Bauman, Wilhelm and John Blessing, Johan Weidenbach, Magdalena Elser,
Gottlieb Nathan, Frederick Biel, Karl Elser, Peter Kast, Andreas Kundert, George
Bender, George Zeller, Wilhelm Krausz, Paul Wildermuth, Martin Scheid, Johannes
& Peter Heckenlaible, Friederick Wosnuk, John Kerner, Christian Salzsiedler,
Johann Linderman, Peter Junker, Karl Bechtold, Ludwig Boehler, Friedrick
Rennich, Karl Roemich, and John Hummel filed claims during this period. The
Americans who filed claims were Charles J. Beebe, Barth Caldon, Myron Sommans,
Com Parsons, Frank C. Howard, Spenser Seldon, Carl Anderson, John Fade, Harvic
P. Hall, B.P. Adams, James Cummings, Klaas Hans, George W. Hielschen, Ellenhouse
Vitus and Amy Dybshroony.

In 1889, the first Germans from Russia settled in Walworth County in the
Highland and Adams Townships. The Spiry brothers Philip, Fred, and Karl, with
their father Frederick, settled in Highland Township in 1889. Shortly thereafter
they were joined by Philip and Jakob Aman, Jakob Merkel, John Rosin, George
Haux, Peter & Florian Hartman, Karl & Johannes Krause, Johann Kurle, Frederick
Jesser, Christian & Ludwig Helm, Jacob Pleines, Karl Wahl, Gottlieb Boehler,
Frederick Kramlich, Johannes Hochstetter, Jacob & Gottlieb Fiechtner, Jacob
Ochszner, Christian Pfitzer, Johann Kalmback, Karl Schlepp, Karl Schnaible,
Jacob, Gottlieb & George Schock, Johann Schuh, Jacob Stiegelmeier and Wilhelm
Moser. These Germans from South Russia came from the villages of Bergdorf,
Hoffnungstal, Gluckstal, Worms, Rohrbach, Annental, Odessa, Rosenberg,
Friedenthal, Helenental, Kassel and from various villages of Bessarabia.

The Chicago-Milwaukee Railroad purchased the McDowell claim in 1900 and an
additional purchase of the Payne claim made up the townsite of Java, located in

SPRING LAKE TOWNSHIP
The Germans from Russia who settled in the Spring Lake Township were the
families of Leonhardt Berreth, Frederick, Jacob, Johann & Michael Buechler,
Jacob Ehret, Gottlieb Fiechtner, Christian Horst, Martin Krueger, Fred Perman,
John Rosin, John Sackman, Jacob Schaeffer, Wilhelm Schuck, Frederick Walz, John
Weiszhaar and Christian Wolff.

By 1900, each township had from 30 to 35 farms. Each family had as many children
as 10 or 12. Transportation was still horse and wagon, and Java became the
closest trading center. The farmers hauled their grain and drove their pigs and
cattle to the Java market. In turn, they purchased building material, fuel,
machinery, clothing and food from the Java merchants. This explains the
phenomenal trade growth of Java during the period of 1900 to 1910.

By 1905, all available land had been claimed in all directions of Java. There
was truly a good mixture of people who made up the community: Americans,
Hollanders, Austrians, Hungarians, Scandinavians, Germans and Germans from
Russia. The Germans from Russia were somewhat clannish and found Java to their
liking. It became their trading town, and later they retired and moved into Java
to be close to their friends and their church, which was very important in their
lives. There has been an out flow of people from the Java trading area from 1903
on. There are a number of reasons why this has occurred in rural America. All
land had been filed upon and it became apparent that a one-quarter parcel of
land could not support a family. Grown sons married and could not obtain land
close to their parents, so they moved into new areas like western SD and ND, MT,
WA, CA, and Canada. Poor crops, low grain prices, heavy debts and Canada's new
immigration and land policy lured a fairly sizeable group to immigrate to
Canada. As people left the farms, the neighbors would pick up their acreage and
thus, they were able to prosper. In the 1930's with the Depression, banks
closing and dust bowl days, many farmers were forced to move to town and to CA,
WA, ID, and OR, to seek employment. Others left farming and were employed in
larger towns such as Mobridge and Aberdeen. During WWII, the size of farms
remained fairly stable, but from 1946 on, the number of farms declined
astronomically. At a rapid rate, farm after farm was purchased by neighbors to
expand their holdings, or by corporations and "side-walk" farmers. With
improvements in rural road systems, better transportation, and competition from
discount businesses, the business places in the town of Java were forced to
close. This also has had a direct affect on schools and churches in the
community. The number of farms in a given township is now under 10, where it
once was 30 to 35; the number of children per family is two to three, where once
it was 10 to 12. There are no longer any rural schools or rural churches in this
community.

Information on many of the individual Pioneer families is sparse for the period
of 1883, from the time of arrival in pre-Java, and to the early days of the City
of Java. One source that revealed large amounts of data on the early pioneers of
pre-Java history is the Java East Cemetery. Although the cemetery was founded
after 1900, a fairly sizeable number of Pioneer families and their offspring
were buried here before 1900. Those with markers who were buried before 1900 are
Abraham Bowlus (1807-1889), George Bruckner (1827-1899), Johnnie Bruckner
(1894-1895), Marie Bruckner (1891-1893), Jacob Consolver (1810-1889), Thurman
Corson (1849-1893), who was a Civil War Veteran, Rhoda E. Goodwin (1869-1892)
and August Hoffmeyer (1831-1887). Those with markers who were buried after 1900
and through 1910 are Emma S. Adams (1845-1910), Elizabeth Bruckner (1902-1903),
baby Christopherson (1909-1909), Diana Consolver (1822-1905), Rena Corson
(1878-1902), George Erbe (1862-1905), Melba Erbe (1900-1901), Charles O. Farnarn
(1866-1902), John A. Hoffmeyer (1905-1907), Raymond Kelley (1900-1903), A.
Kirkhoven (1866-1902), Cornelius Noble (1874-1903), Nicklos Noble (1868-1909),
Trynje Noble (1844-1905), Ida May Stewart (1866-1908), Edward B. Stowell
(1899-1910), Esther Stowell (1902-1910), Susannah Winkley (1836-1906) and
William Pitt Winkley (1829-1910).


ROSELLA
By Fritz Clement
[Edited excerpts from the Feb. 2, 1973 issue of the Java Herald
 and the Selby Record]

A lot of sweat and blood and hard labor went into the development of SD and when
we turn back our memories to the time, in those early 1880's when the hardy
pioneers made their first appearance in this area, we must realize that what
they had to endure in order to survive those first few years was something that
is hard for us to believe in this day and age.

There were no roads, and sources for supplies necessary to preserve the family
were miles in the distance. Heating of homes posed problems. In many instances
the heaters were the type fashioned by hand and were fueled by twisted hay, cow
chips and what little wood that could be obtained. There were no thermostatic
controls. There were no telephones, no electricity, and no running water.

These are the kind of situations that existed when the little trading store of
Rosella came into being back in the early 1880's. Rosella could not rightfully
be called a town or a community, although it did have a post office with the
mail being brought from either Eureka or Bowdle. The John Hofmeyer store was all
there was to this little spot on the map that had much to do with shaping the
future course of that area.

The historical legend of Section 5, 124-75, which is in Walworth County, shows
that it was homesteaded July 24, 1900, by Maria Hofmeyer. Post office site:
Rosella Halben (this is the present site of the Art and Dwight Helm farm).

Taken from the Walworth County records, were the following warranty deeds:

Sept. 5, 1900: Maria Hofmeyer, a widow, to John Hofmeyer, a single man (her
son).

Jan. 10, 1907: John Hofmeyer and Ellen (Beckman), husband and wife to Ludwig
Helm.

Sept. 23, 1918: Ludwig Helm and Margaretha Helm, his wife, to Christian L. Helm.

Jan. 7, 1958: Christian L Helm and Rosina Helm, husband and wife, to Arthur H.
Helm.

Mr. and Mrs. August Hofmeyer came to SD from NY, and settled in the Rosella
area, perhaps on the site of the store. August died Aug. 20, 1887, indicating
that the parents had arrived some time prior to that date. He was buried in a
family lot near Rosella but after the sale of the property, was reburied in the
East Java cemetery.

John followed his parents to Rosella and John and his mother were responsible
for building the store building at Rosella; like many buildings of that era, it
was of sod with wooden siding. Part of the building served as a home for the
family and the other section was devoted to the post office and store. This
could have been some time before 1894 for records show that Rosalie Hofmeyer, a
wife of George Hofmeyer (brother of John) was the postmaster at that time. This
family tired of the country and George and Rosalie went back to NY shortly
thereafter, because the next postmaster is shown as Catherine P. Beebe, who was
commissioned Dec. 6, 1900, and in March 3, 1903, the post office was
discontinued and moved to Sutley.

The Hofmeyer store was a sturdy structure; the floor rafters were 2 x 12's and
the ceiling 2 x 10's. The building was built of sod with walls 24-inches thick.
The outside and inside walls were finished with lumber. It is a very substantial
building and has withstood the elements all these years. Three generations of
the Helm family have lived there.

When the Hofmeyers operated the store, he had constructed a ramp at the west
side on which he could drive a team of horses pulling a wagon loaded with grain.
This ramp enabled them to reach the attic door easily and this is where the
grain was stored. Some of the grain was traded for merchandise, but most of it
was raised on the farm. Hofmeyer would pick up supplies at either Eureka or
Bowdle, making a weekly trip to one of these places, oftener when business was
brisk. Only bare necessities were stocked, except at Christmas time, when a bit
of color and frills were added. The floor plan of the building was conveniently
arranged so that the family living quarters were separate from the store portion
and thus there was some privacy.

When the Milwaukee Railroad extended its line beyond Bowdle, John Hofmeyer
realized that with the new town of Java getting started, the day would come soon
when his business would be going south to the new town and the railroad.

In Dec. 1904, John sold his farm, 140 acres going to Peter Schneider, 140 acres
to Frederick Helm, and 280 acres to Ludwig Helm, it being on this latter piece
that Rosella was located.

[According to Walworth County records, Rosella post office was discontinued Mar.
3, 1903. Records show that there was a post office in the Hofmeyer store in
1894.]


SUTLEY
By Fritz Clement
[Edited excerpts taken from The Selby Record, Nov. 16, 1972]

When the pioneers who helped to build up this section of the state arrived here,
back in the late 1880's, in order to take care of their needs, little
communities or trading posts were established and for a number of years, these
were the only means by which the settlers could buy merchandise needed for their
homes.

In Campbell County, the names of such towns as LaGrace, Vanderbilt, Flint,
Thule, Hein, Campbell, Tislo, Grass, Gale, Applegate and Sutley appeared on an
atlas dated in 1900.

Sutley was across the road from what is now the Leslie Rau farm. The people of
this community, and other such communities, had much to do with the development
of Walworth and Campbell counties, and of the town of Java.

The little community of Sutley was located approximately 9+ miles north of Java,
in Campbell County, about two-and-a-half miles from the north Walworth County
line.

While the people who came to settle the Sutley area were from South Russia,
their language was German, as were many of their customs. These people were of
German descent whose families had settled in Russia, enticed by a colonizing
program, which gave each settler land, money and freedoms. According to a 1920
census, 900 Germans from Russia lived in Walworth County and 847 in Campbell
County.

It was said that a post office, creamery, and two general stores were located
north of the Reformed cemetery. How and when this little community was founded
is not known, but reports are that David Blinderman operated a general store,
Albert Lange operated a store in the front part of his building, which also
housed the post office, and the rear part of the store was the creamery and
Gottlieb Freimark carried mail to and from Sutley to Eureka. After the Lange
store was closed, the post office was moved to the A.O. Berreth farm, where Toby
Biel now lives. From there it went to the Goodwin place and later was
discontinued. When the Milwaukee Railroad extended their lines west of Bowdle
and the towns of Java, Selby, Glenham and later, Mobridge, were founded, the
life of the little community existed for only a few more years after 1900.

Among the first settlers may be found the names of Banek, Bauer, Bender,
Berreth, Bertsch, Biel, Boehler, Buckenberger, Buechler, Delker, Freimark,
Geigle, Hauck, Heuther, Hirning, Hirsch, Junker, Kary, Kast, Krueger, Kundert,
Oswald, Rau, Schneider, Sieler, Took, Wosnuk and Zeller.

Other families living near the area were Maier, Brockel, Vollmer, Hinzman,
Klingman, Ackerman, Bauer, Metzger, Linderman, Bieber and others. The original
settlers acquired one-quarter through homestead operation and as needed, more
land was added.

The first two churches established in the area were the Reformed and
Evangelical. The Reformed Church was built in the NW part of the cemetery, where
many of the early pioneers were buried. A sod building served both churches in
the beginning, but later, the group separated and the Evangelical Church was
built about one-half mile from the Art Kolb farm. Later, a Congregational Church
was built in Walworth County one-half mile south of the Campbell County line and
north of the Wilmer Boschee farm. In 1930, this church was moved to Campbell
County and was situated just south of the Leslie Rau farm. A Seventh Day
Adventist Chruch was built near the Oswald farm and a Lutheran Church was
established about one-and-a-half miles north of the then John Zeller farm.

The education of the children who grew up in the area was provided by eight
rural schools. These served the Delker, Buckenberger, Bender, Ackerman, Sieler,
Blessing, Kundert and Bertsch vicinities. By 1960, all of these schools were
closed.

According to the files of the Java Herald, Sutley was still in existence in 1904
and weekly news items appeared in the pages. A writer known only as The Hayseed
would write weekly happenings from the Sutley area. A few such items and the
dates they appeared are:

The Jan. 7th issue told of a Miss Hart, who was a school teacher, and chronicled
a Goodwin family reunion.

The Jan. 14th issue of 1904 told about a spelling match at the Krause School in
Walworth County. Names mentioned among the news were Peter Junker, A.O. Berreth,
who was county commissioner; Fred Hirning, Rev. Oeder, who conducted services at
the Evangelical Church.

The next issue states that the Wolff Brothers were drilling a well for Simon
Hirsch. Mrs. Fred Hirning (nee Geigle) died shortly after giving birth to a son.
The name of Henry Buckenberger also appears in the news.

After an absence of several weeks, the Sutley news again appeared in the Herald
and reported that a spelling team was going to Java for a spelling bee.

It was established about this time that there was a Baptist Church in the area,
as a news item states that a Rev. Hilslinger of Eureka delivered a sermon in a
church of that denomination. An item told about a George Jardine making a deal
with the McCormick people to represent this company in the Sutley area.

There is nothing physical left of Sutley other than a few store and concrete
foundations, which supported the buildings. There used to be a large iron or
steel boiler, which was said to have been a part of the creamery, but this has
long departed. The Reformed Cemetery is the only indication that a community
once existed in the vicinity.

[Acknowledgement given to LeRoy Bender and Herbert Geigle for their
contributions to this article]

The Women of the Prairie
Imagine what it must have been like for the homesteading women to leave their
extended family circles, friends, and all things familiar to them, regardless of
their point of origin. They arrived on the vast prairie with nothing but earth
and sky. They had no house in which to live at the on-set, and no conveniences
to give them a sense of comfort. Incompatibility had to exist, for there were
women from refined families of the city, those who came from a rural life in
different states, and those who arrived from other countries, carrying little
with them but their dreams. The loneliness must have been terrifying. Indeed
some came to this country to meet family members already arrived, or traveled
with their immediate family and others with whom they were familiar. They were
the more fortunate. As time passed and common grounds were discovered among the
women, they blossomed, as did the land from the labor of the men.

Nothing was easy. There was always work to be done on a homestead. The woman had
no modern equipment to lighten her burden and she accepted sacrifice as her
duty. Her household tools were a broom, flatiron, and washboard. She raised a
garden, gathered wild fruits, cooked, canned or dried the food for winter's use.
She had no refrigerator and no trading post near enough to replenish the food.
She raised poultry for food and for eggs to sell, and milked the cow for milk
and butter, and to sell butter and cream. She harvested herbs and was the home
doctor, who often practiced midwifery; mustard plasters, Watkins ground black
pepper, cooked cherry juice, or the fuzz of a peach were often used to cure
ailments. A sock filled with oats and heated in the oven was a sure cure for an
earache, while chamomile, Queen Anne's Lace, or sassafras root were used for
indigestion. Onions were considered a cure-all. She spun yarn, knitted socks and
mittens, made all of the family's clothing, and darned the clothes. She scrubbed
the floors, tub washed the clothes, roasted her own coffee, and made soap, and
butter, and quantities of baked goods. She raised and taught her children, and
helped her husband plow the land; amazingly, she found time to attend
neighborhood events. As more land was plowed and farming techniques improved,
her work was increased when she cooked large meals for the large threshing
crews.

How many of the women of the prairie wept as they looked at the withered gardens
in which they had labored, pulling weeds, hoeing, and picking potato bugs until
their arms ached? She bore many children, rocked them in illness, kissed the
bumped head or scratched leg until the pain disappeared. How long before she had
a first name to give her identity? Old obituaries too often refer to a deceased
female as 'Mrs.', with no first name ever mentioned. These women carried on the
religious traditions and cultural aspects with which they had been raised,
teaching their families the importance of the church and a treasured way of
life. The Prairie Woman was the backbone of the family, and of the growing
society. She is to be admired, praised, and remembered.

The Sod House
The farmer on the plains usually had no wood at all. Many stories of the early
settlers told of living under the wagon in which they arrived. Others told of
living in caves, or a hollow that was dug out and covered with branches and
prairie sod. When a more permanent structure could be built, furrows of sod were
plowed and cut crosswise into blocks about 12 to 18 inches wide, two to three
feet long, and four to six inches thick. Rows of these sod blocks were piled on
top of each other to make walls, and covered with a roof made of branches,
thatch and sod. The end walls were built to a point in the center and a
ridgepole was placed from end to end. Sometimes wood was brought with the
pioneers and they built a frame to support the roof, or found a little wood
nearby. The floor was just the hard-packed earth, which could be swept and even
mopped. Windows and doors were often made from old boxes the pioneers brought
with them. A sod house remained warm in winter and cool in summer, but it had
its disadvantages. Dirt sifted down on the food, crumbled from the walls, and
rose from the clay floor. Rodents lived in the thatch, and gophers often dug
tunnels through the walls or floor. Later, settlers often improved their houses
by whitewashing the walls and bringing in lumber for doors, ceilings, and
floors. The energies and love of the mothers and daughters turned the interior
of this house into a home. The remains of a few sod houses still dot the Java
countryside, standing as reminders of a time long past.

(Photo:) 1961 at the Herb Schneider farm

(Photo:) Early day wedding.  Photo courtsy of Delila Biel.

Stoneboat
The idea of a vehicle called a "stoneboat" was brought with the Volga Germans
from Russia to the U.S. It was made of tree logs about a foot in diameter; the
front of the logs were tapered in such a way so they would not dig into the
ground. Each log was placed about four feet apart, and a sturdy cross member was
notched about 12 inches from the front. The cross member had a chain or rope
fastened around it and was hooked to a horse, or later to a tractor. There was
also a cross member at the end and boards were attached along the entire length
of the vehicle. It would run close to the ground, and when it would go over a
medium sized stone, the stone would run under the stoneboat until it came out at
the back end. The vehicle was used to haul the stones out of the fields so a
better crop could be raised, and later, so the stones wouldn't tear up the
machinery. Thus, it is known as a "stoneboat".

The Threshing Crew
Harvest season brought the Threshing Crew, which consisted of about 15 men, who,
in the 1920's, often would have a gasoline machine, probably a
McCormick-Deering, and teams of horses to haul bundles on an average field. Some
would have a steamer that burned coal. The younger men would "work the grain
wagon," which meant that they would shovel the grain to keep it evenly
distributed in the grain wagon to avoid numerous trips to the farm yard to
unload the wagons into the granaries. One method of threshing was pitching cut
grain that had been placed into large stacks. The farmer would place two stacks
close enough so the machine could be pulled between them. The crew would pitch
the grain directly unto the feeder of the machine. Horses were used for the
grain wagons.

In bad weather, the crew would pass time by playing cards, some for money and
some for fun. The farmer's wife would feed them, setting up a board on ten-
gallon cream cans where wash basins, soap, and water could be found to clean up
before the meal. Usually the meal consisted of potatoes, soup, chicken and
homemade bread. A mid-afternoon lunch of watermelon, bread, or sometimes kuchen,
would be served. The members of the crew would take out blanket rolls and sleep
in a farmer's hayloft if they were too far from home, or it was too late to
travel. They slept in their work clothes on one blanket and covered themselves
with another. Excitement on the farm must have been high when the threshing crew
arrived, much like the excitement of today when the combiners show up, a sign
that harvest is soon to be under way.

The Advent of Java
By LeRoy C. Bender

"Hear that train a'comin, Comin 'round the bend." These words from a well-known
song may very well be reminiscent of the events preceding the founding of the
town of Java.

It is not exactly known when the officials of the Chicago, Milwaukee, and St.
Paul Railway came to the decision to extend their railroad line from Bowdle to
the Missouri River; however, it appears such a decision was reached shortly
before the turn of the century, or just after. This extension of the line
ultimately resulted in the rise of four new towns along its course.

Early in Feb. 1900, a survey crew comprising of nearly twenty men commenced the
survey of the new grade for the planned extension, heading due west from Bowdle.
Rumors and speculation ran rampant as to where the new railroad would be built.
One faction claimed that the shortest distance between two points is a straight
line and surely the survey crew would follow such a line of thought. By the 23rd
of Feb., the survey crew met its first obstacle: the hills north of Spring Lake.
The survey skirted these hills, going north where easier grading and less
construction expense seemed to justify the additional distance. Continuing in a
westerly direction, the survey crew found a gradual decline to the Missouri
River by way of Blue Blanket Creek, which proved to be the only acceptable route
to the river.

About the middle of Apr. 1900, grading began at Bowdle, and on the 21st of the
same month, grading work began at the western terminus, where the town of Evarts
was to be founded. In June, it became known that four new towns were being
planned along the Milwaukee extension, the first on the McDowell claim, which
had been purchased by the Milwaukee Land Company for townsite purposes. An
additional purchase of the Payne claim, adjoining the McDowell claim, was
consummated, enlarging the proposed townsite property.

Early in July, the settlers in the northeastern portion of Walworth County were
circulating petitions praying for the immediate platting of a town upon the
newly acquired townsite property. It had been found that the McDowell claim was
encumbered by a school mortgage and efforts were underway to legally lift this
mortgage in order to plat the land and offer lots for sale, for it was contrary
to railroad regulation to sell any lots not absolutely perfect in title.

Later in July, on the 17th, the laying of rails began west of Bowdle. By the
28th of the month, the new townsite was being surveyed and advertisements in
area newspapers alerted the pubic to watch for the opening date for sale of
lots, and encouraged prospective businessmen and others, to purchase and locate
on them. Applications were to be made to the Land Department, C.M.&St.P. Ry.,
Milwaukee, WI.

During the grading and rail-laying period, a large encampment of laborers was
situated on a portion of the townsite property. According to one of the older
residents of the present town, much fighting occurred among the men, and deaths
were not uncommon. It is most interesting to note that these laborers dubbed the
prospective new town "Java" in honor of the good coffee served at a small shack,
which was situated where the town's stockyards were later built. By Oct. 20, the
name "Java" was made official, and so it has remained these one hundred years.

The Dedication Plat for the town of Java was filed Oct. 23, 1900, and the
following day, lots were placed on sale at the home of James C. Corson, the
Townsite Agent for the Milwaukee Land Company. From available information, it
appears the first purchase of lots was made by John Hofmeyer, who had been
operating a pioneer store at Rosella, Post Office, in Highland Township. Mr.
Hofmeyer, by his own claim, was the first to break ground for a business
establishment; however, the distinction of having the first building and
business in the new town belongs to Henry Thielen, of Bowdle, who had a small
store in the area where the stockyards came to be erected, and this building and
business may well be the same one that served that "good coffee" to the railroad
crews.

On Nov. 23, 1900, a route inspector for the Post Office Department visited Java,
gathering information relative to prospective mail routes, not only in town but
also for the surrounding areas of settlement. Among the first applicants for the
postmastership of Java was Mr. T.B. Bowlus, a pioneer resident of the vicinity,
and it was Mr. Bowlus that received the appointment as the first postmaster,
near the end of Dec. 1900.

By Dec. 1, 1900, three buildings were in the construction process; by Jan. 5,
1901, several businesses had been established and the new town boasted of having
24 buildings. Java was booming, with the boom lasting for several years. The
town did not draw its business houses and citizenry only from other defunct
towns in the immediate area, but was made up largely of those from outside areas
wishing to embark on business ventures of their own, by local settlers, and by
operators of pioneer stores and Post Offices such as Rosella, Spiry, Beaulieu,
and others, which had given service to the various settlements. Several branch
offices from business establishments in other communities also began operation
in the new town. The growth of Java was phenomenal. One of the pioneer settlers
of the area, Mr. Hessel Dyk, whose name and person is remembered by many, stated
in his remembrances that, "I had never seen a place grow like Java did the first
years of its existence. It seemed like we would go to bed at night and wake up
the next morning to find that three or four new buildings had gone up
overnight."

As early as the middle of Mar. 1901, Java became linked with the outside world,
not only by the railroad and Post Office, but by telephone connections as well,
when a telephone line was completed from Buchecker's Junction.

An article which appeared in the Jan. 5, 1901 issue of the Walworth County
Record, authored by a gentleman, presumably of the Java area, who signed himself
only as "Farmer Joe," and extolling the very early virtues and accomplishments
of Java, contained an ending which is appropriate now as then: "Long Live Java!"


                                   THE CITY

1900 From its inception in the autumn of 1900, shortly after the Chicago,
     Milwaukee & St. Paul Railway Line was extended from Bowdle to the Missouri
     River, and for approximately three years thereafter, the status of Java was
     simply that of a village, possessing no special form of government. Its
     growth had been steady during this period, the population being estimated
     at about 150 souls.

1903 Early in Oct., after a meeting of the citizens, it was decided to
     incorporate from a village to the status of a town, with a regular form of
     government suitable to its size and class. On Sept. 5, of that year, State
     Surveyor George Merriman of Bowdle was in Java to survey the town site
     preparatory to incorporation. Early in October, the following notice was
     advertised in the local newspaper:

                              NOTICE OF ELECTION

Notice is hereby given, that an election will be held on Monday, October 19,
1903, by the legal voters of the proposed incorporated Town of Java, Walworth
County, South Dakota to vote upon the question, whether or not said proposed
incorporated town shall be incorporated or not as such Town of Java.  The voters
who favor the inforporation of such Town shall have upon their ballots the
words, "For Incorporation, Yes," and the voters who do not favor such
inforporation, shall have upon their ballots the words, "For Incorporation, No."
Said election will be held at the store of W.P. Winkley within said proposed
incorporated town and polls will be open from 9 o'clock a.m. of said day, the
19th day of October, 1903 until 4 o'clock p.m. of said day.

Dated at Bangor, Wlaworth County, S. Dak. October 7, 1903.
SEAL
By Order of the Board of County Commissioners of Walworth Couty, S. Dak. Geo.
W. Ryan, County Auditor.

     The results of this election showed 47 votes being cast, 45 for
     incorporation, and 2 against. Since a large majority of the citizens had
     previously favored incorporation, the result was not unexpected. After the
     polls were closed, the Java Cornet Band played some fine music out on the
     streets in honor of the event. During the evening, the Cornet Band
     serenaded each business place in Java, completing a day of celebration,
     with all the citizens participating.

     On Nov. 23, 1903, an election was held for the purpose of electing a Board
     of Trustees. Selected to serve on the first town board were:

     David Blinderman, 1st Ward; William F. Ewald, 2nd Ward and John Hofmeyer,
     3rd Ward.

     The Board of Trustees of the Town of Java held its organizational meeting
     on Nov. 27, 1903, at the store of John Hofmeyer, with all the elected
     trustees and town clerk, Christian Huether, attending. The following is a
     brief outline of the business transacted at this meeting:

     Upon motion by William Ewald, John Hofmeyer was elected president and thus
     the Board of Trustees was organized. The president received instructions to
     order the necessary books and proper blanks for recording their future
     transactions. William Ewald was charged with selecting a permanent meeting
     place for the Board. Upon motion, duly seconded and carried, to engage the
     services of an attorney to draw up the necessary ordinances as well as
     executing the other legal affairs of the new corporation. Carl F. Clement
     was hired at a salary of $30 per month, to serve as long as deemed
     necessary by the board. The clerk was instructed to purchase a star and
     billy for the marshal.

     The Board of Trustees met again on Dec. 3, 1903, at which time ordinances
     number 1 and 2 were read and approved. Jacob Schafer was appointed as the
     town fire warden.

     The following day, Dec. 4, the board again met, designating the office of
     the Mississippi Lumber Co. as their regular place of meeting. At this
     meeting, the following took place: W.F. Dyer was named treasurer; Martin
     Gehrki Jr., assessor; Jacob Schafer, Marshal; Fred Krause, Justice of
     Peace; and Joseph Bosch, Overseer of Highways. Prior to adjournment,
     ordinances number 3 and 4 were read and approved.

     At this time the small town of Java began to prosper and its development
     and expansion was rapid for a number of years.

     A $3500, two-story schoolhouse was built in this year, a big achievement
     for the town.

1904 The first notable improvement after organization came when the Dakota
     Central Telephone Company installed a telephone booth and switchboard at
     The Java House, early in the year, as well as a number of new telephones
     within the town, filling a long felt need.

     Other improvements followed during the spring and summer, one of which was
     the erection of the first municipal building, a jail, being located on the
     lot west of the present municipal building. Jacob Fiechtner built the jail
     building at a bid price of $239, while another bid submitted by John Hill,
     (known as the old Captain) lost out being six dollars higher. Later the
     jail building was moved to the lot in back of the old city hall, and for a
     time served as a dwelling and shoe repair shop before being sold and moved
     to an area farm.

     Streets were laid out, graded and graveled; a new engine house was built
     and equipped with a fire engine, hoses and related items. In the course of
     time, wooden sidewalks were built, a water reservoir was constructed, a
     town hall erected, and a town well dug and equipped with a windmill. These
     early improvements were paid by warrants issued by the town. In 1906, a
     bond issue was passed in the amount of $2000 to remove the indebtedness
     caused by these needed improvements.

                                       The
                                    NEW TOWN
                                     of JAVA

Is an incorporated town in Walworth County, South Dakota, on the Chicago,
Milwaukee & St. Paul Railway about 70 miles west of Aberdeen.  Although only
three years old, Java has about 280 inhabitants and supports a fine graded
school, one church, five general stores, drug store, bank, newspaper, two
liveries, four implement warehouses and various other places of business.  Java
has three large grain elevators, a gristmill and two lumberyards.

The town is growing fast in its pace to keep up with the demands of the large
and rapidly developing territory tributary thereto.

If you are seeking a new business location, look well into the inducements
offered by Java.  For prices and terms of sale, call on
                                            J.B. Corson, Local Agent, Java, S.D.

1905 The Kupp Brothers, J.C. and George, supervised the installation of a more
     permanent telephone system in the town, for the Dakota Telephone Co.

     The town of Java was in contention as a site for the courthouse, having
     filed a petition with the County Commissioners. Java later withdrew its
     petition when a legal question arose concerning the registration of
     qualified voters within the county.

     Java's population was now at 277.

1907 The town had progressed considerably, having provided such things as fire
     protection, organization of a cemetery association, adequate water supply,
     municipal buildings, improved telephone facilities, met with educational
     needs, to name a few, a very commendable achievement for a small town in
     those times.

     Another indication of growth was noted when the Milwaukee Land Company had
     their property north of the track surveyed and another addition to the town
     was platted.

1908-09 The railroad company rerouted its track, passing north of the town
     approximately one-half mile. This event was considered a rather severe
     setback to the town. A proposal from railroad officials, to move the town
     to the north, was refused by the citizens. A spur line constructed by the
     company served the town, thereafter.

     The citizenry of Java increased to 473 in 1910, and showed a decline to 410
     by 1915. The intervening years between 1909 and 1915 were relatively quiet
     ones. The South Dakota Gazetteer stated that Java had a population of 473
     in 1913.

1914 City notice that all hogs were to have been removed to outside the city
     limits by Oct. 23. The town marshal was instructed to notify all violators.

1915 In the Third Census of South Dakota, Java was listed as having 4 colts
     under 1 year; 6 horses age 1 and over but under 2 years; 40 horses 2 years
     and over. No mules or asses. Five calves, 4 heifers, 26 cows kept for milk,
     4 cows not milked. In bushels, 7 Parsnips, 16 Tomatoes, 26 Carrots, 113
     Onions, 7 Turnips, 653 Cucumbers, 40 Beets, and 152 Melons. It showed
     130,000 pounds of milk, 2625 pounds of butter and 270 pounds of cheese.
     There were 1209 chickens, 12 ducks, 1 turkey, 7254 dozen eggs and 13 acres
     of Potatoes with 1232 bushel yield total. There were 410 inhabitants, 211
     male and 199 female.

     A major improvement occurred in the town during the summer. The wooden
     sidewalks along Main Street were removed and replaced with cement
     sidewalks, the first along the business places of August C. Schlepp and
     Emanuel Baer. Many residents also improved their properties by replacing
     wooden walks with cement. Later that year the town hall was remodeled and
     the jail was moved, the work performed by George Berreth. In addition, a
     bell tower was constructed, with the bell serving as a fire alarm and to
     announce the curfew hour.

1916 In Jan., the Board of Trustees passed a resolution to build more cement
     sidewalks next spring. Walks to be built were on both sides of First Avenue
     from the corner of Lange's Store, west as far as the corners of John H.
     Wolff's property and up to the Pres-byterian Church. Other walks in Payne's
     Addition will naturally follow.

     A petition circulated in the spring called for a special election by the
     qualified voters, to determine whether or not the town should issue bonds
     amounting to $8,000 to be used in constructing a municipal light plant. The
     date of the election, June 4, saw 80 votes cast, 48 in favor and 32 against
     the bond issue. In July bids were opened, with A.F. Kaufman of Appleton,
     MN, submitting the successful bid for the plant in the amount of $5,730.
     The contract for the building to house the plant was given to Gunder
     Johnson, at $875. Near the end of Sept., all work was accomplished and the
     electric current turned on.

1918-21 Perhaps the greatest building boom was witnessed, primarily in the
     residential portions of the town, when many of the finest homes in town
     were built in the west and north additions. The Java Cooperative Creamery
     was launched in 1920, and during 1921, the educational needs were met when
     a fine new fireproof schoolhouse was built, and many of the town streets
     were re-shaped and re-surfaced with gravel. It was at this time that a
     change in the town's status took place, when Java was incorporated into a
     city, and adopted the Mayor-Alderman form of government. Serving as the
     first mayor under this type of government was Carl F. Clement. Others were:
     W.C. Hicks, Philip Spiry Sr. Albert Lange, Martin Gehrki Jr., Charles
     Schlepp, William Kunz, August C. Schlepp, Col. E.C. Weatherly, I.R. Krause,
     Joe Zarka, Wesley Frank, Paul Jacobs and John Zeller.

1923 A 50-horse power engine was purchased to power the electric light plant,
      necessitated by an increased demand for electricity.

1924 Improved fire fighting was added with additional hose and two chemical
     engines.

     Power and lights were made available from 6 a.m. to midnight.

1925 The building housing the electric light plant was renovated when yet
     another new and larger, 60 h.p. Diesel type & Fairbanks-Morse, engine, and
     a new generator were purchased to update and adequately meet
     ever-increasing demands for electric service. Also at this time the city
     streets received additional gravel.

1926-35 The next ten years passed rather uneventfully. A compressed air whistle
     had been installed at the Java Auto Garage, to function in sounding the
     alarm in case of fire. This was later moved to the city power plant. 1931
     found Wm. Kunz serving as Mayor, A.C. Schlepp, city auditor, and councilmen
     Clement, Gehrki, Schlaht, Schadler, Pfitzer & Bauer.

1936 An extensive street program was instituted, which included the opening of
     Chicago Street, leading to the nearby county highway. In the autumn
     followed the strategic placement of hydrants to provide improved fire
     protection, in connection with the beginning of a waterworks system. Soon a
     project was undertaken to enlarge the waterworks system in order to include
     commercial and private users.

1939 The waterworks planning was culminated when a WPA project was begun.
     Another outstanding milestone was reached with the completion of this new
     waterworks system. The water tower and tank were completed, and the pump
     house was almost finished by July 29, 1939.

     Java Municipal Band presented concerts each Weds. evening during the summer
     months at the city square on Main, A.C. Schlepp, director.

     Another improvement to provide additional fire protection was noted with
     the purchase of a truck, which updated the fire fighting equipment of the
     Java Volunteer Fire Department.

1940-46 Attention again focused on the need for further municipal improvements,
     and architect Roland Wilcken formulated plans for a new municipal building.
     With the approval of plans and specifications, a WPA project began in the
     autumn of 1940, with work continuing during the winter. This building of
     reinforced concrete, measuring 75x50 feet was completed in 1941. All
     concrete work was complete in Jan. 1941. Building and interior finishing
     were next on the schedule.

     Electric plant equipment again was updated with the purchase of a more
     adequate light and power system.

     The city council purchased a fire truck, a used Model "B" Ford, for $125,
     in 1940. Volunteer members did the work and furnished materials to convert
     it into a modern fire truck. At a special meeting, the City Council
     definitely decided to go ahead with previously discussed plans for the
     construction of a new fireproof structure to house the city electric plant.

     In 1946 an election was held, resulting in the decision to sell the power
     plant equipment to Montana-Dakota Utilities Company, a 20-year franchise
     was approved with that company; they then constructed a complete
     transmission system in the town. The town continues to be served by MDU.

     Also during 1946, street improvements were made with Main Street receiving
     major attention. The old city hall had been sold to a Mr. Moore of Leola,
     who in turn resold it to a group of concerned Java citizens; they then
     turned the site and building over to the LaVerne Bauer Legion Post, where
     this organization functioned until their present facility was built.

1947 This year saw the creation of a park board that carried out its duties by
     establishing a city park on a piece of property just west of the
     schoolhouse. The park later was improved with playground equipment, picnic
     facilities, water piped in, and was regularly maintained for use by the
     public. Also during this year earnest attention was given to a project to
     provide a much needed and sought after sewer plant and disposal system. A
     bond issue passed and revenue bonds were issued; construction began in
     1948.

1948 Chief of Police Ed Goetz resigned. C.R. Hochstetter appointed to the
     position at $100 a month for the first month, and $125 a month thereafter.

     Designated two more street lights and two more park lights and one light in
     the alley behind the Liquor Store.

     Discussed food, drink and Bingo stands for the 4th of July celebration.

     Approved extending the sewer on Pacific Ave. from east Main, on north
     Chicago to Pregitzers, and on north Helms St. to Martin Fiedlers.

     Purchased coal heater for the Liquor Store.

1950 Marking 50 years of progress, Java celebrated its Golden Jubilee on June 14
     and 15. Extensive plans had been formulated for this occasion, which was
     largely attended. Programmed events included: Most excellent parades,
     baseball games, rodeo, street sports, orations, free stage shows, band
     concerts, whisker judging contest, movies, dances, and a carnival,
     providing everyone in attendance with a most enjoyable time. E.C.
     Weatherly, depot agent, was elected as Mayor, replacing A.C. Schlepp, who
     had served in that capacity for 14 years.

1951 Approved building a Ladies Rest Room and made arrangements to look for a
     suitable place. Purchased Lot 11 in Block 2 from A.C. Schlepp for $75. In
     Aug. of 1951, a special meeting was held for the purpose of hiring a
     caretaker for the Rest Room. Mrs. A. Buckenberger got the bid at $10 a
     month.

1954 City Liquor Store showed gross profit of $6,850.03.

1955 Purchased a Police car.

1959 Martin Gehrki, Auditor for the City of Java, or Finance Officer, resigned
     after many years. Others that followed in this position were Julius
     Pfitzer, LeRoy Bender, Leon Kast, Louella Aman, LaRayne Schlepp, Calvin
     Aman, LeRoy Bender (another term), Jerome Lee, Donna Bieber, Kima Allbee,
     Carol Allbee, Becky Witlock and presently, Carol Allbee.

     All of Main Street was given an oil mat, and blacktop was placed on the
     road from the Kary corner north to the cemetery.

1960 It was reported that minors were receiving alcohol from someone. The City
     board warned there would be consequences if caught.

1962 An emergency was declared and an agreement made with Independent Well
     Drilling Co. of Aberdeen to drill a new well.

1970 A new sidewalk was put down in front of the Liquor Store.

     Main Street resurfaced at 25 cents per square yard

     Bigger street lights were put in

1971 LeRoy Bender was the Justice of Peace.

     Julius Pfitzer donated a Burglar Resistant Safe.

1972 The City could be found repairing new sidewalks on the west side of Main.

1974 New lights were put up in town.

1975 Java celebrated its 75th Anniversary. The Municipal Liquor Store was to
     charge 30 cents for pop.

1977 Mayor Wes Frank, Councilmen Wolf, Melcher, M. Pfitzer, Kast, Fiedler, R.
     Pfitzer. LeRoy Bender, Auditor and Steve Biel, Treasurer. Chief of Police,
     Sewer and Water Superintendent and Street Supervisor was Mike Darling.

     Orville Stangl presented a deed for the cemetery east of Java, to the City
     of Java. A Perpetual Care Fund was enacted later.

1978 Mayor Wes Frank resigned and John Zeller was chosen as Java's Mayor.
     Clifford and Bernice Grenz leased the Municipal Liquor Store.

1979 Rinel Schneider purchased the old jail for $50. Located in City Hall, it
     had to be cut up to get it out.

1984 The Council decided to use remaining un-appropriated Revenue Sharing Funds
     and Sewer Water Funds to pay for replacing the water tower standpipe.

     A Fire Phone was purchased.

     The Board decided to use Entitlement 16 Revenue Sharing funds to complete
     one block of sidewalk on the east side of Main Street.

     The City of Java switched back to The Town of Java, when Council President,
     Vivian Witlock, and all five aldermen, who were Jon Bradley Bender, Oliver
     Goetz, Dwight Helm, Dean R. Moser and Jeral Schreter, signed a petition. At
     this time, it was decided to become a three-person Board of Trustees, those
     being Bradley Bender, Dwight Helm and Oliver Goetz. Those who have served
     as President of the Board were Marvin Pfitzer, Greg Biel, Gerhardt Fiedler,
     Vivian Witlock, Bradley Bender, Larry Dobson, Burton Sheffner,  Art Frank,
     Elroy Ketterling, Art Frank (another term), and presently, Virgil Biel.

1985 WEB water filled the Java Hill reservoir, progress evident at all the WEB
     construction sites. The dome went on at the Java Hill reservoir in Nov.

1986 Larry Dobson met with the board to discuss starting a Library. Permission
     to use space in City Hall was given. The cost to the City would be $300.

1988 Ordinance 135 granting a franchise to install Cable TV, effective Mar. 31,
     1988, signed Jon Bradley Bender, President, and LeRoy Bender, Auditor.

     Ordinance 136 designated Java Community Arts and Education Council for the
     purpose of expanding the cultural and artistic resources for the people of
     Java.

     $2,000 Revenue Sharing money used to chip and seal Main Street. Applied for
     a Grant.

1989 Java held a big SD Centennial celebration with a large attendance from out
     of state and the surrounding area.

     A special school district reorganization election was held. The plan called
     for combining the Glenham, Java and Selby school districts into the Selby
     Area School District. Voters in the three schools went to the polls on Nov.
     21 and voted for reorganization.

1990 The First Annual Kuchen Festival was held July 14, sponsored by the Java
     business people.

     The Java Public School was closed.

1994 A new Fire Siren was purchased.

1996 The residents of Java voted to again have a five person Board of Trustees.
     At the present time, Trustees are Fred Carpenter, Viola Goetz, Jerome Lee,
     and Alan Schaefer.

1998 The Java Community Club, the Gold Committee and Ray Langston family
     Memorial donated a picnic shelter for City Park.

     An estimate was received from Jensen Rock and Sand to resurface Main
     Street.

     Java adopted a one-cent city sales tax to help with the street resurfacing.

1999 Preparations were in full swing for the 2000 Java Centennial, the
     celebration of heritage and survival.

     Main Street was resurfaced by Jensen Rock and Sand of Mobridge.

     Bud Allbee leased the Municipal Liquor Store.
