                       Java Business Community - One Hundred Years

(Photo:) Untitled

No doubt among the earliest transactions connected in any circumstance with the
town of Java would be the acquisition of the railway right-of-way and townsite
property, followed by the sale of townsite lots by the Milwaukee Land Company,
through their townsite agent, James C. Corson, who conducted the sale of lots at
his home located about a half-mile east of the town.

John Hofmeyer, who had started a grocery store at Rosella, made the first
purchase of lots.

HENRY THIELEN: First among the actual town businesses was that of Henry Thielen
of Bowdle, who began building about Nov. 8, 1900, and soon stocked it with a
variety of goods. It is also probable that Mr. Thielen operated the refreshment
shack near the railway siding, which served the railroad construction crews
during the summer of 1900.

LUMBER: John Erbe became the town's earliest dealer in lumber and coal, having
on hand a fine stock of quality merchandise.

BAUER, HOFF AND STOLLER: John Bauer, Jacob Hoff, and Jacob Stoller came from
Eureka, constructed a large store, 26x50, in Block 3, on Lot 13, and stocked a
fine line of general merchandise, opening for business in Dec. 1900, under the
name of Bauer, Hoff, and Stoller. In 1905 an addition was built to the south to
expand the business. Mr. Hoff left the partnership in 1908, with Bauer and
Stoller continuing the venture. From about 1904 until the middle of 1913, this
store housed the post office, as Mr. Stoller had been appointed postmaster; and,
with his efficient deputy, Miss Annette Stoller, had given the patrons very
creditable service. In 1915, Jacob Stoller dissolved the partnership. The firm
then operated as Bauer & Sons for many years. In later years Miss Evelyn Bauer
and her brothers, John Jr., and Fred E. continued the business.

When Java celebrated its 50th anniversary in 1950, Bauer & Sons was the oldest
pioneer store remaining, not only in Java, but in Walworth County as well. A
disastrous fire in the later years of the store's existence severely damaged the
original portion of the store. It was sold in 1960 to Chris Pfitzer who operated
a cream station and also sold veterinary supplies. Pfitzer Creamery was
discontinued and the shelves were restocked with paint. Part of the building was
remodeled and housed Dee's Beauty Salon, operated by Dee Fiedler.

HOFMEYER'S SQUARE DEAL STORE: Shortly after Bauer, Hoff and Stoller opened for
business, another general mercantile was completed across the street to the
south of their store on the west side of Main, that of John Hofmeyer, who came
to Java from Rosella in Highland Township. He built an all lumber, two-story
building that was three lots wide and was 80-100 feet long, located in Block 4,
on Lot 1. He sold groceries, millinery, shoes, clothing, and other general
merchandise items.

Mr. Hofmeyer was best known for his genial way of doing business. He continued
in business until early 1912, when he sold to Wm. Curran, who, in a short time,
sold to Albert Lange in April of that year. Mr. Hofmeyer was a member of the
first town board; the original business meeting of the town of Java in 1903 was
held at his store. The Hofmeyer family left Java in 1912, settling in an eastern
state.

The Square Deal store was a landmark for many years. Following the death of
Albert Lange in 1935, his wife continued operation of the store for a number of
years, and then the building was sold and dismantled. During its existence this
building was the center for many civic and social events, the upper story
serving the community for lodge meetings, dances, movies, lyceum programs, local
community meetings, stage shows, church services, and Sunday schools. A couple
of Java men recall roller-skating being held in the upper story of this
building. It was in this hall that the remaining members of the famous Welsh
Singers gave a concert. Most of the members lost their lives in the sinking of
the Titanic. In the May 14, 1903 issue of The Rising Sun, John Hofmeyer
advertised a complete line of suits for old and young, bargains in boy's 2 piece
vestee, norfolk and blouse suits, men's worsted suits at low prices. "We also
carry a large general stock especially strong in mens and boys hats, gloves,
shirts, underwear, etc. We also carry a large stock of reliable shoes, dry
goods, etc. We want your butter and eggs."

THE SPIRY BROTHERS: The Spiry Brothers, Philip and Fred, built a 26x50
structure, which housed their machinery business in 1900. They carried a line of
general farm machinery, buggies, and stated that no farmer need let his crops go
to waste as they handled the type of machinery needed for trouble-free service.
This business continued until Jan. 1905, when the Huether Brothers, Henry and
Christian, purchased the premises. The Spiry brothers had the distinction of
being the first farm machinery business in the new town.

LAKEMAN, COOK & COMPANY: Lakeman, Cook & Company had begun erecting a building
in the fall of 1900, in Block 2, on Lot 5. The walls had been set up when a
severe winter storm tore down all that had been done; this forced them to begin
anew, and it was not until about mid-Mar. of 1901 that this establishment was
opened for business. Arrangements were made to hold Java's first masquerade ball
there on the evening of Mar. 22, 1901. Mr. Jarvis, a Bowdle fiddler, and one
other person, unknown, supplied the music. Business was brisk at Lakeman, Cook,
and Company, often taking in from $250 to $300 cash in a single day as more and
more settlers moved into the area. After six months, an addition was built on
the north side of the original store to house a farm machinery section. Later,
another addition was erected on the south side of the original building; this
addition housed a full line of furniture, and soon this store was selling
everything from needles to a threshing machine, with a full stock carried at all
times. An advertisement in The Rising Sun of May 14, 1903 read: "For Bargains.
Go to Lakeman, Cook & Co., of Java, S.D. Farm Machinery at Greatly Reduced
Prices, a 16 inch Columbia High lift Sulky Plow with 3 Horse Equalizers for $32;
Corn Planters & Cultivators. Also a full line of Hardware, Furniture, Groceries,
Boots & Shoes. The highest market price paid for butter and eggs."

(Photo:) Furniture, Hardware, Groceries, etc.

For several years, from five to seven clerks were employed to handle the
business. In 1910, Arend Lakeman, Sr.,  retired, and sold his share to his
partner and to his son, Arend, Jr. The firm was known as Cook and Lakeman, until
1911, when Arend, Jr. decided to get into the dairy business and sold Cook and
Lakeman to H.J. Cook. Sometime later the store was forced to close for lack of
patronage. While Dirk Lakeman, Sr. served as Java's second postmaster, the post
office was located in this store. The building was on the corner across the
street and to the north of the former Central Hotel. Other businesses in the
building were Sacketts Drug Store, the John H. Wolf Garage, and J.C. Perman's
first implement business. In 1945, Ole and Esther Naasz opened Ole's Electric,
which was closed in about 1956. The Walworth County Hightway Dept. later owned
the building. It was torn down and replaced with the present structure.

DAKOTA CENTRAL TELEPHONE COMPANY: As early as the middle of Mar. 1901, Java
became linked with the outside world, not only by the railroad and Post Office,
but by telephone connections as well, when a telephone line was completed from
Buchecker's Junction. The Java telephone line moved into the area about 1899 as
Dakota Central. In 1900 they moved the office into town, and were completely in
operation by 1915. They converted to an all-relay dial in 1940. Erna Hochstetter
Werre started as an operator in Java on Mar. 18, 1936. On Mar. 25, 1939, she was
Agency Chief operator in Java and worked for two weeks as an operator in Selby,
where she was transferred. She later moved to Aberdeen.

(Photo:) Early telephone office.  Myrtle Ewald McCoy at switchboard, Bertha
         Spiry Hay is standing.

BLACKSMITH SHOP: The first blacksmith shop was opened and operated by John
Banik, later adding a line of farm machinery, buggies, pumps, and windmills.
Simon Bitzer became a partner in 1904 and added a wagon shop.

TAYLOR'S CENTRAL HOTEL: H.A. Taylor, Java's first hotel man, moved a building
into Java, remodeled it, and served the needs of the early community. It should
be noted that the building Mr. Taylor moved into town came from Campbell County,
and was moved entirely with horses providing the motive power and with
considerable difficulty for all concerned. This building had been situated in
the area adjacent to what was known as "Feinstein Lake" and was a major stop
along the "Ipswich Trail," the route used by many of the early settlers in the
1880's. Mr. Taylor sold the hotel property in May 1901, to his brother-in-law,
ex-commissioner H.P. Hall.

(Photo:) The east side of south Main, at left, behind trees is Central Hotel

THE JAVA HOUSE: Mr. Hall operated "The Java House" in conjunction with a feed
barn and stable until Jan. 1904, when Fred Diegel purchased the property. This
hotel was located on the east side of Main Street, opposite from Hofmeyer's
Store. In the May 14, 1903 issue of The Rising Sun, H.P. Hall advertised an
enlarged, remodeled and refinished, most comfortable hotel in Java, with good
meals and pleasant rooms, and a feed barn in connection.

DRAYLINE: Phillip Flemmer had the distinction of being the town's first drayman.
He operated a large-scale business, hauling supplies as needed in the bustling
new town.

BLINDERMAN BROTHERS: David and John Blinderman advertised for business before
having a suitable structure in which to operate, erecting their business
building in Feb. 1901. They dealt in groceries, general merchandise, and scrap
iron.

MEAT MARKET: Java's first meat market was opened and operated by John (Jack)
Feeney some time in 1901 and remained in business until 1904 when the property
was sold to Andrew Naasz, who opened a saloon, and then the building was
commonly known as the Naasz building.

JAVA MEDICAL DRUG STORE: Dr. Sigmund Rosenthal came to Java from Evarts and
became the first doctor to serve Java and community. He operated the drug store
in a small building where the old Java Equity Exchange Lumber Yard now stands;
he moved to other quarters at a later date. Dr. Rosenthal remained in Java for a
lengthy time, serving well in his chosen profession.

LAW & REAL ESTATE: An office opened in May 1901, housed in a small building
built by Senator LeClair and his partner, a Mr. Ham. Its location is uncertain.

MARTELL SALOON: The inevitable saloon soon made its appearance. It is generally
conceded that August Martell of McPherson County opened the first such
establishment on the west side of Main Street, north of Bauer, Hoff and Stoller.
August Martell advertised in the May 14, 1903 issue of The Rising Sun: "August
Martell Keeps nothing but the very best Wines, Liquors, Cigars, etc. Courteous
treatment and good drinks for everybody. Java, S.D."

In 1904, Doerr Brothers purchased the business, and Mr. Martell engaged for a
time as a cattle buyer; later he returned to McPherson County, where he went
into business. August Martell was a colorful figure, a veteran of the Spanish-
American War, an intimate friend of President Theodore Roosevelt, serving,
according to reports, as Roosevelt's personal messenger, being with Roosevelt
during the Rough Riders' savage and bloody assault up San Juan Hill.

DEPOT: During the spring of 1901, a construction crew came to Java to erect a
depot to provide service to patrons of the railroad. They commenced work about
mid-May, completing the structure approximately July 15. In service for the
Chicago, Milwaukee, and St. Paul Railway at the depot was F.A. Miller, general
passenger agent, and A.D. Mashek, regular station agent. This depot continued
in service for many years; a number of years ago the service was discontinued.
After being vacant for a period of time, the building was purchased by the Java
Equity Exchange, remodeled, and served as a warehouse.

(Photo:) Untitled

GRAIN ELEVATORS: At about the same time, grain elevators were being built along
the course of the railway. Bauer, Hoff & Stoller Elevator: Prior to the
establishment of banking facilities in Java, Bauer, Hoff, and Stoller paid their
own grain checks at their store. In time, the Bauer, Hoff, and Stoller Elevator
was moved to a point east of the Potter, Garrick and Potter Elevator being
operated by that firm. McCabe Brothers acquired the combined facility and
continued in business for many years. It was then sold to the Java Equity
Exchange.

Crown Elevator was purchased by the Java Equity Exchange and was used into the
70's, when it was dismantled and a larger and more modern facility was
constructed at the site. Bagley Elevator Co.: arrangements were made with John
Hofmeyer to pay their grain tickets, as did Hofmeyer for the Crown Elevator. The
Bagley Elevator was consumed by fire in the 50's.

(Photo:) Bauer, Hoff & Stoller elevator is closest; sign on far elevator
         advertises "Montivideo Roller Mill Co., Cream of West Flour"

A smaller building located west of the elevators, used for a beer storage and
cooling warehouse, was purchased by Carl Jacobs. In preparation for moving, this
building was loaded upon moving dollies. Before it could be moved, tornadic
winds toppled the structure and reduced it to debris. Other grain-handling firms
were Hunt & Son Elevator and the Java Grain Company, which for a time operated
in the Potter, Garrick and Potter Elevator.

WINKLEY'S: William P. Winkley, another of Java's early-day businessmen,
conducted a grocery store in his building located on the west side of Main
street on Lot 1, Block 3. This building later housed businesses of Blinderman
Brothers, L.A. Gershin, the Gershin Brothers, E.R. Kary Grocery, the G & L Store
(1951), operated by Mr. and Mrs. Gilbert Schlepp, all being grocery concerns.
After setting vacant for some time, it was a part of the Java Equity Complex and
used as a warehouse until it was torn down.

CENTRAL LUMBER COMPANY: Early in March of 1901, the Central Lumber Company was
preparing to begin a lumber yard at Java, with Henry Thielen in charge. Mr.
Thielen continued his general mercantile interests, later selling to Bauer, Hoff
and Stoller.

JAVA STATE BANK: In 1901, The Milwaukee Land Company sold Lots 3 and 4 in Block
4 in the Town of Java to William Baker of Spiry, Walworth County, SD.
Construction began for a greatly needed bank. A Mosler vault door was brought
from Freeman, SD, where it had been in the Freeman State Bank. [This vault door
is now in a private home in the state of WA.] The Java State Bank opened for
business in 1902 with C. Buechler as president, B. Buechler as vice president
and C. Buechler as cashier. In 1903, John Feiock of Freeman was given the
position of bookkeeper, Christian Buechler received ownership, and he and his
wife Barbara sold the property to Java State Bank. The bank failed and was sold
on Jan. 15, 1905, to First State Bank of Java. The building housing this bank
was located on the west side of Main, south of the Hofmeyer store.

FIRST STATE BANK of JAVA: Almost immediately after the collapse of the Java
State Bank, the First State Bank of Java, with E.G. Hicks as president, F.B.
Pease as vice president and J.E. Carroll as cashier, opened its doors. By Sept.
1, 1904, Ward McCafferty was in charge of the bank with E.G. Hicks, president;
John Hofmeyer, vice president; and W.C. Hicks, cashier. The bank continued
operation until about 1932. It went into suspension and was liquidated in Apr.
1944. The Board of Directors at that time were E.H. Noteboom, Jacob Ochszner,
Anton Stangl, John Ochszner and William Kunz. The property was sold to Albert E.
Helm in June 1944, who sold it to Jacob Helm in Mar. 1945. Jacob sold it to
Katie Helm and Katie sold it to Phillip Spiry. The back rooms of the building
were used as a residence (the Emil Fiechtner family moved into the rooms in
1940). Later, the building was purchased and Emil Boehler established The Barber
Shop.

(Photo:) July 1904, L-R in photo are Jacob Schlaht, George Schlaht, August
         Martel, John Schlaht, Sam Oster (with black hat), George Zeller, Mike
         Goehring, ?, Rudolph Weiszhaar, and ?

SCHLAHT BROTHERS: Among the early-day businesses in the booming new town of Java
was the partnership known as Schlaht Brothers, under the proprietorship of
Jacob, George and John Schlaht.

First locating on Lot 9, Block 2, of the original town plat, the brothers
engaged Alex Heiser of Selby, their brother-in-law, to erect a building in
January of 1902. The business consisted of a saloon and billiard hall, and the
new establishment grew and prospered.

In 1904 brother George left the partnership to take up a homestead 9 miles east
of Mound City, in Campbell County and the firm continued as Schlaht Bros., with
Jacob and John at the helm. Aside from the usual line of refreshments, sundries
and entertainment, an occasional bowery dance was held.

It became apparent that a larger and more modern building was necessary to house
the increasing volume of business, and in June of 1907, the pool room building
was moved to the rear of the lot, and a fine new two-story building was erected,
being 24 by 30 feet with 16 foot posts. On July 4, 1907, a Grand Ball was held
to dedicate the new building, with a fine lunch served throughout the
celebration. Later in July of the same year, new fixtures were received, and by
year's end elegant new bar fixtures were installed and two new pool tables were
added; these improvements were adjudged by many as being the finest in this part
of the state.

The saloon room and billiard room were so arranged that it was possible to pass
from one to the other via a walkway between the two. The upper story of the new
building contained rooms used as living quarters. In later years this building
housed another business familiar to many Javaites, the drug store operated for
many years by August C. Schlepp.

In July of 1908, the business was advertised for sale, the property consisting
at this time of two business houses, a fine new 8 room residence, and two
business lots and three residence lots, however, the business continued under
the Schlaht Bros. until January 23, 1909, when by mutual consent, the
partnership between Jacob Schlaht and John Schlaht, under the firm name of
Schlaht Brothers, was dissolved; John retiring from the saloon business, with
Jacob as successor of the firm.

Jacob Schlaht continued in business until Feb. 1910, when he sold the saloon
business to Jacob and Rudolf Weiszhaar, father and son, who took possession on
that date. John Schlaht, continued his residence in Java for many years as a
prominent businessman.

SCHLEPP DRUG STORE: In 1910, Carl Schlepp sold his building to his son, A.C.
Schlepp. The building housed a recreation parlor, which the family operated
until 1927, when the fixtures of the recreation parlor were sold and replaced
with drug store fixtures. The drug store and barbershop were operated until 1956
when the stock and fixtures were sold and the business closed. The building was
razed a few years later.

New businesses were started every year during the boom of Java. Many changed
ownership, with partners selling out to partners, brothers selling to brothers.
It is nearly impossible to account for all business transactions in the early
days of Java. The following business changes and years can, at best, give the
reader an idea of just how active was this community.

Java Herald and Rising Sun of Bangor, In Sept. 10, 1903, Java was blessed with
   its own newspaper. Carl F. Clement, who had been employed at The Frei Press
   in Eureka, in partnership with George P. Vick, purchased the printing
   equipment of the Hoffman Brothers at Bangor. Moving the heavy equipment with
   horse and wagon proved quite a task; however, on Sept. 10, 1903, the first
   edition of the combined paper became a reality. Fritz Clement, a son of the
   founder, and his wife Ida later published the paper.

At the north end of Main, looking south and to the west, an empty space beside
the Java Community Cafe was once the location of the former David Blinderman
building, which in turn was sold to H.J. Cook, and under the operation as H.J.
Mercantile. In 1917, Louis A. Gershin also became owner of the business. He made
great improvements and operated it as Gershin General Store until Jan. 1, 1943,
when the store was closed. In 1944, Emmanuel and Gertie Kary purchased the
building and opened a grocery business known as Kary Super Valu Store. Gilbert
and LaRayne Schlepp took over ownership in 1951, and operated it as G & L
Grocery. It was then owned by the Java Equity and used as a storage complex
until it was knocked down in Oct. 1990. Clerks working in this building over the
years were Ida Gerhardt, Emma Wiespfenning and Rosie Spiry, among others.

Another one of Java's oldest buildings was the Winkley Building, later taken
over by D. Blinderman. Other businesses housed here were: Gershin Mercantile,
Kary's Furniture, Speidel Recreation, Hirsch, Oster, and Neumiller Recreation.
In 1953, E.E. Schlepp took over ownership and operated as Schlepp's Cafe until
1959, when a nephew, Elmer Schlepp, became owner. It is now the Java Community
Cafe.

A small building south of the Cafe had served as a cream station for owners such
as John Schlaht, John Dufloth, Joe Bosch, Art Freimark, Art Schumacher and Chris
Pfitzer. This building was later destroyed by fire.

The building to the south of what had been a cream station has quite a history.
On Nov. 22, 1902, the Milwaukee Land Co. sold Lots 3 and 4 of this Block (3) to
John and Henry Herman, and in Apr. 1903, the Milwaukee Land Co. sold Lot 5 in
this Block (3) to Sigmond and Sophie Rosenthal. The Rosenthals sold the north 13
feet of Lot 5 to David and John Blinderman, Christian Wolf and Louis Gendel, co-
partners. The Hermans sold the co-partners the south 22 feet of Lot 4 in Nov. of
that year. Eventually, Gendel sold his share and Blindermans and Wolf partnered
with Gottlieb Freimark, who sold his interest to Blinderman and Wolf. Christian
Wolf and David Blinderman made furniture and coffins in the first level, and the
upper level was used for receptions, meetings, and other social activities. Jan.
1905, Blindermans and Wolfs sold 1/4 interest to Christian Himmerich. In Mar.
1905, David and Edna Blinderman sold 1/4 interest in the E1/2 of Lot 2, Lots 3
and 4, and the N1/2 of Lot 5 to Gottlieb Knodel. They also sold their  share in
"the stock of merchandise now owned by the firm of Blinderman Brothers, Wolf and
Himmerich and located in the buildings on Lots 2, 3, 4, and 5 in Block 3." The
stock consisted of groceries, dry goods, boots and shoes, crockery and
glassware, notions and furniture. By Nov. 1905, John and Rebecca Blinderman sold
their entire share to Gottlieb Knodel. And In Feb. 1911, Gottlieb and Louise
Knodel and Christian and Rosina Wolf sold all that they owned to Christian
Himmerich. Christian Himmerich passed away and the property was divided among
the heirs, two of whom were Katharina and Ludwig L. Helm. They sold the property
to Friedrich and Ludwig Helm, who sold it to Jacob Helm. On Mar. 20, 1925, Jacob
and Katie Helm sold the property to Arend and Kittie Lakeman, Sr. The Lakemans
operated the Lakeman Cafe and lived upstairs. Kittie Lakeman sold the property
to Ed Gill in 1943. Ed operated Gill's Hardware until Ervin Wolf took over the
business and named it Wolf Hardware. Tillie and Minnie Job purchased the
property in 1963 and operated as Job's Cafe  until 1969, when Claudia Pfaff
became owner and operated Claudia's Cafe for two years. Private owners are
presently using the building.

(Photo:) Untitled

The buildings occupied by the previous Municipal Liquor and the Job Cafe was the
former Schnaible and Krause Busy Bee Store. In 1942, Minnie and Tillie Job
operated the Job Cafe until they purchased the former Lakeman Cafe in the
1960's. Both buildings were dismantled after their vacancies.

(Photo:) Untitled

Pfitzer & Eisenbeisz Pool Hall was formerly a saloon and pool hall, previously
operated by Naasz, Lutz, Martell, Doerr and Schlaht. It was later owned and
operated as Eisenbeisz & Son until 1965. It was sold and used as a Recreation
Hall operated by Elmer Wolf. A short time later it was closed. In the spring of
1980, Courtney Neal of Nashville, TN began renovating the building, with plans
of opening a variety store. By mid-summer, Neal's Department Store was opened,
with a partial stock on hand. The store was closed in the wintertime, when Mr.
Neal made business trips to Nashville, returning in the spring with additional
merchandise. The store was in operation for a period of time but eventually was
forced to close. The building is now under private ownership.

(Photo:) Untitled

On the next block, south of the former Bauer store was Langes Mercantile Store,
which has been dismantled and is now a vacant lot. Next to the lot was the First
State Bank building, which later housed the Emil Boehler's Barber Shop. The next
structure south was known as the Telephone building, which housed the telephone
switchboard in the early days of Java. An apartment was in the back rooms of the
building. In 1972 it was dismantled.

A large building, known as the Hicks and Helm Garage, was later the Charlie
Schlepp Garage. Many years later Hepper & Son became owners and also had a Ford
sales franchise. The building has been dismantled.

A building south of the Garage was known as The Java Printing Office, which was
later moved to Selby.

The former E.G. Heerwald building still remains and is the Mona Schlepp
residence. It served previously as a Millinery and Hairdress Parlor, operated by
Ida Spiry and Anne Banik. In 1935, Lydia Wolf (Shaver) operated it as a Beauty
Salon.

A Sterling service station, operated by Ed Hochstetter and John Lutz, was across
from the school, where the present Fire Hall is located.

Across Main Street, east of the Mona Schlepp residence, is Otto and Betty
Schnaible's residence, which had served as a dress shop in the early days of
Java. In later years, it became a doctor's office.

The building that was north of the Otto Schnaible residence was the site of the
Old Fire Hall. Years later it served as the Java City Hall, until 1941, when a
new City Hall was built. Meetings of the Java Legion and Auxiliary were held in
this building until a new structure was erected. The Java City Band, A.C.
Schlepp, director, practiced on the 2nd floor on Tuesday and Thursday evenings.
Birthday parties and other social events were held here, as well. Fred Permann
purchased the building and operated Permann Plumbing & Heating. In 1965 Wilbur
Kary purchased the inventory and moved it to his farm home. In the late 60's and
early 70's, Rev. Martin Bieber used the building for his antique collection. He
set up a "display of the past" in his building for Java's Diamond Jubilee in
1975. The building was destroyed in 1992.

A wooden bell tower was located south of the hall, used to alert firemen to a
fire and announce the beginning of a 9 p.m. curfew. Youngsters under 16 were not
allowed to be on the streets "downtown" or "uptown" depending upon where they
lived. Any youngster caught after curfew was escorted home by the City Cop.

Immediately behind the building were the city windmill, an electric power plant,
and a large community water tank. The power plant had DC current and was
operated by Fred Krause and Shorty Wolf. Residents used the tank to water their
milk cows. Many residents had their own cows, usually one to a family, as a milk
supply.

(Photo:) Adam Lorenz Shoe Shop, 1934. Fred Walther, Anna Marie and Adam Lorenz.

Adam Lorenz Shoe & Harness Shop was north of the Old Fire Hall building and was
in operation for many years. Due to automation, Adam was forced to close his
shop in 1940. This building has also been dismantled.

North of the Lorenz Shoe & Harness shop was a large structure, which was the
former Banik Garage. Sold to the Spirys, it was operated as Spiry & Son Ford
Garage. In 1945, Chris Pfitzer took over ownership, which he operated as a
garage and machine shop for four years. After being vacant for several years the
building was dismantled.

The next building was known as the Library, which was operated by Mrs. Noble.
Later it was the residence of Ella Buckenberger and is now owned by a private
party.

The Post Office building near the former Buckenberger residence is still
standing. I.R. Krause carried out his appointment as Postmaster for 22 years in
this building. Julius Pfitzer was the next appointee who served as Postmaster
until his retirement. In 1976, an open house was held at the new Java Post
Office; a private party now owns the old building.

(Photo:) Untitled

A small creamery was located north of the Post Office and was served by
operators such as F.C. Pietzke, Schell, Kate Spiry, Jake Nehlich, Fred Krause
and Brown. The building was dismantled in the early forties.

A building on the corner north of the old Post Office was known as the Central
Hotel, which was one of Java's first hotels, owned and operated by H.A. Taylor.
Other businesses housed in this building were a cafe, pool hall and a garage
with other owners such as George Zeller and John H. Wolf and Helm. Spirys moved
their garage and later, Francis Jensen operated it. It later was used as storage
for beehives, and was recently dismantled.

Across the alley to the east was another one of Java's oldest buildings, which
was known as the Blacksmith Shop. The shop was purchased by Anton Weisgram in
1913 from J.H. Wolf and was enlarged two years later. Within a few years, a
brother, Fred, became co-owner and later Frank took over complete management,
operating as one of the best Blacksmith Shops in the surrounding area. Upon
Frank's death, it was closed. The building has since been destroyed.

(Photo:) Lakeman & Cook later became John Wolf Garage, the north part of the
         building held a bowling alley.

(Photo:) Untitled

On the corner across the street of the former Central Hotel was the Cook and
Lakeman establishment, which later served as the Wolf Garage owned and operated
by J.H. Wolf, who had the first Ford Dealership in this area. J.C. Perman took
over ownership and ran an implement business until he moved to a new location
east of this site. In 1945, Ole Naasz purchased the building and operated it as
Ole's Electric. The Walworth County Highway Department used it for storage until
it was torn down and replaced with a new structure.

Across the alley to the east was a Livery Stable, owned and operated by Diegel
and Fiechtner, which was later sold to George S. Wolf. Wolf merged with Adolph
Pfaff Drayline, and after the Livery Stable was discontinued in the later
twenties, Pfaff remained as owner of the Drayline, until he sold it to Adolph J.
Horst in 1946.The Livery Stable was dismantled and presently the city pump house
is located on the lot. Perman Implement was also located on the next lot.

North of the County Highway Dept. building was a large structure erected by
Louis Horst and Fred Dufloth. In 1920, this building was operated as a movie
hall. J.F. Perman took over ownership in 1934 and continued operating it for
movies and other social functions. J.L. Fetzer and son became owners in 1937 and
opened the Grand Theatre. Other owners were: Ed Perman, Ben Stiegelmeier, Herman
Fiedler, and in 1947, the brothers, Art and Wes Frank became owners, continuing
until 1957, when it was closed. It was later dismantled and the lumber was used
for the new Legion Hall, which was built on the adjoining lot. School basketball
games, variety shows, and other events were held in this building. Remember
roller skating in the theatre?

The Schock and Spiry Meat Market north of the Drug Store was dismantled. Adolph
Schuh purchased the lot and in 1949, put up a new building, which housed
Adolph's Repair Shop. This business closed and the building is presently vacant.

The former Campbell Hotel, next to the Meat Market served as a girls' dormitory
in the late thirties and early forties. The building was sold and moved to
Leola.

The late Gottlieb Zeller residence served as a dentist's office in the early
years of Java, and is now the Kent & Holly Wolforth residence and home of
Holly's beauty shop.

Schmierer Garage opened in 1957 on the west end of Java. Business was expanded
in 1958, operated by Rueben Schmierer. The Garage became a gathering place for
some of the local men, in the later years, and was closed when Mr. Schmierer
passed away. The property was sold to a private party and is now vacant.

Jensen Excavating was established in 1958 with five pieces of equipment. Mr.
Jensen has since retired and no longer runs the business.

Carlson Custom Blacksmith was established in 1961, Oscar Carlson, owner. He
continues to operate his business from his farm south of Java.

Goetz Repair Shop was established in 1969, located west of Java on Highway 103;
Jerry Goetz, proprietor.

Hochstatter Antique Shop was established by Christ Hochstatter and his son
"Turk". Located near their home in Java, it was operated until 1973, when the
Turk sold out and moved to WA.

The Flower Garden began in 1970, with Hazel Zeller as owner. Gladiola bulbs,
bulblets and seeds were sent to England, New Zealand, Russia, Canada, and 18-20
states, especially among the northern third of the U.S. Cut flowers, perennials
and unusual house-plants were also sold on a local basis. In 1980, Hazel
received the John Robertson Award at a banquet of the SD Horticultural Society.
She was appointed to a five-year term as a director of this society. Hazel sold
her beautifully landscaped property and moved into the Low-Rental Apartments.
Hazel passed away on Mar. 17, 2000 in WA.

Mike Kary Salvage was located NE of the railroad track. Operation was
discontinued when Mike died.

Vivian Witlock established a home-based beauty salon, Viv's, in 1973 with Susan
Goetz as assistant operator. Vivian closed the shop in Java when the family
moved to Selby; she continues operating her beauty salon in her Selby home.

DC&M opened in 1995 when the Java school building was sold for $1 to Freeman
Paquet and Guadalupe Arellano, co-owners of a welding business. The dumpster-
building business relocated to Java from Mobridge. Freeman sold out to Guadalupe
and the business continued until late 1999, when personal matters forced the
closure.  Presently, the former Java school building stands vacant.

BEAUTY PARLORS and/or SHOPS

Ida Spiry and Anne Banik operated a Millinery and Hair Dress Parlor in the
former E.G. Heerwald building, which is the present home of Mona L. Schlepp.

Emma Wolf Steigelmeier worked as a Hairdresser in Kansas City and Aberdeen
before she opened her own shop in her Java home. She was in business from 1927
to about 1934.

In 1935, Lydia Shaver Wolf operated a Beauty Salon in Java in the front part of
the Heerwald building, until about 1941. Viola Schadler Fiedler took over the
Salon on Apr. 1942 and operated it until the building was sold to Mr. and Mrs.
John Naasz, who made it their home. Viola bought the business and equipment and
moved it into a house that later belonged to Amelia (Molly) Wolf Arbach. Viola
had her shop until 1947.

Dee (Ken) Fiedler opened her own shop and operated it for about a year in 1963.
Her shop was in the front of the newly remodeled Bauer & Sons building, which
was then owned by Chris and Lillian Pfitzer and was operating as the Paint
Store.

During this time, Margie Eisenbeisz Mueller also had a shop in her home a block
east of south Main Street.

Vivian Gill Witlock and her family moved into Java. She had an addition built
onto her home and opened Viv's Hair Shop in Aug. 1973, with Susan Goetz
assisting. The family moved to Selby in 1990, where the operation of Viv's Hair
Shop continues, with Traci Sandmeier Frank working with Viv.

Holly (Kent) Wolforth opened Hair Country in Oct. 1992. A #1 Miami Dolphins fan,
Holly spiffed up her shop using the Dolphins color theme. She states that it has
become her Shrine.

JAVA COMMUNITY CAFE

Elmer and Erna Schlepp purchased the cafe from Elmer's uncle, E.E. Schlepp, in
1959 and operated Schlepp's Cafe for 25 years less one month. They retired in
Dec. 1984 when they sold the business to Paul and Sandy Jacobs, who ran the cafe
for five and one-half years. Bernice Grenz leased the business for six months.
The Jacobs decided to close the cafe and no one came forward to purchase it.

The community got together and on Feb. 26, 1990, held an organizational meeting
where the Java Community Cafe Corp. was formed. Officers elected were Ted
Schneider, chairman, LeRoy Sandmeier, vice-chairman, Donna Bieber, secretary,
Merlyn Melcher, treasurer and Delila Biel, member-at-large.

The cafe doors opened Mar. 19, 1990 with Linda Langston as manager. Linda
resigned in May and Dorothy Schneider became acting manager.

In Jan. 1996, Teri and Mark Nelson purchased the business from the Cafe Corp.
and operated it until June 1997. Christina and Alan Schaefer became the new
owners, operating the cafe from June 1997 until Nov. 1998. The cafe was then
turned back to the Nelsons, who tried selling the business through advertising.

The business went on the auction block in 1999. Marvin and Lois Wolf purchased
the business from the Nelsons, and made financial arrangements with the Cafe
Corporation. The community once again opened the doors for business. Pat Aldrich
was named manager in July 1999 and submitted her resignation in early Dec. due
to family health problems. Christ Schaefer took over as interim manager until
"Ellie" came to work. Eloise (Mueller) Lassle became the manager of the Java
Cafe on Feb. 1, 2000. Not only is she a good cook, but also "loves to cook" and
is familiar with the type, and quantities, of food the patrons from this part of
the country like best.

JAVA EQUITY EXCHANGE

The first Equity meeting held in Walworth County took place at Selby in July of
1911, conducted by C.O. Drayton, who came here on a return trip from the
territory along the Milwaukee railroad west of the Missouri River, where he had
made a number of addresses and interested many farmers. About a week after the
Selby meeting a similar gathering took place in Java at Lange's Hall, and
sufficient interest was aroused so that an organization was formed. This first
setup as such organizations are now called, was known as a Local Equity Union
and the number of the Java charter from the National Union was 9, which shows
that Java was a real pioneer in the cooperative movement. It was social and
educational, much like our present-day community clubs. At every meeting there
was talk of cooperation and the day when farmers could unite to buy and sell
collectively and save the exorbitant profits often taken by dealers.

On Dec. 2, 1911, the Equity Union elected Arne Strand, G.W. Ryan, H.C. Erbe,
Martin Thorson and Thomas Murray directors, evidently with the intention that a
start should be made in business. These men met and applied for a charter from
the state, which was granted Mar. 1, 1912. However, nothing more was done until
Nov., when a group of determined farmers met at the Erbe schoolhouse SE of Java
and pledged a dozen shares of stock at $25 each in the new enterprise. H.C. Erbe
was elected president, and G.W. Ryan, secretary-treasurer.

The annual meeting was held on Dec. 6, 1912 and A.R. Gordon became president,
A.E. Borg secretary-treasurer, with Fred Bieber, G.W. Ryan and Ernest Noteboom
as the other directors. Nothing further was done until the summer of 1913 when
twine, elevator site and similar subjects were mentioned much in the minutes of
the meetings. The Crown Elevator was negotiated for in a meeting held June 28,
and on July 5 the contract was completed. The price was $3,500. The keys were
received from Henry Bauder and on July 21st, the board hired A.E. Borg as
manager. Of interest is that notes for $1500 were part of the deal for the
elevator.

(Photo:) Wm. Kunz (right) with H. Buckenberger in Equity office

Late in 1913, William Kunz was hired to assist A.E. Borg. When the implement
business was purchased, Mr. Borg took over the management of that while Mr. Kunz
stayed in charge of the elevator. During his years as manager, in addition to
his elevator duties, he also handled and shipped thousands of head of livestock.
Mr. Kunz continued as manager until 1945, when he retired after 32 years of
faithful service.  Charter Members of Feb. 3, 1913 were

A.R. Gordon       George Sebert      Anton Stangl
Geo W. Ryan       Phillip J. Merkel  Phillip Noble
James Barclay     Evan Jones         Peter Noble
August Erbe       Fred Bieber        Gaisa Kormandy
Thomas Murray     Geo. Kormendy      W.H. Payne
Joe Stangl        Adolph Stangl      Arne Strand
William Baker

Other First Year Members were

Axel Borg         Jacob F. Wolf Jr.  Jacob Helm
Ed Merkel         Mike Raba          J. Stiegelmeier
Ed Jurgerson      Cornelius Noble    Fred K. Wolff
E. Noteboom       Case Noteboom      L. Kormandy
Jacob Nysse       Emanuel Baer       Wilhelm Moser
Gerrit Noble      Andrew Raba        Martin Thorson
J.C. Campbell     John Raba          Jacob Bender
George Kosters    Heinrich Mueller   Martin Rieger
Wilson Hicks

The implement business was purchased from George Zeller, Feb. 10, 1916. Again,
borrowed money was required and in the autumn of that year, the elevator was
mortgaged. In 1917 the main building of the implement handling building burned
down. The stockholders courageously voted to rebuild. In 1918 a new elevator was
built to meet the needs of the growing business. The implement business never
proved to be a success and was sold to J.F. Perman on Dec. 15, 1925.

In Apr. of 1937, a special stockholders' meeting was held to discuss the
possibility of going into the gas and oil business. A vote taken showed that the
stockholders were in favor of this move, and the bulk plant and service station
belonging to J.F. Perman were purchased for $4,500. A loan for this amount was
secured from the Federal Land Bank. The Consumers Cooperative Assn., now
Farmland Industries, was given the oil and gas contract. This business
prospered, and soon the need for a new service station became apparent. This was
built in 1946 at a cost of $25,000. In 1959 the bulk plant was also enlarged
with the purchase of the Cities Service Oil Co., at a cost of $3,500. When Fred
Helm retired as manager of the Central Lumber Co., Java was left without a
lumber yard as the company decided it was not feasible to remain in the business
here. In 1956, a representative of the company offered to sell the building to
the Equity at a cost of $1,200. The old elevator was torn down in 1971 and
replaced with a new modern $82,000 facility with a 38,000-bushel capacity. A
bulk fertilizer and blender were added in 1974. Merlyn Melcher became general
manager on Mar. 15, 1965.

The service station was updated in 1989 to meet Federal regulations, by
installing two 2000-gallon underground storage tanks.

Java Equity merged with the Ipswich elevator in 1991 and became Ipswich-Java
Farmers Elevator. The bookkeeping system was then changed to computers, thus
enabling the two sites to better serve the patrons.

In the years from 1991 to 1994, more mergers took place, eventually joining the
elevators in Java, Ipswich, Leola, Northville, Wecota, Onaka and Chelsea to
become North Central Farmers Elevator.

An enclosed load-out and larger blender were added to the fertilizer plant in
1993. In 1995, two 30,000-bushel drying bins, an 80,000-bushel storage bin, a
10,000-bushel-per-hour leg and a 1,000-bushel-per-hour dryer were added to
increase the total grain storage capacity to 390,000 bushels. New offices were
constructed adjacent to the elevator building in 1992.

In 1997, North Central Farmers Elevator purchased Cargill Elevator at Bowdle and
in Jan. 2000, merged with Herreid and Pollock.

Presently, two Terra-Gators, two John Deere sprayers, several fertilizer tender
trucks and delivery trucks are operated to serve the patrons' needs. Bulk
chemical was added and the three remaining old elevators were torn down. No
decision has been made, to date, as to replacing the elevators.

Merlyn Melcher was manager until 1997, when his son Mark became manager. Mark
resigned in late 1999 and Karman Stikelstad is acting manager. Employees of the
Java faction of North Central Farmers Elevator are Cliff Bieber and Alan
Schaefer at the service station; Jerry Bauer, Trent Goetz, Merlyn Melcher,
Charlie Neuhart, Arnie Roebuck, and Karman Stikelstad at the elevator. Lorrain
Fiedler is the bookkeeper.

(Photo:) Untitled

JAVA MUNICIPAL LIQUOR STORE

On Apr. 15, 1947, the City of Java held an election with three issues to be
decided by the voter, which were a bond issue for a City sewer system, City
board members, and if the City should own and operate a Municipal establishment.
The bond for the sewer construction was approved and a Municipal Liquor License
for the City of Java was approved by 150 Yes votes to 99 No votes. City board
members at the time were Fritz Clement, E.R. Kary, J.J. Lutz, John Schadler,
John Schlaht, A.C. Schlepp and Ben Stiegelmeier. New board members elected were
Ed Hirsch, Reine Moser and Chris Pfitzer. Remaining on the board were Fritz
Clement, J.J. Lutz, A.C. Schlepp and Ben Stiegelmeier.

In June of 1947, the Municipal Liquor Store began its first month of business in
a building on Main Street owned by Pauline Krause, for $40 rent per month.
Christ Naasz and Jacob Schlepp were hired as bartenders at $140 a month each. A
few months later, the monthly rent was raised to $50 and the bartenders' wages
were raised to $170. Christ Naasz and Jacob Schlepp remained as bartenders for
12 years.

In Aug. 1959, Ben Meier was hired as bartender at $250 per month and 4% of the
gross receipts. In Dec. of 1960 the board approved the application for an Off
and On Sale Liquor License.

In May 1961, the board agreed to hire a contractor to pave Main Street from the
school to the north end of Main Street, for the second time. Liquor funds not
otherwise appropriated were to be used, in installments of $500 a month.

A City election was held Dec. 1962 to determine if the City Liquor business
should continue. The voters chose to stay in the business, continuing to rent
the building from the Krause Estate.

A special meeting was called in Aug. 1963 to discuss a new site. Motion by
Jensen, second by Kast to terminate the present lease and buy the Chris Pfitzer
building for the sum of $2000 was made. Orville Robbins, attorney for the City,
would draw up the papers. The motion carried with a unanimous vote.

Lots 12 and 13, Block 3, were purchased. Discussion followed regarding the
feasibility of constructing a new building over the next months. In a special
meeting held Oct. 24, 1963, Mr. Sackreiter met with the board and offered a
24x60 foot steel structure to be completed on, or before, Jan. 1, 1964 for the
sum of $10,750. Gust Bieber, Herman Fiedler, Marie Hicks, Oscar Schnaible and
Gottlieb Zeller were in attendance. The building would be constructed and leased
for a term of 10 years at $100 per month. The City was given a purchase-option
for any time during the term of the lease, for its cost and 6% interest.

The new City Municipal Liquor Store began operation in late Jan. 1964 in its new
location. Ben Meier remained as bartender and was paid $35 for helping move to
the new location. Ben operated the liquor store until June 1964.

Sam Otterstetter was hired and remained until Feb. 1967; Julius Wolf and Larry
Goetz were hired in Apr. 1967 and continued operating the business until 1974,
at which time Larry and Janice Goetz were hired. They continued until May 1978.

Clifford and Bernice Grenz were the first people to lease the business, from
1978 to 1979. Bernice was then hired as manager and remained until 1983. The
business was leased again, this time to Robert and Jackie Ackerman, from Apr.
1983 to July 1983. Jerry and Mary Meidinger then leased the bar from Aug. 1983
to 1986.

Many turnovers occurred in 1967. Managers included Judy and Clayton Horst, Julia
Skari, Myron Grenz, Mr. & Mrs. Robert Adams, Mr. & Mrs. Allen, and Sheryl
Randall, who ended her employment in Jan. 1989.

Kent and Holly Wolforth leased the The Liquor Store from Jan. 1989 to Mar. 1990,
when Holly was hired as manager until Feb. 1991. Earl Frank was temporary
manager until it was again leased, this time to Dewayne "Hoss" and Joanne
"Sunny" Wanganess from Aug. 1991 to Oct. 1993.

Again it was leased when Jerry and Cindi Miller took over from Sept. 1993 to
July 1994. Lois Aberle then leased the business, remaining from July 1994 to
Jan. 1998. Everett "Bud" Allbee leased the Java Municipal Liquor Store in 1999.

Throughout the earlier years, a great amount of money was transferred out of the
Liquor Fund on a monthly basis. This money was utilized for the betterment of
the streets, walks, and services of the City. This took place when the
population was larger and the "Bar" served as a local gathering place for town
and country folk.

JAVA POST OFFICE

On Nov. 23, 1900, a route inspector for the Post Office Department visited Java,
gathering information relative to prospective mail routes, not only in town, but
for the surrounding areas of settlement. Among the first applicants for the
postmastership of Java, was Mr. T.B. Bowlus, a pioneer resident of the vicinity,
and it was Mr. Bowlus that received the appointment as the first postmaster,
near the end of Dec. 1900.

Between 1904 and 1913, Jacob Stoller was postmaster and his daughter, Annette,
was his deputy. The post office was in the Bauer store at this time.

In 1913, I.R. Krause was appointed Postmaster and remained so for 22 years. In
1920 he put up the "new" building. This building is still standing and is the
property of a private party.

Julius Pfitzer was the next appointee who served as Postmaster from 1935 until
his retirement.

In 1976 a new building was erected across Main Street, on the corner that once
housed the Bauer and the Pfitzer stores. An open house was held at the new Java
Post Office.

In 1984, LaVina Perman retired as Postmaster and Agnes (Alcorn) Johnson assumed
the position. She retired in 1992. Lois Wolf had served as Postmaster, and Terry
Schneider served in a temporary capacity for a time. Agnes and Shirley
Ketterling were the post office clerks. After 1992, Shirley Ketterling took over
the duties and responsibilities of the office, and maintained all operations of
it until 1993, when Richard Wales of Mobridge was appointed Postmaster. Lois
Aberle was post office clerk under Postmaster Wale's direction. Rick continues
as Postmaster, serving the entire Java community.

Earlier, there were three rural mail routes out of the Java office; later it was
divided into two areas. The area north of Java was served by Marvin Pfitzer as
carrier, and south of Java by Chris Pfitzer.

In 1982, following the retirement of the two carriers, the entire rural area was
leased on a contract basis, and Harvey Bonen of Bowdle received the contract. He
presently serves the entire rural area six days a week.

Having a Post Office is a main source of identity for a community. It is hoped
that the roots are strong enough to maintain the Java Post Office for many years
to come.

(Photo:) Untitled

JAVA SUPER VALU

The Java Super Valu store, presently owned and operated by the Java Community
Store Corp., is located in what was, many years ago, the Baer Hardware. It was
later sold to Carl Hepper & Sons for a grocery store and meat market. Years
later, E.R. Kary took over ownership and after World War II, Elmer Biel
purchased the building and fixtures and did business as Elmer's Red Owl. In
1959, Marvin Pfitzer took over ownership and did business as The Java Red Owl.
Some time later, the store was sold to Bob and Joyce Pfitzer, continuing as the
Java Red Owl. In the mid-80's, Merle and Florence Noess took over the business,
which was then known as the Java Super Valu "Your Hometown Store". Merle and
Florence closed the doors Apr. 30, 1996.

Between May and Aug. of 1996, a group of Java Area residents formed a new Java
Community Store Corp. Selling shares, holding fund-raisers and receiving
donations from concerned persons, many who were alumni of Java High School,
raised enough money to purchase the store from Merle and Florence. The store re-
opened for business on Sept. 6, 1996; a gala Grand Opening was held several
weeks later. Founding board members were LeRoy Sandmeier, Oscar Kapfenstein,
Charlotte Monthye, Calvin Aman, and Steve Biel.

Florence Noess managed the store from Sept. 1996 to Mar. 1998. Upon her
resignation, Becky Witlock assumed managership. The store, still in operation
today, carries a complete line of groceries and meats.

MARIN-BIEL INSURANCE

Marin-Biel Insurance, Inc. is located on Main St. in Java. The business, owned
by Steve and Dan Biel, both of Java, is an independent insurance agency,
representing approximately 35 different companies. They handle almost all types
of insurance, including home, auto, farm, crop, life, health, long-term care,
etc. They also still run a small money exchange, which is a carry-over from the
location's long past bank history, when the Hicks family operated a business.

The first business at this location was The German State Bank, operated by the
Philip Spiry family. When World War I broke out, the bank was forced to change
the name to American State Bank due to the negative attitude toward Germans and
Germany. During the Dirty Thirties, the bank went broke. Also about that time,
the bank building burned down. The present-day building was a cream station that
was moved from another location in Java.

After the bank closed, the Hicks family ran Hicks Exchange and Insurance, a
money exchange, tax service and insurance agency. Lewis Hicks sold the business
to Art Eisenbeisz in 1964 and it became Eisenbeisz Exchange and Insurance. Art
sold it to Steve Biel on Jan. 1, 1975. Dan Biel joined the agency in 1996 and
operates the partner-office located in Selby.

MONTANA-DAKOTA UTILITIES

Electricity got its start in Java in 1916, when a municipal light plant was
constructed after a bond issue. The electricity was turned on near the end of
Sept. 1916. In 1923, the plant was enlarged, and 24-hour service provided. In
1925 the building was renovated, and another larger electric generator was
purchased.

In 1927 Emil "Shorty" Wolf went to work for the City of Java Power Plant. The
capacity of the plant at that time was as follows: Two 35kw Fairbank-Morse
generators. These generators were powered by one 50 H.P. and one 60 H.P. Diesel
operated motors.

The history of production and distribution of man's greatest servant,
electricity, at Java and throughout South Dakota has been a very colorful one.
There are still those among us who recall when electric service was provided for
only several hours a day and only on certain days of the week from small,
independently owned, generators. It is they who marvel at the fact that this
area is presently served by a transmission and distribution system that is
capable of accommodating virtually any power demand thrust upon it. The next
time you look at that dependable electric clock or refrigerator that you know
operates 24 hours a day it will help you appreciate how electricity got its
start in Java and this area many years ago.

In 1917 a Mr. Bert Hill, then superintendent of the Milwaukee Railroad in
Mobridge, struck out to give that city electric service with a minimum of
expense. To accomplish this purpose, he ran a steam line from the boilers of the
roundhouse to a generator located in a building in the approximate location of
the old Mobridge Power Plant. A franchise was granted to Mr. Hill and Gus Smith
and they chose to call the newly formed company the Mobridge Light, Power and
Heating Company.

In 1917, Ferris brothers purchased the existing franchise and built the old
power plant building in the city of Mobridge. Ferris brothers changed the name
of the company to the Mobridge Electric and built their first transmission line
from Mobridge to serve the communities of Glenham and Selby. This new
transmission line marked the beginning of a central power source to serve many
electric distribution systems soon to be built in the northern part of South
Dakota. With the advent of this new central power source, residential and
commercial consumers enjoyed a reduction of electric rates from 16 cents to 15
cents per kilowatt-hour.

After World War I, L.P. Runkel and G.A. Stephens acquired the Mobridge-based
company and its property and reincorporated it as the Northern Power and Light
Company. This new firm expanded the business rapidly until they finally served
58 communities in North and South Dakota extending from Lemmon in the west, to
Ellendale, ND, in the east; from Blunt in the south, to Steele, ND, in the
north. Altogether approximately 225 miles of transmission line were used from
east to west and 200 miles to connect the north and south part of this property.
Runkel and Stephens later sold their interests to the United Public Service
Company, which held the property for only a short time. In 1929 it was again
sold to a new firm who called themselves the Middlewest Utilities Company.

In the early 30's these same properties were purchased by the United Public
Utilities Corporation and placed under the management of the Northern Public
Service Company with general offices at Huron. Under this last management, the
Northern Power and Light Company was known as the Mobridge Division and served
some 58 towns in North and South Dakota. This entire area was divided into eight
district offices, each serving approximately seven towns and involving
approximately 796 miles of transmission lines to accommodate almost 7500
customers. E.P. Harrison was Mobridge Division Manager in the 30's and under his
capable direction, normal expansion continued until 1939, when the company was
consolidated with ND Power and Light Company, forming the Dakota Public Service
Company.

In 1941, with the completion of a new municipal building, the Java power plant
was updated and moved into the new building.

In Oct. 1945, Montana-Dakota Utilities Co. purchased the Dakota Public Service
Company. Upon the purchase, Emil Wolf moved to Selby, where he was responsible
for electric service in Selby as well as Java and Akaska. Mr. Wolf remained in
that capacity until he retired in 1967. Upon Mr. Wolf's retirement, Victor Baker
moved into Selby and the service area was expanded to include Glenham. In 1972,
a new building was built for a district office and M.L. "Radar" Bauer became the
district manager, along with serviceman Baker.

In 1981, Mr. Bauer moved to Eureka to assume another position with MDU. In 1987,
MDU sold their office building to D&D Auto Parts. In Mar. of 1991, Mr. Baker
retired after 24 years of service in Selby. Don Bohle assumed his position of
district representative. In 1993, MDU expanded its electric business in Selby by
bringing natural gas to the area during the East River Natural Gas Project,
which saw Pierre, Onida, Agar, Gettysburg, Mobridge, Glenham, Bowdle, Roscoe and
Ipswich also receive natural gas service. Montana-Dakota Utilities Company has
been proud to serve Java for 55 years, and will continue to provide its service
area with safe and reliable service.

SELBY HONEY

When Sandy and Chuck Hanson purchased a beekeeper business, they filed necessary
legal papers and named their business "Selby Honey", expecting to open the
business in Selby. As it turned out, they ended up in Java at the SW corner of
town. In about 1993, Larry and Bette Bermel purchased the operation from the
Hansons and moved to Java with their sons. Requests are made of the farmers and
landowners to set up hives on their property. Honey is brought to the warehouse
in Java from mid-July through mid-Sept., where it is extracted and barreled. It
is then shipped to Sioux Honey Assn., in Sioux City, IA, the world's largest
honey marketer. There are many uses for honey and the by products, such as
baking, in cereals, making candles, medicine, and pharmaceuticals. Bee Pollen
and Royal Jelly are two of the top selling items in alternative medicine. The
Bermels take their bees south in the winter and raise new queens and multiply
the hives.

(Photo:) John Horstink is in front of door of Java Herald; to his left, Carl F.
         & Kate Clement, and to his right, Hessel Dyk

THE JAVA HERALD

Carl F. and Kate Clement, and George P. Vick, established the town's first
newspaper, the Java Herald, in Sept. 1903, a joyous occasion for the citizens of
Java and the surrounding area. Carl's son-in-law, Hud C. Mains, published the
English version, while Carl operated Der Java Herold, the German version. Mains
operated the Herald until July 25, 1908, when it was taken over by Clement. Carl
passed away in 1922 and his wife, Kate, and son, Fritz, continued publication.
In 1946, the Herald building was moved to Selby.

The Clement family continued to publish the Java Herald until Dec. 31, 1983,
when it and the Selby Record were sold to James MacKay, publisher of the Prairie
Pioneer, which covered Pollock, Herreid and the Campbell County area. MacKay
continued to operate the newspapers and printing plant until Oct. 1987, when the
business was sold to Allen and Leah Burke, who came to Selby from Denver, CO.

The Selby Record and Java Herald continued as separate publications until Aug.
16, 1991, when the Burkes combined the papers, and Java features and news were
incorporated into the Selby Record. The paper began as a handset type weekly,
progressing to the hot metal typesetting machine in the 1920's. This method of
typesetting lasted until 1980, when computerized typesetting methods radically
changed the printing and publishing industry.

In June 1996, the Burkes sold the combined paper to Leona Wager of Hoven,
publisher of the Hoven Review. At that time, the building began housing two
businesses, Selby Printing on the north side, and the Selby record occupying the
south offices. Another change in ownership of the newspaper occurred in June of
1998, when Mrs. Wager sold the Selby Record to Sharon Wolff of Selby. We see the
paper today as the Selby Record Continuing the Java Herald.


The Old Home Town
Originally Published in the Denver Post around 1912

Then the evenin' shade is falling at the
Enden' o' the day,
An' a feller rests from labor, smokin' at his
Pipe o' clay;
There's nothin' does him so much good, be
Fortune up or down,
As the little country paper from his
Old Home Town.

It ain't a thing of beauty and its print ain't
Always clean,
But it straightens out his temper when a
Feller's feelin' mean.
It takes the wrinkles off his face an' brushes
Off the frown,
That little country paper from his
Old Home Town.

It tells of all the parties an' the balls of
Pumpkin Row.
'Bout who spent Sunday with sho's girl, an'
how the crops'll grow.
And how it keeps a feller posted 'bout who's
Up and who is down,
That little country paper from his
Old Home Town.

Now, I like to read the dailies an' the story
Papers, too.
An' at times the yaller novels and some other
Trash, don't you?
But when I want some readin' that'll brush
Away a frown
I want the little paper from my
Old Home Town.

                               Family Histories

        B.P. and Emma S. (Benjamin) Adams
Benajah P. Adams was born in West Haven, Rutland County, VT on June 15, 1845. He
was the oldest son of Edward D. and Rhoda (Wicker) Adams. On Sept. 5, 1866, he
married Emma S. Benjamin of White Hall, NY. Mr. Adams was a real pioneer in
every sense of the word, in his help toward settling this great west, honest and
true in all his dealings with his fellowmen. In 1886, Mr. Adams came with his
family to Dakota Territory and, with his son-in-law, settled in Campbell County.

In the spring of 1887, he moved to Walworth County where he took part in the
organization of Adams Township, which was named after him. Some years later he
moved to Java, where he resided until after the death of his wife on Jan. 3,
1910. After her death, he spent the greater part of his life at the home of his
daughter Mrs. H.P. Hall. Mr. Adams, better known as "Grandpa" Adams, was one of
the very few colorful pioneers who figured prominently in the early settlement
of this county. He was active in spite of his advanced age and would seldom fail
to attend any community celebration, old settlers' gathering, or observation of
Memorial Day. He was a member of the Java Presbyterian Church, the Order of the
Eastern Star and the Masonic Fraternity, having raised a Master Mason in Phoenix
Lodge, A.F. and A.M. of the State of SD, as a recognition of his 50 years of
service in the Masonic Lodge.

To this union was born four daughters and one son: Mary E. Hall; Rhoda E.
Goodwin, who died in 1902; Mabel S. Orthmeyer; Ella J. Taylor; and Elnathan B.
Adams. He lived to the ripe old age of 89 and at his funeral service, the
Presbyterian Choir rendered special music. The Masonic Lodge of Java, with V.M.
Graybill of Mobridge acting as master, was in charge, with Rev. F.W. Bruins of
Mobridge officiating. He was interred beside his wife in the cemetery east of
Java.

        Jacob Aman Sr.
Jacob Aman, Sr., and his family left Russia in 1883 and took the long journey to
the land of America. The voyage to the new country was rough and hazardous. With
many of the immigrants becoming sea sick, including Jacob's wife, unsanitary
conditions aboard ship prevailed. Jacob's wife passed away shortly after
arriving in this country. They came to Dakota Territory by train and settled in
the Campbell County area, where they built their first home out of sod, which so
many of the pioneers were doing.

(Photo:) Jacob Aman, Sr. Family. Michael, Mrs. Aman, Rafael, Anton, Rochus, Mr.
         Aman, John

They endured many hardships while trying to work and take care of the family. This family included five boys: Rafael, Rochus, Michael, Anton and John. There were also two half-brothers, Franz and Jacob, and one half-sister, Marianna (Valentine) Kary Sr.

        Michael J. and Christine (Bollinger) Aman
Michael J. Aman, at the age of 9, came to the new country of America, from
Russia, with his parents. They settled in the Campbell County area. He grew to
manhood in the Artas, Mound City and Java areas, and as a young man, worked at
various jobs.

(Photo:) Michael J. and Christine Aman and daughters

He later married Christine Bollinger, who lived in the Artas area. In 1912, they
moved with their little family to Saskatchewan Canada, where they homesteaded,
as did many other families from the States.

Mr. and Mrs. Michael J. Aman had four children: Edgar married and had two
daughters; Alvin married and had two daughters; Mae married Walt Wolf and had
one daughter and one son; and Adeline married Adolph Schuh and had one daughter
and one son.

Mrs. Aman passed away in 1919 during the flu epidemic and then Mr. Aman returned
to SD with his children. He later bought a home in Java, where his children were
educated in the Java school. He resided in Java until his death in 1947.

        Jacob J. and Elizabeth (Stiegelmeier) Aman
Jacob J. Aman was born Jan. 11, 1860, in Landau, South Russia, where he grew to
young manhood. In 1882, he joined the Russian Army and was in the service for a
period of six years. After being discharged from the Army in 1888, he was united
in marriage to Elizabeth Stiegelmeier. The young couple came to America in 1889
and homesteaded seven miles NE of Java, where they built up a farm. Four sons
and two daughters were born into this home.

Jacob B. married Emilie Bender, had one son, Albert A., and two daughters, Irene
and Ellen. After his wife's death he later married Pauline Naasz.  Four children
were born to this union: Calvin, Delila, Iris, and RoxAnn. He passed away in
1955. (See Family History)

John married Christina Wolf and had one son, Erven. John passed away in 1917.

Esther married Fred Mertz and had two daughters and one son.

Edwin married Lydia Zimmerman and they had two daughters and four sons. He was
killed in a tractor mishap in 1942. (See Family History)

Albert R. married Alice Tews and had two sons and four daughters. (See Family
History)

Ida married Louis Gearhart and they had two sons. She is now living in Selby at
the Good Samaritan Center.

(Photo:) Elizabeth and Jacob J. Aman

After deciding to retire from farming, they built a home in Java on north Main
Street in 1919. The Arlo Fiedler family now owns the home.

Here they resided until their death. After a lingering illness, Jacob J. Aman
passed away at his home in 1928. Mrs. Aman continued to live in their home until
the fall of 1937, when she spent the winter in CA with her son, Edwin, and
family. Death interrupted her plans to return to Java when she passed away in
the spring of 1938. She was buried in the Seventh Day Adventist Cemetery NE of
Java.

        Jacob B. Aman
Jacob B. Aman was born to Jacob J. and Elizabeth (Stiegelmeier) Aman on Mar. 27,
1890, on his parents' homestead seven miles NE of Java, in Walworth County. He
was the oldest of six children of whom only one, Ida Gearhart, is living.

(Photo:) Jacob B. and Pauline Aman

He married Emilie Bender and three children were born. They were: Albert A., who
married Jessie Griswold, both deceased; Ellen (Arnold) Sauer, deceased. Arnold
lives in Minneapolis, MN. They had three children: Loren Sauer of Fargo, ND;
Gerald (Terri) of MI; and Sharon (Mark) Hartman of Minneapolis, MN. They have
one son, Scott. Irene (Arthur) Nelson of Minneapolis, MN, had four sons: Darrell
of Minneapolis, MN; Douglas of Minneapolis has three sons, Aaron, David, and
Samuel; Dale (Diane) lives in Hartford, SD. They have one daughter Tami, one
great-grandson, and two sons Paul and Michael; Dennis drowned at the age of
almost 23 in the St. Croix River in northern MN.

Emilie (Bender) Aman passed away in 1924. In 1926 Jacob married Pauline Naasz of
Artas, the daughter of Gottlieb and Kathrine (Krueg) Naasz. Four more children
were added to this family, who were: Calvin A. married LaMoyle Buckenberger in
1953, resides in Java, had seven children (See Family History); Delila married
Virgil Biel, lives in Java, has two sons and one daughter (See Family History);
Iris married Alvin Schuh, lives in Bowdle (See Family History); RoxAnn married
Lyle Nelson, has three sons and one daughter. (See Family History)

Upon Jacob and Pauline's retirement from the family farm, they moved into Java
in 1953. Jacob passed away on Oct. 15, 1955. Pauline continued to live in Java
until her death on Dec. 16, 1993.

The entire family grew up on the family farm five miles north of Java. The house
was moved into Java and is owned by Calvin and LaMoyle Aman, as is the land, the
farm, and the homestead of Jacob J. Aman, a grandfather of Calvin.

        Calvin and LaMoyle (Buckenberger) Aman
Calvin was born Sep. 25, 1927, on the family farm five miles north of Java. He
attended eight years of school at the Sunshine Country School. After Calvin
graduated from the eighth grade, the family moved to CA, where he attended four
months of his freshman year in El Monte High School, Los Angeles. The family
moved back to SD, where he completed his schooling, graduating from Java High
School in 1945. After graduation, he farmed with his dad for five years and, in
1950, was drafted into the Army where he served for two years in the Korean War.

(Photo:) Calvin Aman Family. Back: Craig, Calvin, David. Mid: Cheryl and
         LaMoyle. Front: Nancy, Kathie, and Patricia

On June 14, 1953, he married LaMoyle Buckenberger in Java. After their marriage,
they continued to live on the homestead, where they farmed a few acres of land
and had some dairy cattle.

Calvin, always interested in sports, especially football and basketball, was
scorekeeper and timekeeper for the games in Java for 32 years. He was on the
Java School board for six years, three of which he served as chairman. He also
served on the Java City Council.

Calvin and LaMoyle had seven children: Kathie, Craig, Nancy, David, Cheryl,
Teresa, and Patricia. Teresa passed away on Nov. 9, 1969, at the age of seven,
from complications of meningitis. She was in the second grade. All six of the
Aman children were fortunate enough to attend and graduate from Java High School
before its closing in 1985. Patricia's class was the last to graduate from the
school.

In Oct. 1977, the Aman family moved their house to town, two blocks west of the
school. After moving to town, Calvin helped in farming and worked part-time
mowing for the county. He is now retired.

LaMoyle was born Mar. 9, 1934. She attended Java School throughout her school
years, graduating from Java High School in 1952. While attending school, LaMoyle
babysat, helped out in the Red Owl, owned and operated by Elmer and Clara Biel,
and she worked for Hicks Exchange for four years.

In July 1969, she went to work at the Good Samaritan Center in Selby. She
started working part-time but it soon led to a full-time job. She continues to
work as a Medication Aide-Restorative Aide. She is also an E.M.T. with the Selby
Ambulance Service, and serves as secretary for the Ambulance Service.

Kathie graduated from Java High School in 1972, married Gary Vander Vorst on
June 23, 1973. They have one daughter Carissa who attends UMN. Kathie is part
owner of River Valley Abstract and Title. Gary is CFO for a chain of gas
stations and banks. They live in Hudson WI.

Craig graduated from Java High School in 1973, married Linda Deuter in Ree
Heights on June 15, 1975. They have one daughter, Lindsay, and one son, Nathan.
Craig is the owner of Faribault Tire and Auto Service Center. Linda is Education
Coordinator for Our Savior's Lutheran Church in Faribault, MN.

Nancy graduated from Java High School in 1975, married Dan McClain in St. Paul,
MN on July 2, 1987. Dan is a self-employed floor technician. Nancy is a
Marketing Service Specialist at LeClair Insurance Services. They live in St.
Paul, MN.

David graduated from Java High School in 1976, married Lynn Cordell in Watertown
on Apr. 16, 1994. They have one daughter Dylynn, and one son, Zachary. David is
a Receiving Clerk for Terex-Telelect, and Lynn is owner/operator of The Kids
Depot/Crafters Village. They live in Watertown.

Cheryl, a 1978 graduate of Java High School, married Dan Frost in Pierre on Mar.
12, 1983. They have one son, Christopher, and twins Aric and Sarah. Cheryl is a
secretary for the State of SD Department of Environment and Natural Resources.
Dan is Maintenance Technician for the Pierre Public Schools. They live in
Pierre.

Patricia graduated from Java High School in 1985, married Todd Manolis in Huron
on May 20, 1980. They have two sons, Michael and Andrew. Patricia is a teacher
for the Woolsey Middle School and Todd is owner/operator of Manolis Grocery
Store. They live in Huron.

        Iris (Aman) Schuh
Iris was born on a farm five miles north of Java to Jacob B. and Pauline (Naasz)
Aman on Apr. 23, 1932. She attended rural Sunshine School, completing the eighth
grade, and attended Java High School, graduating in May 1950.

On Nov. 26, 1950, she married Alvin Schuh of Bowdle. They owned and operated the
family farm for over 27 years, moving into Bowdle on Feb. 3, 1978.

(Photo:) Alvin and Iris (Aman) Schuh Family

Alvin and Iris were blessed with four children and 9 grandchildren.

Bonnie, born Dec. 3, 1953, is a Registered Nurse and works for Dr. Michael Houge

Kenneth, born Apr. 16, 1955, owns and operates the family farm. His wife,

Paul was born Sept. 17, 1956. He manages the Schwan Foods Depot at Hillsboro,

        Edwin and Lydia (Zimmerman) Aman
Edwin Aman was born in 1895, to Jakob J. and Elizabeth (Stiegelmeier) Aman.

farmhouse that their grandfather, Jakob J. Aman, built in 1903. The children
were: Edwin, Jr., born in 1920, married Alma Brockel. They had seven children;

married Art Jackson. They had two children; Gene, born 1932, married Joanne

and they had three children.

(Photo:) Edwin and Lydia Aman

Edwin lost his life in a threshing accident in 1942. The family sold the farm to
Jacob B. Aman, oldest brother of Jakob J. Aman.
