        The Anderson Family
Among the first ancestors of the Anderson family to make the long journey to
America from Norway, were Lars Anderson, his wife, Kari Kalstad, and two eldest
sons, Martin and Antone. After arriving in New York, they made their home at
Coon Valley, near La Crosse, WI. Several years later, in 1885, with three
additional sons: the twins, Charlie and Louie, and the youngest of the family,
Otto, came to homestead in Walworth County in the Swan Creek area.

The necessary steps were taken to file on a quarter of land, as a homestead, and
an additional quarter for a tree claim. The town of Lowry is now situated on
Lars' tree claim. Land on all sides adjoining these claims was regarded as free
range. In the years to come, the family had a small income from taking herd
cattle from the farmers as far north as the Java area, and south to Lebanon.
They were expected to get the cattle in the spring and return them in the fall.
The price per head was 25 cents per season.

Kari died in 1914. Lars, born 1843, died in 1922.

Martin Anderson (1868-1942), the eldest son, married Eva Mauch, whose parents
came to America in 1880 and, after homesteading in the Freeman area, came to
live in the Java area. Eva was a sister to Mrs. Jacob (Margaretha) Haux. To them
were born: Edwin, Caroline (Carl) Larson, Raymond and Norman. Mother Eva passed
away in 1957.

Edwin, the eldest son, married Anna Holman, daughter of Engebret and Marin
(Noer) Holman, who immigrated to America from Norway, settling in Bristol, where
they entered the merchandising business.

(Photo:) Anna and Eddi Anderson

Eddie and his family lived on farms in the southern end of Walworth County until
1942, when they purchased the Garret Noble farm SW of Java. They lived here
until 1948, when they moved to Java. Eddie died July 1977 and Anna died Sept.
1979.

Being a baseball enthusiast for many years, Eddie's favorite sports story was of
an incident that occurred the first year he was a baseball pitcher on the Java
team: He was facing his former team mates from Lowry, who were very familiar
with his style, and treated them to a no hit ballgame.

The six children of Eddie and Anna, who all graduated from Java High School are:
James (deceased) married Margaret Job; Earl, married Maryl Wiedebusch; Sylvia,
married Edwin Karst; Mary Anne, married Wilbur Krause, is divorced and lives in
Washington, D.C.; Roger, married Karen Buechler; and Judith, married Gary
Helstrom

        Emanuel and Mary (Schnaible) Baer
Emanuel Baer was born in South Russia Dec. 28, 1880, the son of John and
Margaretha (Herman) Baer. The family immigrated to America in 1893, first to
Freeman and later coming to Walworth County, where his father filed on land and
became quite an extensive farmer, keeping considerable livestock so there was
always plenty of work for the family. Later Emanuel also filed on land south of
the first homestead, a few miles east of Lowry. Emanuel received part of his
education in Russia and what schooling he could in the neighborhood school. He
herded sheep at an early age for the fabulous salary of $8 a month. He clerked
for H.A. Mason in his store in Bowdle, and later worked in Bauer and Stoller
store in Java; later, still, for John Hofmeyer in Java.

(Photo:) Emanuel and Mary Baer

On July 25, 1905, he was united in marriage to Mary Schnaible of Java. Mary was
born Feb. 15, 1887 in Freeman to Karl and Elizabeth (Oster) Schnaible. The
family came to Walworth County in 1889 and lived on a farm three miles north of
Java. Her father raised large herds of sheep and cattle and farmed extensively.
She attended rural school. After marriage they set up housekeeping in Java.

In 1906, Emanuel was elected Register of Deeds for Walworth County and reelected
in 1908, living in Bangor during these terms. When the courthouse was moved to
Selby, the family also moved there. At the expiration of his second term, the
family moved to Java and he engaged in the real estate and insurance business
for four years when he again returned to the office of Register of Deeds. After
another four years he sought, and was elected to, the office of Clerk of Courts
and he continued in this office up to his death in 1925. The family moved to
Selby in 1915.

Emanuel was a life-long member of the Lutheran Church, serving as trustee and
treasurer; member of the Commercial Club, Golf club, and of the early Java band
and men's quartet.

Seven children were born, two of whom passed away in infancy. The children are
Clara, Erna, Leander, Herbert, and Emanuel Dale.

Clara married Alfred Bastian (deceased). They had one daughter Joyce (Herb)
McClellan, and three grandchildren.

Erna married Edward Zabel (deceased) and they had three children. Verne married
Marcella Brockel and they have four children. Arlys married Harold Brown
(deceased) and they had two sons. Sharon married Wayne Wolff (deceased) and they
had two children.

Leander married Martha Birkland at Poplar, MT, and was manager of the Poplar
Montana Elevator Company. He passed away, at the age of 46, in June 1958. One
daughter Virginia Lee was born in 1936 and married Al Hasselbach. They had three
children

Herbert married Hilda Schanzenbach and they had three children. Dennis passed
away Jan. 1972 at the age of 29, leaving his wife Alvina and two children.
Sandra Sue married Terry Stulken and they had two daughters. Judith Marie
married Cecil Ringgenberg. Herbie was affiliated with the Selby Equity Union
Exchange when he passed away in Dec. 1974.

Emanuel (Buster) (deceased) married Maxine Weber at Lincoln, NE. They had four
daughters. Karen married Barry Ellenbecker and they had one daughter; Tanya;
Melanie; and Rogene.

All three sons, Lee, Herb, and Buster, entered the service of their country in
World War II.

While in the courthouse, Emanuel was the adviser and friend of all who came to
him, and was helpful to the German-speaking people in the early 20's.

Mrs. Emanuel Baer passed away in July 1976.

        Gottlieb and Katherina (Haux) Bamesberger
Gottlieb Bamesberger was one of the many pioneers of the Java territory in its
early beginning. Gottlieb was born July 16, 1880, in Hoffnungstal, South Russia,
the son of Christian and Katherina (Orman) Bamesberger. He remained with his
parents until he was 15 years old and then took up a woodworking trade. This was
Gottlieb's work for the next five years until he became 20 years of age and was
military draft age for the Russian army. He decided to come to America and,
within a short time, he and another friend, George Reuer, got passes to come to
America in Apr. 1900. They left Bremerhaven Port, sailed on the ship F. Missler,
and landed in Port New York. They then traveled by train to Bowdle, which was
the end of the Milwaukee Railroad. He worked as a farmhand for one year.

(Photo:) Gottlieb and Katherina Bamesberger

The town of Java was being planned and in a short time many families and
laborers moved to the prospective new town. Gottlieb liked the idea of doing
carpentry work, so decided to come to Java and immediately went to work. He was
in the carpenter trade for about 9 years.

In his early years in Java, he became one of the baseball players for the Java
baseball team and was one of their pitchers. This was one of Gottlieb's favorite
sports and he always found time to play. In 1904, in the Java Lutheran Church,
Rev. Kirchdoerfer performed the marriage uniting Gottlieb and Katherine Haux.

They lived in Java until 1910 when they decided to go into farming, so Gottlieb
and his wife and two children, Christ and Lydia, moved to the Lowry area. They
endured many hardships, but always remarked that America was the "Land of
Opportunity."

        Jakob and Katharina (Stahlicker) Bauder Sr.
The quest for land motivated the immigration of the Bauder family from
Pfullingen, Germany to the Black Sea region. Catherine the Great, the German
princess from Anhalt-Zerbst, issued a manifesto in 1763; however, it was not
until 1804, when her grandson, Alexander I, granted a second manifesto offering
increased privileges, that a mass migration took place.

The privileges, in short, were: (1) Free exercise of religion. (2) Exemption
from land taxes for 10-30 years, and 10 years in the cities. (3) Interest-free
loans for the purchase of equipment. (4) Exemption from military service "for
unlimited time." (5) Self-administration of the community and the school. (6)
Free apportionment by the Crown of 30-80 desseatine of land to each family. [A
desseatine is equivalent to 2.7 acres]

(Photo:) Jakob and Katharina Bauder, Sr.

These colonists were to be models in agriculture. Not everyone qualified. The
requirements were: A letter of good character; cash or property amounting to 300
gulden; and they were to be married men.

Jakob Bauder, Sr., was born Dec. 17, 1844, in the Colony of Hoffnungstal, South
Russia. He was the son of Johann Christoph Bauder, a stocking weaver, who
migrated from Pfullingen, Germany in 1817 to Russia.

Not much is known of Jakob's early childhood. The census registration, District
of Odessa, for the year of 1858 shows that he and two brothers and a sister were
living with their grandfather, Josef Bauder.

Katharina Stahlicker and Jakob Bauder were married on Nov. 5, 1867, in the
village of Hoffnungstal, meaning "hope." Katharina was born Nov. 1, 1847, in
Guldendorf, the daughter of Peter Stahlicker. They moved to Neu-Gluckstal, where
their 9 children were born.

In the colonies where they lived, the family was not permitted to divide the
land. Therefore, the father was often compelled to purchase land from the
Russians, at high prices, for his sons. So it wasn't surprising that the
colonists once more planned to emigrate when the news came from America that the
railroad companies needed them to build the railroads, and that there was land
for homesteading. The decision to leave was made. The first step was to obtain a
passport, which was written in three languages: Russian, French, and German.

According to plan, eight families left the village in Feb. 1894, making an
impressive group. They were: Mr. and Mrs. Fredrich C. Perman; his parents Mr.
and Mrs. Christoph Perman and two sons; and the Adam Mertz, Jacob Mertz, John
Feickert, Adam Schlecht, Gottlieb Oster, and Jakob Bauder families.

After crossing the border into Prussia, they proceeded to Berlin, where they had
to undergo vaccination, as well as have their baggage put through a steaming
process to sterilize it. After these preliminaries, they went on to Bremen,
Germany, where they boarded the big ship on Mar. 8, and began the new experience
of crossing the ocean.

After arriving in New York, the group boarded a train for Chicago and, after a
long trip, during which they were sidetracked over Easter Sunday in a Canadian
city, they reached their destination and then came west to Freeman. Here they
spent a week visiting relatives and purchasing horses, wagons, and other
necessary farm equipment which they shipped on to Bowdle. On Apr. 5, the group
of eight families, accompanied by the Jacob Doerr family who had been living at
Freeman about two years, while waiting the arrival of the group, came to Bowdle.
From here on they scattered, filing on homesteads in Walworth County, McPherson
County, and near Monago, ND.

The Bauders lived on the farm south of their son-in-law, Fred C. Perman, in
Glenn Township, Walworth County. During those early years, church services were
held in the country school about a mile west of their home. The church was a
branch of the American Lutheran Church of Java. They retired to Lowry and their
son, Jacob, Jr., remained on the farm. Jacob, Jr., later sold the farm and moved
to McLaughlin.

Jakob, Sr. died in Lowry on Apr. 21, 1919, and Katharina on Feb. 23, 1927 in
Bowdle.

Their children were: Katherina (1868-1940), m. Jacob Doerr 1891; Christianna
(1870-1952), m. Adam Schlect Feb. 2, 1892; Rosina (1874-1959), m. Fredrich C.
Perman Jan. 16, 1894; Elizabeth (1876-1963), m. Henry Sonnenfeld Jan 24, 1896;
Carolina (1878-1971), m. Christian Miller May 29, 1897; Dorothea (1881-1959), m.
Andreas Lutz 1898; Mary (1884-1957), m. Christ Schilling Jan. 1902; Christina
(1886-1954), m. Wilhelm Schilling Mar. 13, 1906; Jacob (1890-1937), m. Caroline
Mertz Jan. 11, 1916.

        John and Christina (Buckenberger) Bauer Sr.
Hon. John Bauer, Sr., of Java, represented his district in the state legislature
and was prominent in public affairs. He was also an important factor in the
commercial life of his community as he was engaged in merchandising and the
success, which he gained, was doubly creditable in that he was a self-made man.
He was born in Russia on Nov. 29, 1855, a son of Frederich and Mary (Hager)
Bauer, both natives of Russia, who lived their entire lives in that country. His
paternal grandfather, George Bauer, was a native of Wurttemberg, Germany, and
moved to Russia in 1807. The maternal grandfather also moved from Wurttemberg to
Russia.

John Bauer was raised and educated in his native land and continued to reside
there until 1884, when he came to America and made his way to Yankton,  where he
remained for a short time. In 1886 he took up a homestead in Campbell County,
and after two years, moved to McPherson County, where he acquired title to land,
on which he lived until 1909. In that year he moved to Java where he was engaged
in merchandising in partnership with his two sons, Fred and John.

Mr. Bauer was married Sept. 14, 1880, in Russia, to Christina Buckenberger. They
were the parents of 10 children: Maggie, Katherine, Fred, John, Eveline,
Ottilie, Ida, Martha and Hertha, twins, and Huldah.

Mr. and Mrs. Bauer were members of the German Reformed Church. Mr. Bauer served
on the school board for several years and as an assessor for two terms. In 1904
he was honored by election to the state legislature. He took great interest in
the development of SD and was willing to sacrifice personal interest to the
general welfare.

        John Bauer Jr.
John Bauer was born Jan. 17, 1888, on a farm in Campbell County, where his
parents had homesteaded. Later his dad bought a farm one mile SE of Eureka,
where he grew up and attended grade school. In 1900 he was put in charge of the
farm and his dad went to Java and started the first store, in partnership with
Hoff and Stoller. The store was named Bauer, Hoff and Stoller. The post office
was also housed in this store for a few years. Later the farm was rented out and
the family moved to Java.

In 1908, John went west and filed claim on a homestead near White Butte, but
remained there only a year before he returned to Java. John, his dad, and
brother Fred, bought the Hoff and Stoller partnership and named the store Bauer
and Sons.

(Photos:) John Bauer and Lydia Bauer

On Apr. 20, 1912, John married Lillian Heerwald and to this couple two children
were born: Duane, born Jan. 23, 1914, married Dagney Nelson. Irene, born Aug.
30, 1913, married Leonard Rickard.

After the death of his wife, he married Lydia Fiechtner on Dec. 9, 1919. Lydia
Fiechtner was born Jan. 26, 1902 on a farm three miles east of Java, where she
grew up and attended grade school for four years.

John and Lydia had four children: LaVerne, born May 22, 1922, served his country
in World War II as a Flight Officer and Pilot of a B-29, and was killed in China
in 1944; Marjorie (Herbert) Buechler was born Jan. 28, 1924 and was a teacher;
Della (Julian) Ackerman was born June 19, 1926 and taught school at Wessington
Springs, Webster, and Herreid, and at Oceanside, CA (deceased); Delores,
(Harvey) Teske, born Mar. 4, 1928, was employed at Daytons in Minneapolis, MN,
and taught school for one year before she was married. She passed away in 1968
in Aberdeen.

John was owner and operator of Bauer and Sons until 1960 when he passed away.
Lydia remained living in Java until her death. She was a life-long member of St.
Paul Lutheran Church, became a member of the Ladies Aid in 1945, (now WELCA) and
served four years as local group chairman of India Missions and two years as
group chairman. She was appointed District Group Chairman of ND and SD, where
she served for two years, and also was a charter member of the Church Altar
Guild, which was organized in 1960.

        Fred G. and Rosina (Fiechtner) Bauman
Friederich Bauman, Sr., and Christiana Fiechtner were born in Hoffnungstal,
Kherson, in 1869, where they went to school and were married in 1891. They came
to Walworth County when their son, Fred G., was a year old. Fred's parents took
up a 160-acre homestead and started to farm. They raised four boys and two
girls. Fred G., the oldest, was born in Russia in 1892.

(Photo:) Fred G. Bauman Family. Standing: Martin, Clarence, Harold. Seated: Fred
         G., Hilda, Rose, and Rosina (Fiechtner)

Rosina Fiechtner was born in Hoffnungstal, Kherson, Ukraine in 1902, was
baptized and went to school there. She was the daughter of Matheis and Katherina
(Brosze) Fiechtner. When she was 10 years old, in 1912, she came to the U.S.
with her parents and family to Lehr, ND. In 1919 she came to Walworth County
with her family and settled on a farm 10 miles south of Java.

On Oct. 3, 1920, Fred and Rosina were married, by Rev. Kirchdoerfer, in their
Hoffnungstal Church. They bought land five miles east of Java, built a home, and
started to farm. They were blessed with five children: Martin F., Clarence,
Harold, Rose Emma,  and Hilda.

Clarence and Marilyn Bauman, living in Bismarck, ND since 1954, were both born
on their parents' farms east of Java, where they were reared and attended the
one-room Alamo Country School. Clarence is the son of Fred and Rosina Bauman;
Marilyn is the daughter of William and Mathilda Sauer. Their farms were five and
six miles east of Java. Both families were members of St. Paul Lutheran Church
in Java, where Clarence and Marilyn were confirmed. As a young boy, Clarence
remembers the Hoffnungstal Gemeinde Kirche five miles NE of Java, where the
Bauman family attended church. Rev. George Kirchdoerfer was Minister during that
time and until 1930, when the congregation joined with the church in Java.

In 1945 Clarence entered the Navy and served aboard ships in the Pacific
Theatre, being discharged in Oct. 1947, then came back to work on the family
farm. Clarence and Marilyn were married at St. Paul Lutheran Church on July 16,
1950 and resided on the family farm until 1952 when a farm injury forced them to
discontinue farming. During the year of 1953 they spent some time in OR, WA, and
ID. They moved to Aberdeen, where Clarence attended college until June 1954,
when they moved to Bismarck, ND, where Clarence became associated with Capital
Commercial College and also had his own accounting and income tax business.

Marilyn became manager of the Drumstick Cafe, located in Bismarck, which she
purchased in Apr. 1973. Marilyn and Clarence operated the cafe until May 1995,
and then sold it to a former employee. After selling the cafe, Marilyn started
her own business dealing in collectibles, dolls, and antiques, while Clarence
continues with tax preparation and accounting. "Marilyn's Keepsake," the name of
her business enterprise, occupies a booth in a local Bismarck antique shop.

Clarence and Marilyn have four children, all now living in Bismarck. The oldest,
Steven, born Feb. 28, 1951; Clyde, born Aug. 15, 1953; William, born June 8,
1960; and Amy, born June 11, 1966.

Clarence, born Feb. 18, 1923, and Marilyn, born Sept. 30, 1932, are active
members of the "Germans from Russia Heritage Society" headquartered in Bismarck.
They have helped organize new chapters in ND and SD. Clarence served the society
as Vice President from 1984 to 1987 and President from 1988 until 1991.

"Preserving our Heritage" should always remain a priority with the friendly
peoples of Java, who need to be ever mindful that it was our ancestors with the
courage to seek freedom and a new life from Russia to America 100 years ago.
Their stories, this Centennial Book, with the history of our Pioneers, along
with the town of Java and community and all the memories contained therein shall
remain forever in this "Centennial Book." -- By Clarence Bauman

Rosina (Rose) Emma  was born Jan. 16, 1927, in rural Java. She attended the
Alamo Country School, graduated from Java High School in 1944, attended summer
school at NSTC in Aberdeen, and taught at the Alamo School for three years.

Wilmer Stiegelmeier was born Sept. 19, 1920, in rural Java, the son of Jacob B.
and Katherina (Berg) Stiegelmeier. He attended the Edison Country School,
graduated from Selby High School in 1939 and from SDSC at Brookings in 1943 with
a BS degree in Economics. He was inducted into the Army in 1943 and was
stationed at Camp Howes and Camp Walters, TX; Ft. Robinson at Little Rock, AR;
Camp Blanding in FL; and Ft. Jackson in SC. Wilmer was honorably discharged in
1946 and began his life's occupation of farming and ranching.

Wilmer married Rose Oct. 5, 1947, in the St. Paul Lutheran Church of Java. They
farmed five miles SW of Selby.

Rose was a 4-H club leader for 14 years, served a number of years in offices of
the American Lutheran Church Women (ALCW), and for the Germans from Russia
Heritage Society. Rose is a 51-year member of the Handy Homemakers Extension
Club.

Wilmer is a member of the American Legion. He and Rose are members of the
Germans from Russia Heritage Society and St. John Lutheran Church in Selby. They
have been blessed with four children and 12 grandchildren. Diana and her
husband, Paul Moxness, each have a doctoral degree in Musical Arts and teach at
Mankato State University at Mankato, MN. Dawn and her husband Jim Anderson work
in various Christian organizations in Minneapolis, MN as Pastor and leaders.
Their children are Aaron, Michael, Nathan, and Amy. Mark and his wife Becky are
farming SW of Selby. Their children are Adam, David, Joshua, Hannah, Levi, and
Elissa. Paul and his wife Marie live in Bismarck, ND where he works for A.G.
Edwards and Sons, Inc. Their daughters are Karen and Shaina.

Hilda married Otto Schaefer. "On Nov. 11, 1928, I was born on the family farm
four and one-half miles east of Java, the youngest of five children of
Friederich (Fred) and Rosina (Fiechtner) Bauman, and here is where I grew up.

I attended Alamo School in the country for the first eight grades, just as did
brothers Martin, Clarence, Harold, and sister Rosina. The year I was in the
first grade (1934-1935), all five of us were attending Alamo School at the same
time, with Martin being in the eighth grade. Our mother packed the lunch for all
of us in one empty syrup gallon bucket!

In the fall of 1942, I started my high school years along with sister Rosina,
who was a junior at that time, and brother Harold, who was a senior. The first
two years, during the severe winter months when country roads were impassable,
Rosina and I stayed in the Girls' Dormitory in Java, and brother Harold stayed
in the sleeping quarters made up for the boys in the high school building.

After graduation, I attended college at NSU in Aberdeen (then called Northern
State Teachers College), and I taught in rural schools and later in the primary
grades of city schools in Hosmer, Java, Mobridge, and Roscoe.

On Dec. 20, 1953, I was married to Otto Schaefer of Mobridge, the son of Emanual
and Caroline Schaefer, and we were blessed with two daughters. Merry Beth was
born Dec. 18, 1956, in Mobridge, and Elizabeth Ann was born June 30, 1963, in
Minneapolis, MN, where we were living at the time.

While we were in Minneapolis, I worked in the Minneapolis School System for many
years, and in the Sears Roebuck Department store, and I also had my own business
as a personal seamstress, working out of our home.

Otto was Sales Manager of the Maytag Company in Bloomington, MN, and in 1977 we
were transferred to Dallas, TX for a year and a half. While living in Dallas I
was employed as the Data Supervisor for a large oil-consulting firm.

In the fall of 1978, Otto was promoted to Northwest US District Manager with the
Maytag Company and we located to Lodi, CA, where I have resided ever since. Ten
months after moving to Lodi, Otto passed away on Aug. 16, 1979. I had just
recently gotten the position as secretary to the Manager of Central Bank at
Stockton, CA and daughter Elizabeth Ann was a sophomore at Lodi High School, so
here is where we stayed.

Over the years I have been an executive secretary for a distribution corporation
in Stockton, organist for Emanuel Lutheran Church in Lodi, a member of the
Stockton Chorale and the Lodi Symphony Orchestra Chorus.

Daughter Merry Beth was married to Rick Starkey on Oct. 31, 1981, and they have
one daughter Johna Marie. They own Ft. Niangua River Resort near Lebanon, MO.
Daughter Elizabeth Ann was married to Tony Petrali on Dec. 20, 1986, and they
have three children, Gregory Adam, Julianna Rose, and Joseph Franco. They live
in Elk Grove, CA."--By Hilda Bauman Schaefer

Fred G. Bauman was an active community leader, being an officer in the rural
telephone company, the school board, and he was County Assessor for many years,
a rural mail carrier, as well as the organist for the Lutheran church. He also
directed the German Choir at St. Paul Lutheran Church for many years, played the
church organ every Sunday and for special occasions for 40 years or more.

Rosina (Fiechtner) Bauman helped on the farm, taught Sunday school, boarded
schoolteachers, helped with Ladies Aid projects, and for many years sang soprano
with the German Church Choir.

After the Baumans retired from the farm in 1951, they built a two-bedroom home
in Java less than two blocks south of the church, which was a very central part
of their lives, and continued to serve in various capacities whenever and
wherever needed. When Mr. Bauman's health forced him to give up playing the
church organ, his son, Martin, stepped in for a number of years, and then his
daughter Hilda took over the duties as organist for several years.

During 1981-82, when the "Germans from Russia Heritage Society" was forming a
chapter in the Java-Eureka areas, Rosina Bauman was an encouraging and
enthusiastic supporter. She helped recruit members, organize meetings, and
donate financially to the chapter, which was given the name "Die Deutsche
Freiheit" Chapter. The German heritage was always very dear and important in the
lives of the Bauman family. In later years Fred and Rosina spent several winter
months at Mesa, AZ. The dry climate was beneficial to Fred's health.

Fred G. Bauman passed away on Nov. 20, 1988, having reached the age of 96 years
and five days, and was interred in the St. Paul Lutheran Church Cemetery at
Java. "Java was their home, No other place would do. From pioneer to modern
times, the Dear Lord helped them through."

        Gerhardt and Hildegarde (Jakober) Bauman
Gerhardt Bauman was born July 7, 1909, in Walworth County five miles east of
Java, the youngest child of Friederich and Christiana (Fiechtner) Bauman. His
brothers were Friederich (Fred G.), Jacob and Gustave, and his sisters were Emma
and Christina. His mother died in Apr. 1923.

Gerhardt spent his time on the farm until the age of 15 years, when his father
moved to Bowdle. Gerhardt continued his education there, and did some musical
entertaining on the accordion. He was also involved in business until 1929 when
he sold his service station and went into the music orchestra business on a
larger scale.

He married Hildegarde Jakober of Hosmer on Mar. 8, 1936. This same year the
couple started the Gamble Store in Hosmer, which they operated for 62 years.

Gerhardt was involved in community affairs, served on the church board and the
town board. He was a member of the Civic Club for 36 years, served on the
volunteer Fire Department, was a member of the Sportsmans Club, and was a member
of the Edmunds County Zoning Committee. During all this time he kept up his
musical career on the accordion. He was inducted into the SD Music Hall of Fame.

Gerhardt died May 22, 1992, at the age of 82 years.

Hildegarde was born Dec. 28, 1912, at Hosmer to Christian and Margaretha
(Vilhauer) Jakober. She attended grade school and graduated from Hosmer High
School.

The Baumans were blessed with two children: son, Paul, is a Doctor of Divinity
serving as Pastor at St. Andrew Lutheran Church in Sheboygan, WI. He is married
to Rae Blevins and they are blessed with three children: Michael, Kathryn, and
Andrew. Daughter Margaret is married to David Trefz. They live at Webster, where
she has been teaching vocal music in the school for 29 years. She also has a
major in English. They are blessed with three children: Rachael, Matthew, and
Maryann.

        George and Christina (Mauch) Bender Sr.
George and Christina (Mauch) Bender immigrated to the U.S. from southern Russia
near Odessa, after his brother wrote telling them about favorable conditions in
SD.

They left their homeland with five children: Bill, George, Christina (Brodehl),
Katherine (Lange) and Jacob.

Seven more children blessed their home: Adam (his twin sister Eve died at
birth), Emily, Emanuel (they both died as teenagers), Theophil, who died Nov.
19, 1918 while serving with the Allied Forces, Freda (Opheim) and Ben completed
the family.

(Photo:) Geore Bender, Sr. Family. Back: William, Christine, Katherine. Center:
         George, Sr., and Christina (Mauch). Front: George M. and Jacob M.

The family purchased land in Campbell County NW of Java. As the finances were
available, more land was purchased. Sometimes wheat was the medium of exchange.
A large farm home was built along with barns and other outbuildings. They raised
wheat and sheep until the family moved to Java in 1908.

Their son, George, married Rose Jenson and lived on the farm.

George Sr. suffered a stroke in 1919 but recovered completely, only to be struck
down with liver cancer at age 65.

Christina Bender lived in Java many years after the death of her husband and
then made her home with their youngest son, Ben. She died at the age of 93. She,
her husband, and five of their children are buried in the family cemetery east
of their farm in Campbell County.

Some of the land, including the site of the original farm, remains in the
family. Mark Rubida is the fifth generation to farm the land.

Jacob and Elizabeth (Hauck) Bender
Jacob Bender was born in the village of Worms, Odessa District, South Russia, on
Aug. 5, 1863, where he received his education and grew to young manhood.

In 1886, he made the decision to leave his native land of Russia and came to
America, coming to Yankton, Dakota Territory. He settled there for about two
years, living with relatives. In 1888, he came north to homestead in Campbell
County, filing on the SE quarter of Section 6, Township 125, Range 74.

Mr. Bender hired out breaking horses and made his mark as an accomplished
horseman. He made trips to Montana, selecting and purchasing wild broncos,
bringing them back to Eureka, where he broke them and in turn, they were sold to
area farmers.

On Nov. 24, 1890, Jacob was married to Elizabeth Hauck, the daughter of Mr. and
Mrs. Karl Hauck. Mrs. Bender was born Oct. 3, 1865, in South Russia, and came to
the U.S. with her parents in the spring of 1890. The young couple made their
home on the E1/2 of Section 8, Township 125, Range 74, in Campbell County, which
remained their home until they retired from farming. On Sept. 22, 1921, Mr. and
Mrs. Bender moved into a fine new residence in Java, where they resided until
their passing, Mrs. Bender on Dec. 19, 1934, and Mr. Bender on Aug. 18,1939.

(Photo:) Jacob and Elizabeth Bender

Mr. and Mrs. Bender were the parents of 10 children: Elizabeth (Gottlieb)
Zeller, Emily (Jacob B.) Aman, Emma (Edward F.) Biel, August, Lydia (Fred)
Stoebner, Carl (died in infancy), Albert, Henry, Martha (Henry H.) Wolff, and
Edward (died at age 4).

        Russell and MaeNerva (Hoffman) Bender
Russell Bender, son of Albert and Susie (Flamang) Bender, is the grandson of

homesteaded north of Java in Campbell County.

The Albert Bender family lived on a farm in Campbell County until 1943, when

Russell and MaeNerva continue to reside in Java.

        Henry and Martha (Jundt) Bender
Henry Bender was born in southeastern Campbell County on Oct. 6, 1903, to Jacob
and Elizabeth (Hauck) Bender, on the family farm in the area once known as the
Sutley Community. He attended rural school and after his schooling farmed on the
home place. In Sept. of 1921, his parents moved to the town of Java, where they
had erected a new residence.

Henry was married to Alvina Schlaht in Mound City on Feb. 9, 1928. They made
their home on the Bender farm. To this union one son, LeRoy, was born. In the
fall of 1944 Henry held a livestock and machinery auction at his farm and later
in that year purchased a residence in Java. In the autumn of 1945 Henry and his
son moved to Java.

On Aug. 20, 1946, Henry was married at Eureka to Martha Jundt of Eureka. Martha
was born Jan. 12, 1902, to Johann and Katharina (Schumacher) Jundt on the family
farm east of Eureka in McPherson County. In 1920, her parents moved to Eureka
and she accompanied them and made her home with them. Prior to her marriage to
Henry she was employed in the food service department at the Eureka Hospital.

While on the farm, Henry raised registered Shorthorn cattle, both beef and
dairy.

(Photo:) Martha and Henry Bender

After moving to Java Henry continued grain farming until 1967 when he retired.
During his retirement he enjoyed gardening and fishing. In their retirement
years Martha was a member of the Java Garden Club, a sewing club, and was active
in several organizations of their church.

Mr. and Mrs. Bender both passed away at Bismarck, ND, Henry on Sept. 4, 1912,
and Martha on Feb. 4, 1984. They are both buried in the St. Paul Lutheran
Cemetery at Java.

        LeRoy and Hilda (Kurle) Bender
LeRoy was born July 13, 1929, at Eureka to Henry and Alvina (Schlaht) Bender. He
attended the Bender School in Campbell County near their farm home. He attended

1947.

On Nov. 29, 1950, he enlisted in the Air Force and trained to be a B-36 Bomber
Mechanic. He received an honorable discharge in  Sept. 1954. After coming home,

In Dec. 1974, LeRoy was hired to be the Java City Auditor, and then hired again
in 1987.

        Larry and Bette (Sannes) Bermel
The Larry Bermel family moved to Java in May of 1993 from Fertile, MN after
purchasing the Selby Honey Company from Chuck and Sandy Hanson. The family
consists of Larry, Bette, Heath, and Reid.

Larry was born in Randolph, NE to Don and Darlene Bermel in 1950. Elementary
education was obtained at District 22, a one-room schoolhouse six miles from
town. Larry attended high school in Randolph, graduating in 1968. Two days after
graduation he bought a $9, one-way bus ticket to Fertile, MN to work with his
uncle in the bee business. In the fall of 1968 through Jan. 1970, he attended
the University of NE at Lincoln. He volunteered for the draft, spending two
years in the Army, one of which was in Vietnam. After the Army, he went back to
working bees for his uncle.

Larry and Bette met in the spring of 1972 and were married in Jan. 1974, leaving
soon after to go to TX to work bees. Bette was born to Art and Norma Sannes in
Crookston, MN. She attended school in Fertile. After graduating she attended
Moorhead Tech. in Moorhead, MN. Bette played piano and taught Sunday School at
Crookston Lutheran Church. In May 1976 Heath, the first of two sons, was born.
Bette drove school bus for the school district. Larry had quit the bee business
and was hauling chicken feed and gravel for a local trucker. In the spring of
1976 the family moved to the country on a five-acre homestead.

Reid was born in Feb. 1978, the same time the Bermels were building a new home.
Larry was then managing a 2000-acre farm. In 1986, Larry quit farming and
started driving school bus with Bette. A year later he was the manager of the
busses. In 1988, Larry went back to the bee business and has continued it ever
since. Since coming to SD the Bermels have wintered their bees in Mississippi
and continue to live in Java.

Heath attended schools in MN and in TX in the winters of his 7th and 8th grades.
Heath was active in 4-H and from age 9, showed pigs and cattle until he
graduated in 1994. In the 9th grade, Heath started FFA and showed pigs,
attending numerous judging contests. Also while in FFA and 4-H he took up
welding and master woodworking. Heath also was in electricity and bees in 4-H,
he also took small engines and went to the State Fair with many of his projects.

Reid attended school in MN and TX. He was also in 4-H and enjoyed woodworking
and showed pigs and cattle. Reid was in the performing arts and went to the
State 4-H and many other competitions. He played basketball from the 7th through
12th grades and went to State his junior year, where the team took 2nd place.
Reid attends NSU in Aberdeen and comes home in the summers to help with the
bees. He plans to become a chiropractor.

        Fred and Rosina (Hausauer) Bieber
Fred Bieber was born in Gluckstal, South Russia, Dec. 20, 1879, and came to
America in 1884 with his parents, Johann Jacob and Christiana (Ritter) Bieber.
They settled near Eureka. In 1902, he married Rosina Hausauer who was born Dec.
22, 1882, at Nesselrode, South Russia, a daughter of Karl and Johanna (Klein)
Hausauer. She came to America with her parents in 1885, and also had settled in
the Eureka area. After their marriage, they lived two years with his parents on
their homestead five miles NE of Eureka. During this time, a son was born who
died in infancy. Later a daughter Emilie (Ferdinand) Walz was born. They moved
SE of Java on the Parker farm, which is now owned by the Dale Bieber family.
Later they moved to the James Kane place. During this time, a son, Arthur, was
born. He died at the age of nearly three years. After two years they bought the
Bieber homestead and moved back to Eureka.

(Photo:) Fred Bieber Family. Back: Arthur, Emilie, Ottilie, Magdalena, Herbert.
         Front: Gustave, Mr. and Mrs. Bieber, Albert

The children born here were: Gustave W. (who married Marie Schreter), Magdalene
(Henry E.) Schreter, who lives in Java, and Ottilie (Oscar) Schnaible.

He sold his farm in Eureka and in the spring of 1911,  bought a farm seven miles
south of Java, where the three younger children were born. Arthur F. married
Letha Haskell; Herbert F. married Henrietta Sayler (deceased) and remarried to
Mrs. Pauline Maule; and Albert J.

Mr. Bieber was actively associated with church and community affairs. He was one
of the original stockholders of the Java Equity Exchange, and served as a
director of that organization for many years. He was also a board member of Ryan
School District.

They retired and moved to Java in Oct. 1939. On Apr. 28, 1949, Mr. Bieber passed
away and Mrs. Bieber passed away Oct. 12, 1974.

        Gustave and Marie (Schreter) Bieber
Gustave Bieber was born Mar. 1, 1907, at Eureka to Friedrich and Rosina
(Hausauer) Bieber. At the age of four, his parents moved to a farm seven miles
south of Java. He attended grade school at the West Ryan School but being the
eldest son, he attended very little school because he had to help with the farm
work.

(Photo:) Gust and Marie Bieber

Marie Schreter was born to Henry J. and Marie (Baer) Schreter on Mar. 10, 1909.
She attended country school at Surrey School near Lowry.

Gust and Marie were married on Easter Monday, Apr. 1, 1929, at Lowry Lutheran
Church. The ceremony was not to interfere with the spring work and they couldn't
get married during Lent, so they were married on April Fool's Day - Easter
Monday. Purchasing the Henry Leidholt farm, 11 miles south of Java, they lived
there until 1974, at which time they retired and moved to Mobridge.

Soon following their marriage came the "Dirty Thirties" where nothing grew but
thistles. The first years on the farm were difficult. They picked cow chips,
corncobs, and old wood for fuel to heat the house. Only two rooms of the house
were heated to conserve energy. During this time, they battled many hardships:
dust storms, Mormon crickets, grasshoppers, and armyworms. Thistles were used
for feed for the cattle, and when available, molasses was poured over it to make
it more enticing. Due to a lack of feed, the government killed some of their
cattle and their horses were moved to ND for the winter.

Perseverance saw Gust and Marie through those difficult years and as times got
better Gust continued to farm and raise fattened prime cattle. Transported first
by train and later by truck, the cattle were shipped to packing plants in Sioux
City, IA, Huron, Fargo, ND, and St. Paul, MN.

Gust was known to be very particular as his cattle were fed and fattened to
exact measures, and his cornrows were planted perfectly straight. During calving
season, he helped his neighbors, expecting nothing in return. Such acts of
kindness earned him the nickname "Doc." He also serviced and dug many of his
neighbors' wells.

Marie (Mary, to her family) had many interests of her own. In her spare moments
she enjoyed working in her yard, where she created ornately decorated gardens
filled with beautiful flowers, shrubs, and trees. She continues to display her
talent of flower arranging in local garden shows, where she has collected
various awards and ribbons for her creativity.

Another interest of Mary's was her embroidery work and quilting. She shared this
hobby with her many friends, and with their help she quilted bedspreads for each
of her three daughters and her 10 grandchildren.

Gust and Mary enjoyed attending cattle and horse sales. Together they both
enjoyed riding horse and in their later years, were active in the Senior Center
in Mobridge. Some of the clubs they enjoyed over the years were the following:
Saddle Club, Garden Club, Extension Club (Home Arts and Fair View), WELCA,
Square Dance Club, and the Moose Lodge. Gust also served on the West Ryan School
board. They were members of the Trinity Lutheran Church.

They raised three daughters. Lorraine married Floyd Biel and they lived north of
Java. Shirley married Adrian Kast and their home is in Haynes, ND, and Pam and
her husband, Ray Reiss, are currently living on the home place.

They have 10 grandchildren and 13 great-grandchildren. Gust passed away on Sept.
4, 1995.

        Fred C. and Lila (Weisgram) Bieber
Fred C. Bieber was born Jan. 20,1914, on the family farm in Walworth County,
south of Java. His parents, Johann and Elisabeth Bieber, had come to this
country with their parents as small children, from Gluckstal, Russia, and lived
in the Eureka area. After they were married, they homesteaded south of Java
where they reared their 11 children.

(Photo:) Lila and Fred C. Bieber

Fred's mother Elisabeth, born Dec. 30, 1872, died in 1930. His father born on
Nov. 14, 1869, died in 1932.

Fred married Lila Weisgram on Mar. 3, 1935. Her parents were Emma (Bauman) and
Anton Weisgram. Lila's mother was born Feb. 8, 1895, and died Aug. 5, 1981.
Anton was born June 10, 1890, and died Dec. 16, 1966.

After their marriage, Fred and Lila moved on the old Schwartz brothers' farm
three-and-a-half miles SE of Java, where their three sons were born. Harry
Gerhardt was born June 14, 1937. He married Virginia Voller and is now a retired
Data Processing Administrator of Job Service in Bismarck, ND. They have two
children. Debra is married to Rick Stoppler and has two daughters, Alissa and

graduated from a college at Salt Lake City, UT. Ross J. was born June 23, 1950.
He graduated from Denver Automotive and Diesel College, and farms and ranches on
the home place.

The early years were rough. Those were the drought years with no crops, dust
storms, and low prices, but Fred and Lila considered themselves pretty lucky.
Everyone else was having the same difficulties.

Fred and Lila retired and moved to Java in Aug. of 1982. They celebrated their
50th Wedding Anniversary in 1995. They spent their winters in Phoenix, AZ. Fred
passed away Oct. 25, 1988.

        Jacob C. and Eva (Perman) Bieber
Jacob C. and Eva (Perman) Bieber were born, raised, and attended schools on
farms about 10 miles south and SE of Java. Jacob was born in 1896 and Eva Perman
in 1900. They were married Dec. 31, 1918, and settled on a farm 10 miles south
and one-quarter mile east of Java, where they farmed and raised cattle. Their 10
children were all born while they lived on the farm and all were members of St.
Paul Lutheran Church in Java.

The first years of their married life were rough going as they had very few of
the conveniences that we have today. Cow chips, corncobs, and old wood were used
for fuel, as coal was expensive and few families could afford it.

Then came the "Dirty Thirties" starting about 1933 through 1936. The Biebers
were fortunate for not having any of their cattle shot on orders of the
government, as many had, because of lack of feed. They bought and shipped in hay
from out of the state and later rented pasture in the Conde area and SE of
Gettysburg.

(Photo:) Jacob C. and Eva Bieber

They, with the help of the family, milked 25-30 cows, which supplied the food
and the clothing for the family. There were no gardens because of the drought.
The dust would blow so hard the sky would be dark, obstructing the sunlight.
Lights would have to be burned during the day. The harvest wasn't much as there
were about as many thistles as stalks of grain in a bundle, and grasshoppers
were thick, taking what little grain there was left. In 1936 many horses and
some humans contacted encephalitis (sleeping sickness) in SD. In the summer of
1937 an outbreak of Anthrax took 11 of the best milk cows and other cattle.

A happier highlight of the "Thirties" was a trip to the Worlds Fair in Chicago,
late in 1933.

In 1945 the Jacob C. Biebers retired and moved to Gettysburg where they bought a
home.

Their 10 children were: Martha, married Jacob Heier; Rueben (deceased), married
Irene Schneider; Ellora, married Jack Patterson; Alma, married Alvin Heier;
Meta, married Vern Overgaard; Duane; Venoye, married Duane Hughes; Jerome;
Henrietta, married Wm. Wright; and Kenneth.

Jan. 6, 1967 was a day to celebrate! Irene married Arthur Fiedler, born Feb. 24,
1911, the fourth of seven children born to Martin and Marie (Pleinis) Fiedler.
Art and Irene made their home in Java and Art continued to farm at his home
place five miles north of Java until his retirement.

Art and Irene have many happy memories of their 11 grandchildren, one deceased
granddaughter and 9 great grandchildren. Anyone is welcome to stop in to say
hello and will probably be offered a piece of Irene's famous kuchen, or may find
Art uptown playing cards.

(Photo:) Irene (Schneider-Bieber) and Art Fiedler

        Rev. Martin Bieber
Martin was born Sept. 24, 1904, near Java, to John and Elizabeth (Schmaucher)
Bieber. He grew up wanting to be a farmer, but several incidents led him to
become a Minister. He was ordained on June 14, 1931, at St. Paul Lutheran Church
at Bowdle. He started his preaching in IL. He celebrated his 50 years of
ministry in 1954. He continued to be Vacancy Pastor in a lot of area churches
for many years.

He married Irma Knoppe on Aug. 8, 1931. She was the daughter of Martin's
professor when he attended college at Wartburg College in IL.

Irma and Martin had four children. Gerald, Stanley (died in infancy), Murriel,
and Beverly. Irma died Feb. 22,1963. Martin married Hilda Hoss on Nov. 17, 1969.
They lived in Hecla where they operated a motel and in 1979, they moved to
Ellendale, ND. Martin collected antiques and rocks over the years.

Hilda died Apr. 4,1989 and Martin died Mar. 6,1990.

Hilda's daughters are Donna Barton of Ellendale, ND and Florence Noess of Java.

        Christoph and Karolina (Keller) Biel
Christoph Biel was born Jan. 7, 1877, at Golgalofore, South Russia. In 1894 he
came to America with his parents and settled in the Sutley Community, north of
Java.

Karolina Keller came to America in 1880 with her parents and they settled in the
Campbell County area. On Dec. 11, 1900, she was married to Christoph Biel. They
resided on a farm in the Sutley Community until 1929 when they bought a home in
Java to live a retired life.

(Photo:) Christoph and Karolina Biel

Four children were born, who were: Bertha, married Jacob Kary; Theodore C. Biel,
married Martha Zimmerman; Fred C. Biel, married Dorothy Huber; and Leo Biel,
married Ella Wolff.

On Nov. 11, 1938, Christ Biel suffered a stroke, later followed by a serious
stroke in 1947. He never regained his health completely and passed away in Dec.
1948. Mrs. Biel passed away in Jan. 1952.

        Theodore C. (Ted) Biel Family
Theodore C. "Ted" Biel was born Oct. 23, 1903, to Christoph and Caroline
(Keller) Biel on a farm eight miles north of Java, where he attended school and
grew up.

Martha Zimmerman was born May 17,1906, to Jacob and Caroline (Grenz) Zimmerman

moved to his farm five miles north of where Ted Biel grew up.

(Photo:) Martha and Ted C. Biel

Ted and Martha were married Sept. 19,1926, at the Reformed Church north of Java.
They made their home on a farm 10 and one-half miles NW of Java. They had three
children: Virgil, born Aug. 19, 1927, married Delila Aman. They also made their
home on this farm and had three children, Dick, Todd, and Roberta; Priscilla,
born Dec. 6, 1930, married Ervin Mueller of south of Java, where they still live

Construction from 1959 to 1968, when he became self-employed as a painter for
many years. Martha did baby-sitting and also baked homemade bread, kuchen, and
rolls for people.

Ted had been ill for four months with Crohn's disease and passed away Nov. 27,
1979 at the Mobridge Community Hospital. Martha later suffered a stroke and
entered the Good Samaritan Center at Selby, where she lived for 121/2 years. She
passed away Dec. 26, 1994.

Their grandson, Todd, and his family are now living on the farm.

        Fredrick and Barbara (Ottmar) Biel
Fredrick Biel was born at Odessa, South Russia on Feb. 1, 1869. He grew to young
manhood and was united in marriage to Barbara Ottmar, who was born Jan. 21,
1870, and also lived in Odessa.

The Fredrick Biel family left their home in Annental, Russia and undertook the
long journey to come to the U.S. One daughter Louisa, and Fredrick's parents
accompanied them to the U.S. They landed in New York Port in Apr. 1894, then
traveled by train to Roscoe and later went to Eureka, where they joined other
relatives and friends.

The Biel family homesteaded seven miles north of Java in Campbell County, where
they farmed numerous years and also raised a family of two sons and three
daughters. Mrs. Floyd (Lorraine) Biel resides in the home and Leonard Starks,
son-in-law of Floyd and Lorraine, owns the homestead.

(Photo:) Fredrick Biel Family

The children of Fredrick and Barbara were Louisa (Christ) Rau; Edward F.; Emma
(John) Kary; Theodore F.; and Lydia (Carl) Rueb.

Time progressed and Fredrick bought another farm, which was known as the Ted F.
Biel farm. He farmed until 1919 when he bought a home in Java.

        Edward F. and Emma (Bender) Biel
Edward F. Biel was born Oct. 6, 1896, and attended Sutley School. He helped his
parents on the farm and later was drafted into service in 1917 during World War
I. Edward served three months in battlefield at France, and served in the Army
of Occupation in Germany for six months. He returned home and was discharged
June 7, 1919. Edward married Emma Bender in Oct. 1919, and they took over his
father's homestead. They farmed for many years, raised a family of four
children, who were educated in the Java Public School.

(Photo:) Ed F. Biel Family. Floyd, Emma, Elmer, Ed F., Deloris and Kenneth

married, and one daughter, Jill. Elmer passed away July 1999. Deloris (deceased)
was married to Albert Schreter and had one daughter, Pam. Floyd married Lorraine
Bieber, had six children (See Family History). Rev. Kenneth married Caroline
Levi, had two sons and two daughters (See Family History).

        Floyd and Lorraine (Bieber) Biel
Floyd Biel was born Nov. 20, 1923, at Campbell County to Edward F. and Emma

Floyd and Lorraine bought the farm and continued to farm at the Biel Homestead.

        Rev. Kenneth and Caroline (Levi) Biel by Rev. Kenneth Biel
The farm on which I was born is seven miles north of Java. My grandfather,
Friederich Biel homesteaded this farm, when he and his wife came to the Java
area from South Russia in 1893.

(Photo:) Rev. Kenneth and Caroline Biel

My father, Edward F. Biel, was born the following year. He grew up on this farm,
returning to farm there following his term of service in World War I. He married
Emma Bender and to this union four children were born: Elmer, DeLores, Floyd,
and myself.

In 1942 I graduated from Java High School. In the fall of the same year I
enrolled at a college in Yankton, which is now defunct. There I received my
Bachelor of Arts degree and also in Theology. I was ordained at Eureka in the
Congregational Church. Later the denomination was named "The United Church of
Christ."

My first pastorate was in a small town in rural MI, named AuGres. In Aug. of
that year, 1947, I married Caroline Levi who lived at Zeeland, ND and had
attended Yankton College.

We have been blessed with two daughters and two sons. We have lived in several
states and for the past 22 years have resided in Littleton, CO. Until 1991, I
was pastor of Columbine United Church, and since then have been serving as
Pastor Emeritas and serving as Pastor of Visitation.

        Theodore (Ted) F. and Albina (Mayer) Biel
Theodore F. (Ted) Biel, son of Frederick and Barbara Ottmar Biel, was born Apr.

Shirley, and Ronald in the Sutley Community 9 miles north of Java. They worked
very hard and had tough times through the Thirties, living in a sod house until
1945 when they built a one and a half story home.
