        David Blinderman Family
Before Java was established in 1900, a number of small stores and combination
post offices were established in Walworth and Campbell counties. The Blinderman
family, David and John, were homesteaders but also merchants, or peddlers, who
opened stores in their homes. David Blinderman homesteaded the west half of NE
quarter and the south half of NW quarter of Sec. 26 in Blessing Township,
Campbell County, in 1898. For a short time, he and Albert Lang operated a store,
creamery, and post office in Sutley. The creamery was located just north of the
present Leslie Rau farm. In 1900 John sold the land to Simon Eisenbeisz and took
up a claim in Highland District, the north half of NW quarter in Sec. 13. His
brother David had filed a claim in 1898 on 40 acres of the SW quarter of NW
quarter and the west half of NW quarter of Sec. 24 in Highland District. Here he
established the Spiry post office and store on the Spiry homestead north of the
present site of Java. David Blinderman was one of the first merchants in Java,
coming here and establishing a successful mercantile business when the city was
in its infancy. In Dec. 1905 John and his family moved to Zeeland, ND.

On Jan. 5, 1906, a notice appeared in the Java Herald that Edna Blinderman, wife
of David, died at 2 o'clock at the age of 39 years, 7 months and 20 days. The
cause of death was from a complication of diseases. Her body was shipped to
Minneapolis where she was to be buried under the Jewish Rites in the Jewish
cemetery of that city. Dr. Sigmund Rosenthal accompanied the remains.

Edna was born in Grossliebental, South Russia, where she and David were married.
In 1886 they came to the U.S. to New York City, then to MN, and to SD. Mrs.
Blinderman was highly respected. In the Mar. 16, 1907 Java Herald it was
reported that David Blinderman was happily married to Miss Anna Gershin. She was
a sister to L.A. Gershin, who operated a store in Java, until 1941, when he sold
the business to Emanuel Kary. A baby boy was born to the David Blindermans in
1913, and died a few minutes after birth. On May 20, 1926, David's son, Myron
graduated from Java High School. On May 26, 1927, Frieda, born Mar. 10, 1910 in
Minneapolis to David, graduated from Java High School. In the June issue of the
Java Herald it was published that a former Java pioneer businessman had
succumbed after a prolonged illness. Mr. and Mrs. Blinderman left Java several
years before to make their home in Minneapolis as both of them had begun failing
in health and wished to be near their children. He was survived by his wife, who
had taken faithful care of him during his long illness, one son, Myron of
Minneapolis, a daughter, Frieda, Mrs. Leonard M. Besner, of Red Wing, MN, and a
grandson, besides a host of other relatives and friends.

        The Boehler Family
Born in 1766 in Soufflenheim, Hagenau District, Alsace, Peter Boehler and his
wife Anna Barbara immigrated to Rohrbach, Beresan District, Odessa, South Russia
in 1809 with their children Philipp, Johann Peter, David and their daughter
Margaretha (Heinrich) Hofmann.

Their son, David Boehler, was born in 1802 and married Elisabetha Keller (b.
Nov. 1, 1800 in Alsace). Their children were Peter; Barbara (Johannes) Moser;
Philipp; Margaretha; Christina (Johannes) Moser, who had married her sister's
widower; Eva Maria; David; and Friedrich, who married Margaretha Kerner.

Philipp Boehler, son of David and Elisabetha (Keller) Boehler, was born in 1829
in Rohrbach. He married Elisabetha Bachmann and they had Philipp, David, Jacob,
Ludwig, Johannes, Sophia, Friedrich and Gottlieb. Elisabetha Bachmann Boehler
died about 1875 and Philipp married Katharina Ehly nee Schock on May 30, 1875 at
Neu-Freudental, South Russia. Philipp and Katharina had Margaretha, Peter, and
Maria Eva.

Ludwig Boehler, son of Philipp and Elisabetha (Bachmann) Boehler, was born Aug.
18, 1855 in Rohrbach. He married Christina Elser in 1884 and they immigrated to
the U.S., arriving at New York Port on Nov. 1886. They filed claims in Blessing
Township, Range75W Section 27 and 34. Christina Elser Boehler died in 1903.
Ludwig married Christina Oswald Kunz on Aug. 20, 1903 in Mound City at the
Congregational Church. They were members of the Odessa Reformed Church in Sutley
Community. In 1910 Ludwig retired from active farming and he and his wife moved
to Java. Christina Oswald Kunz Boehler passed away in May 1925 and Ludwig died
Sept. 24, 1926. Ludwig had an adopted daughter, Emma, who married Jacob Gill of
Eureka; Christina Oswald Kunz Boehler had two children, Wilhelm and Christine
Kunz. Ludwig and  Christina are buried in the Reformed Cemetery NW of Java.

Sophia Boehler, daughter of Philipp and Elisabetha (Bachmann) Boehler, was born
Oct. 18, 1863 in Rohrbach. She married John Ochsner (b. May 27, 1855) of Worms.
Sophia came to the U.S. with John's family in 1885, while he completed his
service in the Russian Army. He joined her at Sutton, NE in 1886, where they
settled until 1898, when they moved three miles west of Zeeland in Emmons
County, ND. John died Mar. 1921 and in 1924, Sophia married Anton Allmendinger
of Selby. Some time after Anton died, Sophia moved to Zeeland, where she passed
away on Jan. 19, 1948. She is buried in the Friedens Reformed-Heinz Cemetery.
Sophia and John had Elizabeth (Karl) Hofmann, Theophiel, Gustav, Leah (Ludwig)
Pfeifer, Olinda (Edwin) Boschee, Sarah (John) Ellwein, and John.

Friedrich Boehler, son of Philipp and Elisabetha (Bachmann) Boehler, was born
Aug. 16, 1870 in Rohrbach. He served in the Russian Army from 1892 to 1896 and
married Clara Albrecht on Feb. 3, 1898. They emigrated to the U.S. from Bremen,
Germany to New York on the Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse, arriving on Mar. 15, 1901.
They filed claim in Township 127N Range 78W Section 2 in Campbell County. They
settled on a farm near Herreid, later moved south of Pollock, where they lived
until 1940 when Fred retired and they moved into Pollock. Fred and Clara had
Friedrich, Jr., who was born in Russia, Emilia (Gust) Ochsner, Arthur, and
Edward. Friedrich (Frederick) passed away Mar. 26, 1952.

Gottlieb Boehler, Sr., was born to Philipp and Elisabetha (Bachmann) Boehler on
Dec. 4, 1872 in Rohrbach. He immigrated to the U.S. in 1892. (See Family
History)

Peter Boehler, son of Philipp and Katharina (Schock) Boehler, was born Sept. 19,
1885. He immigrated to the U.S. in Apr. 1905, arriving in New York. He married
Karolina Lindemann (b. 1886) in 1906. They came to the Java/Selby area, then
moved to Isabel, SD. Peter and Karolina had Peter, Karoline "Carrie" (Oscar)
Liebelt, Philip, John, and Erma (Charles) Fergerson. Son Philip was born Feb. 7,
1910 in Java and married Lottie Ellwein in Nov. 1937. They moved to Timber Lake,
where Philip passed away June 15, 1989. Son John was born May 21, 1912 at Selby.
He married Helen Stadel in Timber Lake, and died July 13, 1996 in Mobridge.

Maria Eva, daughter of Philipp and Katharina (Schock) Boehler, married Konrad
Ackermann on Nov. 10, 1902. They immigrated to the U.S. in 1913, arriving in
Java on May 18. Konrad died June 4, 1927 and was buried in the Lutheran
Cemetery. On Sept. 17, 1927, "Mary" (Boehler) Ackermann married Fred Spiry, who
had lost his wife in 1924. Fred Spiry passed away Mar. 1931 and Maria Eva (Mary)
married Anton Hertz of Fairfax on Feb. 4, 1932.

        Gottlieb and Eva (Wolf) Boehler
At the age of 19 years, Gottlieb Boehler traveled from Rohrbach, Russia to
Bremen, Germany, where he boarded a ship to the U.S. He arrived at Baltimore
Port in June 1892, and made his way to Sutton, NE, where his sister Sophia
(John) Ochsner and her family had settled. Gottlieb stayed with the Ochsners,
working as a wheelwright, which was a traditional family occupation from as far
back as the days in Alsace. After he reached the legal age to file on land,
Gottlieb came to the Sutley Community in Campbell County, where he stayed with
his brother Ludwig. He filed his claim, which he later sold to Ludwig and filed
claim in Walworth County, in the Highland District, just a short distance west
of the village that would become the Town of Java. In May of 1895, Gottlieb
filed his Declaration of Intent in Campbell County.

Gottlieb Boehler, Sr., was born Dec. 4, 1872 in Rohrbach to Philipp and
Elisabetha (Bachmann) Boehler. After living in the Java area for a time, he
married Eva Wolf. At the time of their marriage, Gottlieb's address was Rosella.

Eva Wolf was born in Bergdorf, South Russia on Apr. 4, 1873 to Friedrich (Fred),
Sr., and Elisabetha (Maeule) Wolf. Fred Wolf, Sr., was born Oct. 9, 1842 in
Bergdorf to George and Elisabetha (Amann) Wolf. Elisabetha Maeule was born Nov.
16, 1843 in Bergdorf to Martin Michael and Katharina (Mittleider) Maeule. Fred
and Elisabetha were married on Oct. 13, 1864 in Kassel. After Elisabetha
(Maeule) Wolf died in 1880, Friedrich (Fred) married Eva Kurle on Jan. 20, 1881
at Bergdorf. Fred and Eva (Kurle) Wolf and their family immigrated to the U.S.,
Java, in 1890, where they settled on land NW of the town.

Gottlieb and Eva farmed and ranched nearly all of their lives. They had built a
new house in the town of Java, presently owned by Violet (Buckenberger) Goetz,
but had lost it during the Depression years while they struggled, like nearly
everyone in the area, to hang on to their land. They moved back to the
farmhouse, built in 1905, where they remained for the rest of their lives.
Gottlieb passed away Apr. 25, 1949, at home. Eva stayed on the farm with her
sons, David and Emil, and passed away Dec. 7, 1955. Gottlieb and Eva are both
buried in the Lutheran Cemetery NW of Java.

(Photo:) Gottlieb Boehler Family

Gottlieb and Eva had 12 children, all born in rural Java with help from either
Mrs. Kundert, a midwife, or Dr. Rosenthal. Lidia, born Oct. 1901, died on Aug.
10, 1905. The other children of Gottlieb and Eva are:

Emma married John Schuh, Jr. on Apr. 20, 1913. She died Nov. 9, 1953 and John
died Aug. 8, 1965. They are both buried in the St. Paul Lutheran Cemetery, Java.
They had three children, who were: Ellsworth, Raymond and Loretta. Ellsworth
married Freida Frazier on June 21, 1939 and farmed NE of Java. Freida taught
school in the area, retiring from full time teaching in 1977. Ellsworth passed
away and Freida lives in Mobridge; Raymond married Luella Hochstatter and they
had three children; Loretta married Cornelius Schnaible and they also had three
children.

Linda was born in 1897 and graduated from Highland School District #16. She
married Fred Pregitzer. Fred was a carpenter and the Java school janitor for
many years; Linda painted houses, cleaned houses and was always there to help
whenever needed. Fred and Linda loved to fish. Linda passed away July 21, 1988
in Mena, AR, where she had been with their only child, daughter Virginia (Bill)
Medford. Linda is buried in the St. Paul Lutheran Cemetery, Java.

Elizabeth (Betty) was born in 1898 and graduated from Highland School District
#16. She worked in McLaughlin and then moved to Mobridge, where she was employed
at the Brown Palace Dining Room. She married Carrol Turner at Mobridge in Jan.
1926. They lived in IA until she moved to Indianapolis, where she worked with
their only son, Raymond, in his mail order business. Betty passed away July 7,
1978, and is buried in the St. Paul Lutheran Cemetery, Java.

Gottlieb George was born in 1900 and attended rural school. He married Irene
Butler and worked for the Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad Company, and
was a barber on the Atchison-Topeka-Santa Fe Railroad. In 1955 he purchased a
Barber Shop in Chicago, where he lived. Irene and George also owned a tavern in
Chicago, which she managed. He was a member of the Masonic Lodge. George passed
away Oct. 31, 1962 and was buried in the St. Paul Lutheran Cemetery, Java.

David was born in 1903 and attended school in Java. He was a member of the Moose
Lodge of Aberdeen, Farmers Union, and a past director of the Java Equity
Exchange. He remained single and farmed the homestead with his brother Emil.
Dave lost an arm in 1940, in a farm accident, yet he continued as the machinery
mechanic. Dave loved to dance and visit. He passed away on June 9, 1982 and is
buried in the St. Paul Lutheran Cemetery, Java.

Ludwig (Louis) G. was born in 1905 and graduated from Java High School in 1925.
He was a clarinetist and played with Lawrence Welk in the Hotsie-Totsie Band.
Louis was Auditor for the City of Java. He married Evelyn Lutz, daughter of
Eugene and Ida Lutz of Eureka. They moved to Montana, where Louis died on Apr.
24, 1969. Louis and Evelyn had one son, Lyle, who lives in Ft. Collins, CO.

Lydia (Lieta) was born in 1906 and attended rural school for the first five
grades before attending Java Public School. She was a member of the Glee Club,
and was on the girls' basketball team for four years, on which she was captain
in the year the team was undefeated. Lieta graduated from Java High School in
1927 and went to NSC. She was a teacher in the Hawthorn and other rural schools
in Walworth and Campbell counties. Lieta married Wm. F. "Red" Haux in 1933. They
lived in Mound City, where he was a barber until they moved to Aberdeen, where
he operated the Sherman Barber Shop. He was a member of Yelduz Shrine, the
Shrine patrol and the Elks. Their house in Aberdeen is the present location of
Brides and Belles, owned by Paul and Gayle Jacobs, Jr., and Sandy Jacobs,
formerly of Java. Red and Lieta moved to Frederick, where he ran a Barber Shop
and was a member of the Masonic Lodge. Wm. F. "Red" Haux died in 1956. Lieta
married Judge Harold Calkins and lived in WI until his death, when she returned
to Java. Lieta passed away on Nov. 12, 1989 and is buried in the St. Paul
Lutheran Cemetery, Java. Lieta and Red had one daughter, Marlene (Carl) Craig of
Grand Junction, CO.

Jacob (Jake/Jack) Roy was born in 1909. He attended Java Public School,
graduating in 1929. Jack was a member of the boys' basketball team for four
years. He joined the CCC with his brother Emil, and married Elizabeth "Toots"
Noble in 1934. Jack served in the Army in the Philippines during World War II.
He married Dorothy and lived in Bremerton, WA, where he was employed. Their
children were Michael J., Jacquelyne Rose, and Georgia Lynn, all of Washington.

Emil was born 1911, attended school in Java and graduated from Java High School
in 1932. Emil, also known as "Jew," graduated from Twin City Barber College in
Minneapolis. He enjoyed and played basketball on the Independent team and was a
member of the Java baseball team. In 1934 he moved to the Black Hills, living
and working near Hill City until 1936, then moved to Toppenish, WA with his
brothers Dave, Jack and Rueben, where he was employed. He joined the Army in
1941 and later was on active Army Reserve. Emil farmed the homestead with his
brother Dave and owned and operated a Barber Shop in Java. He was a member of
the Moose Lodge and Mobridge Country Club. Emil spent many winters in Las Vegas,
where he enjoyed his favorite sport of golf. He also enjoyed reading, learning,
and was known for his great sense of humor. Emil passed away at his home in Java
on Aug. 18, 1980 after a long battle with cancer.

Arthur was born 1913. He attended school in Java and graduated from Java High
School in 1933. He was a charter member of the "J" Club and was active in track.
Art married Maxine Riddle and they had one daughter, Bonnie Kaye. He joined the
Army during World War II, and was at Normandy. His second marriage was to Julia
Starkweather and they had two children, Quinton, who lives in OK and Linda. Art
bought, reconstructed, and sold several businesses, and was also in the cemetery
and monument business. Art passed away Aug. 3, 1973.

Leonard Rueben was born 1917 and attended the Java school, graduating in 1936.
He married Margaret Nies and they had two daughters, Jeanne and Kathy. (See
Family History)

        L. Rueben and Margaret (Nies) Boehler
Leonard Rueben Boehler was born July 23, 1917 on the Boehler homestead west of
Java. He attended the Java school, graduating in 1936. Right after graduation,
Rueben went to Toppenish, WA with his brothers and worked at a creamery. That
fall, all jobs died and no employment could be found. He moved to Bismark and
worked at the Patterson Hotel.

Margaret Louise Nies was born Nov. 2, 1919 to Peter L. and Ethel (Ryan) Nies in
Pierre. She graduated from Java High School in 1937 and moved to Wala Wala, WA,
where she worked as a housekeeper. She then took care of an invalid woman in
Reardon, WA. Alvin and Susie Spiry were in Reardon, also, and when they came
back home, Marge came along. She worked in Bismarck as a housekeeper for $3.50 a
week plus room and board.

Rueben and Margaret were married on Feb. 18, 1940, in Java. They lived in an
apartment at Wahl's house, which later was the home of Peter Schneider. Marge
recalls cooking on a kerosene two-burner stove in the hallway, and baking bread
in the oven that was placed on top of the stove. Marge and Rueben then moved to
Pullman, WA, where Rueben was Superintendent at the Muscovite Mine outside of
Deary, ID. Marge was a waitress at Pullman. They then moved to Moscow, ID, where
their first daughter, Jeanne, was born. Rueben worked for the Bureau of Mines as
a Jr. Mining Engineer for one year when he was called into the Navy in 1945 and
was stationed at Great Lakes. Marge and Jeanne lived in Chicago with Rueben's
brother George and his wife until Rueben received his honorable discharge and
the family returned to Java. Rueben was the Selective Service Clerk for Draft
Board #19 from 1947 until 1955, and helped his family on the farm west of Java.
Daughter Kathy was born in Mobridge.

Rueben is a charter member of the LaVern Bauer American Legion Post, #275 and
was a member of the Java Chamber of Commerce. Marge is a charter member of the
American Legion Auxiliary and of the Sew and So Extension Club.

In 1955, Rueben took a position with the U.S. Army National Guard in Mobridge
and the family moved to that town. When the National Guard unit of Mobridge was
activated in 1961, Rueben, known as "Sarge," Marge and Kathy moved to Louisiana,
where Kathy attended school in Leesville until they returned to Mobridge. Marge,
who received her training at the Alex Johnson Hotel in Rapid City, was a
waitress at the Embers Fireside, Silver Grill Cafe, the Arcade and Brown Palace
for over 20 years.

(Photo:) L.R. Boehler Family. Kathy, Rueben, Marge and Jeanne

Jeanne Marie, born Nov. 17, 1943 in Moscow, ID, attended Java Public School
through the first half of the 7th grade. She graduated from Mobridge High School
in 1961 and furthered her education in CA at LBCC, LBSC and UC Irvine. She was
married in Long Beach in 1966. Her husband's business transferred them to Kansas
City, where Jeanne taught at a Head Start school in the inner city, coached a
cheerleading team, and was involved with the Crosslines community service
organization. Transferred, again, to Chicago for one year and back to CA to
Marin County in the San Francisco area, where Ron continued his employment with
INA. Jeanne, an Accountant Auditor, also taught Yoga and Aerobics classes, was
an active member of the domestic abuse program Hot Line, a member of Kasai
Honorary Society and the Soroptimists. She was also politically active as a
chief negotiator, was on the Communications Advisory Council, and Affirmative
Action chair in Marin. She was published in 1980. Jeanne and Ron divorced in
1981 and Jeanne moved back to SD in 1983, when Rueben became ill. She married
Dennis Schneider on Feb. 17, 1984 at St. Paul Lutheran Church in Java. They
presently live and farm seven miles north of Java. (See Family History)

Kathy Louise was born July 3, 1950 in Mobridge. She was the first child entered
on the St. Paul Lutheran Church Nursery Roll. Kathy graduated from Mobridge High
School in 1968 and from Presentation College in Aberdeen. She was employed at
St. Luke's Hospital and later was Assistant Coordinator of the Alternative Care
program of Northeastern Mental Health Center. She married Wayne Godkin in 1969
in Aberdeen. They had one son, Cameron, born Jan. 8, 1973. Kathy and Wayne
divorced and Kathy and her son moved to Rapid City, where Kathy was Chronic Care
Manager at Dakota Psychiatry 16 years. She then was Clinical Director of Family
Planning for SD Public Health until 1997, when she moved to Mobridge to be
closer to her parents. Kathy is presently an RN at Beverly Health Care Systems
in Mobridge and is a Nurse Massage Therapist, Nationally Certified in
Therapeutic Massage and Bodywork. Her son Cameron lives and works in Sioux
Falls. He has a daughter MaKayla Marie.

Marge and Rueben moved back to Java in 1983 after Rueben's health failed. They
are members of St. Paul Lutheran Church. Both enjoy gardening, company and
travel.

        Lawrence and Velma (Sauer) Bonen
Lawrence E. Bonen, born Sept. 3, 1932, to Emil and Emma (Haberer) Bonen near
Hoven, was schooled at country schools near Hoven and Bowdle, entered the Army
in 1952, was discharged in 1954, and went to work for various farmers. In 1955
he went to work for Ruben Aldinger at Aldinger Hide and Fur. He married Velma J.
Sauer on Sept. 2, 1956, at St. Paul Lutheran Church at Java. Velma was born to
William and Mathilda (Rosin) Sauer on May 16, 1938 at the Sauer homestead five
and one-half miles east of Java, and attended the Alamo Country School for eight
years. She graduated from Java High School in 1956. After marriage, they moved
to Lead, where Lawrence was employed at the Homestake Gold Mine. While living in
Lead, three sons were born: Lance Kevin on June 1, 1957, David Craig on May 19,
1958, and Douglas Jay on May 26, 1961. The family moved to Hosmer in 1963, where
they owned a bar and grill. In 1979 they moved to Bowdle, where they both were
employed by Aldinger Hide and Fur. Ill health forced Lawrence to retire in 1988.
Velma continued working for another year, as bookkeeper, then dabbled in second-
hand and antiques. Larry and Velma still reside in Bowdle and enjoy flea
marketing, spending most of their summers in Rapid City, doing flea marketing
with their son, Doug.

Lance married Melody Peterson, has a daughter, Aliesha Lynn, and resides in
Hosmer.

David married Penny Aldinger. Their children are Craig David, Rhonda Lee, and
Mary Ann. They reside in Hosmer.

Douglas Jay married Dora Haar. Their children are Douglas Jay Jr. and Daniel
Ray. Dora died in a car accident near their home east of Java.

        Douglas J. Bonen
Douglas Bonen was born May 26, 1961, to Lawrence and Velma (Sauer) Bonen in
Deadwood. When he was two and one-half, the family moved to Hosmer, where Doug
attended school and graduated from Hosmer High School. After graduation, he
attended Springfield College for a short time and then returned to the area. He
married Dora Lynn Haar, daughter of Dewayne and Lila Haar, in Nov. of 1981.

They moved to Casper, WY, where Doug worked in the oil fields. Douglas Jay
Bonen, Jr. was born in Casper on Nov. 28, 1982. The family returned to Bowdle in
1983, where Doug worked at Aldinger Hide and Fur and Dora at the Bowdle Nursing
Home. Daniel Ray was born Feb. 14, 1985.

Doug and Dora then bought the Ellsworth Schuh home five miles east of Java and
enjoyed living in the country, where Dora loved the yard work and flowers.

Doug was employed at the Java elevator until 1993, after which, he became self-
employed in D.B. Furs, with his brother David. He does flea marketing in Rapid
City during the summer.

Dora died in a car accident in 1992. Doug and his sons still reside on the farm
east of Java, and Doug, Jr. and Daniel are in high school in Bowdle.

        Henry and Marie (Merkel) Buckenberger
Henry Buckenberger was born Aug. 9, 1878, in Menno and married Marie Merkel on
Feb. 25, 1900. She was born in Marienberg, South Russia on Dec. 13, 1873 and
came to America with her parents in 1899, residing in Campbell County.

They lived on a farm in Campbell County after their marriage until 1909, when
they moved to Java. They had 9 children, two of whom died in infancy.

Henry first operated a meat market. Later, he started a harness shop on the east
side of Main Street, beside the former Post Office. He sold this to Helm and
moved to what was the Lumber Yard. He operated the hardware store and harness
shop with his oldest son in 1922, located in what is now the grocery store. He
sold this to Baer of Bowdle and he and his son went across the river for one
year to break land. Coming back, he opened a shoe shop.

In 1936, his wife and son, Albert, died of food poisoning. Henry was a Rawleigh
salesman at that time. He then moved to Kennewick, WA. He returned several years
later and opened his shoe shop in the Lang building. He left again, returning
and setting up another shop in the Schock building. In 1945, he sold out and
moved to WA to live with his daughter. He passed away on Nov. 19, 1950, in
Eureka, shortly after moving into the rest home.

Henry and Marie's children were:

John A. was born Apr. 15, 1901 at Sutley. (See Family History)

Arthur R., born May 19, 1902 at Sutley, died 1972 at Kennewick, WA. He married
Mary Arbach in 1938. They had one son, Ronald.

(Photo:) Henry Buckenberger family and others in early Java Main Street scene

Edward F., born May 25, 1906 in Sutley, Mrried Pauline Teske. Later he was
married to Viola Rieger. They had two children.

Martin, born Dec. 7, 1907 at Sutley, married Frieda Naasz on Nov. 7, 1933. He
farmed with his brother John for several years in Campbell County. He retired
from the railroad in 1953. They had one son, LeRoy.

Albert, born Feb. 25, 1909, in Java, died June 18, 1936 of food poisoning. He
was a Java High School graduate and worked for the Milwaukee Railroad until his
death.

Alvina, born Sept. 26, 1912 in Java, was a Java High School graduate. She
married Alvin Martell of Kennewick, WA. They had one son, Jim.

Ben A., born Mar. 22, 1914 at Java, graduated from Java High School. He bought
the garage from Louie Helm, sold out and went into partnership with Herbert
Fiechtner, operating a recreation parlor in the Dave Blinderman store. In 1936
he married Hazel Nies, daughter of Pete and Ethel Nies of Java. Ben was in the
retail clothing store business for many years in CA, where he was also a partner
with his brother-in-law, George Nies, in a mobile home park in Palm Springs, CA.
Ben and Hazel had three children, Bob, Larry and Sharee. Hazel passed away Oct.
6, 1995 at Pebble Beach, CA, where they lived. Ben is now residing in San Diego
near his son, Larry, two of his grandchildren, and a great grandchild.

        John A. Buckenberger
John A. Buckenberger was born at Sutley on Apr. 15, 1901, to Henry and Marie
(Merkel) Buckenberger. He married Dorothy Wolff on Sept. 29, 1921. She passed
away in 1934. He married Ella Wolf on Feb. 14,1936.

(Photo:) Violet, Calvin, LaMoyle, John and Ella Buckenberger

There are three children. Calvin in Kennewick, WA, married Georgia Jones. They
have five children, Patricia, Mike, Terry, Bobby, and Veronica. Violet married
Oliver Goetz. They have two daughters, Carol and Jeanne. Husband Oliver passed
away Nov. 5, 1992. LaMoyle married Calvin Aman. They had seven children, Kathie,
Craig, Nancy, David, Cheryl, Patricia and Teresa, who passed away Nov. 9, 1969,
at the age of seven.

John farmed in Campbell County, worked with his father in the hardware store and
the harness shop. He worked for the Milwaukee Railroad and at Perman Implement.

Ella worked as a Nurses Aide in the Bowdle Nursing Home. She also took in
washing when REA came to the area.

John passed away Feb. 15, 1965. Ella passed away Jan. 1998.

        Michael and Magdaline (Herman) Buechler
Mr. and Mrs. Michael Buechler, nee Magdaline Herman, were married in Russia in
1878 and came to America in 1882. They came to the Java area and homesteaded on
a farm about 10 miles east of Java. They went through long hardships while
trying to raise a family of five children. In 1921 they bought a home in Bowdle
and retired. The children were: Katherine, who married Jacob Himmerich; Maggie
married Jacob Gross; and Jacob, John, and Henry.

In 1938 the Michael Buechlers celebrated their 60th Wedding Anniversary, in
Bowdle, with their children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren.

(Photo:) Michael and Magdaline Buechler

        The Campbell Family
In 1904 or early 1905, Wilbur E. Campbell, his wife Mae, and two daughters,
Verna and Eunice, in the company of his brother, Albert G. Campbell and family,
came to the Bowdle area from Denison, IA, to be near an older brother, Walter J.
Campbell and family, who operated a general store in Bowdle, and later in Selby.

Albert G. became a Methodist minister in the Black Hills region. Wilbur E.
farmed in the Bowdle, Java, and Selby areas until 1913, when the family moved to
Java, purchasing the Java Hotel business from the Zeller sisters. Later, Mae
Campbell purchased the Rosenthal building and continued the hotel in that
location.

(Photo:) The Campbell Family in 1914

Wilbur's activities included auto mechanics with Schlepp Garage, operation of
the Java Light Plant, the south rural mail route, and operating the separator
for John Wolff's threshing outfit each fall for about 20 years.

The Campbells were divorced in 1928. Wilbur remarried, moved to Memphis, NE,
where he died in Apr. 1933.

Mae married Dwight Hall in 1943, lived in Portland until his death. She returned
to Billings and died there in June 1957.

Verna married Arthur J. Stuart in 1921. They lived in Billings, MT until her
death in Dec. 1947.

Eunice married Orville L. Griggs in Dec. 1925. They moved to Billings in 1930.

        Oscar E. and Dorothy (Thomas) Carlson
Oscar E. Carlson was born to Hans O. and Elizabeth (Gimbel) Carlson on May 5,
1924, on the homestead south of Java. Simon Gimbel, Oscar's grandfather, founded
the homestead, in the early 1880's.

On Feb. 9, 1948, Oscar married Dorothy Thomas from Bowdle, who was born Apr. 25,
1925. Four children were born to Oscar and Dorothy.

Diane, born Nov. 23, 1948, lives by Canistota and is a 6th grade school teacher.
She married Michael Merrigan, born Feb. 2, 1949, from Canistota. He farms and is
very active in the Canistota Fire Department and the medical rescue unit, where
he is a Certified EMT. They have one son, Bartholomew, who was born June 2,
1984.

Dinah, born Aug. 23, 1950, lives by New Effington, SD and works part-time with
the Head Start program. She married Frank Konda Jr., who was born June 25, 1947,
from Marion. He is a high school science and chemistry teacher in Sisseton. They
have seven children. Travis, born Oct. 19, 1974, is a civil engineering student
at SDSU in Brookings. Daren, born Mar. 26, 1976, is a civil engineering student
at SDSU in Brookings. Loren, born Nov. 7, 1978, is a machine tool graduate of
Lake Area in Watertown. Alan was born Aug. 24, 1981. Kerry was born Mar. 26,
1984. Neal was born Mar. 15, 1986, and a daughter, Kama, was born May 18, 1991.

(Photo:) Oscar E. Carlson Family

Perry, born Nov. 18, 1956, lives in Aberdeen, where he presently works for
Cunningham Electric. He married Bonny Allbee, born Nov. 21, 1956, of Aberdeen.
Bonny is director of sales at Dakota Electric. Perry has one son, Zachary, born
July 20, 1978.

Dinal, born Jan. 1, 1967, lives by Garretson and is a part-time Certified Dental
Assistant in Sioux Falls. She married Bruce Carlson born Jan. 21, 1966 from
Garretson. He is a service technician at Eugene Beckman & Sons Implement in
Garretson. They have three children. A daughter, Krysta, was born Dec. 19, 1990;
Austin, born Sept. 4, 1993; and a son, Jaden, born June 21, 1998.

After graduating from Java High School in 1941, Oscar began farming and did a
lot of blacksmith work, which he learned on his own and from his father. He also
did much plumbing and heating work, whereas the name of his business became
Carlson Custom Blacksmith. He did a lot of work in the Selby and Java area.

In June 1988, Perry became a partner in the business with his dad. They
purchased an acreage and building from Ken Thorstenson in the Thorstenson
addition of Selby. On July 19, 1991, a railroad section house was purchased from
Harvest States and moved to the business site. An addition and improvements were
added for storage in 1992. The business was run from the Selby shop until Aug.
1997, when Perry moved to Aberdeen. Oscar, who continues to do excavating,
heating, and blacksmith work from the farm place, is still running Carlson
Custom Blacksmith, by Java.

All four of Oscar and Dorothy's children graduated from Java High School. Their
daughter, Dinal, was one of the graduates to end the era of Java High School in
1985.

        The Clement Family
The Clement family was among the early pioneers of Java, coming in 1903 when
they established the Java Herald, a two-page weekly newspaper printed one half
in German and the other half in English. Equipment was from the old Rising Sun
at the then county seat of Bangor.

Carl F. Clement was born May 14,1859, at Lockport, NY and was a graduate
minister in the Lutheran faith at Wartburg Seminary, Dubuque, IA in 1880 but his
love for the newspaper business led him to give up the ministry. He came to SD
from Napoleon, OH after he had operated a number of newspapers in that state and
also was a city superintendent of schools at Napoleon and Wapakoneta, OH. He
came to SD in 1902, where his family soon joined him.

Carl F. Clement, his wife Kate, and three children, Carl W., Freya and Fritz,
had spent the winter months at Canning, SD, where Mr. Clement taught a country
school. That summer Mr. Clement worked on a German newspaper in Eureka. He gave
a Fourth of July speech in German at a celebration in the new town of Java. At
that time, he was asked if he would start a newspaper there. Money was raised
and the first issue of the Java Herald made its appearance in Sept. of 1903.

A son-in-law, Hud C. Mains, published the Java Herald while Carl operated Der
Java Herold, the German version, which was a separate paper. In July 1908, Mr.
Mains went to Aberdeen and Carl continued publication of the Java Herald until
his death on Mar. 23, 1922. His son Fritz took over the publication, keeping the
business in the family.

Carl F. Clement also graduated from a law school and practiced law in addition
to operating newspapers in OH and SD. He was Java's first city attorney and
mayor, and later became states attorney for Walworth County for a number of
terms.

Mrs. Clement was born July 31, 1869 in Sidney, OH. She married Carl on Feb. 2,
1895. In addition to the three children mentioned above, another daughter,
Marguerite (Gretchen), was born in 1906, married M.C. Munson and died in 1999.
Two daughters by a previous marriage of Mr. Clement were Ella (Hud C.) Mains and
Laura (C.O.) Reed. Both lived in Java for a number of years, where Laura taught
elementary school. Both are now deceased. Freya, who passed away in 1923, also
was an elementary teacher in the Java schools. Mrs. Clement passed away in 1958
at Selby.

(Photos:) Carl F. Clement and Kate Clement

The Clements were active in civic affairs while living in Java. Father and son
Fritz took part in local activities, and Fritz was a member of the city council
for fourteen years. Carl F. Clement was a lover of music and organized many
musical groups during the early days of Java when most of the entertainment for
the area people came from local talent groups.

Carl W. Clement passed away in Feb. 1972 at Millbrae, CA, where he lived with
his wife Mildred (Hadley) and daughter Leilani.

(Photos:) Fritz Clement and Ida Clement

The Clement family continued to publish the Selby Record and Java Herald until
Dec. 31, 1983. Ida Clement died in Jan. 1982 and Fritz died in June 1993. Fritz
and Ida Clement were named to the SD Newspaper Hall of Fame in 1985, Fritz
having been in the newspaper business for over 60 years.

After James MacKay took over operation of the papers in 1984, Fritz divided his
time between Selby and Mesa, AZ.

Other members of the family include Bruce Clement, Selby, who continued to work
at the printing plant after the sale until 1987, when vision problems gradually
reduced his work time. He then joined his father in the trips to AZ for the
winter.

Bunny Clement Mead, with her husband Wendel, moved to Selby from Maryland in
1990. They also spend winters in Mesa, AZ. They have two daughters and four
grandchildren living in Maryland.

Mildred Moore and daughter Leilani reside in CA. Leilani Marshall has a son in
CA and a daughter in CO.

        James C. and Kezia (Young) Corson
James C. Corson was born in Shelby County, OH, on Sept. 23,1856, and Kezia Young
was born in the same county on Aug. 17,1862. They were married on Apr. 23, 1881.
The oldest child, Martha Alice, born in Shelby County, OH, on Jan. 11, 1883,
moved with her parents to Dakota Teritory in 1886.

The Corson family homesteaded on land two miles east of Java, where the first
sod house was built 14 years before the town of Java was started. They later
moved into Java and their home is now the Ed Allbee residence.

Thurman Corson built the first grain elevator on the Milwaukee Railroad. Corson
County was named after J.C. Corson, who also worked for the railroad, selling
lots in new towns as the railroad extended westward. Mr. Corson was also the
first landowner in the new town of Java. He and one of his brothers owned the
first threshing rig in Walworth County, an old Buffalo Pitts steam engine and a
Red River separator. Many long winters were spent moving from one farm to
another, threshing wheat that had been in stacks for months waiting for this
machine to arrive.

(Photo:) James, Alice, Grace, Merl and Kezia Corson

The rest of the children were born to the Corson family while they were living
in the Java area. Alice, Grace, and Merl were all educated in the Java school,
and Gerald spent four terms in the Java school, commuting from TX to SD. The
long cold winters caused an illness that forced them to move to a warmer climate
and, in 1910, a move was made to TX.

Alice married Gerrit Noble of Java, and one son, Leonard, was born Nov. 27,
1904. Gerrit passed away in 1938, and Alice in 1974.

Merl, born in Java on Feb. 23, 1887, married to Leafy Ruyon in 1907. Three years
later they moved to TX with his folks and raised a large family of 9 children,
of which four were burned to death in a fire that destroyed their home in 1925.
Leafy passed away in 1961 and Merl passed away in 1964, leaving five children
and a number of grandchildren.

Grace, born in the Java area on May 28,1888, married Arthur Johnson, who was an
engineer for the Milwaukee Railroad. He was killed in a train wreck in 1910.
They had one son, Howard, born in 1909, who married Alma Merkel in 1928. They
moved to TX where Howard passed away in 1964. They had one son, Jack. After
Arthur's death, Grace moved to TX, where she remarried. She died in 1972.

Gerald, born in Java on Mar. 8, 1903, married the former Alma Merkel Johnson.

James C. Corson died Apr. 12, 1938 at the age of 82 years, and his wife, Kezia,
died Apr. 21, 1949 at the age of 87 years. Both died in Houston, TX.

        Jacob and Katharine (Bauder) Doerr
Jacob Doerr was born Mar. 15, 1867, in Neu-Kassel, South Russia, son of George
Friedrich and Barbara Becker Dorr. Katharine Bauder was born Aug. 17, 1867, in
Neu-Gluckstal, daughter of Jacob and Katharine Stahlecker Bauder. Jacob and
Katharine Bauder Doerr were married on Nov. 26, 1891, in Kassel. They immigrated
to America about 1893 and had first lived in the Freeman area before moving to a
farm near Java. Katharine took sick so they had an auction sale and moved into
town.

Jacob and his brother Carl ran a saloon in Java from 1904 to 1908. The brothers,
known as the Doerr Bros., were also into raising cattle and hogs. In 1908, Jacob
sold his part of the business to his brother Carl and then moved his home out to
the farm where he took up farming, again. Carl purchased a bowling alley in
Selby, which he put into operation in Java. Carl became a Watkins salesman about
May of 1914 and left the Java area to work the Potter and Sully Counties.

Jacob and Katharine had 9 children who were: Jacob Frederick, born Nov. 1, 1892
in Freeman, died Oct. 31, 1967 at Bowdle. He married Rosina Buechler in 1916.
George, born Apr. 7,1895 in Java, died Mar. 17, 1961 in Tacoma, WA. He married
Elizabeth Merkel in 1921. Gottlieb, born Aug. 7, 1897 in Java, died Mar. 12,
1977 in Sioux Falls. He married Olga Anderson in 1947. Elizabeth born Aug. 17,
1899, died Oct. 11, 1958 in Bowdle. She married Jacob L. Merkel, Jr. in 1921.
Eva, born Jan. 26, 1902, died Feb. 15, 1991 in Bowdle. She married Garhard
Blumhardt in 1923. Christine, born Apr. 26, 1903, died Nov. 24, 1995 in Bowdle.
She married Lloyd "Stormy" Koch in 1932. Rosina, born June 16, 1906 in Java,
died Jan. 6, 1924. Albert, born Apr. 24, 1909, still living in Red Wing, MN. He
married Mary Wentz Dore in 1934. Caroline (Carolyn) Doerr, born Feb. 12, 1912 in
Java, died Jan. 4, 1989 in Red Wing, MN. She married Fransis Malloy, divorced;
married Harold Babberl in 1949.

(Photo:) Eva Blumhardt, George Doerr and Elizabeth Merkel

Jacob and Katharine moved to Bowdle in 1920, where Jacob built a house at 4076
9th Street. Jacob died on June 23, 1930, and Katharine on Oct. 10, 1940.

        Adam and Margaretha (Pfitzer) Eisenbeisz
The origin of the name Eisenbeisz is not certain. The first half of the name
"Eisen" means iron. The second half "Beisz" is a variation of the verb "to
bite." Speculation is that the first Eisenbeisz was a blacksmith who made
portions of bridles for horses' mouths (iron bite). Another thought is that this
name refers to the vise a blacksmith uses. Nonetheless, IRONBITE is quite a
name.

The first recorded name of Eisenbeisz appears in the Black Forrest area of
southwestern Germany. Three brothers are listed in the archives of the alpine
village of Freudenstadt, which is located SW of Stuttgart. The oldest, Hans
Eisenbeisz, was born in 1561, the second brother, Michael Eisenbeisz, was born
in 1570. Gidius Eisenbeisz, a third brother, was born in Reutin, as were his
older brothers. Gidius had one son, Simon Petrus Eisenbeisz. Most of the 10,000
Eisenbeisz's now living in the U.S. are descendants of Gidius.

(Photo:) Margaretha and Adam Eisenbeisz

History records that, in German lands in the late 1700's, conditions were ripe
for mass migrations of an impoverished oppressed people. This was all due to:
the many years of religious and governmental revolts, the Feudal system where
people could not own land, the nobles whose supremacy was entrenched in the
countryside, the peasant population - scattered, unprotected, just trying to
survive. Russia came to the rescue of many troubled German people. The Turks had
left the Ukraine territory in South Russia located by the Black Sea. This large
area was in need for many willing workers to come, settle, and build up this
land. In the late 1700's, Catherine the Great of Russia (a German-born bride who
had married the Russian Czar) issued proclamations inviting Germans to settle on
the southern steppes of Russia. The invitation read something like this: come
live in my country, no taxes, you won't have to serve in the army, free land,
run your own churches and schools, etc. The only stipulations are that you have
a skill or trade, a family, and  some money. Germans in the tens of thousands
chose to uproot and undertake lengthy, difficult journeys to an unknown foreign
frontier. About 30,000 of them accepted the offer of  Catherine the Great in the
1760's. Many more would follow during her grandson's rule (Alexander I).

In 1805, Bernhard Eisenbeisz (Adam's great-great grandfather and a descendant of
Simon Petrus Eisenbeisz) and his family emigrated from Dornhan, Germany to
Gluckstal/Odessa/Cherson in South Russia. Cherson is a huge area of land in the
Ukraine on the NW shore of the Black Sea. Later, Bernhard's descendants would
move to Hoffnungstal/Bessarabia.

Several generations would pass, as the Germans in Russia over a period of a
Century would establish villages, schools, and churches. They built an
agricultural center that became the 'bread basket' of the European world. By the
late 1800's the Germans comprised only 10 percent of the population but owned 90
percent of the land. Many Russians were working for the Germans as hired hands
and servants. In the late 1870's, the tide began to turn. Russians had been
complaining about having to serve in the army while the Germans did not, and the
Germans ran too many of the towns, churches, and schools. In time, the new
rulers of Russia began to change the laws. Courts began to rule against the
Germans in all decisions. Over time, things got worse and some Germans left
Russia. The final straw came when the Russia rulers forced Germans to start
serving in the Russian army. Thousands of Germans packed their belongings and
said good-bye.

In 1898 Adam, age 17, his brother and three sisters immigrated to Java with
their parents Christian and Rosina (Oster) Eisenbeisz. They settled NE of town
near friends and relatives from Hoffnungstal, where they resided for 11 years.

On Mar. 16, 1905, Adam married Margaretha Pfitzer at the Lutheran church in
Java. In 1908 they moved to Akaska, where he farmed for 11 years. In 1919 they
moved back to Java, and in the spring of 1920 Adam, and his two brothers-in-law,
Mathias and Julius Pfitzer, purchased a business from Carl Hepper, which became
known as Pfitzer and Eisenbeisz. In 1928 Adam purchased full interest and
operated a recreation parlor with his son, under the firm name of Adam
Eisenbeisz and Son. Failing health due to a threshing machine accident resulted
in Adam's early retirement in 1947.

Adam and Margaretha had four children. The only son, Arthur, married Rose
Stoecker; their daughters Katherine, married Fred Goetz; Martha never married;
and Margaret married Joe Mueller. All the children lived in Java and are now
deceased.

Joe and Margaret Mueller had one daughter, Madeline, who is now living in
Lancaster, CA with her daughter Tracy.

Arthur and Rose Eisenbeisz had two sons. Virgil, the oldest, married JoAnn Wolff
and they have three children: Deborah Tiff, who has a son, Justin; Douglas
married Roberta Biel. They have a son, Derek, and a daughter, Allison; and
Cheryl, who married Jason Lorenz. They have two sons, Brett and Aaron. Virgil's
entire family resides in Aberdeen.

Gene, the youngest son of Arthur and Rose, married Ann Engelhart. They live in
Aberdeen. Their two children, Khristine and Joel, live in Minneapolis, MN.

(Photo:) Rosie and Art Eisenbeisz

        Herman and Pearl Erbe
Our known Erbes came from Barchfield, Hesse-Cassel in east central Germany,
where many Erbe families lived. It seemed impossible for them to make a living
so our Erbe family immigrated to the U.S. in 1852. They went to Dane County, WI
and while there, one of the sons, John Erbe, my grandfather, met his wife to be,
Johanna Berger. They married and in 1883 moved to Walworth County to homestead
on free claim land. They built a shanty on land six miles west of Bowdle and
about eight miles SE of Java.

Herman and Pearl met right at the farm, where they lived for about 60 years. At
this time, 1909, Herman's brother, Howard, and his wife, Ethel, were farming
this farm, the homestead of their father John Erbe.

Later, Pearl moved with her family to WI; soon thereafter, Herman boarded the
train and visited her. There in WI they were married on Mar. 19, 1913. The next
day they returned to the farm near Bowdle to plant their crop.

(Photo:) Herman Erbe Family. Willard, Dorothy, Velma, Raleigh, Leonard, Marge,
         Pearl, and Herman

On Mar. 5, 1914, their first baby was born, a son, Leonard; then Raleigh in
1916, Willard in 1918, Velma in 1919, Dorothy in 1922, and last of all, Margie
in 1932.

In 1949 Herman and Pearl, Leonard, and Margie took a trip to the West coast to
visit relatives and friends. This was the only vacation they took during their
married life.

Herman's parents passed away in 1938 and 1939, and Pearl's parents in the
1950's. Herman and Pearl lost their daughter Velma in 1955.

Herman and Pearl were surprised on their 25th Anniversary when the Spring Lake
ladies put on a "mock wedding" for them at their home. They celebrated their
50th  at the Bowdle Legion Hall, their 60th  at the farm with friends arriving,
and their 62nd at the Bowdle Nursing Home where they lived, with family.

Their entertainment was visiting neighbors, Community Club, house dances. The
family was always included - no baby sitters in those days.

Like the neighbors around the area, all went through the Dirty Thirties. Many
people moved west. The Erbes are a frugal, determined bunch and they stuck it
out. The 40's brought wetter years and better prices, so they experienced the
bad and the good, and it made them stronger because of it.

Java was the Erbe's rural route address for many years. The Fourth of July
celebrations at Java were the highlight of our summers. Java always went all out
to provide good entertainment for their surrounding community, and we considered
ourselves a part of that.

Dorothy graduated from Java High School and calls Java her hometown.

Willard, their third son, remembers the "Dirty Thirties:" "I remember the Dirty
Thirties when dad had to put up Russian thistles to keep his small herd of
cattle alive. Dad would hitch up the team of horses on an old horse mower and
mow what thistles and grass he could find. We boys would help rake and haul them
in. Then Dad would pitch the thistles and hay up through a small door in the
upstairs of the barn. Dad and Leonard, my oldest brother, would pitch the
thistles up and Raleigh, my other brother, and I would move them to the back.
These Russian thistles were kind of salty. The cattle had to eat them because
there was nothing else for them. We lost a number of calves and cows through
this drought. I think the railroad company bought many of our cattle and killed
and buried them. We had a couple of hogs which we fattened up so our family
would have a meat supply for the winter months."

Pearl passed away in Oct. of 1975, and Herman in Oct. of 1978. They both reached
the age of 87 at the time of their death.

The children were:

Leonard, who passed away in Aug. 1992; his wife, Irma, lives in Custer. They
were married 41 years.

Raleigh lives in Ipswich. His wife, Martha, died Jan. 1996. They were married
almost 50 years.

Willard lives on the home place in a trailer house, west of Bowdle.

Velma passed away in Nov. of 1955.

Dorothy lives on a farm SE of Selby. Her husband, Ted Manke, died Jan. 1998.
They were married nearly 55 years.

"Ted Manke was born Sept. 13, 1917, on the Manke farm eight miles SE of Selby,
to Albert and Dora (Kruse) Manke. He grew up on a farm and attended grade school
and high school in Selby.

(Photo:) Ted and Dorothy (Erbe) Manke

Ted served in the CC Camp and also the Army for a short time, then came home to
help his dad on the farm.

I, Dorothy, was born May 19, 1922, at the Erbe farm six miles SE of Java, to
Herman and Pearl (Carter) Erbe. I grew up on the farm, attended country grade
school, and graduated from Java High School in 1940.

I stayed in the girls' dormitory located on the east side of Main Street. There
were many hilarious times there. There was a building right next to one of the
dorm rooms and the roof was even with one of the dorm windows - so we climbed
out on there one night (well, maybe more than one) and walked out to Gertie's
home out in the country. I think perhaps we were late for school the next day.
Our Dean, Mrs. Noble, was such a great lady, but kids will try to pull the wool
over your eyes whenever possible. We never did do anything too destructive.
Sometimes we went to the dorm basement to get oranges. We got hungry! One
Halloween the outhouses got lined up on Main Street. I was not in on that, but I
did help push a hayrack from out on the farm just west of town. Maybe we took it
into town?

I believe we had a reunion 10 years after graduation, in 1950, and then I helped
with the organizing of the reunion held in 1986. That was the end of the good
old school days at Java High.

Ted and I met at a dance at the Opera House in Selby in the late 30's. We didn't
see each other for a few years, then met again in the early 40's, courted, and
married on Feb. 20, 1943. We settled in on the Manke farm with Ted's folks, for
a year and a half. Ted's Pa and Ma moved to town in the fall of 1944 and we were
on our own. The first act we did when their pickup left the yard was to make a
Hollywood bed out of the cast iron one that they left in the house for us. How
many of you know how to make a Hollywood? This is how: You saw off the head of
the bed and turn the bottom end of the bed around for the head, and there you
have it! Exciting, huh? It was for us, especially when, while we were doing
this, Ted's folks came back to the farm looking for their mattress they had lost
off their pickup as they were moving their belongings to town. We were
embarrassed, but they never said a word about our "surgery" on the bed, and I
don't think they ever found their mattress.

Our first year of farming on our own, in 1945, was a heartbreaker; our crop was
hailed out slick and clean. Fortunately, Ted had insured the crop for hail. His
dad sold his machinery and milk cows to us for $1800 and we were to pay for them
with money we would get from our wheat crop. This is what happened: We got $1800
for our insurance payment for the hailed-out crop, and just handed it over to
Ted's dad for the cows and machinery. We had no debts and we had no money, but
we did have milk cows and we sold cream and bought groceries, so we made it
through to the next crop year. "Our Lord supplies all our needs according to His
riches and glory by Christ Jesus." Philippians 4:19

We decided to have a family. Ted wanted girls and he got them. Betty was born in
1949. She lives in St. Paul, MN, is single and works with Home Care. Mary
arrived eight years later. She lives in Pierre with her husband, Jay Livermont,
and their three children, Mark, Kristine, and Jason. Jay is a carpenter and Mary
works with Social Services.

We spent all of our married life on the farm, except for a couple of years, so
that was almost 55 years. Ted farmed until 1991 and then rented out the land,
but we continued living on the farm. Ted belonged to the Java Equity and did
most of his business there during the 70's and 80's. I think I could almost
write a book about all of the amusing experiences we've had on and around our
place, but that will be for another book. Ted passed away on Jan. 26, 1998. I
miss him!

Time passes fast. Find the best in each day and in each other - and enjoy
it!" - by Dorothy Erbe Manke

Margie lives in Aberdeen. Her husband Chuck died in June 1993. They had been
married 40 years.

There are 57 grand and great-grandchildren. Lyle, Wayne, and Eric are the only
ones to carry on the Erbe name in the Herman Erbe family tree.

Willard Woodrow Erbe
"CONGRATULATIONS JAVA ON YOUR ANNIVERSARY" by Willard W. Erbe

Congratulations Java on your 100th anniversary. You have a clean little town.
The lots are all neatly mowed and very few dead trees. Java is the Coffee Town -
it should be called the Flower Town.

Your NW cemetery is sure kept up good; the markers are in nice straight rows.
Well-taken care of, one of the nicest in Walworth County. Java used to be a real
interesting town. A friendly bunch of people. They used to have Number One
baseball and basketball teams. Carnivals on the midway, several rodeos. The
Hepper Bros., Bill and Bob, in charge of them. Snow fence for the arena, cars
would circle the outside, always big crowds. I think the Hepper Bros. had the
butcher shop. Full line of business places on Main Street.

A nice big schoolhouse on south Main St., a city park west of the schoolhouse. A
clean park.

Java had some big celebrations, ball games, horseshoes, rodeos, big carnivals on
the midway, parades, two dance halls, and fireworks.

Alvin Spiry and Ellsworth Schuh played for many old-time dances, lots of fun or
lots of "spass," in German. Martin Bauman helped out on the drums. Good old
accordion music is the best. The good old days and nights. Lots of good old beer
was drank.

The main street of Java, nice and wide. I'm sure it helps prevent fender
benders.

My uncle Henry Erbe used to live in the Flower Town. The Boehler Bros. bought
the house and moved it to north Main Street. "Jew" Boehler used to have the
Barber Shop.

(Photo:) Willard Erbe

At harvest time the elevators were overloaded with cars and trailers, tractors,
trucks, semi's. All lined up ready to get on the scales. The elevators and bins
are overloaded at harvest time.

I live here on the John Erbe homestead, where I was born and raised. I went to
school, little old country schoolhouse one mile west, known as the Spring Lake
School. Two of my old school buddies are still at large in my neighborhood:
Orville Stangl and Dwayne Lee. The old schoolhouse is SE of Java on the Merle
Noess farm.

I'll be 81 years young Oct. 13, 1999, served in the First Cavalry Division in
World War II. Saw New Guinea and Japan.

My Home-Sweet-Home is six-and-a-half miles west of Bowdle and 9 miles east of
Java.

When I started this write-up, I was outdoors in the shade of a big elm tree. Now
it is finished.

Life goes on. The Almighty takes good care of us. Will sign off, have a cup of
"Java," leave the Flower Town.

God Bless you all, good luck, you stay well - you all have a good celebration!!!

        Ward Winton and Marva Jean Ferguson

We retired here in 1996 after Ward had been a licensed plumber for 35 years in

        Gottlieb and Karolina (Wahl) Fiechtner I
Gottlieb Fiechtner I, was born Mar. 7, 1830, and grew to young manhood in the
village of Hoffnungstal in the Kherson territory. Gottlieb married Karolina
Wahl, who was born Apr. 10, 1830, and lived in the southern Russian area for
many years. They came to America when they were in their early fifties and most
of their children were grown and married.

They homesteaded land east of Java, near his son, Gottlieb II, and his family,
and farmed for a few years. His wife died a short time after they came to
America, then Gottlieb lived in a small home on his son's farm. A number of
years later, he came to live with his granddaughter, Louisa (Christ) Sauer, and
family. Several years later, he passed away.

(Photo:) Gottlieb Fiechtner I

This couple was blessed with seven children, which were: Mathias, a doctor in
Russia, was married. He passed away in Russia; John married and later
homesteaded in NE; Gottlieb II, married Karolina Spiry and homesteaded near
Java; Karolina married Christ Sauer Sr., who passed away, and she later came to
America with her two children, John and Christian Jr. She settled in CA, and
later married Jacob Kapfenstein; Katherina married Gottfried Zweigart and
homesteaded in Bridgewater; Christiana married Fred Bauman Sr., and homesteaded
in Bridgewater, and later five miles east of Java.

        Gottlieb and Karolina (Spiry) Fiechtner II
Gottlieb Fiechtner II, was born May 28, 1855, and grew up in the Kherson
Territory. He married Karolina Spiry in 1882. Karolina, the daughter of Fred
Spiry, Sr., was born Mar. 22, 1863, and lived in the Ukraine area of Russia.

After several years of hard labor trying to make a living for his family,
Gottlieb, his wife and three children - Louise, Kary and Gottlieb III, undertook
the long journey to come to the promised land of America. In 1886, they departed
from the Odessa port and, after several weeks, landed in the port of Baltimore,
MD. They remained in Baltimore for some time, as the three children became very
sick and had to be hospitalized. Gottlieb's wife had to work in the hospital to
cover the necessary expenses.

(Photo:) Gottlieb and Karolina Fiechtner II

After leaving Baltimore, they journeyed by rail to the Scotland and Bridgewater
areas to join other relatives. They were there a short time when Gottlieb
contacted his parents in Hoffnungstal to persuade them to come to America, as
there was more land available to be homesteaded. When the Fiechtner family had
saved enough money they, too, journeyed to America and landed at Port Detroit in
1893. They traveled by train to the Bridgewater area to join their son, Gottlieb
II, and his family.

Several months later, Gottlieb and Karolina and their children Louise, Kary and
Gottlieb III, moved to the Java area to be near Karolina's parents. Gottlieb's
parents and other relatives also made the move to settle near the Java area.
Gottlieb and his wife homesteaded four miles east of Java, now the Marlow
Schaffer farm, where they built another small house for Gottlieb's parents. Nine
more children were born to Gottlieb and Karolina, which were Jake, John,
William, Katie, Minnie, Rose, Mary, Lydia, and Amelia.

Before Gottlieb's death in 1908, he served as Walworth County Assessor for a
number of years. His wife, Karolina, died in 1952.

        Gottlieb and Christine (Naasz) Fiechtner III
Gottlieb Fiechtner III was born in Hoffnungstal, South Russia on Sept. 24, 1884.
He was a little boy when his parents undertook the trip to come to America. It
was a long but somewhat exciting to the three Fiechtner children. They
homesteaded in the Scotland and Bridgewater area in 1887, settling amid friends
and relatives that had previously lived amongst them in South Russia.

(Photo:) Christine and Gottlieb Fiechtner III

In 1893, when Gottlieb was six years old, his parents moved to the Java area,
where his father and mother filed claim on some land east of Java. Things looked
promising for the Java area, due to the extension of the railroad, which was
being built westward.

Gottlieb had little time for school, as he had to help out with the farming,
which was done mostly by oxen and mules. He grew to young manhood and later
married Christine Naasz, who too, came to this country with her parents, George
Naasz II, at the age of two years. They were married Apr. 4, 1907, in a small
country church near the Fiechtner and Naasz homes. They lived on his father's
homestead for many years. Four children were born to the Fiechtners while they
were in the Java area. Gottlieb also owned and operated a livery stable in 1919
but, after three years, he sold it and farmed until 1928 when the Fiechtner
family moved to Montana. They farmed in the Crow Rock area. No rainfall and hail
and his wife's illness forced Gottlieb to move back to SD. They moved to Java,
where Gottlieb found employment with the railroad for many years and later was
employed at the City Power Plant until he retired. The family belonged to St.
Paul Lutheran Church.

The Fiechtner children were:

Emil (deceased) married Hilda Hirsch and had one daughter, Janet.

Albert (deceased), married Martha Hirsch, and had two sons, Jack and Lyle.

Gary married Phyllis Simpson (deceased) and had two sons, Dennis and Bret.

Erna, married Elmer Schlepp, and has one daughter, Marlys, who married Neal
Pfitzer, and one son, Douglas, who married LaNette Hettich. (See Family
Histories)

        John and Emelia (Naasz) Fiechtner
John Fiechtner was born Aug. 23, 1891, at Bridgewater, the son of Gottlieb and
Karolina (Spiry) Fiechtner, who immigrated to Dakota Territory in 1886 from
South Russia (originally of German descent).

His family remained in the Bridgewater vicinity until 1893, and came to Walworth
County and homesteaded about three miles east of the Java town site. John
remained on the homestead and took over the responsibility of operating it after
the death of his father in 1908. His mother sold the farm in 1918 and moved to
Java. His grandfather, Gottlieb Fiechtner also lived on the homestead in a house
by himself.

Emelia Naasz was born Sept. 24, 1894 on the Naasz homestead in Walworth County,
five miles east of the Java town site, the daughter of George and Magdalena
(Graf) Naasz. Her parents emigrated from South Russia (originally of German
descent), and arrived on their homestead May 5, 1893. They built a two-room sod
house, and this remained their home until they built a three-room house with a
summer kitchen that was built with stone, straw and mud. An additional room was
built on later for her grandmother Naasz, and she lived there for a while.
Emelia moved to Java with her parents at age 13 in 1907.

John and Emelia were united in marriage on Nov. 18, 1913. They moved on the
Naasz homestead, having purchased it from her parents. Their three children,
Herbert, Irene, and Gertrude, were born there. The years of farming were lean,
and they could not keep up the payments. They left the farm and lived briefly in
Mobridge and then Java. After that, they moved onto the Kapfenstein farm and
from there to a farm four miles SE of Java, living there for five years. The
children attended the Spring Valley School.  When the Depression hit in 1930,
they moved to Java, and worked wherever jobs were available. Their children
graduated from Java High School. After a few more years of farming, they moved
to Mobridge. John died in June 1948. Emelia stayed in Mobridge until 1951 when
she sold her house and moved to Lodi, CA.

(Photo:) Emelia and John Fiechtner

One incident that remained clearly in their minds was the Flu Epidemic of 1918.
They went from one place to another to look in on the sick and give assistance.
Flu hit the Adolph Naasz home south of Java:  people living there at the time
were as follows: Mr. and Mrs. Naasz and their children, Ted, Art, Adolph Jr.,
Alvina, Emil, Esther, Herman and Irene; Mr. and Mrs. Jake Fiechtner (Lydia
Sackman) and their children, Hertha and Alvina; and Grandma Sackman (Mrs. John
Sackman) and her children, Tillie, Andreas, Reinhold and Herman. All of them
were sick in bed except Adolph Naasz. This house was sorrowed by the death of
four of the occupants - Mrs. Jake Fiechtner, Alvina and Esther Naasz, and
Grandma Sackman. The Karolina Fiechtner family had the flu also. The people that
resided there were as follows: Rose, Minnie, Bill, Lydia, Mary and Emelia. Rose
and Minnie came from Kansas for a visit when the flu hit. Jake Fiechtner and two
children moved back here too, after the death of his wife. At John and Emelia's
home, which they shared with Mr. and Mrs. Gottlieb Fiechtner on the Naasz
homestead, the following were sick with the flu: their children, Herbert and
Irene; Gottlieb and Christina, and their two sons, Emil and Albert. Emelia
didn't get sick with the flu until about a month later, after everyone was well.

Herbert married Ida Klein. They farmed east of Java until they retired to Bowdle
in 1973. They had six children. Phonia married Harvey Diedtrich and they reside
in Eureka. They are both employed in the Pierre area where Harvey is a tutor in
the Crow Creek Middle School and Phonia works in the Cultural Heritage Center.
Their son, David, married Linda Mehlhaff and they live near Brighton, CO. David
is a certified industrial hygenist and Linda is employed by an orthopedic clinic
in Denver. David and Linda have three children, Derrick, Angela and Robert.
Angela and her husband Geno Fuentes have one daughter, Jericha, and also reside
in Brighton. Daughter Susan is married to Larry Czarnowski and they are the
parents of a son, Stephen. Susan is a Kent County, MI employee, and Larry is a
Kalamazoo County, MI employee. Terrance married Arliss Schilling, They reside in
Titusville, FL and are both retired. Terry, a chemical engineer, served in the
military, worked for DuPont in IA for several years, moved to FL and worked for
the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, retiring in 1994 after 31
years. Arliss is a Registered Nurse. She has worked at different hospitals and
also for The Hospice of St. Francis, before retiring. They have three children.
Curtis married Michelle DeSart and they have three children, Jermaine, Anna and

        Walter and Viola (Zweigardt) Fiechtner
Waldemar (Walter) Fiechtner was born in Hoffnungstal, South Russia on Nov. 29,

and later moved to a farm east of Java.

of Gottfried and Magdalena (Spiry) Zweigardt.

Walter and Viola moved to the state of Washington in July 1936. They worked on a

        Gottfried and Karolina (Reimer) Fiedler
Gottfried Fiedler, born Jan. 22, 1857, to John Jacob and Anna Helena Martin-
Fiedler, and Karolina Reimer-Fiedler, born Sept. 27, 1860, the daughter of John
and Florentina Hildebrandt-Reimer, were both born in the village of Rosenberg, a
colony in South Russia, to where their parents had migrated in the early part of
the 19th Century. Here they were to enjoy complete liberty in church and school,
local ordinances, military exemption and grants of Crown land, in exchange for
the tilling and planting of it and large groves of timber.

After 10 or 12 years, when privileges were being renounced, our grandparents
knew definitely that America was where they would go to once more seek full
freedom. It was not easy to leave their comfortable homes, but after a year's
preparation their whole village was ready to leave by May 1876. A cross-country
train trip took them to Berlin and Hamburg, where they embarked on the Kaiser
Wilhelm, one of the finest ocean liners of that day. After several weeks at sea,
they reached their port of entry, Ellis Island. A new experience there was to go
to New York City, via a submarine tunnel and about the city on an "elevated".

Another cross-country train trip brought them to their destination of Yankton,
Dakota Territory, which was the capitol. Getting their families settled in town,
our grandfathers set out to buy homes and found suitable places not too far out.
Having arrived in June 1876, they found much excitement due to the Black Hills
gold rush but too, the countryside was at its best.

(Photo:) Gottfried and Karolina Fiedler

Our parents were married Nov. 18, 1878 and for a few years lived in a small log
cabin in grandparents Fiedler's yard near Mission Hill. As land became available
nearby, they purchased a place of their own a few miles farther out, with no
improvements on it. Lumber was hauled from Vermillion to build their first frame
house, granary etc. In the spring, trees were planted for shade and fruit and
the shelterbelt contained 400 black walnut seedlings. Ground was prepared for
seeding, taking all of father's time, leaving mother with the care of house,
yard and garden, besides small children. As the season advanced and the work
increased, father purchased a reaper for himself and a sewing machine for
mother, each serving as an extra pair of hands to help.

They moved to Freeman, which was their post office, and attended church and
school in town. Having lost two infants, who were buried at Mission Hill,
another son was born to them here, Jan. 1, 1901. The very level land had
attracted them, but after three years of above normal rainfall and no drainage,
they saw that another move was necessary.

They came to Java in Mar. of 1903 and located about seven miles NW of town. The
oldest son, who had a small business in town, had married by the end of the
first year, as had their second daughter, and both lived in town. The oldest
married just before they moved and remained at Freeman. In 1904 their youngest
daughter was born and the last half of the family received their public and
religious education here. The schoolhouse was located on their land, a
quarter-mile from the house, and the country church, two miles, with the parish
church in Java, where we were all confirmed.

Our parents retired in 1924 and moved to Mobridge to build their last home.

They celebrated their Golden Wedding here Nov. 18, 1928, but could share only
eight years here together before father became ill and passed away May 1, 1932.
Mother continued to live here for 15 more years until, in 1947, three more of
her children moved to Canistota. She went with them for company-sake, as most of
the family had left this area during the Depression years. Mother passed away on
June 15, 1948.

The children, all deceased, were: Gottfried, Helena, Florentina, Albert, John,
Henry, Wilhelmina, Caroline, Marie, Elizabeth, Anna, and Ruth.

        John and Caroline (Helm) Fiedler
John Heinrich Fiedler was born on Jan. 4, 1885, to Gottfried and Karolina Reimer
Fiedler at Yankton. In 1900, he moved with his parents to Freeman, and in 1903,
he moved with his parents and the rest of their family to Java, where they
settled on a farm seven miles NW of Java.

In 1908, he married Caroline Helm at the Friedens Church NW of Java.

In 1909, John and Caroline homesteaded in Perkins County and lived there until
1911 when they proved up their homestead and moved back to a farm NW of Java.

In 1943, they moved to a poultry farm one-half mile east of Mobridge until 1947,
when they moved to Canistota. Caroline passed away in 1949 and John then moved
back to Walworth County and lived with family members until his death in 1960.

John and Caroline had three sons, John Fredrick, married to Emma Schaffer, Oscar
Reinhold, married to Olga Schnaible, and Norman Ervin married to Lorrain Naasz.

        Oscar and Olga (Schnaible) Fiedler Sr.
Oscar R. Fiedler, Sr., the second oldest son of John H. and Caroline (Helm)
Fiedler, was born Dec. 11, 1913, on his parents' farm four miles north of Java.
He completed eight grades at a rural school there and then worked on the family
farm. In 1935, he married Olga W. Schnaible, daughter of John and Maria (Weber)
Schnaible of rural Java. They lived on a farm seven miles north of Java. In the
fall of 1939, they rented a farm three miles north of Lake Hiddenwood. In 1943,
they moved to Olga's parents' farm 10 miles south of Java. The next year they
moved to, and eventually purchased, a farm 9 miles SE of Java, which was their
home for the rest of their lives.

(Photo:) James, Arlyn, Oscar, Jr., Olga, and Oscar Fiedler, Sr.

Oscar and Olga had three children: Oscar, Jr., married Carol Mueller, lives on
his parents farm, and has four children, Dale, Renee, Michele, and Lance. James
married Darlene Schuh. They live in Clark and have three children, Todd,
Douglas, and Lori. Arlyn, married to Sylvia Knoepfle, lives in Bowdle and has a
daughter, Kim.

Like all young couples in the Thirties, Oscar and Olga struggled to make ends
meet but, through perseverance, they were able to purchase and build up their
farmstead. Oscar enjoyed talking about the old-time barn dances where he played
the accordion. Olga passed away in 1996 at the age of 82, and Oscar passed away
in 1997 at the age of 83.

        Oscar and Carol (Mueller) Fiedler Jr.
Oscar Fiedler, Jr., the oldest son of Oscar R. Fiedler, Sr. and Olga (Schnaible)
Fiedler, was born at the home of his parents north of Java. In 1943, he moved

School and then his enjoyment of farming led him to stay and work on the family

Oscar, Jr. and Carol were married in 1955 and made their home six miles SE of

(Photo:) Dale, Renee, Carol, Oscar, Jr., Michelle, and lance Fiedler
