        Mike and Viktoria (Kovach) Horvath by Henry Kosters
Mike Horvath was born in Tsaramorovisa, Hungary in the County of Horvath to
Michael Steven Horvath and Mary Schatmary Horvath on Mar. 25, 1895. At age 25
Mike Sr. was injured in an accident and died of blood poisoning. Mike Jr. was
two years old at the time.

Mary (Schatmary) Horvath later married Wendall Kais and four children were born:
Steven, and three sisters. Mary Schatmary Horvath Kais died of pneumonia at the
age of 41 at Tsaramorovisa, Hungary.

Mike's stepfather, Wendall Kais, served in the 1,000th Battalion of the Austro-
Hungarian Army. During that era in Hungary (Austria/Hungary), every young man
was required to register for military service when he reached the age of 16
years. Between the ages of 21 and 24 years, every young man was required to
serve on active duty for a three-year hitch in the Austro-Hungarian Army.
Wendall Kais advised Mike that he should leave Hungary and go to the U.S.
Wendall believed that a war in the near future was inevitable and that one
result of that war would be to have the Soviet Communists take over Hungary.

Mike was raised on his stepfather's small farm, an acre or so, just outside the
town of Tsaramorovisa, Hungary.

Wendall Kais provided Mike with a letter of introduction to a friend to help him
gain employment in Germany, as he began his journey to the U.S. Mike left
Hungary and went to Germany, where he worked outside of the small town of
Wostervitz, near the city of Notre Dam (Germany). Mike worked in the potato
fields as a farmhand and drove a team of four oxen in this work and he worked in
Germany through the growing season of 1911. For his work he was paid in produce
(potatoes), which the Germans used for making alcohol. Mike was able to sell his
potatoes to pay for his passage and for additional pocket money, which was
required for those desiring to immigrate into the U.S.

When Mike left Germany he traveled from Wostervitz to Veerhagen at Hamburg,
Germany and boarded the ship American Gunnard, which was bound for New York and
Ellis Island. With the money he had earned he purchased a single ticket, which
included the steamship passage to New York and the train trip from New York to
Milwaukee, WI, his final destination. Mike left Hamburg, Germany on Dec. 20,
1911 and arrived in New York on Christmas Day after a five-day ocean voyage.

Mike had lied about his age by one year to be admitted more easily into this
country and to avoid the draft requirements in Hungary.

The Great Northern Railroad and the State of NE were the next set of adventures
for Mike. His work with the Great Northern Railroad only lasted two months and
he then went to work for the Northern Pacific Railroad between Grand Forks, ND
and Winnipeg, Canada. Again the work with the railroad was of rather short
duration and Mike was forced to pick up work as a farmhand. He then worked for a
time in the Elk Point area of SD.

Mike followed the crops up into ND. Finally he started south again and came to
the vicinity of Java. He traveled between jobs wherever he could find them and
then hopped a freight train and allowed the rails to select his next
destination. Much of his work at this time was in the harvest fields and on
threshing crews. In the Java area he found employment with a Dutch farmer named
Peter Noble; first on his threshing crew and then as a hired man.

Mike and Viktoria were married in 1914. Peter Nobel, Carl Schlepp, Henry Mueller
and George Kosters all contributed to getting the young couple into the business
of farming. The type of farming done in the Java area at that time was
considerably different than the Hungarian ways Mike knew best. Mike had a great
deal to learn about small grain farming even with his experience as a farmhand.

Viktoria had $500 from an insurance policy from her late husband Gaza Kormendy.
Viktoria also had the land Gaza had homesteaded to contribute toward getting
started. This was the origin of the American branch of the Horvath Clan of
Gypsies.

World War I was underway by this time and during 1916, Mike, and Joe Zarka,
another Hungarian friend and neighbor, were both summoned by the draft board to
serve their country. However, Mike was exempted from the military draft with the
stipulation that Mike not only maintain his own farming operation, but that he
provide assistance to neighboring farms where the men had been called to
military service. He and Viktoria had added a baby girl (Helen) to their family.

Mike served as the Clerk of the Spring Valley School board for a period of two
years. During the time of his service on the school board he made the motion to
more than double the salary of the teacher Emma Stangl, from the grand sum of
$35 per month to $76 per month. He said it was worth $2 per child per month to
provide a good teacher for the education of the children of the Spring Valley
School.

During his time of service on the school board, the Walworth County
Superintendent of Schools was Mrs. Marshall. The County Superintendent was
required to visit the schools frequently. One of the teachers in the Spring
Valley School, Tiny Noble, had boarded with Mike and Viktoria for a time. Mike
learned to read and write some English during the time Tiny boarded with them as
well as learning from his family as they went on to school. He also learned from
neighbors and in business dealings.

Mike and Viktoria left the original homestead after about 10 years of marriage
and moved to the Carl Schlepp place, located along U.S. Highway 12, which they
had purchased. Mike and Viktoria lived on the Schlepp place, which became known
as the Horvath place, for the next 11 years. At that time Highway 12 was in the
process of being upgraded to a U.S. Highway; they were re-grading and
re-gravelling the road. The Horvath's youngest children and their grandchildren
would play in the pasture near the highway during the construction. They would
pick flowers and walk through what the writer thought must have been the largest
culvert in the world under the now highway. It is worthy of note that old timers
in the Java and Selby areas still refer to that hill as Mike Horvath's Hill, but
the shape of the hill has changed dramatically with reshaping of Highway 12
through the years. On that hill today there are two large markers, WEB water
tanks, which provide water for thousands of people over several hundred square
miles.

Times became very tough in the 1930's for many South Dakotans. There was the
combination of drought, grasshoppers, farm products and those products they
could sell brought very low prices. It was more profitable to burn than to sell
the corn and buy coal. These factors caused many South Dakotans to leave the
state as they lost their farms. They could not feed and house their families.
Many farmers burned grain they produced as it brought so little on the market
that they couldn't buy the coal they needed. Dried cow manure (called Buffalo
chips) was gathered from the pastures and barnyards for heating and cooking.
Finally the Horvaths made the decision to quit tje farming operation and move to
IL.

In Aug. of 1937 Viktoria and the children, except Mary, boarded the train for
Harvey, IL, where Viktoria's brother George helped them out for a time. Mike
stayed behind for a time to complete closure of the business and the farm
auction, which was held in  Sept. of 1937.

On Dec. 28, 1931 Elizabeth Mary Horvath married Henry Jacob Kosters, the son of
longtime neighbor and friend George Kosters.

Mike sought advice about the sale of the farm property, machinery and livestock
from Louis Gershin, a friend and merchant in the town of Java. Mike and Viktoria
had quite a list of machinery and livestock. The list included a gear-drive
McCormick Deering Tractor. Mike followed Mr. Gershin's advice and repaired all
of the machinery for the sale.

During Mike's stay in SD, George Kosters, Henry Mueller, Carl Schlepp and the
Raba families were his good friends, neighbors and advisors. There were a number
of Hungarian farmers in the area who were his good friends such as: Andrew Raba,
John Raba, Joe Zarka, Steve Timar, Joe Zambo and Loy Miklos. There are others
who should be included in this listing and apologies are extended for those
omissions.

During World War II Mike was drafted once again. This time he was assigned to
work for the Pullman Car Company at West Pullman, IL. At the Pullman Car Company
Mike helped to build the troop trains used to move troops across the country.

Michael Steven Horvath II died at his home at Harvey, IL on Oct. 5, 1979. He had
worked for the combination of Kickert Brothers/Neilon Chevrolet for many years
as the new-car serviceman. At the time of his death he had been retired for
fifteen years and enjoyed working in his showcase garden. His love for the soil
and growing things never left him (You can take the boy from the farm, but you
can't take the farm from the boy).

Funeral services for Mike were held on Oct. 9, 1979 at the Ascension Catholic
Church in Harvey and he is buried at the Assumption Cemetery. He had lived in
Harvey and Phoenix IL for a total of 40 years.

Michael Steven Horvath II was survived by five daughters; Mrs. Henry (Mary)
Kosters and Mrs. Mark (Verna) Raba of Selby, Mrs. Mike (Rose) Gutyan of
Schererville, IN, Mrs. Andrew (Helen) Hovantzi of Chicago, IL, Mrs. Margaret
Pellaccio of Santa Fe, NM; one son, Michael Steven Horvath III, of Spearfish; 25
grandchildren, 48 great grandchildren, and two great-great grandchildren. He was
preceded in death by his wife Viktoria in 1976, and an infant son Paul.

        Viktoria Kovach Horvath (Nagy Mama) by Henry Kosters
In about 1910 Viktoria came to the U.S. and the Chicago area. Her brother George
provided the passage money. Apparently she was not terribly enthusiastic about
leaving Hungary. She had good employment and lived a rather good life as the
employee of a very wealthy family. Her prospects for marriage were probably
rather limited due to the type of employment and the mobility required in her
job. One might guess that she was encouraged to come to the U.S. by uncle
George. In 1911 Uncle George Kovach accompanied his little sister Viktoria to
Java, to meet Gaza Kormendy and his family. Viktoria had met Gaza in Chicago at
a Hungarian get-together shortly after her arrival in this country. Gaza had a
homestead, near George Kosters, Henry Mueller, Carl Schlepp, George Kormendy,
and Ladislaus Kormendy, which was about five and one-half miles south and two
miles east of Java.

Gaza Kormendy and Viktoria Kovach were married in the spring of 1911. There were
two children born to this union, Elizabeth Mary on May 4, 1912 and Rose on
Sept. 1, 1913. Gaza suffered from consumption (Tuberculosis) and his health
began to fail. He died during the winter of 1913. Gaza left a wife, two
children, a homestead and $500. Gaza Kormendy is buried at the "old" Java
Cemetery.

In 1914 Viktoria met and married Michael Steven Horvath Jr. At that time Mike
was working at the farm of Peter Nobel. Viktoria and Mike settled on the
homestead left to her by Gaza. The $500 in insurance money helped them get
started in farming.

Viktoria Kovach Horvath was born in Tamesvar, Hungary near the city of Budapest
on Apr. 20, 1882, to Istvan and Elizabeth Kovach. They were poor people who
worked as laborers on a wealthy man's farm. The landowner provided living
quarters for the laborers. These living quarters provided a common earthen oven
and stove for the four families that shared each of the laborer's dwellings.

Viktoria had one brother, George, and at least two sisters. These two sisters
(Veronica and Rose) immigrated to Argentina in South America and no one has
heard from them in some time. Her brother, George immigrated to the U.S. and
settled at Harvey, IL.

Viktoria was a small (about 5'2") attractive woman. She had a beautiful soprano
voice. She very much enjoyed singing. For the most part the songs she would sing
were songs from her youth and Hungarian ballads. Her husband, Mike Horvath,
disapproved Viktoria's singing in public. He only approved of her singing for
and with the family. One can recall her singing Hungarian tunes at many of our
family gatherings.

Viktoria Kovach Horvath died at her home on July 24 1976. The funeral mass was
conducted at Ascension Church in Harvey and she is buried at the Assumption
Cemetery. Her family was her life, especially the young children. These
youngsters could always bring a twinkle to her eyes.

Uncle George Kovach enjoyed life and made and lost several fortunes according to
his own tales. In his declining years, as a pauper once again, he worked at the
Buda Factory in Harvey, IL. He then worked as a tailor in the "Old Folks Home"
at Oak Forest, IL, where he resided in his declining years. He died in 1951, and
is buried at Oak Forest, IL. His common-law wife, Helen, preceded him in death
in 1943, and is buried at Franklin Park, IL.

        Christian and Katharina (Geigle) Huether
Christian Huether, the youngest son of Paul and Anna Margareta (Christman)
Huether, was born in 1877 in Neustaz, South Russia. His sister Kathryn and John
Dormaier had homesteaded 12 miles north of Java in Blessing Township in 1888.
The father, Paul, was born in 1831 in Peterstal, South Russia and his wife, Anna
Margareta, daughter Louise, and Christian came to the U.S. in 1889. In 1892 they
filed claims in Blessing Township, Campbell County. His sister, Kathryn (John)
Dormaier, had homesteaded in Blessing Township in 1885. His brother, Paul, Jr.,
and family homesteaded in 1893, where LeRoy Sandmaier farms today. Christian
taught country school and, in 1899, filed his claim. In the same year he married
Katharina Geigle, daughter of Johann Jakob and Katharina Geigle. They were
active church members of the Odessa Reformed Church in Sutley. Christian's
sister Louise and his mother died in 1889, and were buried in Menno. His father,
Paul, moved to Eugene, OR and died there in 1931. His brother Paul, Jr., and
family, left in 1908 for the state of WA. His sister Kathryn moved to WA in
1902. Christian and his family left the farm in 1903 and moved into Java. He was
the town secretary for many years. He and Henry Huether became implement dealers
in 1905. Some time around early 1920 they moved to a farm south of Java. In 1929
the family moved to Hollywood, CA. Six children were born to this union, who
were Edna, Arthur, Gerhard, Alma, Sylvia, and Viola.

        Duane and Venoye Hughes
The family of Duane and Venoye Hughes moved to the Java area in the spring of
1966, when they purchased the J.C. Bieber farm from the estate of Rueben H.
Bieber. Venoye had been born and raised on this farm and attended the Irving
Country School.

(Photo:) Duane and Venoye Hughes Family

The family consisted of five children ranging in age from two to 10 years. The
children attended the Java Public School. Renee, Connie and Kent graduated from
the Java school system. Keith and Carol graduated from the Pierre school system
when the family moved to Pierre.

During the years that they lived in the Java area, Duane served on the school
board and the church council. He worked for the State of SD as the Veterinary
Supervisor of Disease Control Programs and Heat Inspection of North Central SD.
In the fall of 1977 Duane accepted the position as State Veterinarian of SD and
the family moved to Pierre, and in 1987 the family moved to Sioux Falls.

They maintain very close ties to the Java area, as Kent and Miriam Hughes and
their family have continued the ranching operation.

According to the land abstracts some of the land was transferred to Venoye's
grandfather in the late 1800's, which would make Kent's boys the fifth
generation to have lived on this farm in the Java area over the past 100 years.
The roots run deep!

        Carl and Rose Mary (Savelsberg) Jacobs
Carl Jacobs was born in 1898, at Kaukauna, WI. In 1908, he moved with his
parents to Green Bay, WI. In 1917, at the age of 19, Carl followed his sister,
Eva Jacobs Bauer, to Java. Having received training in carpentry at a vocational
school in Green Bay, he began working with a building crew. He helped build the
Helm and Moser houses, some garages, as well as several farm buildings in the
area. In 1921, when mail was delivered by horse and buggy, Carl became a rural
mail carrier.

In 1924 Carl married Rose Mary Savelsberg. Rose was born in 1906 in Sheldon, IA,
and had moved to Glenham with her parents, Mr. and Mrs. Frank Savelsberg. Rose
went to high school there and then on to NSC for two years.

Carl and Rose had five children: Derry, Ardelle (Reginald) Dougherty, Marilyn
(John) Bohan, Jerome, and Paul.

Carl continued as a rural mail carrier, a total of 43 years, until his death in
1964. Rose died in 1965.

        The John Job Family
John Job was born Mar. 17, 1886, at Krontal, South Russia to Martin and
Margaretha (Helm) Job. In June of 1906, he immigrated to the U.S. and worked on
a farm near Pollock for six months, when he moved to a farm six miles north of
Java. On Oct. 30, 1912, he married Justina Doerr, daughter of Rudolph and
Karolina (Koerner) Doerr at Eureka. The young couple established a home and
family north of Java. They struggled through many hardships, but the greatest
blow came in May of 1927, when an infant son and Mrs. Job both succumbed,
leaving children ranging in age from three to 12 years. Mr. Job continued
farming and in 1928, he married Rosina Mohr of Hosmer. This family managed to
survive the "Dirty Thirties" eking out a living as best they could and then
retired to Java in 1944. Mr. Job was called to rest in Sept. of 1956 and Mrs.
Job in Dec. of 1972.

Mr. Job was very active in church and school affairs and was often called upon
to read Scripture in the absence of Rev. Kirchdoerfer, who served the rural
congregation that was attended by the entire family. In fact there was never an
excuse for any member of the family not to attend Sunday school and church
services every Sunday, even though the family had to ride triple deck in their
1928 Chevrolet. Mr. Job also was very much in favor of education and saw to it
that his children attended school regularly, in spite of snow and bitter cold
requiring a horse drawn sled, sheepskin coats and mountains of quilts to get
there.

The children are as follows: Tillie, Robert, Minnie, Frieda (Oliver) McCauley,
Ervin, Rueben, LaRayne (Gilbert) Schlepp, Vina (Charles) York and Delphia
(George) Trudeau.

Robert and Hulda (Forkel), children Roberta, Gaylon and Sharlene; Frieda and
Oliver McCauley, one child, Kathie; Ervin and Janice, two children, Michael and
Barbara; Rueben and Darlene (Kurle), two sons, Paul and Jason; LaRayne and
Gilbert Schlepp, two daughters, Barbara and Carolyn; Vina and Charles York,
three children, Cynthia, Jon and Dale; Delphia and George Trudeau, three
children, Kevin, Keith and Lyle.

        Friedrich (Fred) and Philippina (Doerr) Job
Friedrich (Fred) Job was born at Krontal, South Russia on Dec. 24, 1891, to
Martin and Marguerite (Helm) Job. Fred had four sisters and three brothers and
of this family, three migrated to the U.S., who were Fred, his brother John, and
his sister Christina. John and Fred settled in the Java area, and Christina in
the Hosmer area.

(Photo:) Fred and Philippina Job

Fred immigrated in 1911, at the age of 20, and was employed on farms near the
Java area. Enlisting in the U.S. Army in 1918, Fred served with Company M of the
64th Infantry in France. He received his discharge in 1919 and returned to the
Java area. Again he found employment and on Mar. 18, 1920, he was married to
Philippina Doerr, daughter of Rudolph and Karolina (Koerner) Doerr of Eureka.
The Jobs moved to a farm near Java, and farmed several years, and later moved to
a farm four miles NW of Java.

Six children were born to Fred and Philippina, who were:

Milbert, who passed away in 1954.

Amanda married Herbert Schneider, son of John and Lydia (Kary) Schneider. They
owned and operated a farm north of Java until 1984 when they retired to
Mobridge. They were blessed with three sons, Dean of Denver, CO, Dennis of Java,
and Jerry of Denver, CO. Herbert passed away June 22, 1990. (See Family History)

Esther married Ole Naasz. They owned and operated Ole's T.V., and lived in
Mobridge. They had two daughters, Vickie Adams of Redwood Valley, CA, Gwynn
Hanson of Mitchell, and David of Sioux Falls. Esther passed away June 22, 1992.
(See Family History)

Oscar married Marge Young. They live at Kalispell, MT.

Albert married Marie Arnold in Missoula, MT in 1959. They had one son Jeffery,
and one daughter Jennifer. Jennifer died Aug. 11, 1980 in a car accident. Marie
passed away Mar. 24, 1982. Albert married Doris Frick Anderson July 22, 1989.
They reside in Kalispell, MT as do Albert's son, Jeff, and his family.

Margaret married James Anderson, son of Eddie and Anna (Holman) Anderson. They
had one son Myron, who passed away July 15, 1990 at San Antonio, TX, and two
daughters, Carol Doerr of Hecla, and Connie Bonen of Aberdeen. Jim passed away
Jan. 18, 1996, and Margaret resides in Aberdeen.

        Jacob and Emelia (Walter) Jurief
Jacob Jurief was born Aug. 2,1890, in Simferopol, Crimea Russia to Constantine
and Maria (Mohl) Jurief. Jacob grew up in the village, going to school and
helping his father. When he was 14, he was sent away to school.

Jacob's father owned a saddle and harness shop and during the winter months he
made saddles, bridles, whips, harnesses and did repairs for the villagers.
During the spring and summer months he farmed. Everyone raised their own feed
and grains for animal and family use. Each villager had an area large enough to
keep cattle, horses, chickens and a garden to grow vegetables. When Jacob
returned from school, the farming became his occupation.

In 1908, his father died during harvest season. In the fall, his mother sold the
shop and moved to Toksaba to be near her family. Jacob leased land from the
village landlord and farmed to provide for himself and his mother.

Jacob married Emelia Walter on Sept. 23,1912. She was born Dec. 20,1891, at
Kloestiz, Bessarabia Russia to Michael and Magdelena (Diedtrich) Walter. The
following spring Jacob and Emelia, accompanied by his mother, came to the U.S.,
arriving at Baltimore, MD on Apr. 4, 1913. Traveling by train, the family
arrived three days later in Crookston, NE, where they met Maria's brother-in-
law, Daniel Heinert. They stayed at the hotel that night and left early the next
morning by wagon across the country to Parmelee on the Rosebud Indian
Reservation. It took three days, stopping at farm homes along the way to spend
the night. It was cold and rainy at times. At dusk on the third day, they
arrived at the farm home of her sister.

(Photo:) Stella, Hilbert, Martha, Jacob and Emelia Jurief

They stayed at the farm and learned about life in America. The Heinerts were a
large family and times were hard. To make extra money, they started a bakery in
their home, making and baking bread around the clock. The next morning they
would take the baked goods to town and sell it to the Indians.

The last week in May they left for Butte, NE, to the farm home of Peter Mohl,
Maria's brother. After a short time, Jacob found work on a cattle ranch. The
women stayed at the farm helping with work during the summer. In the fall,
Jacob, Emelia, and his mother, Maria, moved to Onoka, NE. Here they bought two
cows and 12 chickens and set up housekeeping. Jacob then went to work for the
railroad with a section crew. After two years he wanted to try farming. Wages
were a dollar a day. Two daughters joined the family, Martha born May 6, 1913 in
Parmelee, SD and Stella born Sept. 20, 1914 in Onoka, NE.

The fall of 1915 they moved to a farm near Burke, SD. Now a son, Hilbert, was
born Mar. 13, 1916, in Carlock, SD. Later, in 1920, they moved to the
northeastern part of the state, bringing horses, cows, farm machinery, wagon, a
new buggy, and furniture. It was all loaded in a railroad boxcar. Jacob rode
along with the freight train so he could feed the animals. Emelia and the
children came on the passenger train, arriving in Bowdle in mid-Jan. They stayed
at the George Bieber farm west of Bowdle until their farm was vacant. The first
year all that they grew on the farm was wild oats, which was cut for feed.

The fall of 1924 brought an epidemic of scarlet fever. The children all had the
fever and were quarantined for three months and the schools were closed.

In Mar. of 1928, the family moved to Java, where Jacob managed to get a place
with more land to farm. His mother died Oct. 1928. After several years, in 1946,
Jacob and Emelia sold everything they owned at an auction. During the summer
months they traveled and visited friends and relatives in the Midwest. In Sept.
they moved to OR and worked at a maraschino cherry processing plant until they
retired. In 1965, Jacob, Emelia and their daughter, Martha, moved to CA. Emelia
died Jan. 9, 1974, and Jacob died Aug. 7, 1975. They had four children.

Herbert born Oct. 5, 1917, died Sept. 20, 1918 at the age of 11 months.

Martha lived with her parents until they died, and she lived in Stockton, CA
until her death on May 30, 1995.

Stella married Oscar Goetz and lived on a farm NE of Java. They have four sons,
Gaylon, Dwight, Keith and Gordon. Stella passed away Mar. 8, 1992. (See Family
History)

Hilbert married Ottillia Hoffman (divorced). He lives at Klamath Falls, OR. They
have four children. Sylvia married Claude Chambers and has two children, David
and Susan. They live in Castro Valley, CA. Terrance married Peggy Leppert and
has two children, Scott and Kathryn. They live in Klamath Falls, OR. David
married Catherine Bessone and has two daughters, Sara and Amie. They live at
Castro Valley, CA. Diane married Tim Delaney and has two sons, Jess and Jon.
They live in Stockton, CA. Ottillia died Aug. 19, 1994.

Hilbert lived in the Java-Selby area and worked several years for the REA after
he returned from the armed service. He later moved with his family to the West
Coast, in 1955.

        Jacob Kapfenstein
Jacob Kapfenstein, along with many others from Russia, migrated to the U.S. and
eventually settled in SD, east of Java. For a time he lived in Hosmer and later
in Santa Rosa, CA, but later returned to the Java area.

During his early years in this country, he was married and had two children from
his first wife, one boy and one girl. Following the death of his first wife, he
married Caroline Fiechtner Sauer. Three children were born to them while they
were farming east of Java. Mary, the oldest, later married Emanuel Hetterle,
with whom she had three children; Lydia, the youngest, later married Jacob Walz
and they had one boy and a number of girls. John, the only boy, married Martha
Kurle and three boys were born to them, two of whom are still living.

(Photo:) Jacob Kapfenstein

During his later years, and following the death of his first wife, Jacob moved
into Java where he lived until his death in the early 1940's.

        John and Martha (Kurle) Kapfenstein
John and Martha Kapfenstein were well known, long time residents of Java since
1926. In 1948, they purchased what was then known as "the Bender House," making
this their home until 1980. Son Oscar now occupies this house.

John was born east of Java in 1899, to the Jacob Kapfensteins. Martha came to
the U.S. from Russia with her parents, the Christian Kurles. Both John and
Martha were raised, for the most part, in the Java area and were married in Java
in 1926, and continued to live in town until July 1980, when Martha passed away
at the age of 74. John, then, went to live with his son, Oscar, in Wilmot, SD,
until his death in 1983. He was 84.

John worked at various jobs in the Java area including WPA during the "Dirty
Thirties" until about 1911, when he was hired as a section hand laborer for the
Milwaukee Railroad, from which he retired at the age of 67. Martha was a busy
homemaker who was an avid reader, enjoyed gardening and loved to travel. She and
John traveled from coast-to-coast, visiting relatives. Both were life-long
members of St. Paul Lutheran Church in Java.

(Photo:) Martha and John Kapfenstein

They had 3 children: Orville, who died shortly after birth; Oscar, who was a
teacher and principal and lived in several SD communities; and Roger, who was
business manager for the Aberdeen region with the SD Dept. of Transportation in
Aberdeen.

Roger retired June 26, 1993 and he and his wife, former Mona Cressman of
Herreid, continue to make their home in Aberdeen, where Mona is still employed
with the SD Dept. of Transportation in Aberdeen.

        Oscar Kapfenstein
Oscar has come "full circle" in that he started life in Java. After a lengthy
absence from his hometown, he is again a resident of the town of Java.

Oscar, second son of John and Martha Kapfenstein, was born in Java on Mar. 4,
1928. He attended the Java Public School for 12 years, graduating in 1946. He
also worked at Hepper's Market during his school years and, following high
school graduation, worked for two years in local stores and as an extra-hand for
the Milwaukee Railroad prior to entering NSU (then called Northern State
Teachers College). Following one year of college, he taught at Alamo School six
miles east of Java, from 1949-51. In the fall of 1951, he taught in the West
Spring Valley School SW of Java until Sept. 21, at which time Uncle Sam called
him to serve in the Army for two years. After basic and advanced basic training
he was transferred to the 89th AAA Gun Battalion, a perimeter defense of
Washington, D.C., and Baltimore, MD. There he received additional training as
cook and mess steward and was charged with training others as cooks for overseas
duty. Following an honorable discharge from the Army on Sept 21, 1953, Oscar
resumed college studies at NSU in Aberdeen and received a Bachelor of Science
Degree in Elementary Education in 1954. He received a Master of Science Degree
in Elementary Education Administration in 1974. Oscar was an honor student, a
member of the collegiate choir, college fraternity, and has received several
honors and awards since.

(Photo:) Oscar Kapfenstein

Oscar's additional teaching experience included teaching in Java (6 years),
Mobridge (1 year), Herreid (9 years), and Wilmot, S.D. (17 years) - as an
Elementary Administrator and Special Education Coordinator - the first 4 years
in this position, he also served the Summit Schools as an administrator, on a
part-time basis.

After retirement, at the age of 63, in July 1991, Oscar moved back to Java and
following some renovation, moved into the Kapfenstein family home purchased by
his parents in 1948.

Oscar has never married. He is very interested in people and animals, spending
much time, money and effort in promoting the well being of "fellow creatures."
He is also into reading, yard work, TV, volunteerism (church council, Java
Community Store Corp., and several other organizations) and traveling (when he
can spare the time).

Oscar was baptized, confirmed, and is a current member of St. Paul Lutheran
Church in Java, where he has participated in church choirs, men's quartets,
church council. In his earlier years he was Sunday school teacher, Bible School
teacher for many years, and was a substitute organist for German church
services.

        Valentine and Marianna (Aman) Kary Sr.
In 1907, Mr. and Mrs. Valentine Kary, Sr., both born in Landau, South Russia,
decided to make the long journey to America, arriving in the town of Java in
Jan.1908, with their large family of six boys and four girls.

(Photo:) Valentine and Marianna Kary, Sr.

The entire Valentine Kary family left Russia. When they arrived at Germany, the
oldest daughter, Katherine, was unable to continue the trip to America due to
her husband's illness. Although the family received a few letters from her the
first few years, no one has seen her since. The rest of the family arrived in
America on the ship Koln, and the next oldest daughter Rose, and her husband
continued to SD while the rest of the Kary family remained in New York for two
more months because of illness.

Jacob Aman, Sr., brother of Mrs. Kary, met them with a bobsled and brought them
to Java, where they made their home with the Amans for two years.

The Kary family built their first new home in America in the Sutley area of
Campbell County. The home was built of mud and straw, and labor was done by
father, sons, and help from Jacob Aman and sons. The house consisted of three
rooms. The Kary home was located 12 miles north and one-half mile west of Java.
They lived in this home for a number of years.

Later the Karys homesteaded NE of Java and remained on this farm until their
children were grown and married. Mr. and Mrs. Kary retired to Eureka. Marianna
(Aman) Kary passed away on Mar. 20, 1946 at the age of 84. Valentine Kary died
Nov. 12, 1947 at the age of 87.

The Kary family consisted of Katherine (Rinck), Rose (Heinrick), Elizabeth
(Eberhardt), Lydia (Schneider), John, Mike, Jacob, Reinhold, Emanuel, Valentine
Jr., and Albert (born in America). One son died in Russia.

        Michael and Martha (Biel) Kary
Michael Kary was born 1897, to Valentine and Marianna (Aman) Kary, Sr., at South
Russia. At the age of 11 years, Michael came to America with his parents to join
friends and relatives.

(Photo:) Michael and Martha Kary

Michael's first homestead was with the Jake Aman family seven miles NE of Java.
This was the family home until spring, when they moved to various other farms in
the Java area. Michael grew to manhood in the Java area and worked as a farmhand
for many years. On Oct. 9, 1919, Michael married Martha Biel, the daughter of
Mr. and Mrs. George Biel, Sr., who had homesteaded six miles north of Java.

After their marriage, the young couple settled on a farm 9 miles NE of Java,
which is now owned and operated by the LeRoy Sandmeier family. Three children
were born to Michael (Mike) and Martha. Claudia Pfaff Marchewitz lives in
Mobridge. She has three children, Carol Beck, Donald Pfaff and Dixie Schilling.
Alvin had two children, Dianna and Jim. Alvin died Mar. 24, 1966. Wilbur married
Lorraine Boschee and they had two sons, Steve and Terry. Wilbur passed away
1998.

The Michael Kary family lived on various farms around the Java area until they
retired. In 1950, the Karys purchased a home in Java. They operated a creamery
for eight years and then Mike became owner and operator of Mike's Salvage, while
Martha was a housewife. Many years later Mike and Martha helped their daughter
operate Claudia's Cafe for two-and-a-half years.

On Feb. 19, 1976, Martha passed away at the age of 78. Mike entered the Selby
Good Samaritan Center. He died on Dec. 2, 1984, at the age of 87, and was buried
beside his wife at the Java United Church of Christ Cemetery.

        Wilbur and Lorraine (Boschee) Kary
On July 2, 1926, Wilbur was born to Mike and Martha (Biel) Kary at Eureka.
During his childhood, they lived on farms in Campbell and Walworth counties. He
attended Adam's School and was a 1944 Java High School graduate.

The following Dec., he entered the Army, where he served until Nov. of 1946. He
then went back to farming. On Sept. 30, 1948, at the Sutley Congregatinal
Church, he married Lorraine Boschee, born Nov. 10, 1928 at Hillsview. They
stayed on his parents' farm, where they lived until 1998, when Wilbur became
ill.

(Photo:) Wilbur and Lorraine kary Family

Wilbur served as a district and county school board member for eight years. He
was a member of the Walworth County ASCS committee for 10 years. Besides
farming, he operated a plumbing business from the farm.

He retired from farming in 1977, and went to work for Federal Crop Insurance
until 1982. He worked for Northwest G.F. Mutual Insurance in Eureka until 1988,
and then served on the board of directors for three years.

While they were farming, Lorraine did the bulk of the milking. She also worked
part-time at the Java Municipal Liquor Store for a few years.

The Karys moved the farmhouse into Selby shortly before Wilbur passed away in
Aug. 1998.

Wilbur and Lorraine had two sons. Terry Lee Kary was born Oct. 30, 1952 at
Eureka. He married Connie Walz, daughter of Orville and Delores Walz, on June 7,
1980. Terry and Connie are owners of Kary's Lumber Company in Mobridge, where
they reside, and Connie is an RN at the Mobridge Medical Clinic. They have two
sons, Jesse Mark Foster and Levi Bill Kary. Jesse married Denise Mertz on May
29, 1999 and Levi is a student at Mobridge High School.

Steven Michael Kary was born Apr. 21, 1955 at Bowdle. He married Alice Grode on
June 10, 1978. They both work at Hutch Tech. and live in Sioux Falls. They have
two daughters, Jessica Lynn and Lindsey Jo.

        Emanuel "Mandy" R. and Gertrude Kary
Emanuel R. Kary was born Apr. 9, 1903, at Landau, South Russia, the son of
Valentine and Maria Kary. Gertrude Flemmer Kary was born June 5, 1909, at
Eureka, the daughter of Philipp and Katharina Flemmer. The two were united in
marriage on June 14, 1928.

"Mandy" was a barber in Bowdle until he purchased the Louie Gershin Store in
Java in 1941. They were members of the Java Lutheran Church. Gertrude served as
president of the Ladies Aid, taught Sunday school and Bible school. Mr. Kary was
an active member of the Java Chamber of Commerce, serving as president. He was
also active in civic affairs and served on city improvement projects.

In 1951, the Karys sold their store, Kary's Market, to Gilbert and LaRayne
Schlepp and moved to Mobridge, where Mandy worked as a salesman for the Mobridge
Wholesale Company. Later he became a car salesman for Davidson Chevrolet. In
1956, the Karys returned to Java and purchased the Red Owl Store from Elmer
Biel. They sold this store in 1959 to Marvin Pfitzer.

The Karys had three sons: Richard E., who graduated from Java High School in
1949, has four daughters; Dean P. graduated from Java High School in 1952. Dean
has four sons and one daughter. Merlin J. graduated from Mobridge High School
and has two children.

Emanuel "Mandy" Kary died Sept. 1989, and is buried in Zion Lutheran Cemetery in
Eureka. Gertrude Kary resides in Aberdeen.

        Albert and Maggie (Goetz) Kary
Albert Kary, son of Valentine and Marianna (Aman) Kary, was born Mar. 17, 1908
in Walworth County. He attended school in Campbell County. Albert worked many
years as a labor man.

(Photo:) Albert and Maggie Kary

Albert married Maggie Goetz on Sept. 14, 1937, at Java. Maggie Goetz was the
daughter of Charlie and Magdelena Goetz. Maggie was born in Rock Spring in
Rosebud County, MT. She moved to the Java area as a small child with her family.
She attended Hartman School in Walworth County. They moved to a vacant farm NE
of Java, where Albert worked for his brother Jake Kary. They did not have a car,
so Albert borrowed two horses from his brother Jake, and he and Maggie went
places with a stone boat pulled by the horses. This method of transportation
limited them to a trip no further than two and one-half miles. After about two
and one-half years, they bought a 1923 Model T Ford Coup. Albert bought it at an
auction sale for $18.00.

One daughter, Vera (Darling-Osness), was born on Dec. 30, 1941.

In 1947, they purchased a farm on the west edge of Java. In 1959, a tornado
demolished their complete farm. They built a new home in Java in 1960. In 1984,
they sold their home and moved to Groton. Maggie passed away on Mar. 1, 1994.
Albert passed away Mar. 12, 1994. They are buried in the Sunset Memorial
Gardens, Aberdeen.

Albert and Maggie have six grandchildren and 9 great-grandchildren.

        Henry and Paulina (Buckenberger) Kast
Henry Kast was born Dec. 7, 1885, in Odessa, Russia. He was left an orphan at an
early age. His father passed away at the age of 35 and his mother at the age of
38. This left a family of four surviving boys and one daughter. One son passed
away in infancy.

At the age of 16, Henry came to the U.S. with his brothers, Christ, Edward, and
Rudolph, and his sister, Katherine. He worked for his uncle in Lincoln, NE, who
had a blacksmith shop. They did various jobs for people for board and room. In
those days there was no ADC or welfare to take care of the needy, so it was
quite a struggle for the remaining children.

In Feb. 1908, he married Paulina Buckenberger, the daughter of Andrew and
Dorothea (Oswald) Buckenberger, born in Yankton County in Jan. 1884. They
struggled and saved and eventually bought the Buckenberger farm in Campbell
County near Sutley. For some time his brothers and sister lived with them.

(Photo:) Henry Kast Family. Leon, Mr. Kast. Front: Frieda, Mrs. Kast, and Ida

There were six children born to them, two sons and four daughters. The first two
children died in infancy. In Oct. 1911 twins were born, who were Leon and Ida
Kast (Rosin). Ida passed away in 1972 and Leon in 1995. Five years later in Oct.
1916, another set of twins was born to them, who were Frieda and one who died in
infancy.

They remained on the farm until Feb. 1923. Because of ailing health, they had a
farm auction, bought a house in Java and moved to town. The children finished
their education in the Java Public School. Leon graduated in 1932 and in the
same year married Nettie Spiry. They made their home in Java all of their
married life. Two sons were born to them, Adrian and Lynn. (See Family History)
Ida graduated in 1929, and in 1936 she married William Rosin of Selby. They had
three children: Corrine (Rosin) Quenzer, Carol (Rosin) Reuer of rural Hoven and
William H. Rosin, Jr., of Selby. Frieda graduated in 1935 and married Art
Himrich in 1936 in a double wedding with her sister Ida. They had one daughter,
Sharon (Bob) Osborne of Baxter, MN.

The Henry Kasts again went to farming, but farmed from town until 1951, when
they sold their farm to Gust Rau. Henry suffered a heart condition and passed
away in Mar. 1957, at the age of 71. Mrs. Kast continued to reside in Java until
health failed. She spent some time with the children and in the Mobridge Care
Center, until her death in Feb. 1963 at the age of 79.

They were members of the Reformed Church at Sutley and at Java.

They went through many hardships during the drought and grasshopper plague, but
never lost faith in this country. Mr. Kast would often relate his younger days
when he worked in the blacksmith shop. Many nights were spent in the cold with
only a coat to cover and the forge his only heat source. There were many nights
he was so hungry he couldn't sleep.

Most of the things were done together on the farm. At harvest time Mrs. Kast
would help in the fields, as most women were accustomed to doing. Milking 16
cows by hand was not unusual.

        Leon and Nettie (Spiry) Kast
Leon Kast was born to Pauline (Buckenberger) and Henry Kast 12 miles north of
Java, on Oct. 20, 1911. He attended the Buckenberger Country School north of
Java until the age of 10, when he moved with his parents to Java. He then
attended school in Java, graduating with the Java High School class of 1932.
During his high school years he was very active in sports. He was a member of
the 1930 Java High School basketball team that won the District Tournament. He
also played baseball in the summer.

Nettie (Spiry) Kast was born Sept. 3, 1910, on a farm three and one-half miles
NE of Java, a daughter of Fred and Justina (Ernst) Spiry. She attended the
Hawthorne Country School. At the age of 11, she moved to Java with her parents
and graduated from high school in 1929. While in high school she was a member of
the Girls Glee Club and active in sports. In 1925 when she was a freshman, her
basketball team won their way to the State Basketball Tournament at Mitchell.
They traveled by train, which was quite a treat in those days. She was a member
of the "Rainbow Trio," a dance team with two of her classmates.

After graduation, she attended Northern University at Aberdeen for a year, and
taught country school for three years.

Leon and Nettie were married at Mobridge May 28, 1932, and lived in Java all
their years. The "Dirty Thirties," as they were called at that time, were bad.
Weather was very dry and the dust storms were severe. People were all hard up
and had no money. Leon worked on the WPA around Java. After that, he worked for
the Java and Selby Equity for 34 years. He was very active in the community as
he served on the Java School board, Java City Council, church council and was
active on the Fire Department. Leon enjoyed being outside, especially fishing or
working in the garden.

Nettie was a busy housewife and liked to cook and bake. She was a member of the
Lutheran Choir for many years; also a member of the Java Garden Club since it
was organized in 1953. She enjoys gardening and raising flowers and did a lot of
flower arranging and enjoys going to flower shows. She also likes to cook and
bake. When Leon went fishing she accompanied him many times.

Leon died on Sunday, Aug. 20, 1995, at the Mobridge Regional Hospital. He was
83. They were married 63 years. Nettie continues to reside in their home in
Java.

Leon and Nettie have two sons, Adrian and Lynn and three grandchildren and four
great-grandchildren.

(Photo:) Lynn, Nettie, Leon, Adrian Kast

Adrian was born Oct. 25, 1933, at Java. He attended all 12 years of school at
Java. Took up depot agent under Col. Weatherly at Java. In 1952, he went to work
for the Milwaukee Railroad as depot agent. While a depot agent for 20 years, he
worked at 34 different stations, some more than once. In 1970, Adrian went to
signal school at Milwaukee, WI and then worked as signal maintainer at
Hettinger, ND until his retirement. While working for the railroad he was an
officer in the union. He was auditor for the city of Haynes, ND for 33 years,
officer on the church board and the fire district. He served in the Army from
1956 through 1958.

Adrian married Shirley Bieber Aug. 8, 1954, at St. Paul Lutheran Church in Java.
Shirley (Bieber) Kast was born Feb. 19, 1933, at Hoven to Gust and Marie
(Schreter) Bieber. She attended elementary school at West Ryan Country School
and high school at Java. While going to country school, she and her sister rode
horse or walked in all kinds of weather. She worked for the First National Bank
at Mobridge as bookkeeper for several years, was a 4-H leader, taught Sunday
school, and was an officer for the church circle and on the Haynes City Board
for 26 years.

They have two children, Barbara (Kast) Quintus, born Aug. 30, 1960 at Mobridge,
went to school at Haynes and Hettinger, ND. She attended Dickinson State
University and got her teaching degree. She teaches and is a volleyball coach at
Killdeer, ND. She married Steve Quintus Sept. 3, 1983. They have three children,
Matthew, Brian, and Stephanie. They now reside at Killdeer, ND; Scott Kast was
born Dec. 7, 1965 at Hettinger, ND. He attended school at Hettinger and went to
Dickinson State University and North Dakota University. He teaches computer
science at Minot State University. He married Brenda Olien June 22, 1991. They
have two children, Tyler and Sidni, and reside at Minot, ND. Adrian and Shirley
now reside at Bismarck, ND.

Lynn was born in Bowdle on Oct. 17, 1941. He attended school in Java, where he
graduated from Java High School in 1961.

Lynn married Sharon K. Wentz on Mar. 17, 1967, in Bismarck, ND. Shortly
thereafter, he joined the Army and completed his basic training at Ft.
LeonardWood, MO. Lynn was one of the seven in his platoon who was assigned to
Wurzburg, Germany. The remainder of his platoon was sent to Vietnam. Lynn's wife
joined him in Germany and they spent one-and-a-half years there. They had the
opportunity to travel to Holland, Denmark, Austria, Switzerland and Italy during
Lynn's tour-of-duty in Germany.

Lynn was discharged in Mar. 1969 and he and his wife settled in Elkhart, IN.
They have one son Kevin, who also lives in Elkhart with his wife Lesley.

        Adolph (Jeff) and Martha (Sandmeier) Keller
Adolph (Jeff) Keller was born Aug. 29. 1910, to Edward and Magdalena (Wolf)
Keller, near Bison. Martha Sandmeier was born to John and Barbara (Wald)
Sandmeier on Dec. 15, 1915, near Bowdle.

Jeff and Martha were married Dec. 29, 1936, at Selby. The first two months they
lived with her brother, Rudolph, and then moved to Jeff's grandparents' farm.
They herded sheep for Ben Stiegelmeier for $20 a month.

(Photo:) Jeff and Martha Keller

Their first daughter, Irene, was born Apr. 26, 1938. Two years later they moved
to the Adam Mertz farm and stayed there for five years. Shirley was born May 8,
1939. Jeff and Martha drove to town and church with horses many times. Jeff
bought a threshing machine and did some custom threshing in the Bowdle and Java
areas. Darlene was born Dec. 18, 1940. Finally things improved and they were
able to buy their own farm five miles east of Java. They bought 240 acres for $7
per acre, on a five-year term payment. Sometimes it was difficult to make a
payment, but they were lucky to have a good-hearted friend, George Sebert, who
offered to lend them the money for the land payment. They paid him back when
they had enough money.

Jeff loved horses and, at the age of 16, began buying and selling them. Tragedy
struck in 1959, when their house burned down. They lost everything, including
many of Irene's wedding gifts that she had stored there. With the help of good
neighbors, friends, and relatives, they were able to rebuild their home.

Jeff and Martha sold their farm to Paul and Sandy Jacobs in 1972 and moved to
Selby. Jeff enjoyed fishing, playing cards, and visiting friends. Martha enjoys
being outdoors and making quilts.

Irene married Wayne Holder. They live in Selby and had four children. Doreen
died in 1965 and Dean was killed in a car accident at age 9. Duane is married to
Sharon Stotz and they have three daughters, Stephanie, Stacy and Shantelle.
Darlise is married to Bobby Larson and they have three daughters, Rachel,
Samantha and Savana.

Shirley married Arliss Opheim. They live in Selby and have two children. Tammie
married Bobby Ducheneaux and they have two children, Skya and Jayden. Ronnie is
at home with his parents.

Darlene married Tommy Tefertiller. They live in Bozeman, MT and have a daughter,
Echo, who lives in Spokane, WA.

Jeff Keller passed away Jan. 12, 1992, and Martha still resides in Selby.

        Rev. George Kirchdoerfer Family
Rev. George Kirchdoerfer served St. Paul Lutheran Church of Java for 40 years.
He arrived in Java from Germany in May 1902. A year later, Wilhelmina Roth
arrived from Germany and the young couple was married at Marquette, WI,on June
24, 1903.

When Rev. Kirchdoerfer came to Java, the St. Paul congregation consisted of
eight families. The church building was small in structure but in a few years
was replaced with a new structure, 28x60 in size. The original church building
was used as a parochial school. The first parsonage was a two-room affair. In
1903, a new parsonage was built and enlarged in 1915.

(Photo:) The Kirchdoerfer Family. Rev. George Kirchdoerfer, Woldemar, Herbert,
         Minnie, Mrs. Kirchdoerfer, Herman

In addition to serving the Java congregation, Rev. Kirchdoerfer also served in
other towns in Walworth County, as well as Edmunds County, serving seven
congregations in all. He estimated that he traveled 25,000 miles with his ponies
while serving these congregations.

The Java congregation numbered 140 families when he retired in May of 1942. At
that time, he and Mrs. Kirchdoerfer moved to Waverly, IA, where they spent the
rest of their days. Rev. Kirchdoerfer passed away in Mar. 1960, and Mrs.
Kirchdoerfer, June 1972. The Kirchdoerfers had six children; two died in
infancy, Minnie, Woldemar, Herman and Herbert. Woldemar, born Feb. 24, 1910 at
Java, died Dec. 5, 1997 at Woodbury, MN.

        John and Emma (Sonnenfeld) Klein
John Klein was born in Glueckstal, South Russia on Jan. 26, 1892, the son of
Peter and Rosina (Schlichter Kurle) Klein. When his mother married Peter Klein,
she was a widow with three small children, Elizabeth, Jake and Eva Kurle.

(Photo:) Emma, Ida and John Klein

As a result of exposure suffered during a winter storm, Peter Klein developed
pneumonia and never regained his health. He died when John was a young child.
His mother then married a widower, Bratzel. Christ Bratzel was born to this
union. She was widowed for the third time when Mr. Bratzel died in a threshing
accident. Women had no property rights in Russia and life was very hard for the
family. The mother worked as a midwife. Her children stayed with relatives and
John went to live with a childless family and was treated harshly.

Later his mother remarried to Christian Goetz, and a son, Simon, was born. In
1905, Mr. Goetz brought the family to America. The oldest daughter remained in
Russia as her plans were for marriage. John was 13 years old when they settled
in the Lowry-Akaska area. From then on he was self-supporting. He was employed
in the summers as a farmhand and in the winters he spent as a janitor for
various hotels for room and board. Later he found employment with the railroad
at Wishek, ND.

John was living with his half-sister, Eva, and husband, Jake Eisenbeisz, when he
met his future bride. On Jan. 19, 1915, John married Emma Sonnenfeld, daughter
of John and Rosina (Fischer) Sonnenfeld. The young couple made their home with
Eva and Jake Eisenbeisz until 1915, when they settled on a farm seven miles NE
of Java. Their daughter Ida was born here and they remained here until 1938,
when the family moved to Eureka, where John owned and operated a service
station. In 1944, they moved to Bowdle, and remained in farming until 1958 when
their daughter Ida and her husband, Herbert Fiechtner, took over the farm. Emma
died on Jan. 22, 1972, and John passed away Apr. 8, 1972.

Ida and Herbert farmed the home place until 1972, when their youngest son, Joel,
and his wife, Kathy (Mittleider), took over the management of the farm. Their
other children are Phonia (Harvey) Diedtrich, Terry married Arliss Schilling,
Connie (Rodney) Blumhardt, John, Barbara (Norby) Reuer.

        Felix and Verna (Martz) Knittel
Felix was born Oct. 30, 1908, at Hosmer to Christian and Emelia (Pietzke)
Knittel. His father passed away when Felix was three and a half years old. His
mother, brother and sister moved to Bowdle and lived with his grandma Pietzke
for a number of years.

(Photo:) Verna and Felix Knittel

Emelia met Jacob Merkel of Hazelton, ND and they were married and lived at
Hazelton, ND. Felix finished his schooling there. Later he went to Bowdle and
lived with his aunt and uncle, the A.C. Schoenfelders. There he worked on the
dray line and later in the pool hall.

In 1933, he moved to Java and stayed with Gottlieb Schock and Reinhold Baker. He
also worked in the Schock meat market.

On Apr. 28, 1935, he married Verna Martz at the Lutheran parsonage. Rev.
Kirchdoerfer performed the ceremony. They made their home in Java. He served on
the school board and water department, was a fireman and the city cop. When the
co-op station was built, he was the manager.

In 1952, they moved to Mobridge and he was assistant manager at Central Lumber
Company. In 1957, he was transferred to Linton, ND and became the manager. In
1962, he was transferred to Aberdeen to work for Weyerhausan Lumber Company and
U.B.O. After he became very ill, he quit working at the lumber company and later
worked at NSC. He had to retire because of ill health.

Mrs. Knittel worked at the J.C. Penney store. They had two children. Edith
married Joe Chesmore and lives at Watertown. Peggy married Phillip Hoffsten and
lives in Pierre.

Felix and Verna celebrated their 50th Wedding Anniversary in 1985. Felix passed
away 11 days later. He battled cancer for many years. Mrs. Knittel still resides
in Aberdeen.

        Gerard Kosters Family
Gerard (George) Kosters was born in Ottersum, Netherlands, Mar. 12, 1969, to
Peter (1821-1873) and Antonia Verriet (1826-1894) Kosters. When he was 15 years
old he went to Germany and worked in the coalmines. In 1892 he immigrated to the
U.S., going to Bessmer, MI, where he was employed in an iron mine. In 1893 he
came to Appleton, WI, where he found employment in a paper mill, staying there
for about one year. In 1894 he came to Hoven, where he worked as a farm hand.

(Photo:) Gerard and Maria Kosters

In 1897, he filed on a homestead in the Spring Lake District SE of Java. He
married Maria Theunissen of Aberdeen on Nov. 1, 1898, at Sacred Heart Catholic
Church, in a double wedding with her sister, Wilhelmina Theunissen and Joseph
Yoeman. Maria was born at Mook, Netherlands, July 23, 1874 to Hendrikus
(1815-1883) and Wilhelmina Wanders (1835-1884) Theunissen. She came to America
with her parents when she was a young girl.

On May 17, 1902, he signed his naturalization papers. Today, Rodney and Beverly
Ruzsa own the Kosters' homestead. Beverly is the granddaughter of Gerard
Kosters.

George was a man ever ready to help his friends and a booster for both community
and state. He was interested in better schools and did much toward the
improvement of the community in which he lived. He specialized in diversified
farming and dairying.

George and Maria had eleven children: Wilhelmina, Antonia (1901-1907), Gertrude,
Maria, Peter, Henry, Antonia, Garret, Elizabeth, Katherine and John.

George gave his daughter Gertrude's hand in marriage to Steve Bruckner in 1924.
He passed away on July 5, 1925 at the Colonial Hospital, Rochester, MN. He had
one grandson at the time of his death, Fred Bruckner.

Maria was able to attend the weddings of two daughters, Wilhelmina to Gottlieb
Schuh and Maria to George Sebert. She had three grandsons and her wish to have a
granddaughter was granted with Mary Ann Bruckner. Marie passed away at Java on
May 22, 1929.

As of Aug. 1997 there were 80 grandchildren, 200 great grandchildren, 182 great-
great grandchildren, and two great-great-great grandchildren.

Wilhelmina (Min) Kosters was born on Sept. 9, 1899 at Java. Min attended grade
school at East Spring Valley and her younger years were spent helping her
parents on the farm. The Kosters family lost their parents when several of the
children were at a young age, and Min helped raise several of her brothers and
sisters: Antonia, Garret, Elizabeth, Katherine and John. She was a member St.
Anthony's Catholic Church and had served as president of the Altar Society for
several years. She was a candidate for Woman of the Year in 1966, had been a 4-H
leader for 35 years and had worked for a number of years on the Easter Seal
Drive.

(Photo:) Min and Guy Schuh

She married Gottlieb (Guy) Schuh at St. Augustine's Catholic Church in Bowdle on
Nov. 16, 1926. Guy and Min lived with his sister, Louise and John Witlock for
the first year of their married life. In 1929, they moved to their home located
on the south side of Highway 12 - 10 miles SE of Selby, where Min resided until
the time of her death. She died Saturday, Feb. 18, 1967 at the Mobridge
Community Hospital.

In 1942, with the death of her sister, Antonia, Min brought back her infant
nephew, John, and Min and Guy raised him as their own. John Witlock, their
brother-in-law, lived with them for 13 years. Guy continued to live on his home
place until 1974, when he moved and made his home with the nephew he had raised,
John S. Stefanich and family.

Guy and Minnie's old house became an antique and gift shop known as Aunt
Minnie's Attic in 1984. Friends and neighbors helped renovate it after having
been empty for 10 years. Tourists and local people visit all year long.

Gottlieb was born Apr. 18, 1903 to Urban and Mary (Schmidt) Schuh SE of Java.
Both his parents died by the time he was eight. He quit school and went to live
with various relatives until he reached adulthood. Guy's fields of wheat were
his pride and joy. He loved his teams of horses, liked to dance in his younger
days, enjoyed playing cards and meeting his friends at the nutrition site. He
died at the Mobridge Care Center on Sunday, Mar. 16, 1997 at the age of 93. Due
to the hard winter with lots of snow, Guy was not buried until Apr. 18, 1997, on
his birthday.

Gertrude (Gert) Kosters was born on May 22, 1903 at Java. Gert attended grade
school at East Spring Valley and her younger years were spent on the farm
helping her parents. She was married to Steve Bruckner, (son of Ferdinand,
1862-1920 and Julia, 1871-1946 Bruckner, both deceased), at St. Augustine's
Catholic Church in Bowdle on Feb. 20, 1924. Steve was born Mar. 2, 1897 at
Bangor. He grew up in the Bangor-Selby area.

Twelve children were born to them: Ferdinand, Joseph, Mary Ann, Anthony,
Leonard, LaVern, Margaret, Steve, Elizabeth, Francis, Katherine and Florence.

Steve and Gert lived on a farm 10 and one-half miles SE of Selby. In 1946, they
purchased a farm near Ipswich, where they resided until they retired and moved
to Aberdeen, purchasing a new home.

Gert was a member of the Sacred Heart Altar Society and Sacred Heart Band 12,
Aberdeen. She died Jan. 24, 1982. Steve passed away on Oct. 14, 1982. There are
37 grand children and 51 great-grandchildren.

Maria Kosters was born Mar. 23, 1905 at Java. Maria was married to George A.
Sebert at St. Augustine's Catholic Church in Bowdle on Jan. 11, 1928. Nine
children were born to them: Leo, Albert, Arthur, Leonard, Louis, Frances,
Dorothy, Raymond and George. There are 31 grandchildren and 30
great-grandchildren. (See Family History)

Peter (Pete) Kosters was born May 17, 1907 at Java. His future wife, Theresa
(Tracy) Raba was born June 11, 1907 at Selby to Andrew and Theresa (Bertha)
Raba; they were married on Sept. 25, 1929 at St. Anthony's Catholic Church in
Selby.

Nine children were born to them: Virginia; Leander, born Aug. 12, 1932, passed
away at the age of 36 at Fargo, ND; Delores, born Feb. 8, 1935, passed away at
infancy; Laurena; Gerald; Florence; Patricia; Duane and Roger, born Mar. 1,
1952, passed away at the age of 20 on Sept. 23, 1972 at Selby. Peter and Theresa
have 22 grandchildren and 25 great-grandchildren.

Peter and Theresa both attended East and West Spring Valley Schools,
respectively. After graduating from the eighth grade they each helped their
parents on their farms, which were seven miles apart in central Walworth County.
Starting their lives together on the homestead of his father, George Kosters, SE
of Java, they moved to what was the Ladislaus Kormendy farm in 1936.

In 1938, they left farm life and moved to Selby, making their home at the
Lakeman Hotel. Peter worked with the WPA and then went to work for Jake

bought into the John Deere Implement and Ford Dealers business, and it was known
as Rabenberg's Inc. Pete was a member of St. Anthony's Catholic Church. Pete
passed away July 23, 1983. In Sept. 1979, they celebrated their 50th
Anniversary. Theresa is a member of St. Anthony's Catholic Church and St.
Anthony's Altar Society and a member of the Selby Nutrition Site. In 1997, Tracy
celebrated her 90th birthday. She still resides at her home in Selby.

Virginia married John Off and had two daughters. There are five grandchildren.

Leander (deceased Apr. 29, 1969) married Bernadetta Litschewski. They had three
children and 5  grandchildren.

Laurena married Bob Idler. They live in Selby and have two daughters and three
grandchildren.

Jerry and Elaine live in Selby. They have three sons and one daughter. There are
eight grandchildren.

Florence and Roy Karst live in Selby. They have four children and six
grandchildren.

Patty and Gerald "CJ" Niemiller live in Selby. They have two sons and one
grandchild.

Duane and Deb and their four children live in Oklahoma City, OK.

Henry  Kosters was born July 4, 1909 at Java. He passed away Mar. 10, 1976 at
Selby. Henry married Mary E. Horvath, daughter of Mike and Victoria Kovachs
Kormendy Horvath at St. Anthony's Catholic Church at Selby on Dec. 28, 1931.

Henry attended grade school at East Spring Valley. He was raised on a farm south
of Java. During the dust bowl days of the Thirties, Henry and Mary farmed 9
miles SE of Selby known as the Horst place and lived with his sister Maria and
George Sebert for the first year. In 1936, they moved to Harvey, IL and Henry
worked as an auto mechanic. They moved back to Selby in 1950 and ran the Oliver
Implement for 14 years. Henry also worked for Selby Implement and as shop
foreman for the Walworth County Highway Department. Henry was retired when he
passed away. At the time of his death, Mary was a cook at the Good Samaritan
Center, where she worked for 14 years.

Seven children were born to them: Henry (married Ruby Helm) of Pierre; Florence,
born Oct. 26, 1933 at Java, passed away at Selby on Feb. 15, 1937; Morris
(married Janice Helm) of Rapid City; Eugene (married Ruth Quinn) of Tooele, UT;
Elizabeth (married Jerry Schlueter) of Frankfort; Carol (married Darreld Badure)
of Mobridge; and Edward (married Kaylene Greger) of Wright, WY.

Antonia Kosters was born on July 18, 1911 at Java, and passed away at Muskegon,
MI on Jan. 9, 1942. Antonia was married to Frank Stefanich, son of Demeter and
Anna Stefanich (both deceased) at St. Anthony's Catholic Church in Selby on Nov.
8, 1933. Four children were born to them: Delbert July 11, 1934, passed away on

        Johanas and Louise (Weidenlich) Krause
The reason most pioneers came to America was discontentment with their life in
the "Old Country" and to find and settle new land. Such was the case with
Johanas Krause. He sold all his possessions in Russia and came to America,
looking for farmland to provide a livelihood and a place to settle. John must
have chosen his site very well, as the homestead they selected has remained in
the Krause family for 111 years.

(Photo:) Johanas Krause Family. Back: Bertha, Katherine, Israel C. Front: Alex,
         John, Lydia, Louise

John Krause was born Sept. 14, 1865, in South Russia, a son of Karl and Minnie
(Reich) Krause. On Dec. 18, 1886, he was married to Louise Weidenlich, who was
born Mar. 20, 1868 at Friedensthal, Roumania, where she was baptized. Louise was
confirmed in 1882 in Arzis. They had seven children, two of whom, a daughter and
a son, died in infancy; the other two sons and three daughters being: Katherine,
Israel C., Bertha, Alex and Lydia.

The family came to the U.S. in 1889, settling on a farm five miles north of
Java, where the youngest five of their children were born. Here, the family
worked together and endured the hardships, misfortunes and illnesses that were
typical of all their pioneer neighbors.

After living on their farm for 46 years, Mr. and Mrs. Krause built a home in
Java in 1935 and moved to town. Mrs. Krause, 69, passed away in 1937. John
Krause, 91, died on Dec. 23, 1956.

Katherine (Katie) Krause was born Apr. 10, 1890, on the farm north of Java,
where she grew up and attended school. On Oct. 29, 1912, she married Christ M.
Haux at Java, and they made their home on a farm two miles NW of Java. Her
husband passed away on June 29, 1942, and she continued to live on the farm
until 1945, when she moved to town. She passed away on her 78th birthday, Apr.
10, 1968. She was the mother of six children: Robert married Frieda Goetz;
Wilson (deceased); Herman H. (deceased) married Verna Laemmle, and had three
children, Gene, Candice and Darcy; Herbert (deceased) married Esther Haux and
had one daughter Mercedes; Evelyn married Fred Johnle; and Bertha married Ray
Kasper and had three children, LeAnn, Gregory and Raymond.

Israel C. Krause was born May 19, 1891 on the farm north of Java, where he
attended rural school and lived all his life. On Oct. 8, 1935, he married Lydia
Schilling at Bowdle, and they made their home on the family homestead, north of
Java, until his death on Sept. 12, 1973, at the age of 82. Israel was the father
of three children, Harlan lives north of Java, married Ramona Buechler of Bowdle
and has four children, Marcia, Marlys, Sheila and James; Harry lives on the
homestead north of Java; and Stella married Harlan Buechler of Bowdle where they
live on a farm and have three children, Max, Mavis and Marilyn. Lydia Schilling
Krause passed away Dec. 24, 1999 at the age of 96.

Bertha Krause was born Sept. 5, 1893, on the homestead north of Java, where she
grew to womanhood. She was confirmed on Mar. 20, 1910, and was united in
marriage to William Frank of Aberdeen, on May 12, 1921. The couple lived in
Aberdeen for some time, went to Brookings, where Mr. Frank attended school, then
returned to Java. She passed away Jan. 31, 1923, at the age of 29. She was the
mother of two sons: Art, who lives in Java; and Wes, who married Ruth Kurle,
lives in Java, and has two children, Clyde and Colleen.

Alex Krause was born Dec. 22, 1896 at the homestead north of Java, where he grew
up and attended school. Much of his youth was plagued with illness. He spent all
his life on farms north of Java except for the 14 months he spent in the Navy,
enlisting in 1918. On June 22, 1931, he married Mary Boettcher at Selby. They
moved from their farm north of Java, into town in 1964. Alex died Dec. 9, 1980.
Mary Krause now resides in Aberdeen in New West Senior Housing, an assisted
living home. As of Aug. 1998 Mary remains healthy and very happy.

They had one son, Wilbur, who lived on the farmstead north of Java with his wife
Mary Anne and family until 1975, when he divorced and moved to Java. He then
moved to Woonsocket before moving to Prescott Valley, AZ, where he worked for
Better Built Manufacturing until retiring in 1997. In Oct. 1981, he married
Maxine Kistler. Since both are now retired, they moved back to their home state
of SD in 1997. They currently reside in Alpena.

Mary Anne (Anderson) Krause is working for the Federal Government. Since
accepting this job, she has lived in the countries of Venezuela and Jamaica. She
still continues with this job as of 1998 and now resides in Washington, D.C.

Wilbur and Mary Anne had seven children. Cynthia (Kevin) Rau resides in Aberdeen
and is an RN for St. Luke's Hospital. They have two children Heather and
Matthew; Chloe (Courtney) Kaelberer resides in Bozeman, MT. She works as an LPN
in a doctor's clinic. They have two children Mandi and Brittney; Cathy (Nolan)
Lindemann resides in Aberdeen. She works as a Deputy in the Register of Deeds
office for Brown County. They have one daughter Sanessa; William (Wendy) Krause
resides in Tuscon, AZ where he and Wendy started their own landscape design and
nursery business "Terra Designs." They have two children Evan and Erin; Robert
is enlisted in the Air Force and as of Aug. 1998 is stationed in Anchorage, AK.
He has one daughter Madison, and she is living with him in Alaska; Ben died on

Before his death Ben had graduated from Woonsocket, enlisted in the National

        The I.R. Krause Family
Mr. and Mrs. Israel R. Krause and their parents were among Java's earliest
residents.

I.R. Krause was born in Bessarabia, South Russia of German parentage in 1882 and
came to the U.S. with his parents, Karl and Wilhelmina (Reich) Krause, and  his
brother Fred, and sister Ledia in 1890. The family settled on a homestead near
the farmstead of another older son, John, who, with his wife Louise, had come to
the U.S. in 1889.

I.R. Krause attended rural school near his home and, after completing the 8th
grade, taught that school for a number of years. In 1904, he and his brother,
Fred, established the Krause Mercantile Store, one of Java's first businesses.
He also did some barbering in his early years and was a member of one of Java's
first dance orchestras. He possessed unusual natural musical ability. He took
only a few lessons by correspondence course, yet could play practically any
instrument by ear, as well as by notes.

In 1913 he was named postmaster at Java and operated it in the north side of the
former Krause Mercantile store building, along with a jewelry and clock and
watch repair business. At that time, the Krause Mercantile store was
discontinued. As a sideline he also sold made-to-measure suits for men for many
years, as well as phonographs and records. He built a new Java post office
building in the fall of 1924; the local telephone switchboard was also moved to
the post office building, operating from there for a number of years. After
serving as postmaster for 23 years, he was replaced in that office by J.S.
Pfitzer. Mr. Krause then devoted full time to his favorite vocation, that of
tuning and fixing pianos and organs, serving a large area in this part of SD as
well as ND. He could repair or tune almost any instrument and also did sewing
machine adjusting.

He served as Justice of Peace of Java for many years. One of the anecdotes told
about him while he was serving in that office was typical. A traffic offender
had been brought before him and, after the case he told the defendant that the
fine was $25. "Oh, I've got that right in my pocket," quipped the man. "And one
day in jail!" continued Mr. Krause, "Have you got that in your pocket, too?" He
also served as Mayor of Java for two terms in the 1950's, and was a lifetime
member of the Java Fire Department.

He was a member of the Java and Selby bands for many years and directed the Java
school band for several years while serving as dean of the Java school dormitory
in the 1940's. He served as organist of St. Paul Lutheran church for 33 years
and as choir director for many of those years. He also organized the first
Little German Band at Java. Members of the original group were: Sam and Philip
H. Spiry, August C. and Gilbert Schlepp, Gerhard Bauman, and Mr. Krause and
daughter Cecelia and son Levi. For many years he also served as secretary of the
Modern Woodmen of America lodge at Java.

On Nov. 14,1905 he married Anna Mary Diegel, and they spent the remainder of
their lives in Java.

Mrs. Krause was born in 1885 on a farm near the eastern edge of Campbell County
south of Eureka, a daughter of Fred and Anna Maria Diegel. At the age of 13 she
moved with her family to a farm NW of Java and in 1902 to Java, where they
operated the Java Hotel for a number of years, Mrs. Krause serving as the chief
cook though she was only a teenager. After her marriage she was active in St.
Paul Lutheran Church and was one of the early members of the Ladies Aid of the
church. For many years she and her husband were members of a singing club
consisting of a group of couples who would gather on Sunday evenings for hymn
singing. Mr. Krause served as accompanist. She was also a member of the Sewing
Club, which was later known as the Thimble Club. Mrs. Anna Mary Krause passed
away in 1938.

(Photo:) Anna Maria and Israel R. Krause - 1905

In 1945, I.R. Krause married Katie (Haux) Pfaff of Java, and they continued to
make their home in the family residence. Mr. Krause died on May 4, 1966, and
Mrs. Krause died Oct. 15, 1969. She had two children, Arthur Pfaff and Clara
(Elmer) Biel.

        William and Katharine (Hirning) Kunz
Christina (Oswald) Kunz, recently widowed, and her two children, William, age
six, and Christina, age four, traveled to this area with friends and relatives
in 1884, after emigrating from Russia in earlier years. They settled 12 miles
north of Java, in the Sutley area of Campbell County. Christina married Ludwig
Boehler on Aug. 20, 1903 in Mound City. She passed away in May 1925 and Ludwig
passed away in Sept. 1926.

(Photo:) William and Katharine Kunz - 1901

William married Katharine Hirning at the Sutley Reformed Church in 1901.
Katharine (Katya) had arrived in the U.S. in 1893 with her foster parents when
she was 12 years old. The couple farmed on William's farmstead until 1910, when
they moved into Java.

William worked for the Crown Elevator Company in Java and Katya fulfilled the
contract as Mail Carrier, driving daily over the prairie from Sutley to Eureka
in a small two-wheel sulky.

For 32 years William operated the Java Equity Exchange. He was also president of
the Board of Education, belonged to the Woodman's Lodge, served as Mayor of Java
for two terms during the 1930's, served as Fire Chief for many years and was an
active church member.

When William retired from the Java Equity in 1945, they moved to Mobridge in to
be near their daughter, Erna, and her husband, Dr. A.W. Spiry. William passed
away Apr. 22, 1957, and Katya on May 6, 1972.

They had six children. Edward, born Nov. 17, 1904, graduated from Java High
School in 1923. He married Bertha Schuh and they had Ines and Nancy. Erna was
born Oct. 23, 1906 and graduated from Java High School in 1926. She taught
school for many years and married Dr. A.W. Spiry. She passed away Jan. 15, 1989,
preceded in death by her husband. They had Joyce and Bill. Nettie was born Sept.
10, 1908 and graduated from Java High School in 1926. She married Henry Hauck, a
teacher and coach. Nettie was a teacher for many years. They had Chloe and Bill
(See Family History). Wilfred was born Jan. 27, 1911 and graduated from Java
High School in 1929. He married Hazel Nupen and they had one child, Cindy
Dykema. Wilfred and Hazel operated a men's clothing store in Bismarck. Ervin,
born Nov. 8, 1913, graduated from Java High School in 1930. He married Verna
Lutz, a hospital registrar. He was once a teacher, wrestling coach, sales
trainer and management director. They had one daughter, Kathy, and two sons,
Bill and Dick. Ervin served in the Armed Forces during World War II. Howard was
born July 24, 1920 and graduated from Java High School in 1938. He married Verna
Hartman. They had Vicki and Marsha. Howard was a recipient of the Purple Heart
as a result of the Japanese skirmish on Leyte, the first island to be taken by
the American invasion on Oct. 20, 1944. While leading a reconnaissance group,
they stepped on a Japanese mine, which exploded and seriously injured all of
them. Howard spent months in an army hospital.

All but one of William and Katharine's children married residents of the Java
area.

        Christian and Karolina (Hafner) Kurle
Christian and Karolina (Hafner) Kurle and family entered the U.S. at Boston, MA

        Adolph and Edna (Speidel) Kurle
Adolph, son of Christian and Karolina (Hafner) Kurle, was born at Bergdorf,

(Photos:) Adolph Kurle and Edna Kurle

Edna was born to Christian and Eva (Ritter) Speidel on Oct. 19, 1910, on a farm

Jordon, MT near Miles City. Edna's father passed away in 1915 at Miles City at
