        Adam and Christina (Hoehn) Leno
Adam Leno was born Dec. 26, 1861, in Helental, South Russia. He was the son of
Heinrich Peter Leno, who was born in the same village. Heinrich was the son of
Peter Leno and the grandson of Johann Leno, both of whom had been born in
Prussia and migrated to Peterstal near Odessa in 1815.

Adam and Christina Hoehn were married in Helental on Dec. 20, 1883. In Aug.
1884, they came to America, landing at Scotland, Dakota Territory. After staying
with friends there for a short while, they took a train to Aberdeen and from
there to the small town of Ipswich, where the railroad ended. With the help of
Adam's cousin, Gottlieb Sieler, they bought a wagon, a breaking plow, some
tools, a pair of oxen, a cow, and a few chickens. They then set out for Sutley
in Campbell County, where they filed on a homestead.

(Photo:) Adam Leno Family. Back: Christina, Henry, Jacob, Peter and Johanna.
         Front: Mr. Adam Leno, George, Mrs. Adam Leno, Emmanuel

Their first house, including the roof, was built of sod. The floor was made of
tamped clay. In the fall and spring, barrels of water and sacks were always kept
handy to combat prairie fires. The Dakota winters were formidable natural
enemies of the pioneers. One of the worst on record was the winter of 1888. A
severe blizzard came early in the fall. Tunnels had to be dug from the house to
the barn and the well to provide food and water. Adam and seven of his neighbors
walked to Ipswich, about 65 miles, each carrying home 50 pounds of flour.

In the late fall of 1890, Adam's family and their neighbors experienced an
Indian scare. Stories of horrible massacres of whites by Indians spread
throughout the area. Hardware dealers, it seems, made sure that the settlers
heard these reports in order to promote the sale of firearms. So, when the rumor
of an impending attack spread through the area, a huge throng of settlers from
the Sutley territory fled to Eureka, the railroad terminal, to escape on trains.
Before reaching Eureka, however, many heard that it was a false rumor and
returned home. The Leno family witnessed a terrible diphtheria epidemic, which
broke out in their neighborhood and spread over a large area. Many did not
believe it to be contagious and visited the sick, taking their children along.
As a result, hundreds of children died in the Sutley area.

The homesteaders in the Sutley community experienced some very hard times. In
1889, the year the two Dakotas became states, they suffered a grasshopper
plague. A heavy frost on the night of July 4, 1894, turned all the crops black
by morning. Drought damaged the crops in 1894, 1898, 1900, 1901, and 1902. Like
many of his neighbors, Adam had to mortgage his homestead. In 1902, he
surrendered it and moved to a farm six miles from Java, which was owned by a Mr.
Banik, a Java businessman. In 1903, he and a group of friends and acquaintances
went to look at some land in western ND, which the government had opened up for
homesteading. They filed claims on land about 28 miles south of Hebron, ND and,
in the spring of 1904, they moved to their new locations with covered wagons and
all their personal property, including livestock, crossing the Missouri River on
a ferry somewhere near Cannonball, ND.

All of the children were born in Campbell County, north of what is now Java.
Henry, the oldest of the children, was born in 1886 near Sutley, Dakota
Territory.

        Louis (Loy) and Elizabeth (Simmon) Miklos II

(Photo:) Miklos Family. Ida, Sophia, Louis II, Joseph, Esther and Ella

served for three years.

Raymond Miklos was born Mar. 13,1945 at Mobridge. He attended grade school at

        Viola (Schlepp) Mittleider by Viola Mittleider
Viola (Schlepp) Mittleider was born Nov. 21, 1924, to Fred and Magdalena (Goetz)
Schlepp.

I grew up on a farm seven miles NE of Java, in a sod house built by my great-
grandparents, Karl and Rosina Oster, who with my grandparents, Gottlieb and
Christina (Oster) Goetz, came from Hoffnungstal, South Russia to America in 1897
and took up land through the Homestead Act. William McKinley was President at
the time. They built sod farm buildings within a quarter of a mile from each
other. This land has been in the same family for over 100 years.

The children of Karl and Rosina Oster were: Christian Oster, his wife Elizabeth;
Samuel Oster, his wife Wilhelmina; Adam Oster, his wife Katharina; Katharina
(Christian) Pfitzer; Rosina (Philipp) Spiry (Dr. Spiry's mother) and Christina
(Gottlieb) Goetz (my grandmother).

My grandfather Gottlieb Goetz passed away in 1911 and in 1919, my grandmother
Christina married Christian Pfitzer, in Java.

My grandparents, Gottlieb and Christina (Oster) Goetz, had a large family, My
mother, Magdalena (Goetz) Schlepp, was the 10th child and the only girl in her
family. Two of her brothers died in infancy, My dad died in 1947 and in 1957, my
mother married Samuel Schlepp.

The children in my mother's family are: Gottlieb and Barbara (Wallentin), their
children are Robert, Julius, Leo, Arnold, Edith, Hilda, Olga, Rosella, Elsie and
Amelia; Charlie and Magdalena (Horst), their children are Maggie, Oscar, Edward,
Ferdinand, Harold, Irene, Erna, Howard and Calvin; John and Othelia (Eisenbeiz),

had no children; Magdalena, Mrs. Fred Schlepp, had one daughter, Viola.

My grandfather, John K. Schlepp, came to America from Neudorf, South Russia in

My Dad's parents made their home on a farm four miles NE of Java. In 1918, they

I married Fred Mittleider in 1947. We lived on our farm until 1955, when we

        The Moser Family by Stanley Moser
Wilhelm Moser was one of Karl and Philipina (Lorenz) Moser's 15 children. The
family was living in South Russia in the 1880's when Wilhelm, in his late teens,
reportedly joined a group of explorers climbing Mt. Ararat in search of Noah's
Ark. In 1884, Wilhelm married Shanna Hartman and they began a family.

(Photo:) The Moser Family - 1905

Probably due to land shortage and loss of freedoms that most Germans were
experiencing, Wilhelm traveled to the new world with the Hartman, Aman and
Stiegelmeir families, arriving April 2, 1889. The trip, by ship and railroad,
took the group 18 days.

They filed for homesteads shortly after arriving in Eureka. The families settled
eight miles NE of present-day Java, with the Moser property sharing the eastern
property line with the Hartmans, and the western line with the Amans. The
Stiegelmeiers settled near the Amans.

As soon as possible, Grandpa Wilhelm Moser returned to Russia to bring his
family to their new home. A baby boy, Jake, had been born to the family in June;
there was also four-year old Bill, Jr., and two-year old Katy. The family of
five arrived in Eureka in Oct. 1889.

They had to rush to build shelter that first winter, which came early and was
particularly harsh. Their supplies ran low, and the family was hungry, but they
did not resort to eating any of the seed wheat - Grandpa Moser protected that at
all cost!

Wilhelm and Shanna built a two-room sod house the first summer. One room was for
the animals and one room for the family. The family continued to grow when
Emmanuel was born in 1891 and Edward in 1895. In 1899 another child was
expected, and they began adding on two additional rooms. Shanna did her share of
heavy manual labor up to the day before delivery; she repeatedly hoisted heavy
adobe up to her husband. Shanna died shortly after giving birth to Uncle Adam in
1899.

With six children to raise, Grandpa Moser went to Germany to bring another wife
and mother for his children. A widow, Elizabeth Aman, became his bride in 1899.
Two more children were born, Martha in 1901 and Reinhold in 1904.

The children from the two marriages were: Bill, Jr., born 1885 and died 1965;
Katy Moser Baliet, born 1887; Jake, born 1889, died 1922; Emmanuel, born 1891;
Edward, born 1895; Adam, born 1899, married Florence Shumway in 1925; Martha
Moser Stiegelmeier, born 1901; Reinholt, born 1904, died 1988. All eight are
deceased.

With the labor of his teenage sons and technology of the steam tractor and
McCormick harvesters, Wilhelm Moser became quite prosperous.

There is a story about Wilhelm and his first car. Anxious to try out his new
'toy', he drove the car onto the sloping yard. As the car accelerated, he pulled
back on the steering wheel and cried, "Whoa! Whoa!" Before he remembered to step
on the brake, his new car punched a hole in the barn. He died in 1934.

Karl Moser, Wilhelm's father, came to the U.S. in 1909. He settled in the
McLaughlin area with relatives. At the time of Karl's death in 1917, he had 91
grandchildren.

Bill, Jr., farmed in ND. Jake and Manuel Moser were privileged to serve in the
Army during WWI. Manuel owned an auction barn in Selby and Bowdle.

Jake married Elsia Oswald and they farmed. Jake took his threshing machine and
steam engine tractor as far as ND for threshing. He died in 1922 of cancer of
the blood, leaving his widow with two young daughters. Elsia remarried and
settled in Alberta, Canada. Laura is a nurse living in OR and Verna lives in
British Columbia.

Katy and Martha both married and moved to Lodi, CA. Martha married Abe
Stiegelmeier and they had one daughter, June. Abe built houses and even a motel,
which he operated till it was sold.

Reinhold, my father, married Doris Shumway of Watertown. He became a farming
partner with Uncle Adam until the disastrous 30's, when Uncle Adam moved to
Chicago and became a painting contractor. Reiny served as a Walworth County
Commissioner for several years.

I vividly remember the dismal 30's, the drought and the grasshoppers. The leaves
didn't come on the trees that spring and temperatures soared to 115 degrees. The
only relief from the heat was in the cellar. Dust storms and swarms of
grasshoppers darkened the sky, making it difficult to see. My father (Reiny)
left the house at 4 a.m. morning after morning to buy a daily load of straw from
a farmer in Roscoe. He would hammermill the straw with green tumbleweeds to feed
to the farm animals in a desperate attempt to keep them alive.

My sister, Bonita, and brother, Dean, were born in the 30's. I attended the
Hartman Grade School, just one-and-a half miles from home. Usually the walk was
not too bad, but one morning I stopped at the Meckler place just a half-mile
from the school. I asked Mrs. Meckler, "Could I come in? I'm so cold."

She was so kind to not only let me come in to warm up, but she also gave me a
warm drink. What kind neighbors we had!

I remember spending Saturday nights in Java, running up and down the streets
with schoolmates or seeing a movie for 18 cents. Candy bars or soft drinks were
only 5 cents.

The youngest member of the Reinhold Moser family was Mearl, born in the 40's. I
learned about his birth while staying in the dormitory. I returned home the next
Friday anxious to see my new brother.

My father and mother had four children:

Dean married Gladys Oster and they had three boys, Dick, Greg and Kevin. Dean
and Gladys live in Java and have five grandchildren.

Bonita married Wally Spiry. They have two sons, Dan and Steve, and one daughter,
Vickie. Bonnie and Wally live in Rapid City and have five grandchildren.

Mearl married Paulette Naasz in Dec. 1999 and they live near Selby; he has a
daughter, Melody, and Paulette has a son, Jerome.

I, Stanley Moser, have two children, David and Debbie, and three grandchildren.
I live with my wife, Cheryl, in Dana Point, CA. (Near Laguna Beach)

The pioneers were not only patriotic, but also church goers who trusted in God.
As an example, I think of Florence Moser, who taught many years in the Java
area.

All the families who settled in Java and the surrounding area contributed to
make this country great, and they made Java a wonderful place to grow up.

        Heinrich and Martha (Bollinger) Mueller
Heinrich Mueller was born in Immenschlag, Post Gastern, Austria, on July 3,
1885. He lived there with his parents until 1906, when he immigrated to the U.S.
He came as far as Waterville, MN, where his brother Joseph lived. He worked
there for a while for $15 a month. Not liking city living, he decided to come to
his cousins' place (The Stangl brothers), near Java. He worked for the Stangl
brothers for three years, and then homesteaded on a rocky quarter of land west
of Spring Lake.

(Photo:) Heinrich and Martha Mueller

He was a bachelor for two years, living in his claim shanty 14x16 feet. He then
met and married Martha Bollinger, who had immigrated to the U.S. with her
parents from Neudorf, Russia. They married on May 24, 1911, at the farm home of
Adolph Stangl. They lived in their claim shanty and spent many hours working
very hard. They purchased their first milk cow and Heinrich had to take on an
extra job with a road crew to pay for it. They had many memories of the hard
times they had the first few years, such as their wheat running six to seven
bushels to the acre and selling for 70 cents a bushel. Also the first year they
planted potatoes; the gophers dug them all up and ate them before they could
even start growing. Their 9 children were born on this homestead.

Henry, the oldest son, was born Mar. 6, 1912 and he married Molly Nafts of
Huntley, MT. (See Family History)

Otto was born Oct. 11, 1913 and he married Anna Hofmann of Worden, MT. They live
in Java and have five daughters. (See Family History)

Anton was born Sept. 14, 1915, and he married Evelyn Jackson of Ayden, NC.

Carl was born on Aug. 11, 1917. He married Eunice Erbe. They have three sons and
four daughters.

Emma, the Mueller's first daughter, was born Oct. 17, 1919. She married Gay Raba
and they have two sons and three daughters.

Marie was born Feb. 7, 1922. She married Albert Schreter and they had one
daughter. Marie passed away during heart surgery in Nov. 1943. Her little
daughter, Charlotte, then made her home with her grandparents, the Heinrich
Muellers, living there until her marriage to Ervin Monthye, Jr., of Mound City.
(See Family History)

Harold (Chuck) joined the family on June 19, 1924. He served in World War II
with the Army Air Force in the Philippine Islands. He married Beverly Jones on
Oct. 22, 1950 at the Congregational Church in Huron. Bev was born Oct. 18, 1930
in Ipswich, Edmunds County, to Thomas and Nora Jones and is also one of 9
children. Thomas Jones came to SD from MO and Nora was born at Ipswich. In 1942,
the Jones family moved to Huron.

Children born to Chuck and Bev are Kandice and Tom, born in Mobridge, and Scott.
Kandice married Rick Boomsma and they have Jennifer, Jeff and Tim. They live in
Hitchcock. Jennifer is married to Troy Styer and has Alex and Ashley. Scott and
his wife, Brenda, have Jessica, Jacquelyn and Janelle. They also live in
Hitchcock. Tom resides in Huron.

The Muellers farmed in the Spring Lake area near Java from 1950 through 1957
when they moved to their present farm in Pleasant View Township near Hitchcock.
The original farm house was built before the blizzard of 1888 and was occupied
by the Mueller family until 1974, when they built their present home just west
of the original site. The Scott Mueller family moved into the original farmhouse
in 1988.

The Muellers are members of the Congregational Church in Huron and are active in
many community affairs.

Anne was born on May 21, 1926. She married John Witlock and they had two sons
and four daughters. (See Family History)

Ervin joined the family on May 4, 1929. He married Priscilla Biel, and they have
one son and two daughters. They still live on the family homestead SE of Java.
(See Family History)

Mr. and Mrs. Mueller both worked very hard to make a living for the large
family. They had many happy, and also sad, memories of the days gone by. Mr.
Mueller was one of the men that helped organize the Java Equity. He also served
on the Board of Directors there for many years, as well as on the school board.
They were life-long members of the Lutheran church in Java, and celebrated their
60th Wedding Anniversary there in May 1971. Mrs. Mueller passed away May 3, 1973
at age 82, and Mr. Mueller passed away Aug. 18, 1974 at age 89.

        Henry J. and Molly (Nafts) Mueller
Henry Joseph Mueller, the oldest son of Heinrich and Martha (Bollinger) Mueller,
was born on the family farm one mile west of Spring Lake on Mar. 6, 1912. He
completed the eighth grade at East Spring Valley School and worked on the family
farm.

During the Depression in the "Dirty Thirties", Henry learned that there was work
to be had in the irrigated sugar beet fields in MT. He, his brothers Otto and
Carl, and other local young men went there to be employed. While there, he met
and married Molly Nafts, daughter of William and Elizabeth (Schleining) Nafts of
Huntley, MT. They returned to SD in 1935 and moved to a farm six miles SE of
Java, which was to be their home for the rest of their lives. Molly was very
homesick, as living conditions were not favorable due to the drought. She
recalled leaving a broom outside overnight and in the morning it was eaten by
grasshoppers. In 1943, they were greatly saddened by the lengthy illness and
death of their first-born son, William.

(Photo:) Molly and Henry Mueller

Henry and Molly had four children: William, deceased; Carol married Oscar
Fiedler, Jr., and lives in rural Java near her parents' farm. They have four
children, Dale, Renee, Michele, and Lance (See Family History); Morris is
married to Nancy Ruden and they live in Rosemount, MN and have two children,
William and Teresa; Mavis is married to Harold Kempf. They live in Aberdeen and
have two daughters, Karla and Kerry. Morris and Mavis are twins.

Henry and Molly were both very active in the St. Paul Lutheran Church and in the
community. They both enjoyed gardening and maintaining a beautiful yard. Henry
passed away in 1979 at age 67, and Molly passed away in 1980 at age 70.

        Otto T. and Anna (Hofmann) Mueller
Otto T. Mueller was born Oct. 11, 1913, to Heinrich and Martha (Bollinger)
Mueller at their homestead south of Java. He attended school at East Spring
Valley through the eighth grade. He grew up with his eight brothers and sisters,
working on and enjoying the farm.

Throughout the year of '34, Otto and others migrated west to MT to find work
hauling sugar beets and shipping hay. During this time at a Fourth of July
dance, he was introduced to Anna K. Hofmann, a young college student. She was
born Dec. 22, 1917, to Frank and Marie (Herzog) Hofmann at Worden, MT. She
attended public school in Worden through the 12th grade and one quarter at
Eastern State Normal College in Billings. They were married in Forsyth, MT on
Feb. 11, 1935, and headed to the Mueller homestead, where they made their first
home with Otto's parents for a couple of months.

They moved to a farmhouse one-half mile west of the homestead and lived there
with Otto's brother, Henry, and his new wife, Molly. In 1937, they moved to the
Carlson farm a bit further south and began farming on their own. Their first
child, Marvin Donald, was born in this home on Nov. 15, 1937.

Wanting to own something of their own, they bought 440 acres of farmland three
miles north of Java from the Federal Land Bank in 1941. They moved into the
small sod house in 1942 and shortly thereafter, Marvin died of leukemia at the
age of five.

Their second child, Marlene, was born Sept. 5, 1943. She is married to Kenneth
Stadel, lives in Aberdeen, and has three sons. On Dec. 8, 1944, Irene Shirley
was born. She is married to Roger Spiry, lives in Bemidji, MN, and has three
children. Marjorie Louise was born July 10, 1947, married Ronald Fiedler, lives
in Java, and had four children. Eloise Ann was born Oct. 23, 1949. She is
married to Clarence Lassle and lives in Bowdle. She has four children. Susan E.
was born Nov. 28, 1956. She is living in Watertown with her husband, Steven May,
and their two children.

In 1947, Anna and Otto bought and moved onto the Fred Spiry place a one-quarter
mile to the west. They remodeled the house and improved and expanded the land.
In 1968, their daughter and son-in-law, Marj and Ron Fielder, joined them in the
farming operation.

Otto served on local school and church boards and was a Walworth County
Commissioner for 16 years. Anna has always been an active member of the church
ladies group.

(Photo:) Anna and Otto Mueller

In 1964, Otto and Anna bought the Margaret and Red Haux home in Java, did some
remodeling and moved in. Otto continued to farm commute-style, while Anna made
the house into a home and set up a large garden. The farm was sold to Ron and
Marge in 1992. Otto slipped into semi-retirement, filling his time with long-
awaited hobbies such as fishing, hunting, card-playing, auction sales and
visiting. Anna now has time for quilting, crocheting and making rugs. They both
enjoy visiting their children, 15 grandchildren, and 12 great-grandchildren.

        George Naasz Family
The Naasz family originated in Sessenheim, Alsace, with the first George Naasz
born about 1771. He married Maria Heintz on Jan. 31, 1791, in Sessenheim. Maria
was born about 1773; her father was Marzolf Heintz. They had three children, all
boys, of which two passed away as infants. The surviving son, Georg Friedrich
Naasz was born Apr. 26, 1800, in Sessenheim. He migrated to Bergdorf, Odessa,
Russia, where he married Elizabeth Catharina Schaible in 1822. She was born Nov.
12, 1799, in Grombach, Germany, to Johann Martin and Elizabeth Schuhmacher
Schaible. The Schaible family migrated to Russia in 1817.

Georg Friedrich and Elizabeth (Schaible) Naasz had three children.

Jacob, born Jan. 7, 1823, in Gluckstal, Odessa, married Wilhelmina Schulz on
Jan. 10, 1846, in Klostitz. They had 9 children, six of whom survived, but
little is known about them.

Georg Naasz, born May 1, 1825, in Bergdorf, married Margaretha (Muller) Miller
Dec. 12, 1846, in Klostitz, Odessa. Georg Naasz died July 9, 1880, in
Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia. His wife accompanied her children, all born in Russia,
to America. They left to seek new homes and escape political and military rule
in Russia. The oldest son, Adam, remained in Russia, while his son, Adam, Jr.,
accompanied the rest of the families to the U.S.

Magdalena, born May 8, 1828, in Bergdorf, married Ludwig Laib on Feb. 5, 1848,
in Klostitz. Ludwig and Magdalena had 14 children, of which eight survived. Some
of their children came to the U.S. in 1902 and settled in eastern WA.

        George and Magdalena (Graf) Naasz II
George Naasz II was born in Hoffnungstal, South Russia on Sept. 8, 1855, son of
George Naasz I and Margaret Miller Naasz. He was united in marriage with
Magdalena Graf on June 29, 1877. She was born in Hoffnungstal, Romania on May
18, 1855. George's brothers and sisters were: Ludwig, Magdalena, Louise,
Christian, Fred, Andreas, Margaretha, Adam and William. Magdalena's brother and
sister Katherine and Adolph died in Romania; her Hofer half-brothers and sisters
were Adolph, John, Frederick, William, and Carrie (Martin) Rieger, who all
immigrated to the U.S.

(Photo:) George and Magdalena Naasz II

The family immigrated to America, in May 1893, for the same reasons that many
other families did - to escape the political and social conditions and the
military rule in Russia. The five older children, Adolph, Magdalena, Ludwig,
George, and Christina, came over with their parents. Christ was born on the
ship. Emelia and Edward were born on the homestead in Walworth County. The
oldest daughter died in Russia, and two other children died on the homestead.
Their hardships and difficulties were similar to that of hundreds of other
immigrant farmers, and they met them with fortitude and courage.

They homesteaded on a farm five miles east of present Java. Their first concern
was to provide some sort of shelter. They built a two-room sod house as a
temporary dwelling in a corner of the yard, and lived in this until the stone
house was built - of stone, straw and mud. They built three rooms: one for the
folks, one for the children, and a kitchen, and then an additional room for a
summer kitchen. A barn was built onto the house, just one room enough for a few
horses and cows. Everything was built in a row. Later there was a wooden barn
built, and the other was torn down. When his mother lived with them, they built
an additional room for her to one side of the house. A stone fence was built to
enclose the garden, which had cherry, apple and other trees; rhubarb,
raspberries, vegetables, and hops for yeast to make bread. They built a sod pig
barn. A round smoke house was built of mud, and onto the smoke house, a round
mud oven was built. The oven was about three feet high, and they would start a
fire with straw, wood, cow chips, etc. until it was real hot. Then they would
take out all of the ashes and place in the loaves of bread. Ten loaves of bread
could be baked at one time; even kuchen was baked this way. Everything would
bake nice and firm. They had a metal door on this and would seal it with mud.
The smoke house was enclosed with a metal door and had a pipe out of the roof.

They drove to Hoffnungstal Church, about four miles away, with a horse and
wagon, and in winter, with a sled. Some of the families attending the church
were those of George and Fred Naasz, Bauman, Zweigardt, Hindemith, Horst,
Schlepp, Kapfenstein and Fiechtner. Before this church was built, services were
held in the homes, each taking their turn. From the start, they were without a
minister. The people that lived in this community built the church.

They moved to Java in 1907. George, his brother Ludwig, and David Blinderman
bought a mercantile store and operated it in 1907 and 1908. George sold his
share to young Lou Helm. Then George and his son-in-law, Gottlieb Fiechtner,
bought the livery stable, and Gottlieb operated it for about two years. The five
older children were married, and Christ, Emelia, and Edward moved to town with
their parents.

They lived a quiet retired life, and were true and devoted Christians, being
members of the Lutheran faith all their lives. George passed away Mar. 28, 1924,
and Magdalena died Jan. 30, 1926.

Adolph married Margaret Miller and had three children - Theodore, Arthur, and
Adolph, Jr. After the death of Margaret, Adolph married Pauline Sackman, and
their children were Emil, Herman, Irene (Arthur) Pfaff, Edgar, Reuben, Marvin
and Milton. Their two daughters Alvina and Esther died during the 1918 flu
epidemic.

George III married Lydia Gross, and they had Ida (John) Goetz, Alvin, Albert,
Herbert and Clifford. (See Family History)

Magadalena married Christ Schnaible, and they had Berthold, Otto, Arnold,
Traugott and a daughter, Laile, who died in 1919. (See Family History)

Ludwig married Louise Wahl, and they had Martha, Edgar, Edwin, Igan, and DeLila.

Christina married Gottlieb Fiechtner and they had Emil, Albert, Gerhardt and
Erna (Elmer) Schlepp. (See Family History)

Christ married Tillie Sackman and their children were Othmer and Violet
(Vernard) Sieler. (See Family History)

Emelia married John Fiechtner and they had Herbert, Irene (E. Levi) Krause and
Gertrude (Edgar) Pietzke. (See Family History)

        Christ and Mathilda (Sackman) Naasz
Christ Naasz was born May 2, 1893, on board the ship to the U.S. from Russia, to
George II and Magdalena (Graf) Naasz.

He grew to manhood on a farm east of Java, where his family had homesteaded.
Years later, he went into business owning and operating a saloon in Java. Christ
married Mathilda (Tillie) Sackman on Dec. 26, 1918, in the Lutheran church in
Java.

(Photo:) Mathilda and Christ Naasz

Christ sold his saloon and the young couple moved to his parents' farm east of
Java. They farmed for 18 years with help from Tillie's brother, Herman Sackman,
who lived with them for many years. The family moved to Java in 1938, where
Christ was employed by Helms Lumber Yard and later by Eisenbeisz Pool Hall. He
became the manager of the Java Municipal Liquor until his retirement.

Christ and Tillie were devout church members and assisted in janitor services at
the St. Paul Lutheran Church for many years. Tillie was a member of the church's
woman's society and also a member of the church choir, until her death in 1967.

Two children were born to the Christ Naasz family. Othmer (Ole) was born Nov.
16, 1919 and married Esther Job (See Family History), and Violet, who married
Vernard Sieler (See Family History).

        Othmer (Ole) and Esther (Job) Naasz
Othmer "Ole" Naasz was born Nov. 16, 1919, at the family homestead east of Java.
When the family moved to Java in 1938, Ole went to work for Spiry & Jenner until
it burned down. He then worked for Gershins General Store and Heppers Market,
before joining the military on Apr. 12, 1942. He served in the Southern Pacific
during World War II. He was a Radio Chief and Assistant Communications Chief for
the 1st Battalion Hdqs., 128th Infantry of the 32nd Red Arrow Division. He was
honorably discharged Nov. 27, 1945.

In 1948, he opened Ole's Electric and Furniture in Java. He married Esther Job
on Feb. 4, 1951, in the St. Paul Lutheran Church in Java. Esther was born June
10, 1925, on the family farm outside of Java, to Fred and Philippina (Doerr)
Job. In 1951, Ole sold his store in Java and they moved to Mobridge. He briefly
worked in car sales before moving to Oakes, ND in 1954. They returned to
Mobridge in 1955, when he was offered a position in Gambles Store. In 1967, Ole
and Esther opened "Ole's Radio and TV" in Mobridge. They retired and sold the
store in 1981.

In 1977, Esther developed kidney disease, which required trips to Aberdeen for
Dialysis three times a week, until she passed away June 22, 1992. Ole still
resides in Mobridge; though retired, he still manages to find time to repair
windshields. Ole and Esther had:

        Edward and Martha (Mayer) Naasz
Edward Naasz, born Oct. 4, 1901, was the son of George Naasz II, who immigrated
to America and settled four miles east of Java. Edward grew to young manhood
while working as a farmhand for various farmers. He later was employed at the
Schlepp Drug until he married Martha Mayer, daughter of Michael and Christina
Mayer, on Aug. 14, 1924.

(Photo:) Edward and Martha Naasz

They farmed on the homestead of George Naasz for many years and later moved on
the Lakeman farm, but remained there only a short time and then moved on the
Spiry farm north of Java. A few years later they moved on the Jake Helm farm and
remained there until 1932, when they moved to Java. He was employed by the
County Highway Department, until his death in Jan. 1972. Martha was a cook for
the Java Public School for 12 years.

        Fredrick and Rosina Naasz
Fredrick and Rosina (Schuh) Naasz were both born in Hoffnungstal, South Russia,
where they grew up and were married. Fredrick was the son of George and Margaret
(Miller) Naasz.

On May 2, 1888, Fredrick, Rosina and children, John and Fred, along with his
mother, brother Andrew, and sisters Margaret (John) Ehret and Louise (Karl)
Wahl, left Russia, to make a new home in America.

(Photo:) Fred and Rosina Naasz

After many long days on the ship, they arrived at New York and from there,
traveled by rail to Dakota Territory. They arrived in Eureka and remained there
long enough to buy food and other provisions to aid them on their search for a
homestead. They settled in Walworth County and homesteaded six miles NE of Java.
Here they built a sod house and started farming and raising livestock.

Fredrick and Rosina raised a family of four children who were - John and Fred,
who came to America with their parents; and Margaret and Jacob, who were born at
the homestead.

In 1919 the Naasz family retired from farming and bought a home in Java.
Margaret moved to Java with her parents, where they resided until their deaths.

        John and Kathryn (Hofer) Naasz
John Naasz was born in 1886, in Hoffnungstal, South Russia, and came to the U.S.
with his parents, at the age of two.

John grew to young manhood on his parents' homestead six and one-half miles NE
of Java. He worked hard helping his parents raise livestock and farm grain.
Little time was spent in school but religious services were attended regularly.

(Photo:) John and Kathryn Naasz

to the U.S. with her parents in 1903.

The young married couple bought a farm three and one-half miles from his
father's homestead. They remained on the farm until they retired. Five children

In 1942, John and Kathryn retired from farming and purchased a home in Java,

        Jacob and Clara (Fiedler) Nehlich

        Charles (Karl) and Louisa Nies
Charles (Karl) Nies was born in Baden, Germany, in 1854 and Louisa Beissenherz
was born in 1860, in New York City. Charles met Louisa while she was filling a
stage engagement as Florence Hathaway in Lincoln, IL. They were married Mar. 8,
1878 and lived near Lincoln for about six years. Joining the tide of emigration
toward the west, they lived for a time in IA and NE before coming to Java with
their family. They resided on the Buchecker farm, later known as the Seyer farm,
south of Java for eight years. They later settled on a ranch east of Ekalaka,
MT, where they lived for the remainder of their lives. Louisa died June 12,

        Peter L. and Ethel (Ryan) Nies
Peter Leo Nies was born in Wayne, NE on Feb. 29, 1892, to Charles and Louisa

Pete Nies, like his father and brothers, was a born cattle rancher. Pete and

        The Noble Family
The Cornelius Noble family came, by steamboat across the Atlantic Ocean to the
U.S., from Alkmaar, Holland in 1874. They landed in New York and then traveled
by train to Aberdeen and on to Ipswich, where the railroad ended. Here they
purchased a wagon and team of oxen and other necessary tools for farming. They
arrived at the Java area on May 1, 1884.

The Nobles and their four sons settled on land two miles SW of present-day Java.
Their first home was a small house with only the bare necessities, without
comforts or luxuries. Their time and energy were spent in working the land and
providing food and clothing.

Pioneers had to travel by ox team to the nearest railroad to buy the staple
food, clothing and seed and to sell the grain they had raised.

Philip, Peter, Gerrit and Nick all attended school nearby; school was held only
part of the year.

As the years went by, Philip married Grace Harris and acquired the farm one mile
south of Java. Peter Noble married Anna DeVries in 1899. He purchased the Van
Alst farm and filed on a tree claim three miles SW of Java. Gerrit Noble married
Alice Corson and farmed his father's farm two miles SW of Java. Nick farmed
three miles south of Java. He passed away Oct. 25, 1909, of heart failure, while
duck hunting near Spring Lake.

In 1905, Grandmother Noble became ill and passed away in Oct. of that year.

(Photo:) The Noble Family. John, Dick, Peter (father), Cornelis, Anna (mother),
         Tina, Jansje, Cornelius (grandfather)

It was here near Java that they all went through the hardships of pioneer days.
There was much worry about prairie fires, Indian uprisings, droughts, snow
blizzards, black blizzards and grasshoppers. Neighbors, in early days, joined in
rabbit and coyote round-ups to prevent crop destruction and loss of stock.
Neighbors also got together with teams and wagons and drove to the Missouri
River to pick buffalo berries, grapes and plums. They helped one another with
harvesting and threshing, and in times of illness. The Depression days brought
on the greatest hardship and worry to the health of these early pioneers.

Philip and Grace (Harris) Noble had: Philip, who married Cathryn Wosnuk and they
had Ronald; Grace McMacken-Alcott had Jimmy and Sue Grace McMacken; Elizabeth
Noble Coture (deceased); Nick Noble (deceased) married Clara Wolf; Laura Noble
married Timon Oltman and had Lorna Oltman. Philip Noble passed away Mar. 23,
1932.

Peter and Anna (DeVries) Noble had: Tina; Dick (deceased); Cornelius married
Addie Lutz (deceased), and they had Jane Noble Abel and Joan Noble Riddle; John
Noble is deceased; Jansje Noble married Oliver Wilson and they had Donald,
George and Peter. Peter Noble passed away Nov. 1, 1937.

Gerrit and Alice (Corson) Noble had: Leonard, who married Esther Olson
(deceased) and they had Robert, and Jean Noble Schuchardt. Gerrit Noble passed
away Mar. 21, 1938.

        Nick and Clara Noble
Nick's granddad was born in Holland and came to America with his wife and sons,
Nick, Peter, Garret and Philip. They homesteaded on the farms, which have been
known as the Noble Brothers farms.

(Photo:) Nick and Clara Noble

Nick grew up in Walworth County. He was born on a farm one mile west of Java,
and moved in 1917 to Java, where his father, Phillip, ran the Java Equity
Machine shop.

Clara Wolf was born two-and-a-half miles west of Java, where her folks had a
farm. They moved to town in 1918 to go to school.

Nick and Clara were married Jan. 1, 1932 in Java. Nick worked on WPA at Lake
Hiddenwood. They left SD in 1940, to live in Lakeland, FL. They stayed until
July 1943, and then went back to SD for a short visit, then left for Vancouver,
WA, to work in the shipyards. They were both welders until the end of the war.
They then went to Camas, WA to work in the Crown Zellerbach Paper Mill. Nick
died Jan. 28, 1969, and Clara is also deceased.

        Merle and Florence Noess
Merle and Florence Noess moved to the Java area in Feb. 1972, from Ellendale,
ND. They had 500 sheep and no barn for lambing and no fences to keep them in.
That year, the snow banks helped them manage and, with the help of their three
sons, they got everything done. They raised sheep for about 10 years, until the
coyotes liked them better than did the Noess family. They sold the sheep and
went into the cattle business.

(Photo:) Merle and Florence Noess Family

In 1986, Merle and Florence bought the Java Red Owl from Bob and Joyce Pfitzer.
Two years later, the name was changed to Java Super Valu. In Apr. 1996, they
closed the store and in Sept. 1996, the Community Corp. purchased it. Florence
managed the store until she became employed at the Good Samaritan Center in
Selby.

Merle suffered a stroke in Apr. 1992, so they had to sell their cattle and part
of their land. In Jan. 1997, they moved into the Sunrise Apartments in Java
because of Merle's health and the abundance of snow. They recently moved into
their own home, near the Lutheran church.

Their three sons all graduated from Java High School and all were active in
sports activities.

Wayne lives in Marion, SD and works at Hutchinson Technology in Sioux Falls. He
has three sons, Derek, Joshua and Heath.

Merlen lives in Sac City, IA and is manager of Simplot Soilbuilders. His wife,
Carolyn, operates a cake decorating business from their home. They have a son,
Eric, and a daughter, Amy.

Leslie lives in Java and is Maintenance Operator for Walworth County. His wife,
Bobbi, works as an RN at Bowdle Hospital. They have a daughter, Samantha, and a
son, Sheldon.

        Christ W. and Margaretha (Pleinis) Nusz
Christ Nusz was born Apr. 6, 1888 at Freeman, SD, to Mr. and Mrs. Heinrich Nusz,
Sr., who had emigrated from South Russia to Freeman in 1875. Christ was 13 years
old when he moved to a farm six miles north of Selby in 1901.

(Photo:) Christ W. Nusz Family

In 1907 he married Margaretha Pleinis from the Java area. Mrs. Nusz was born in
1889 to Mr. and Mrs. Jacob Pleinis, Sr., who lived north of Java. She attended
school in Highland District north of Java. In 1901 she worked in the first
restaurant in Selby. She worked for Captain Newton Kingman for $2.50 a week, and
also worked for the D. Reillys. He was with the Walworth County Bank. Mr. and
Mrs. Nusz lived in the Java area for most of their early-married life, except
for a few years spent near Hettinger, ND.

When Christ's father moved into the town of Selby, they moved to the home place
near Selby and farmed the land. In 1920, Christ and his brother, Robert, bought
a threshing machine and threshed for the entire neighborhood.

By this time there were seven children in the Nusz family, and Mrs. Nusz was
very busy washing clothes on a scrub board, baking all of the bread, raising
vegetables, and canning all of the vegetables as well as the beef, pork and
chickens. She also sewed all of the clothes for the entire family.

The Depression came and there were many dust storms, but they continued planting
grain until the grasshoppers ate everything. There was no feed for the cattle,
so they raked up thistles, mixed them with old straw and salted it down for feed
for the animals. Times were very hard, so when a daughter, Mrs. Fred Stadel, who
had moved to CA earlier, found a farm for her parents near Cottonwood, CA, they
had an auction sale and moved in Oct. 1936.

Mr. and Mrs. Nusz were the parents of 11 children. Ferdinand, (deceased),
Albert, Theodore, Donald and Walter, Esther (Fred) Banek, Engelena (E.R.)
Stuhlmiller, Elsie (Fred) Stadel, Hulda (A.E.) Berreth, Edna (Jake) Orth and
Lillian (Argo) Giese.

Mr. and Mrs. Nusz celebrated their 63rd Wedding Anniversary in 1970. Mr. Nusz
passed away Jan. 31, 1971.

        Della Nusz
Della Nusz, born at Leola to Otto and Mary Breitag, had seven brothers and three
sisters. She married Edmund Nusz Oct. 10, 1937 and moved to a farm 5 miles north
of Selby. Eddie died Nov. 29, 1985, and Della remained on the farm until Dec.
1995, when she moved into an apartment in Java.

Eddie and Della had two children, Norlyn, who died Nov. 1995, and Diane Sauer
lives in Fargo. Della has two grandchildren, Rod and Jodi Sauer, both living in
Fargo. She also has two great-grandchildren, Logan and Samantha.

Della is best known for her home-baked bread and egg coffee. She places a lot of
smiles on her neighbors' faces in Java. They love the aroma that comes from her
apartment and they get to share her bread and coffee.

        The Obenauer Family
Philipp, the oldest son of Friedrich and Johanna (Singer) Obenauer, was born
June 3, 1856 in Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia. He married Katharina Maier in 1886,
and they had two children, who died in infancy before the family came to the
U.S. in May 1889. They settled in the Eureka area, where Katharina died in 1900.
Philipp and his three small children then moved to Java, where they lived with
Friedrich and Karolina. Philipp and Katharina had Magdalena, born 1889, married
Oscar Olson and lived in Billings, MT, where Magdalena died; Jacob, born 1892,
was an Army veteran of World War I and lost an arm while in the military. He
settled in Minneapolis, where he married Ida Hagen. They had Eleanor, born 1922.
Both his wife and daughter died from carbon monoxide poisoning; Christian, born
1899, lived in Java with the Friedrich Obenauers until after World War I, when
he moved to Billings and married. He died there in 1985. The only known survivor
of the Philipp Obenauer family is Chris, Jr., who lives in Billings. Philipp
Obenauer died July 2, 1926 at Java.

(Photo:) Friedrich Obenauer Family

Friedrich Obenauer was the third son of Friedrich and Johanna (Singer) Obenauer.
He was born April 17, 1860 in Hoffnungstal, South Russia. After completing his
military obligation in the Russian army, he married Karolina Sackmann on Jan.
22, 1888. She was born Dec. 4, 1859 in Borodino, Bessarabia, the daughter of
Andreas and Eva (Beutel) Sackmann. Adam, their oldest son, was six months old
when they came to America in May 1889, with Friedrich's brothers Philipp and
Johann, and their families. The family lived in McPherson County and then moved
to a farm NE of Java, where they lived until they retired and moved to Eureka in
1919. They lived there until their deaths, Friedrich on Mar. 7, 1942 and
Karolina on Jan. 21, 1953. At the time of her death, she was the oldest citizen
of Eureka. Their home was the "landing place" for many of the Obenauer and
Sackmann siblings when they arrived in America from South Russia. Friedrich was
a frequent correspondent for the Staats Anzeiger, the German-language newspaper,
sharing the news with friends and relatives in America and Bessarabia.

The Obenauers had eight children, three who died in infancy.

Adam was born Nov. 20, 1888, in Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia. He married Lydia
Wolff, born Nov. 8, 1893 in rural Java, to Johannes and Katharina (Ketterling)
Wolff. Adam and Lydia died instantly in a car accident near Leola on Nov. 27,
1957. Adam was the Case Implement agent for many years in Eureka. They had three
children - Albert, born in 1913, married Leona Wagner in 1938, and they lived in
Startup, WA, where Albert died Aug. 14, 1985. Their daughters are Sandra (Bruce)
Kennedy and Dianna (David) Harris. Leona lives in Seattle. Theodore was born in
1916 and married Leah Bertsch in 1938. Ted was a World War II veteran and died
May 11, 1960. They lived in Eureka, Leola and Aberdeen, where Leah still lives.
Viola was born in 1920 and married Paul Burger in 1946. She died Feb. 26, 1983
and Paul now lives in Sheridan, WY. They have three children, Linda (Joe)
Brockel, Steven and Patricia (Mark) Morrison.

John was born Feb. 14, 1892 in rural Java. He married Kathryn Gross of Bowdle in
1917 and, after living in Eureka for many years working as a real estate agent,
they retired to Lodi, CA, where John died in 1963 and Katie in 1980. Their only
son, Harold, was born in 1918 and married Esther Noehre of Roscoe. He died on
"D" Day of World War II. Their son, John Paul, is an attorney in Sacramento, CA
and Esther lives in CA.

Fredrich was born Oct. 26, 1894 in rural Java, and on Jan. 9, 1916, married
Rosina Schlepp, daughter of John J. and Helen (Doebele) Schlepp. They lived on
the Obenauer family farm near Java and later on a farm near Eureka, before
retiring to Eureka, where Rosie died Dec. 8, 1970 and Fred died Mar. 16, 1975.
They had eight children: Ida, born 1915, married Peter P. Schmidt and had twin
daughters, Karyn and Karyl; Hertha, born 1917, married Wallace Hay, who died
Nov. 13, 1942, in the service of his country in World War II. She married Rueben
Fischer May 14, 1948, at Herreid. Hertha died Apr. 25, 1988 at Loma Linda, CA
and Rueben died Dec. 24, 1988 at Fontana, CA. She had two sons, Walter Hay and
Kenneth Fischer; Ervin, born 1919, married Ruth Wiedrich and lived in the Eureka
area. Ervin died Mar. 3, 1998 at Bowdle. He had two sons, Floyd and Ervin;
Elsie, born 1921, married Eugene Ellis in Aug. 1943, and has Betty, Rose and
Robert. Eugene is deceased and Elsie lives in Frazier Park, CA; Edna was born in
1923 and died in 1925 at Bowdle; Violet, born 1928, married Ray Koerner and has
Jerilyn, Carole, Kathleen, Steven and James; Janice, born 1931, married Elmer
Opp and has Karen, Janet, Gaylynn and Alan; Leroy, born 1937, married Lois
Peterson and has Tammy, Kerry, Rosina and Danielle.

Magdalena was born June 12, 1898 on the family farm in rural Java. After leaving
the farm where she was born and raised, she went to Aberdeen, where she was
employed at the Radison Hotel for several years. Prior to 1942, Magdalena moved
to Eureka to take care of her aged parents, where she remained for the next 14
years. She married Raleigh Erickson on Aug. 15, 1955. They lived in Aberdeen,
where Raleigh was employed with the Milwaukee Railroad. Raleigh died July 28,
1965 and Maggie died Oct. 4, 1982.

Bertha was born Feb. 21, 1900, in rural Java, and married Richard Ketterling on
Jan. 18, 1927. Richard was born Apr. 15, 1900, at Bow-dle, to John and Olga
Ketter-ling. They made their home in Mercer, ND. Richard died in 1969 and Bertha
died Feb. 23, 1988. They had two daughters, Loretta born 1934 and died in 1935,
and LaRose.

        Jacob and Eva Ochszner
Jacob Ochszner was born April 8, 1871 at Worms, Russia, one of 15 children. At
the age of 13, he, with his parents, immigrated to the U.S. and settled on a
farm in Hutchinson County, near Yankton. In 1889, he moved on a farm five miles
NW of Java. He married Elizabeth Wolf, Jan. 4, 1894. They remained on this farm
until his retirement in 1920, at which time they moved into Java.

Elizabeth passed away Dec. 13, 1928, and Jacob married Eva Pregitzer in 1929.
They made their home in Java, until he passed away Sept. 30, 1952.

Eva Ochszner was born Dec. 13, 1889 at Gluckstal, South Russia to Karl and
Johanna (Kiesz) Ritter, one of 11 children. At the age of 9, she, with her
parents, immigrated to the U.S. and established their home on a farm seven miles
south of Eureka. In 1907, they moved to a farm a mile west of Mound City, where
she lived, met, and married Christian Spiedel, in Oct. 1909.

The Spiedels lived on a farm NW of Mound City until 1912, when they moved to the
wide open spaces of MT, about 50 miles NW of Miles City. The settlers out there
were far apart with no close neighbors and nothing but prairie and sky, as far
as the eye could see. The only living things in abundance were wild life,
especially coyotes, and lots of sagebrush and rattlesnakes. The sagebrush was
used for heating the homes and also for cooking.

(Photo:) Eva and Jacob Ochszner

Two children were born to this union, one daughter and a son, who died in
infancy. In the spring of 1916, Mr. Spiedel passed away. Then Eva and her
daughter moved back to SD. She later married John Pregitzer in the fall of 1916.
They made their home on a farm two-and-a-half miles NW of Java, where they lived
until the fall of 1928, when they moved into Java, where Mr. Pregitzer passed
away in Dec. of that year. One son was born to this union, who died at the age
of seven.

Eva married Jacob Ochszner in Oct. of 1929. They lived in Java until his death
in 1952. She stayed on in her home, until the spring of 1971, when she entered
the Good Samaritan Center in Selby. Eva had Edna (Calvin) Baumann, two
granddaughters, Dalles (Erwin) Zeller and Darlene (Aaron) Hartman, and four
great grandchildren, Mrs. Dave Hasselbery, Cindy Zeller and Paul and Jason Job.

        Carl and Rosina (Wagner) Oster
Carl (Karl) Oster was born Aug. 24, 1841, in Gluckstal, Russia, where he was
confirmed and grew to manhood. On Feb. 21, 1863, Carl was united to Rosina
Wagner at Klostitz, South Russia.

(Photo:) Rosian and Carl Oster

Carl and his wife made their home at Hoffnungstal, South Russia, where their
seven children were born, who were: Katharina (Christian) Pfitzer, born Nov. 25,
1863, Christian born 1865, Christiana (Gottlieb) Goetz, born 1867, Magdalena
(Fred) Buechler, born March 19, 1874, Johann, born Sept. 12, 1877, Samuel, born
Nov. 22, 1878, and Adam, born July 5, 1881.

Carl and Rosina, and their family of unmarried children, undertook the trip to
America. In 1889, they settled in Walworth County and homesteaded on a farm
eight and one-half miles NE of what now is Java. He became a naturalized citizen
on April 10, 1897. Some years later, Carl and his wife moved to Java, where he
resided until his death on Dec. 27, 1909. Rosina died Oct. 21, 1918 at Java.

        Samuel Oster
Samuel Oster was born Nov. 22, 1878, in Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, Romania.
According to the passport record, he moved with his parents to America on April
6, 1889, and became a U.S. citizen through parental naturalization. He married
Minnie (Mina) Kies, and settled on a farm about eight miles NE of Java. Included
in farming, he took pride in raising tobacco. Of the early days of pioneering in
Dakota, he was one of the few farmers in the state who successfully raised
tobacco in a soil and environment far from its native habitat. For many years he
experimented with the growing of tobacco on his farm NE of Java. A careful
understanding of the plant and diligent cultivation produced unusual results. He
raised tobacco for his own and his neighbors' use.

(Photo:) Sam Oster and tobacco plants

Moving to Java in 1919, he discontinued planting tobacco until later in his
life, when he again experimented on a lot near his house. "It took many a barrel
of water during the dry periods to keep the plants growing," but the results
were worth it. He cured the partly green leaves in a barn upstairs. From a small
plot, he produced enough of the leaves for a year's supply for his own use in
his pipe. Wherever he went, one could smell his tobacco. It was strong! His wife
passed away in 1933 and he in 1951.

        Adam and Eva (Schwent) Oster
Adam Oster, born in Gluckstal, South Russia, on Nov. 28, 1863, married Eva
Schwent on June 10, 1891.

Adam and Eva and their foster son, Jacob Oster, came to America in 1901. They
homesteaded east of Java, where they lived for 14 years. They bought a farm two
miles north of the homestead near Horseshoe Lake, where Adam lived until his
death on Jan. 15, 1934. Eva Oster continued to live with her foster son and his
wife. In 1948, the family moved to Bowdle. She continued living with them until
both of their deaths. In 1963, Eva moved to the Eureka Nursing Home, where she
remained until her death, on Jan. 19, 1967.

(Photo:) The Adam oster Family

        Jacob and Katherine (Buechler) Oster
Jacob Oster was born at Gluckstal, South Russia on April 5, 1891. When he was
five, his father passed away and Jacob made his home with an uncle and aunt, Mr.
and Mrs. Adam Oster. In 1901, the entire family came to America and settled in
Walworth County, and homesteaded on a farm eight miles east of Java.

On Jan. 5, 1915, Jacob married Katherine Buechler and the young couple farmed on
the homestead. In 1934, the Jacob Oster family moved to the Adam Oster farm near
Horseshoe Lake, and lived with Eva (Adam) Oster.

(Photo:) Jacob and Katherine Oster

Jacob and his wife retired from farming in 1948 and bought a home in Bowdle,
where Eva continued living with them. Jacob passed away Mar. 20, 1957, and
Katherine passed away Feb. 1, 1963.

Twelve children were born to Jacob and Katherine Oster. Five of these children
died in infancy and the remaining include: Erna (Emil) Sonnenfeld, Theophil
(Ted) married Irene Goetz, Alma (Erwin) Sonnenfeld resides in Aberdeen, Helmuth

        Edwin and Freida (Himmerich) Oster
John Oster, Sr., born 1879 in Russia, and Christina Siewert, born 1885 in
Russia, were parents of Edwin Oster, born May 10, 1909, in Edmunds County near
Bowdle, the oldest of eight children. Jacob Himmerich, born 1888 in South
Russia, and Katherine Buechler, born 1890 in South Russia, were parents of
Freida Rose Himmerich, born Nov. 19, 1911, in Walworth County east of Java, the
oldest of eight children.

(Photo:) Edwin Oster Family. Back: Vernetta, Janice, Floyd, Gladys, Delores.
         Front: Freida, Lyle and Edwin

Edwin and Freida were married Mar. 11, 1934 in the (Buechler) Neu-Glueckstal
Church east of Java. They farmed and lived on various farms NE of Java. In the
fall of 1948, they packed their family of five children and moved to Kent, WA,
where they lived until Mar. 1949. They came back to SD and bought the home place
of Jacob Himmerich, Freida's parents, six miles east of Java. Christian
Himmerich, Freida's grandfather, homesteaded this farm in the late 1800's. The
Osters lived here until 1962, when they retired and moved into Java and sold the
farm to their son, Floyd.

Edwin and Freida spent many winters in LaFeria, TX, as snowbirds, until Edwin
passed away while enjoying one of his favorite hobbies, fishing, on Apr. 25,
1977, at the age of 67. Freida enjoyed a few more winters in TX before selling
the house in Java and moving to Selby in 1984, where she remained until her
death Mar. 17, 1996 at the age of 85.

Edwin and Freida were life-long members of St. Paul Lutheran Church in Java and
are both buried in the Lutheran cemetery NW of Java.

They had eight children, two of whom died in infancy. The living children are:

Delores, born Mar. 25, 1935, married Ruben Deibert on Dec. 6, 1953. They live
near Pollock and have four children, 9 grandchildren, and one great-grandchild.

Gladys, born Aug. 9, 1937, married Dean Moser on Oct. 7, 1956. They have three
sons and five grandchildren and live in Java.

Floyd, born May 15, 1939, married Karen Kludt on Sept. 3, 1961 and lives near
Poulsbo, WA. They have three children and five grandchildren.

Janice, born Jan. 29, 1942, married Merlyn Thorstenson on Sept. 18, 1960. They
live near Selby and have four children and seven grandchildren.

Vernetta, born Apr. 16, 1946, married Norbert Jangula on Oct. 29, 1983 and lives
near Ipswich.

Lyle, born Oct. 1950, married Gillian Roberts on Aug. 4, 1973. He lives in
Northfield, MN and has one son.

        Richard and Sandra (Remus) Osterday
Richard Dale Osterday was born Dec. 6, 1964 in Sidney, NE, to Richard A. and

and attended SDSU until 1985, when he began farming.

Sandra Jean Remus was born Oct. 13, 1962 in Sleepy Eye, MN, to Lynn D. and

Rick and Sandy were married Sept. 13, 1986 and live five miles SE of Java, on

(Photo:) Rick, Sandy, Clay and Blane Osterday
