        Adolph and Adeline (Aman) Schuh
Adolph Schuh was born May 9, 1901, at rural Java, to John and Fredricka
(Schlepp) Schuh. He attended school in the Java area. After school, he farmed
with his father for a number of years and then farmed at McLaughlin for a time.
He then attended a mechanical trade school in Aberdeen, then returned to Java,
and was a mechanic for many years.

Adeline Aman was born Jan. 27, 1908, at Kulm, ND, to Michael J. and Christina
(Bollinger) Aman. At the age of four, she moved with her family to Maple Creek,
Saskatchewan, Canada, where she attended school. Shortly after her mother's
death in 1919, the family returned to the U.S. and settled at Java, where she
continued her education. Adeline was a full-time mother and homemaker.

Adolph and Adeline were married in 1935 and lived in Java for the rest of their
lives. The couple had two children, Robert of Sun City, AZ, and Avis (James)
Sauer of Bismarck. Adeline passed away June 12, 1983 and Adolph passed away June
24, 1983.

Robert was born at Bowdle on Mar. 31, 1936, and lived at Java until early
manhood, graduating from Java High School in 1954. During his senior year of
high school, he was taught the depot agent trade, as were many others from the
area, by Col. E.C. Weatherly. Robert was the Colonel's last student. For the
next three years, he worked on the Milwaukee and Northern Pacific Railroads in
many locations. It probably was the wrong time to go into railroading, being
that modernizing was beginning to take effect and jobs were being cut back.

(Photo:) Robert and Phyllis Schuh

After the railroad, Robert held several other jobs, including working at a TV
station, selling automobiles and lastly, getting a Master Electricians license
and doing electrical contracting. Robert lived in Bismarck from 1955 until 1986.

In 1986, he and his wife, Phyllis, moved to Sun City, AZ, where he worked as a
real estate agent for Ken Meade Realty. In 1994, they recognized his knack to
repair and build computers and he is now their full-time Computer Technician.
Phyllis is employed at Honeywell.

Robert has four children from his previous marriage. They are: Duane, a single
man, working as an electrician in Bismarck; Robert, Jr., also working as an
electrician in Bismarck, married to Denise and has two children; Kathy is single
and attending the U of IN, working toward her doctoral degree; Ronald and his
wife Cheryl, along with their two sons, live in Rapid City. They own the
Morningside Cafe.

Avis was born May 1, 1938, at Bowdle and grew up in Java. She graduated from
Java High School with the class of 1956. In 1957, Avis graduated from the
Aberdeen School of Commerce, and worked as a secretary in Aberdeen, Denver, CO,
and Bismarck. When her sons were young, she was a full-time mother and
homemaker.

(Photo:) James and Avis Sauer

James K. Sauer was born Oct. 8, 1937, at Bowdle, to Christ and Fern Sauer. For
the first five years of his life, he resided with his family on a farm NE of
Java. In 1943, the family moved to a farm NE of Roscoe. He graduated from Roscoe
High School in 1955 and in 1973, from Mary College at Bismarck. After being
employed for 32 years by the State of ND, he retired at the end of 1998 as the
Director of Fiscal Administration with the ND Dept. of Human Services.

Jim and Avis were married Aug. 4, 1957, at Java. They have lived in Bismarck for
40 years. They are the parents of two sons, Shannon and Lauren, both residing
with their families in Bismarck. Shannon and his wife, DeAnn, have two children,
Justin and Lindsey. Shannon is employed with the ND Dept. of Transportation as
the Financial Management Director. Lauren is married to Michelle and is employed
as Coordinator of Mental Health Planning, Division of Mental Health and
Substance Abuse for the ND Dept. of Human Services.

        Pastor Leon and Carolyn Schulz by Pastor Leon Schulz
My name is Pastor Leon E. Schulz. I received a Letter of Call to become the
pastor of St. Paul Lutheran Church in Java. I had not yet graduated from
Wartburg Theological Seminary, in Dubuque, IA, when the Call was received. In
fact, it was during the Easter break of that year in 1967, that I and my wife
Carolyn journeyed to Java to investigate this place where we would live in the
near future. Then following graduation, ordination, and a vacation, we moved to
Java. It was the end of July 1967.

It is, sort of, ironic to know that someone at the Seminary once asked me, about
three years earlier, if I knew where Java was. The person who asked this
question knew that I was from SD. At that time, I said, "It's probably some
little hole up north." I said this, not knowing that I would someday actually
live, for 10 years, in that "little hole up north".

Carolyn was a teacher and began teaching school in the Java school system. This
was a financial asset, which helped to pay off school debts, which were made
earlier. The following June 1968, Carolyn and I adopted a daughter, Sharon
Eileen. In Dec. 1969, our son, Noel John, was born. A few years later, in 1974,
we adopted another daughter, Brenda Kay. We lived in Java for ten years, or
until June 30, 1977.

On July 1, 1977, I became the pastor of Grace Lutheran Church in Menno. Twenty
years later now, I am still serving that church. Carolyn has been working at the
Menno Olivet Retirement Center as the Assistant Activity Director. This
retirement center has 45-50 residents.

Now for a little background as to where our children are living and what they
are doing. Sharon is married to Kevin Elsing. They live in Sioux Falls. Sharon
works in the Barnes and Noble Bookstore, where she is in charge of all books in
the category of fiction. Her husband works for Hutchinson Electronics in Sioux
Falls. Noel lives in Jefferson, SD, but works in Sioux City, IA, as a civil
engineer. He works for Jebro, Inc., which is a company which specializes in
liquid asphalt for road building. Noel is also married. His wife, Jennifer,
works at Elk Point as a physical therapist. They have Marisa, born Dec. 1998.
Brenda is not married as yet. She is presently working as a waitress in Sioux
Falls, with plans to continue her education at a vocational technical school,
following two years at SDSU in Brookings.

(Photo:) Pastor and Carolyn Schulz

Carolyn and I are still living in Menno, and throughout our years there, we have
also had many foreign exchange students living with us, who were from several
different countries in Europe. Our eighth student will be coming to live in our
home very soon.

This concludes the commentary of the Schulz history up to this date. God's
blessings to all of you, who we have come to know over the years.

        George and Katherine (Hessman) Sebert
George Sebert was born Jan. 10, 1858, near Vermont, Dane County, WI. He was the
son of John and Eliza (Klensing) Sebert. In 1883, he came with two of his
cousins, George and August Erbe, and a friend, Wm. H. Payne, to seek land for
homesteading. They squatted on land north of Ipswich. They had difficulty
getting water there, so they came to the Spring Lake area near Java, in 1886.

In 1889, he went back to WI, and was married to Katherine F. Hessman on Feb. 27,
1889. Katherine was born in Bohemia on Mar. 28, 1863, the daughter of Frank and
Anna Hessman. She came to the U.S. with her parents in 1868 and they settled in
Dodgville, then in Mazomanie, WI.

The young couple then came back to SD and lived in their little 12x14 claim
shack. The claim shanty was replaced by a mud brick (sod) house in 1897. This
house still stands on the Sebert homestead. George died Apr. 3, 1942, while they
were living in Selby. Katherine died on the original homestead on May 11, 1951.
They are buried at Selby.

(Photo:) The George Sebert Family

Their oldest son, Everett F., was born Nov. 25, 1892. He married Amelia (Aman)
Stangl on May 11, 1915. Amelia was born Mar. 18, 1895. They farmed in the Lake
Hiddenwood area. Everett died Feb. 21, 1980 and Amelia died Aug. 14, 1993. They
are buried at Selby.

Their second son, George A., was born on July 14, 1895. He married Maria J.
Kosters and they had 9 children.

George and Katherine also welcomed an adopted daughter, Leona (Corson) into
their home in May 1904. Leona was born to Victor O. and Rena Corson on Aug. 26,
1899, and married George Erbe on May 18, 1916. George was born in the Spring
Lake area on Sept. 22, 1893. George died Mar. 10, 1977, and Leona died Apr. 17,
1990. They are buried at Harlowtown, MT. Two sons were born to this union,
Wilbur and Loren Erbe, both living in MT.

        George A. and Maria (Kosters) Sebert
George A. Sebert was born July 14, 1895, on a farm SE of Java. He grew up in the
Java vicinity, where he spent all of his life operating the family farm. At the
age of 22, on Apr. 26, 1918, George enlisted in the Army. He was in the first
All-American Offensive when the St. Mihiel Drive was started (Sept. 12, 1918).
He then experienced the Argonne Positions. The drive continued and, on Nov. 1st,
crossed the Meuse River into Stenay, Germany, the morning the Armistice was
signed. George A. was in the front line from June 27 until Nov. 11, 1918. He was
chosen to stay in the Army of Occupation in Germany until Apr. 1919, at which
time he came back to the states and received his honorable discharge at Ft.
Dodge, IA.

Maria Josephine Kosters was born Mar. 23, 1905, at Java, to Gerard and Maria
Kosters. She attended eight years of school at East Spring Valley, and spent her
younger years on the farm, helping with the work.

George A. and Maria were married at St. Augustine's Catholic Church in Bowdle on
Jan. 11, 1928. They were the parents of 9 children. Leo, who died on Mar. 5,
1992, is buried at Aberdeen, Albert, Arthur, Leonard, Louis, Frances, Dorothy,
Raymond and George M., who still owns the original Sebert homestead land. They
were proud parents of five sons serving in military service at one time: Leo,
Albert, Arthur, Leonard and Louis.

George A. was clerk of the Spring Lake School board for 12 years, a member of
the county school board for three years. He also was a member of the Selby
American Legion and a charter member of the Bowdle American Legion, serving as
commander for a number of years. Maria was a member of St. Augustine's Catholic
Church and Altar Society, and of the American Legion Auxiliary. George passed
away Dec. 23, 1963, and Maria continued to make her home on the farm with her
son George, until she passed away Sept. 18, 1983. There are 31 grandchildren and
30 great-grandchildren.

        Daniel and Katharina (Bauman) Seif
One of the Sutley Community pioneers, who saw this section grow from a prairie
wilderness to a regime of fine farms and growing towns, was Daniel Seif. He was
born Nov. 11, 1859, at Galion, OH, and came to Dakota Territory in 1885, with a
brother and a cousin, to stake some land. His grandparents, Jacob and Margret
(Conewett) Seif, came from Baden, Germany in 1829 and settled in OH. Daniel's
parents, Michael and Catherine (Peaster) Seif, were farming in OH, when Daniel,
his brother, Joseph and cousin, Levi headed to Dakota Territory. They took up
land near the Campbell-Walworth County border and settled in the Sutley area,
where Daniel built his first sod house. This farm is now owned and operated by
Dennis and Jeanne Schneider. Daniel remained here and farmed, and in the winter
months taught school.

(Photos:) Daniel Seif and Katharina Seif

Daniel married Katharina Bauman, born Aug. 12, 1864, the daughter of Heinrich
and Christina (Ernst) Bauman. They were married Dec. 3, 1889, and lived on
Daniel's farm for several years before moving back to OH. While living there,
their first two children, Gertrude and Mary, were born. In 1898, the family
moved back to SD, and homesteaded on a farm 15 miles NE of Java. Here they lived
and farmed for most of their lives. Three more children were born to them -
 Emma, and a set of twins, Fred and Martha.

Farming was done by breaking plow, hand plow and some seeded by hand, as most of
the settlers had done until they were able to purchase horse-drawn machinery.
Grain was cut with the scythe and stacked on piles; corn was planted by hand and
weeded by hoes, which was done by the children. Cook stoves were used for
heating, cooking and baking. Twisted straw, cow chips and dried manure were
stored in buildings and used for fuel in the winter months. Trips were made in
the fall to the Missouri River, where wood was gathered, and fruit picked for
canning and jellies. Oil in a dish was their first source of lights and later,
kerosene lamps were used. Their early bed was made of wood; ticking filled with
cornhusks or straw, served as a mattress, and quilts and pillows were made of
ticking and filled with feathers. Wells were dug by hand, and cisterns were
common until windmills came into existence. Milking was done by hand, which
almost included everyone in the family. The milk was cooled and the cream was
skimmed off for cooking. Later, the cream separator took the chore out of
cooling and skimming.

The Daniel Seif children attended the Delker School in Thompson District. They
also had a little grocery store and post office near their home for a number of
years. During sickness, and when home remedies didn't succeed, Dr. O.H. Gerdes
from Eureka was called.

The children born to Daniel and Katharina were: Gertrude (Gustav) Hirsch; Mary
(Edward) Hirsch; Emma (Gideon) Bieber; and Fred, who remained single. He lived
on the farm until he retired and moved to Aberdeen in 1974. Daniel passed away
at his home in June 1936, and Katharina passed away at the Eureka hospital in
June 1955.

        Henry and Agnes (Blunk) Seyer Sr.
Henry Seyer, Sr., was born at Fehmarn in Holstein, Germany, on Mar. 23, 1874,
coming to America at the age of 15 to Avoca, IA. His father was a shoemaker, and
from their home they could see across the Baltic Sea to the Island of Laaland, a
part of Denmark. It took him a week to find work after arriving at Avoca and his
first job was on a farm near Shelby, IA. He recalled that he worked 11 months
for $50.

On Mar. 3,1896, he was united in marriage with Agnes Blunk, also born in
Holstein on Nov. 30, 1878. She came with her parents to America and Minden, IA,
at the age of 12. They lived in the Minden-Avoca, IA area for 12 years, where
all of their five children were born. They had three sons: Fred (born Mar. 15,
1897, deceased Jan. 26, 1978), Henry, Jr. (born Oct. 12, 1898, deceased June 24,
1995) and Walter (born Apr. 2, 1903, deceased Nov. 23, 1981). They also had two
daughters: Dora (born Oct. 7, 1900, deceased May 16, 1990), and Ella (born Feb.
27,1905).

The young couple started life together on rented farms in the vicinity where
they had lived and were quite successful. However, Iowa land was becoming high
priced and rents were high, and it seemed to them that there were greater
opportunities for them and their family on the cheaper lands of Dakota. Many of
their friends and neighbors thought the same and in the year 1908, the Seyers
came to Walworth County, moving onto the farm six miles south of Selby, then
known as the Abe Taylor farm, which Mr. Seyer had purchased from Otto Lincke,
who moved to Selby to engage in the farm implement business.

In the year 1919, they sold this farm and moved to the Gordon farm in Spring
Valley Township, where they resided until 1925, when he purchased the place
known as the Buchecker farm, four miles south of Java, from Mrs. Anna Noteboom.
This farm was well known throughout the area as being one of the finest farms of
the community. The large house and buildings, along with the 100-foot windmill
tower, were landmarks for many years along U.S. Highway 12.

Mr. Seyer farmed this place with the help of his sons Fred, Henry, Jr., and
Walter. The first farm the Seyers lived on (Taylor place) eventually came back
to the Seyers and was then farmed by Walter and his wife, Mildred, until their
retirement. It then was farmed by his son and wife, Kenneth and Sydney Ann,
until 1980. The original Seyer farm is now owned by the Larry Reede family. Fred
and his wife, Bertha, purchased a farm a mile west of the Buchecker farm known
as the Ritter Place, and began farming on his own. Robert and Pamela Seyer
currently own this farm.

(Photo:) The Henry Seyer, Sr. Family

Henry, Jr. remained on the Buchecker place and farmed with his father. On Feb.
23, 1944, Agnes Seyer passed away. Henry, Sr.'s youngest daughter, Ella,
returned home in 1949 to assist Henry, Jr., with the farm, and to care for her
aging father. Previous to her return to the Selby-Java area, she graduated from
SDSU and taught high school commercial subjects for many years at Redfield, as
well as schools in MI and IA. Henry, Sr., passed away Mar. 12, 1959. Henry, Jr.,
and Ella continued to farm on this place until they retired and moved to Selby
in 1962. The Leo Almendinger family currently owns this farm.

Henry, Jr., and Ella continued to reside in Selby until they became residents of
the Colonial Manor in Ipswich, in the fall of 1992. Neither of them ever
married. Henry, Jr., passed away on June 24, 1995. Ella, the last living child
of Henry and Agnes Seyer, remains a resident of this facility (as of this date,
June 14, 1999). She remains knowledgeable about the past with an interest in the
future, and is an inspiration to those around her.

Dora Seyer was a schoolteacher in Walworth County country schools for a number
of years. She married Kenneth Salmen, a native of White Lake. They made Golden,
CO, their home, where he worked for Golden's Chevrolet Garage. Following his
death in 1954, she continued to live in Golden, and returned to elementary
teaching, which she did until her retirement. She had one daughter, Doris
(married Don Elliot) who lives in Parker, CO. Doris and Don have four daughters,
Julie, Janet, Jodie and Jennifer.

Walter Seyer married Mildred Rischel of Selby. They resided on the original
Seyer farmstead until retiring in 1960 and moving to Selby. After Walter's death
in 1981, Mildred continued to live in Selby, until the summer of 1995. She
currently lives in an apartment in Aberdeen. Walter and Mildred had two sons:
Kenneth married Sydney Ann Zeller (deceased) of Java. They had two children,
John and Janeen. Ken farmed until 1980 and Sydney Ann worked at the First
National Bank (BankWest) in Selby, before moving to Aberdeen. In Aberdeen, Ken
worked for 3M before going to work for the Aberdeen school system, and Sydney
Ann worked at Norwest Bank. Ken still resides in Aberdeen. Marvin has taught
school for many years. He married Judy Geditz of Ipswich, who is a Registered
Nurse. They have four children: Tom, Jim, Terry and Julie. Marvin and Judy
continue to live in Ipswich, where they have resided since being married.

(Photo:) The Walter Seyer Family

Fred C. Seyer, Sr., married Bertha Gosch of Glenham. They had four children.
(See Family History)

        Fred C. and Bertha (Gosch) Seyer Sr.
Fred C. Seyer, Sr., was born on Mar. 15, 1897, in the Minden-Avoca area of IA.
He was the oldest child born to Henry and Agnes Blunk Seyer, Sr. Fred, along
with his brothers, Henry, Jr., and Walter (married Mildred Rishel), and sisters,
Dora (married Kenneth Salmen), and Ella, came to the Selby area with their
parents in 1908. Their father purchased the Abe Taylor farm six miles south of
Selby from Otto Lincke. This farm remained the family home until 1919, when the
family moved to the Spring Valley area south of Java.

Fred entered the IA State Automobile and Tractor School at Sioux City, IA, in
1917. On May 28, 1918, he enlisted in the U.S. Army and served in France during
World War I. Following the signing of the Armistice, Fred was discharged from
the service on Feb. 20, 1919. He returned to the Selby area to farm with his
brothers and father.

Bertha J. Gosch was born May 6, 1912, SW of Bowdle, to Frank and Carrie Schlomer
Lien Gosch, Sr. She has one brother, Frank Gosch, Jr., who resides in Mobridge.
Carrie's first husband, Sebastian Lien, passed away and left Carrie to care for
their two young daughters, Rose Lien (who married John Rabenberg) and Johanna
Lien (who married Ed Beckman). The family moved to a farm east of Glenham when
Bertha was a young girl.

Bertha graduated from Glenham High School in 1930. She then attended Northern in
Aberdeen and received a certificate to teach school. She taught in rural schools
in Walworth and Campbell counties until she and Fred were married on June 16,
1937, at the farm home of her parents SE of Selby, on the farm now owned by
Palmer Miller.

Fred and Bertha made their home on the farm known as the Ritter place, located
in Spring Valley Township, which Fred had purchased from the Kormendy family. It
was there that they raised their family and continued to reside until 1976, when
they moved to Mobridge. Bertha returned to college and received a degree in
Elementary Education in 1970. She taught in the Mobridge school system from
1970, until her retirement in 1977. Fred passed away on Jan. 26, 1978, at
Mobridge. Bertha continued to make Mobridge her home, until entering the Selby
Good Samaritan Center in Sept. of 1997.

Fred and Bertha were both active in their communities. Fred was a charter member
and 59-year member of the Frederick Schauer Legion of Selby. He served many
years on the Spring Valley Township school board, the Federal Land Bank board
and the board of directors of the Selby Equity Union Exchange. Bertha was an
active 4-H leader, member of an extension club, and past president of the
Frederick Schauer Legion Auxiliary. She also served as president of the Java PTA
and Music Mothers. Both Fred and Bertha were active in St. John's Lutheran
Church in Selby. Fred served many years on the church council as treasurer and
was on the building committee when the new church was built. Bertha was active
in Ladies Aid and taught Sunday school.

To this marriage four children were born: Carol (May 8, 193 8), Fred, Jr., (Aug.
7, 1939), Leonard (Nov. 2, 1940), and Robert (Jan. 24, 1949).

Carol attended West Spring Valley School throughout her grade school years and
then attended and graduated from Selby High School in 1956. She continued her
education at SDSU, where she received a degree in Home Economics. She married
Charles Linn of Elm Springs on June 27, 1959, in Selby. Charles, a graduate of
the College of Engineering at SDSU, became employed by the SD Department of
Transportation following graduation. He remained employed with them until
retirement in Jan. of 1998. Carol worked many years in the retail stores of
Lucas and Theim, and Feinstein's in Pierre. They had three children: Clyde,
Laurie, and Tom. In Nov. of 1980 Clyde, a student at SDSM&T, died in a car
accident. Laurie is married to James Brigden and has four children. James is in
the U.S. Navy and they reside in NY. Tom and his wife, Maureen, reside in
Jamestown, ND, where Tom works as an architect.

Fred, Jr., attended West Spring Valley School throughout his grade school years
and then attended and graduated from Selby High School in 1957. He attended SDSU
before receiving a Business Degree from Minot State College. In 1967 he moved to
Las Vegas, where he has worked in the gaming business, and has resided there
ever since. He never married.

Leonard also attended West Spring Valley School before attending and graduating
from Selby High School in 1958. Leonard attended SDSU before entering
Springfield State College, where he received a degree in auto-body mechanics. He
married Dorothy Beaver (deceased) on Oct. 8, 1960, in Mobridge. After living in
Selby, Rapid City, and Mobridge, they moved to Pierre in 1964. Leonard worked
for many years for Beck Motors before starting his own car salvage business,
Pierre Auto Parts. He and his son, Barry, operated this business together until
Leonard's death on Jan. 13, 1999. Leonard had three children: Barry, Jody and
Jackie. Barry and his wife, Karla, live in Pierre and operate Pierre Auto Parts.
Jackie works for the State of SD and lives with her son, Chase, in Pierre. Jody
is married to David Unruh and lives in Fort Pierre with their two boys and one
girl.

Robert attended West Spring Valley School for four years before it closed. He
then attended school in Java before graduating in 1967. He attended NSC for one
year before attending and graduating from SDSU, with a degree in Agriculture.
Following graduation, he returned to the family farm, where he has since
resided. On Feb. 18, 1978 he married Pamela Schneider (daughter of Rinel and
DeLila Schneider) at St. Paul Lutheran in Java. Pamela (born July 30, 1956)
graduated from Java High School in 1974 and attended Pierre School of Practical
Nursing. She worked as an LPN at the Mobridge Hospital until their marriage, and
has since worked at the Selby Good Samaritan Center. They remain members of St.
Paul Lutheran Church.

Robert and Pamela were blessed with the birth of three children. Their family
has been active in the Selby-Java communities, in school, church, 4-H and
community activities. Kelly Rae (born Dec. 7, 1980) is a 1999 graduate of Selby
Area High School. She began her school years attending the Java school. She is
attending NSC. Heidi Jo (born June 6, 1983) will graduate from Selby Area High
School in 2001. She also started her grade school education in Java. Cody Dean
(born Sept. 19, 1985) was a seventh grade student at Selby Area High School,
when he died of an accidental gunshot on Oct. 12, 1998. Although he was only 13
years old when he died, his enthusiasm and love of life touched the hearts of
many people around him. His family and community miss him.

        The Sieler Clan
George Adam Sieler was born in Altenstadt/Geislingen, Wurttemberg, and in late
1700 or early 1800, he and his wife, Johanna, moved to the German colony of
Torschau, Hungary. Around 1807, he and his family emigrated and settled in the
village of Freudental, South Russia. His son, Johann George, was born in 1806.
Johann George married Barbara Schuler and 13 children were born to this union.
Adam Sieler, a son, was born in 1813 and grew up in Freudental, South Russia. He
married Magdalena Pfaff, who was born in Peterstal, South Russia. They moved to
a new village called Helenental. Eleven children were born to this union. Their
son, Henry, who was a schoolteacher, was one of the first Germans from Russia to
immigrate to the U.S. He, with his wife and daughter, and his brother, Peter,
came in 1872 and spent the winter in Sandusky, OH. The following year, Henry
moved to the Menno area of Dakota Territory. Peter left Russia, as he was of
draft age and did not wish to serve in the Russian army. The Russian government
had placed political and economic restrictions on the German colonists. By 1884,
the entire clan, consisting of mother Magdalena and her children and their
families, Adam, Georg Philipp, Henry, Katharina (Jakob) Geigle, Jacob, Nicolaus,
Peter, Eva (Karl) Vollmer, Kaspar, Magdalena (Wilhelm) Ottmer, and Johanna
(Gottlieb) Schaefer, had come to the U.S. Included in this group were cousins
and in-laws, the Klemmers, Schaefers, and Adam Leno and his family.

When Henry and his brother, Peter, arrived in the U.S., they found, and settled
in, Menno, D.T. It was not until 1885 when the last member of the Sieler family
arrived in the U.S. When the last group came to Menno, they found that all land
had been taken and that Campbell and Walworth counties were now open for
homesteading. Thus, in 1885, Adam, the oldest son, and his wife and their seven
children; Georg Philipp, his wife and three grown sons, Heinrich, Adam and
Peter; Katharina (Jakob) Geigle and three children; Eva and Karl Vollmer and
children; Caspar and family; and Magdalena and Wilhelm Ottmer and children, with
their mother Magdalena, who was 65 years old, settled north of Salt Lake in
Blessing Township.

(Photo:) Katharina Geigle, Johanna Schaefer, Eva Vollmer and Magdalena Ottmer
         and husbands

Adam and his wife, Christina (Klemmer) Sieler, immigrated to the U.S. in 1874,
and lived in the Tripp area. In 1885, Adam and his family, along with his
brothers and sisters, settled in Sutley, Blessing Township. As his children
married, they moved to the Plevna, MT area. Adam died on July 7, 1905, of
apoplexy and was buried in the Odessa Reformed Church Cemetery in Sutley.
Christina later married George Wolf, Sr., of Java. She passed away in July 1915.
The Adam Sieler family had 9 children. Their farm was located in the NE quarter
of Section 18 of Blessing Township, which was a short distance NW of Salt Lake.

Georg Phillip was born in 1839, in Helenental, and married Magdalena Bechtold.
He came to the U.S. in 1885 with seven children, three of which were grown men.
Here in the U.S., he was known as Phillip Sieler. He filed his claim on the NW
quarter of Section 9 in Blessing Township, and his grown sons, Henry, Adam and
Peter, filed claims near this homestead. When Phillip died, he was buried in the
family cemetery located in the SW quarter of Section 4, on his own land. The
younger children moved to Plevna, MT. Henry, the oldest child of Philipp and
Magdalena, was born in 1869, in Helenental, South Russia. He married Christina
Tilman and they homesteaded the SE quarter of Section 6 in Blessing Township.
Christina passed away in 1917. Henry and Christina had 15 children. Henry then
married Mrs. Berg and four children were born to this union. Henry passed away
in 1946. Frieda (Art) Helm, the daughter of Henry and Christina, lives in Java.
Adam, son of Philipp, was born in Helenental, South Russia and married Elizabeth
Klingmann. He filed his claim directly north of his father. This union was
blessed with 10 children. Peter, son of Philipp, was born in Helenental, South
Russia and came to the U.S. in 1885, with his parents. He married Lydia Brockel
and they filed a claim NW of his fathers' homestead. They had two adopted
children. In 1938, they moved to Mobridge. Both Lydia and Peter are buried in
the Mobridge cemetery. Marie, daughter of Philipp and better known as Mary, was
born in South Russia. She married Andrew Berreth and they homesteaded in
Thompson Township. Victor Hirsch purchased this farm later. Andrew was a
Campbell County official for many years. Andrew was buried in Eureka and Mary,
in Aberdeen.

Katharina was born May 1851, in Helenental, and married Johann Jakob Geigle in
1869. The first four children died in infancy. On Sept. 27, 1884, with their
children Adam, Katharina and Johanna, they arrived in NY. Mrs. Geigle's aged
mother, Magdalena (Pfaff) Sieler, and a young couple, Adam and Christina Leno,
traveled with them to the U.S. The Lenos settled directly north of the Geigles.
The group purchased their tickets and on Sept. 30, they arrived in Scotland,
Dakota Territory and spent the winter with her sister, Johanna (Gottlieb)
Schaeffer. The next spring, the Geigles, Adam, Philipp and Kaspar Sielers, Adam
Leno, Wilhelm Ottmers, Karl Vollmers, Frederick Klemmer and Gottlieb and
Johannes Schafer, shipped their goods to Ipswich. From here, they traveled by
oxen to Blessing Township in Campbell County and they all settled north of Salt
Lake. Shortly after Sutley was established, in 1885 or 1886, this became their
post office. After 1887, Eureka became their trading town. When Java was
established in 1900, it became their trading town. The Geigles retired to Java
in 1916. On Sat., Mar. 17, 1923, Katharine passed away and was buried in the
Reformed Cemetery NW of Java. Jakob passed away on June 7, 1933, and was also
buried in the Reformed Cemetery. Twelve children were born to this union, four
of whom died in infancy in South Russia. The children are: Adam, Katharina
(Christ) Huether, Johanna (Fred) Hirning, Karolina (Fred) Hirning, Jacob, Rosina
(Matt) Borth, Christina (Herman) Marshall, and Alvina (Simon) Schaefer.

Eva was born Sept. 24, 1855, in Helenental, South Russia. She married Conrad
Vollmer in 1877, and they came to the U.S. in 1874. In the spring of 1885, they
homesteaded in Blessing Township and he developed a sizeable land holding. This
article appeared in the Mound City paper: Conrad Vollmer, a German-Russian
farmer living SE of Mound City, was instantly killed last Monday afternoon,
while on his way from Herried to his home. He had taken a load of wheat to that
town and was driving a young team. When near Mound City and going down a steep
hill, one of the wheels of his wagon struck a deep rut, throwing the unfortunate
man to the ground. The horses became frightened and ran away, dragging him some
distance. His right arm was broken in two places and no doubt his spinal column
injured so much that death came about 15 minutes after the accident. He was 55
years old and leaves a widow and five children. Funeral took place Wednesday
with Rev. H. Reuteman officiating. He was buried in Odessa Reformed Cemetery.
Shortly after the death of her husband, Eva returned to Tripp. She later married
a George Rassler.

Kaspar was born July 16, 1858, and he married Elizabeth Kries on Nov. 16, 1883.
They came to the U.S. on May 5, 1885. He homesteaded the NW quarter of Section
19 on the north side of Salt Lake in Blessing Township. This farm was sold to
Sam Goehring and later to Ed G. Biel. Kaspar and Elizabeth are both buried in
the Pollock cemetery.

Magdalena was born August 21, 1860, in Helenental and married Wilhelm Ottmer in
1882. They came to the U.S. in 1885 and homesteaded in Blessing Township. Some
time around 1905, the Ottmers moved to Wheeler, WA.

        Herbert S. Sieler by Herbert Sieler
My name is Herbert S. Sieler and I was born on a farm 16 miles north of Java. My
father was Henry P. Sieler, who migrated to the U.S., from Russia, with his
father Phillip Sieler (my grandfather) and mother Magdalene (Bechtold) Sieler,
in 1885.

Grandfather Phillip and sons Henry, Adam and Peter, homesteaded land in the
Sutley area, which is Campbell County. Brothers Gottlieb and John did not
homestead land in the Sutley area, instead, John settled in ND. Gottlieb lived
on the land his father homesteaded, after his father died. Gottlieb raised his
family there and moved to MT, in the early 1930's.

The brothers, Henry, Adam, Peter, Gottlieb and John, have all passed away and
very little now exists to show where the old homesteads once existed. All of the
children of these brothers have moved out of Campbell County and the only
Sieler, Frieda (Art) Helm, lives in Java.

I attended three years of high school in Java, having moved from Mound City,
where I completed my freshman year in 1936. I graduated from Java High School in
May 1939.

I recall my father and me hauling wheat to the Java Grain Elevator with horses
and a wagon, and also driving a herd of cattle to market in Java in the late
1920's.

My brother, Phillip, bought a house on the east end of Java and lived there
until he became ill and stayed in the Herreid Nursing home, for many years, and
finally died in a Nursing Home in Bowdle in 1992.

I also purchased a house in Java in the early 1990's and stay in it during my
summer vacation each year.

(Photo:) Herbert Sieler

My father's first wife (Frieda Helm's mother) died and he married Christina
(Schaffer-Berg), who was my mother. Two of my brothers died at birth and brother
Alvin now resides in Jamestown, ND. My sisters, Arlene lived in Denver and is
deceased, Elsie lived in Sacramento and is deceased, and Viola lives in Conde.

The Sieler family has been getting together the last several years in a reunion
with children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren. The reunion has been held
in June each year in Mobridge, and relatives from all over the U.S. attend. All
of Frieda Helm's brothers and sisters, except Rachel, have passed on and their
families are invited to attend the reunion each and every year.

        Vernard and Violet (Naasz) Sieler
Violet Naasz was born Oct. 15, 1923, at the family homestead east of Java. She

        John and Rosina (Fischer-Wolf) Sonnenfeld
John Sonnenfeld arrived in the U.S. in 1884 and spent some time in Menno, where
he worked for an uncle until the spring of 1885, when he and his wife, Rosina
Fischer Wolf, and sons, George and Henry, started for a new homestead by oxen.
They built a sod house on this homestead, but getting no water on that place, he
sold it and moved to Walworth County in 1890 in Adams Township NE of Java.

(Photo:) Emma, John, Jacob J. and Rosina Sonnenfeld

In the third week in June, on June 19, 1894, they finished building a two-room
house constructed of lumber. Mrs. Sonnenfeld had painted the front room with
lime and stippled it with bluing, as was the mode of the day. One evening that
same week, at about seven o'clock, John came to the house, warning his wife to
take the children and come with him to the root-cellar, as there was a storm
approaching from the SW. Never having any experience with a SD twister, Rosina
refused his request and continued with her housework. John and Christ Sackman,
who made his home with the Sonnenfelds, went outside to check on the storm. Just
then the tornado struck and unable to get to the house, they dropped to the
ground and crawled to safety and fortunately were able to get to the root
cellar. The tornado was followed with a drenching rain and almost complete
darkness. By the flashes of lightning, they saw that the house was gone and they
began to search for the family. They found the body of the oldest son, John (5),
who was killed by the twister; about the distance of a city block, they found
the rest of the family huddled together in a lakebed. The younger son, Jake (3),
was unconscious from a head wound. Rosina had a severely cut leg and head
injuries. By all the misfortune, there still was a protecting hand that shielded
George and Henry, as they were unhurt.

Carrying John's body and the unconscious Jake, and supporting Rosina between
them, they made their way to the Adam Wagner homestead, about one-half mile
west. The Wagners were living in a dugout at the time. All their belongings,
including their clothing, were wet. The night was turning cold, everything was
wet and with nothing to kindle a fire, it was very miserable. Everybody was
waiting for the dawn of morning to seek relief. When John came to Bowdle the
next day, Dr. Edwards was out of town and a young Dr. Murdy accompanied him
back. Dr. Murdy stitched Mrs. Sonnenfeld's leg and did what he could to help,
but infection set in. Dr. Edwards made several trips out and finally had to
restitch the leg. When the people of the area heard of the misfortune of the
John Sonnenfelds, they gave them bedding, utensils, furniture, etc., and, after
building a sod house, they were able to set up a home again.

In Aug. 1896, a girl, Emma, (Mrs. John Klein) was born. Rosina never regained
her health and was a semi-invalid the remainder of her life.

In 1918 the couple retired from the farm and moved to Java, where they were
living when Rosina died in 1929 and John in 1936. Jake lived on the farm until
he retired.

Johannas Sonnenfeld, father of John Sonnenfeld, came to America in 1887, and
also settled near Menno before coming to Walworth County in 1889. Two sons came
with him, who were Fred and Henry, and one daughter, who married Karl Kost on
Jan. 12, 1888. Johannas Sonnenfeld was in the big blizzard and froze his feet so
badly that the small toes on both feet had to be amputated.

        The Jacob Sonnenfeld Family
Jacob Sonnenfeld, son of John and Rosina (Fischer) Sonnenfeld, was born Apr. 21,
1891, in Adams Township, Walworth County. He grew up on the homestead 9 miles NE
of Java, and lived there until his retirement.

Adams Township was heavily populated in the early years. According to the tax
list, there were 52 farms in 1902-1905. Everyone in the area did all their
trading in Java, as there were no cars to travel to any distant places. Horses
were the main means of travel, and most people were happy to have these. In
1912, Jake and his father bought a two-cylinder, chain driven Buick at an
auction sale. It had a side crank to start it and a battery ignition system.
They used this car until 1915, when Jake purchased a Model T Ford, one of the
first cars around Java.

Jake started to farm with his father, John, in 1914, which was an eventful year,
as he also married Martha Schlaht on June 4, 1914. They were the parents of five
children, Emil, Erwin and Irene, and two who died in infancy. John Sonnenfeld
retired and moved into Java in 1918, and Jake and his family continued to live
on the homestead. His wife Martha passed away on Dec. 28, 1932.

Maggie Kranzler and Jake Sonnenfeld were married on Sept. 19, 1933, and are the
parents of one son, Donald, born Nov. 6, 1934.

As was the case with all the pioneers, the Sonnenfeld family remembers good and
bad years. In 1934, they too experienced one of the worst droughts Jake could
remember. There was no hay and no pasture. They had to ship in hay to feed the
few head of cattle that they had left. To help offset the lean years, there are
also memories of very good crop years.

(Photo:) Mr. and Mrs. Jacob Sonnenfeld

Being civic-minded, Jake served on the Adams Township school board for many
years. He remembered that most of the children walked to school. The teacher
received wages of $25 per month and had charge of 25-30 pupils. Later the wages
were raised to $28 and $35 per month. In later years, some good teachers
received as much as $100 per month.

Jake and Maggie retired in 1940 and moved to Java, in the home where his father,
John Sonnenfeld resided.

Emil, who married Erna Oster, continued to live on the homestead after his
parents retired. In 1956 they moved to Pierre. Emil passed away Apr. 13, 1967.
They had three children: Kenneth, Loretta and Annetta.

Erwin married Alma Oster and lives in Aberdeen. They are the parents of two
children, Janice and Quenton.

Irene married David Rankin. They were the parents of two children, one died in
infancy, and a son, Allen. She died  Sept. 19, 1948.

Donald married Darlene Voegle and had one daughter.

        Erwin and Alma (Oster) Sonnenfeld
Erwin Sonnenfeld was born in Walworth County on the family homestead 9 miles NE
of Java, on Sept. 16, 1917, to Jacob J. and Martha (Schlaht) Sonnenfeld. He
attended the Norbeck School, a one-room country school, where he graduated from
the eighth grade.

Alma Oster was born in Walworth County about 12 miles NE of Java, to Jacob and
Katherina (Buechler) Oster, on Sept. 3, 1921. Alma attended Horse Shoe Lake
School, where she graduated from the eighth grade.

Erwin and Alma were married on June 18, 1942, at St. Paul Lutheran Church in
Java with Rev. Kirchdoerfer performing the marriage. They lived with Erwin's
brother, Emil, in the summer kitchen on the Sonnenfeld homestead, from June
until Mar. of 1943. At that time, they purchased the Fred C. Wolf farm two miles
north of the Sonnenfeld homestead. They started their farming career with two
black sheep, three cows, a header box, and a Farmall F20 tractor with steel
wheels. All of their belongings fit into the header box, which they used to move
to their new farm home.

There were many good and bad years in farming. However, the good outnumbered the
bad. They recall the price of durum wheat, in the early 1970's, running about
$6.40 to $8 per bushel. They sold a 300-bushel truckload of durum and received
$2000. These good times made it possible to purchase land that belonged to
Erwin's grandfather, John, and land that belonged to Eva Ochszner, and also land
that belonged to Herbert Pfaff.

The Sonnenfelds were blessed with two children.

Janice, born July 1, 1944, is married to Arlyn Bieber. They have one son, Jay,
and live in Kent, WA. Jan graduated from SDSU and is President of the Federal
Way Education Association in Federal Way, WA. Arlyn is self-employed, working as
an electrician and carpenter. Jay is a senior, majoring in political studies at
Westminster College in Salt Lake City, UT.

Quenton, born Apr. 19, 1946, is married to Sharon Dalton and they live in
Golden, CO. Quenton owns and operates Sonnenfeld Enterprises, which specializes
in the restoration of vintage automobiles. Sharon is an administrator in
Jefferson County School District. Their son, Tyler, also lives in Golden. He
graduated from the U of Northern CO in Greeley and is employed at Bandimere
Raceway as the Director of Marketing for Special Events.

In the spring of 1969, eight-year old Cathy Krause came to live with the
Sonnenfelds. She has been a part of the family and is thought of as a daughter.
She married Nolan Lindemann and they live in Aberdeen. Cathy is employed as
Deputy Register of Deeds for Brown County. Nolan is employed at NSU as a boiler
engineer. Their daughter, Sanessa, is in grade school at the Henry Neil School
in Aberdeen.

(Photo:) Alma and Erwin Sonnenfeld

Erwin and Alma retired from farming about 20 years ago and continued to live on
the farm during the summer, until 1995, when they bought a home in Aberdeen and
moved there. They continue to spend six months in SD and six months in AZ, as
snowbirds. Erwin enjoys woodworking and fishing, and Alma is busy with china
painting and gardening. She belongs to a China Painting group in SD and in AZ,
and is a member of the Java Garden Club. They are members of St. Paul Lutheran
Church in Java.

        Philip and Rosina (Oster) Spiry Sr.
The ancestry of the Spiry family originated in the Province of Alsace-Lorraine,
France. The great-grandfather of Philip Spiry, Sr., was an army officer and was
accused of being partially responsible for Napoleon's defeat. He was charged
with treason and convicted to be executed; with the assistance of his friends,
he escaped prison and fled to Germany. He was a surveyor by trade, and later
employed by the Russian government to assist the crown land, which had been
granted by Czar Alexander I, of Russia, to his wife, Czarina Catherine II, a
former German princess.

The land was granted for German colonization with the privileges of religious
freedom, tax exemptions for 10 years, and exemption from military service. Each
family was allotted a portion of the crown land in tracts of about 100 acres.

(Photos:) Philip Spiry, Sr. and Rosina Spiry

The grandfather, Friederich Spiry, was the only son of the family and was born
in 1826 in Kassel, a German colony in the Ukraine of South Russia; he was united
in marriage to Louisa Jesser, a native of Wurttemberg, Germany. Five children
were born to this union: Karl, Philip, Fred and Karolina homesteaded and resided
in Walworth County; their oldest sister, Barbara, resided in Portland, OR.

Philip Spiry, Sr., was born in Kurdumanoff, South Russia, Mar. 20, 1865, and
came to America in 1885 with his brother Fred. They arrived in Scotland, SD, in
a penniless and half-starved condition, having had their last meal in New York
City three days prior to their arrival in Scotland. A kind-hearted merchant,
Henry Sieler, noticed the half-starved lads in front of his store and finally
questioned them. After hearing of their circumstances, he invited them into a
restaurant and bought them their first meal in Dakota Territory. They were
invited into his store and, before the end of the day, landed their first jobs
on farms. They were employed as farm laborers in the vicinity of Menno and
Scotland, until they learned that free government land was available for
homesteading in Walworth County. In Mar. of 1888, they and two other families
arrived at Ipswich in an emigrant car.

Philip brought with him one ox, one horse, a farm wagon and a breaking plow,
while Fred had two ponies. From Ipswich, they proceeded in a westerly direction
and finally arrived at Hiddenwood Creek. They followed the creek looking for
water weeds, which would indicate shallow water. They knew that well-drilling
equipment was not available for miles. They dug a well with a spade and found a
plentiful supply of water at the 6-8 foot depth. Their sod house was completed
in a few days at the cost of $24.

Philip married Rosina Oster on Dec. 5, 1889, at Bowdle, and homesteaded on a
farm three and one-half miles north of Java. In 1896, he was elected as county
assessor and served for two years. In 1900 he entered the farm implement
business in Java, in partnership with his brother, Fred. In 1902, he was elected
County Treasurer and served to the end of 1906.

In the spring of 1903, the Spiry family moved to Bangor, the county seat of
Walworth County. In the spring of 1905, they moved their residence to Selby. A
short time later, litigations arose and the court ordered the county seat to be
returned to Bangor. A new frame building was erected, and the county records
were returned; again it became necessary for him to make his daily trips to
Bangor, until the end of his term.

In the fall of 1906, the Spiry home was sold to E.C. Wilson and in Mar. of
1907, the family moved to Java. He started the German State Bank in 1906,
renaming it the American State Bank during World War I. He was actively engaged
in the banking business until poor health caused his retirement. After the death
of John H. Wolff in 1918, Philip purchased the Ford Garage, which was known
thereafter as Spiry and Sons Ford Garage. His sons managed the garage for many
years.

In 1924, he served as City Mayor. He was treasurer of the Board of Education,
president of the board of trustees and, during the 31 years of residence in
Java, held many other offices. He passed away at home on Jan. 28, 1936.

Philip and Rosina had 11 children: Magdalena Zweigardt Aman; Philip H.; Charles
Frederick (Fred); John E.; Bertha Hay; Samuel; Rosie Hochstatter; Dr. Arthur W.;
Theodore; Annette Heezen; and Edwin Alvin.

        C.F. (Fred) and Rosie (Zeller) Spiry
Carl Frederick Spiry, known as "Fred", born Dec. 16, 1892, on a farm three miles
north of Java, was the second oldest son of Philip and Rosina (Oster) Spiry. On
Aug. 30, 1914, he was married to Rosa (Rosie) Zeller. They had one child,
Harold, who served as superintendent of the Java City schools for many years and
as a business teacher in Aberdeen and Mobridge.

For several years, Fred was associated with his father and brothers in the
operation of the German State Bank, later known as the American State Bank.
After the death of John H. Wolf in 1918, Philip Spiry, Sr., purchased the Ford
Garage, and Fred managed the garage business. The Spiry and Sons Ford Garage was
under his management from 1918 until 1940. Associated with him in the operation
of the garage were his brothers. After Fred's death, his wife, Rosie, and his
brother, Sam, operated the garage for approximately 20 years. In his earlier
years he also was an active participant in the operation of the Spiry Meat
Market, which was operated by Fred and several of his brothers. Active, in some
capacity, in the operation of the bank, garage, and meat market were brothers,
Fred, Sam, Johnny, Philip, Arthur, Ted and Alvin.

(Photo:) C.F. and Rosie Spiry

Fred served as a member of the Java City Council for over 10 years, was a member
of the Java Volunteer Fire Department and school board, and was prominent in
Republican circles in Walworth County for many years.

His wife, Rosie, and her sister, Lena, operated the Central Hotel in Java for
several years prior to 1914. Rosie was active in community affairs, extension
clubs, Republican circles, the Spiry Garage, the church choir, the G & L
Grocery, and other service organizations.

Fred passed away on Apr. 4, 1940. Serving with him on the Java City Council at
the time of his death were A.C. Schlepp, Mayor; John Lutz, Ed Gill, Louis
Boehler, Fred Bauer, C.L. Hicks, Fritz Clement, and John Schlaht.

        Harold F. Spiry
Harold F. Spiry, the third generation of the Spiry family to live in Java, was
born in Java on June 7, 1915, the son of C.F. (Fred) and Rosie Spiry. He
attended the Java Public School all 12 years and was graduated from Java High
School in 1933.

Harold then went on to college at USD, where he was graduated with a Bachelor of
Science degree, magma cum laude, and Phi Beta Kappa, in 1940.

He spent his lifetime in the teaching profession, which numbered some 50 years.
He served as Superintendent of the Java Public School for 9 years and an
additional five years as a classroom teacher. During his teaching career he also
served as a classroom teacher in Roscoe, Streeter, ND, Lennox, Milbank, Mobridge
and Aberdeen.

Harold served as president of the SD Business Teachers Association, and was a
member of the SDEA and NEA. He is presently a member of the Masonic Lodge and
Eastern Star in Mo-bridge, where he taught in the high school for some 20 years.
Also in Mo-bridge, he was a member of the Mobridge Rotary Club, the Toastmasters
Club, and several other clubs and organizations.

(Photo:) Harold Spiry

He is a lifetime member of St. Paul Lutheran Church in Java, where he directed
the choir for 20 years. Harold earned many awards in the field of vocal and
speech work, where he was awarded many Division I ratings, including several
superiors in State Competition. An avid writer, he has had numerous articles
published in national business magazines. Additional honors include dedication
of high school yearbooks, both in Java and in Mobridge. After receiving his
degree in Vermillion, he did graduate work at NSU in Aberdeen, UMN in
Minneapolis, and Columbia University, New York City. After retirement, Harold
returned to Java, where he now resides. [Editor's note: A Superior rating to the
best typing instructor ever!]

        Samuel E. and Hertha (Hauck) Spiry
Sam E. Spiry was born May 3, 1900, to Mr. and Mrs. Philip Spiry, Sr., on a farm
three and one-half miles north of Java. When Sam was two, the family moved to
Bangor, where his father was Walworth County Treasurer. When the courthouse was
moved to Selby, the family also moved to Selby. The Spiry family moved to Java
in 1906, where Mr. Spiry went into banking business. The family consisted of 12
children. In 1918 the Spirys purchased the garage from Mrs. John H. Wolf, which
was later known as Spiry and Sons.

(Photo:) Hertha and Sam Spiry

Hertha Hauck Spiry was born Nov. 23, 1906, to Mr. and Mrs. Karl Hauck, Sr., on a
farm 12 miles NW of Java in Campbell County. Hertha and younger brother, Henry,
moved to Java with their parents in 1919. The family consisted of four boys,
Fred, Carl, Ted and Henry, and six girls, Katherine, Bertha and Hertha, Alvine,
Lizzie and Alvina, who passed away at an early age.

Sam and Hertha were married on Sept. 9, 1924, in Java. Sam and his brother Fred
owned and operated the Spiry and Sons Standard Oil garage for many years. After
Fred died, Rosie, his wife, and Sam continued to operate the garage until 1961,
when it was sold to Francis Jensen and Sam retired from the garage business.

Four children born to Sam and Hertha were a son, who passed away in infancy,
Wallace, Betty and Tim.

Wallace was born on Dec. 1, 1931. He married Bonita Moser on Oct. 18, 1953, at
Java. Wallace and Bonita had three children, two sons and one daughter. They are
Daniel A., Steven D. and Vickie L. (Charles) Sandvik. Daniel is married to Joan
Buller and they have two daughters, Erin and Rachel. They are living in Lincoln,
NE. Vickie is married to Charles W. Sandvik and they have three children, Carl,
Wesley and Heather. They live in Enumclaw, WA. Steven is living in Rapid City.
Wallace and Bonita are retired and live in Rapid City.

(Photo:) Bonita and Wallace Spiry

Betty was born on Oct. 23, 1935. She married Marvin Pfitzer on Feb. 12, 1956.
Four children were born to them: Lori passed away in 1961 of cancer, Ivy, Gwen
and Kent. (See Family History)

Tim was born on Nov. 16, 1945. He married Virginia Schmierer on Oct. 2, 1966.
Three children were born to them: April Ann, who passed away in infancy,
Michelle and Sherri. They live on a farm near Bowdle.

Sam was a volunteer Fireman for many years and also, in his early years, played
the bass horn in the Java-Selby band. Hertha belonged to the Java ALCW for 43
years and the Thimble Sewing Club for 35 years.

        Vaughn and Luella (Pies) Spiry
Vaughn Spiry was born to Alvin and Suzie Spiry on Nov. 3, 1938, at Mobridge. He
was later joined by two younger brothers, Fredrick (deceased), and Roger, who

Vaughn attended elementary and secondary school in Java, and graduated from Java

(Photo:) Luella, Vaughn, Twyla and Arvyn Spiry

        Fred and Justina (Ernst) Spiry Sr.
In the spring of 1885, Fred Spiry, Sr., age 17, and his brother, Philip Spiry,
Sr., age 20, immigrated to the U.S. from Kurdumanoff, Russia. They arrived at
Scotland, SD, where they found jobs as farm laborers in the vicinity of Menno
and Scotland. In Mar. 1888, when they learned that free government land was
available in Walworth County, they left their jobs and arrived at Ipswich. They
traveled to Hiddenwood Creek, where they settled.

(Photo:) Fred Spiry, Sr. Family

In 1890, Fred married Justina Ernst from Roscoe, who also was born in Russia.
They built their first home, a sod house, three and one-half miles NE of Java.
They lived in this house until 1900, and then built the house that is still on
the farm and is now owned by Ron and Marjorie Fiedler. While living in the sod
house, they experienced the 1888 blizzard, which lasted four days. Fred and
Philip were in partnership in the implement business in Java for some time.
Later, Fred's profession was auctioneering, which covered a large area. He also
served as county commissioner for eight years, and ran his farm.

Justina was a busy farm wife and did her best in raising their family, which
consisted of: Emil, Minnie (Ed) Wolf, Philip, Sam, William, and Nettie (Leon)
Kast. One child died in infancy. They had 12 grandchildren.

In 1921 they decided to retire, because of Justina's ill health, and moved to
Java. Fred continued his auctioneering for some time. Justina Spiry died Sept.
10, 1924, at age 54. Fred married Mary Eva (Boehler) Ackerman on Sept. 17, 1927;
he passed away Mar. 12, 1931.

        Jacob and Magdalena (Laemmle) Stadel
Jacob Stadel was born in South Russia in 1865. He served in the Russian Army for
several years. He was united in marriage with Magdalena Laemmle in Jan. 1889.
She was the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Christ Laemmle, Sr.

(Photo:) Jacob and Magdalena Stadel, Sr.

Jacob and Magdalena immigrated to America right after their marriage and settled
on a homestead 14 miles west of Eureka. They lived there until 1906, when they
moved to a farm 9 miles NW of Java, where they lived until 1927, when they moved
to Java. Jacob passed away in Dec. 1942, and Magdalena passed away in Sept.
1956.

They raised 9 children. Christina Naasz passed away in 1919, NW of Java; Pauline
Lutz passed away in 1965 in Cornelius, OR; Jacob Stadel, Jr., passed away in
Java in 1958; Magdalena Nelson; Regina Schell; Matilda Stadel; Emma Elshire;
Martha Mauch; and Fred.

        Anton and Wilhelmine (Brandt) Stangl
Anton Stangl was born in Gross Eberharts, Austria, on Dec. 6, 1866, and
immigrated to the U.S. in the spring of 1884, settling first near Little Falls,
MN, where he worked as a lumberjack and on an uncle's farm. In the spring of
1888, he came to Dakota Territory, joining his brother, Joe, who had come to
Walworth County two years earlier. These two brothers worked together in the
Spring Lake area for a number of years, tilling the soil and establishing a
farmstead. Anton broke his first sod with a hand plow and a team composed of a
mule and an ox.

Two outstanding events often recalled by these two brothers from the first years
of their life here, were the blizzard of 1888 and the Indian scare of 1890. On
this latter occasion, they, too, being warned by the people going by their place
on the Bangor road, hitched their team to a wagon and joined their neighbors in
the trek to safety in Bowdle, after carefully hiding their ten-gauge shotgun in
the weeds so the Indians wouldn't find it!

1897 was an eventful year for Anton for he became a U.S. citizen, and he married
Wilhelmine (Minnie) Brandt from north of Bowdle. She was born on Mar. 6, 1881,
in WI, and had lived in MN, for a time, before coming to SD. This couple had 9
children, six boys and three girls. Two sons died in infancy. Irving died in
1969 and A. Donal died in 1974.

As was the case with most pioneers, Anton and Minnie worked hard to establish a
home and increase their farm operation. In 1899 two 40-acre plots, which
adjoined the homestead and tree claim, were purchased from the government. The
two brothers continued to live on the same farm until 1904, when Joe sold out to
Anton and moved to a new place a mile away.

Deciding to retire in 1926, Anton and Minnie turned the operation of the farm
over to their oldest sons, Donal and Albert, and purchased a home in Java. Their
residence here was short-lived, for in that fall, Minnie suddenly became ill and
died on Oct. 1. Anton decided to return to the farm, where he continued to live
until his death in June 1946.

(Photo:) Minnie and Anton Stangl

Father Time continued to take members of the family. Albert died in Dec. 1975
and Vina (Ralph) Sawinsky died Mar. 1976. Raymond Lee, husband of Frances, died
in July 1983, and Frances died in Oct. 1987. Herman and Emma (Stangl) Fiedler
sold their home in Java, had an auction and moved to Jackson, MN in Aug. 1993.
Herman died in Sept. 1995. (See Family History) Ella Stangl, widow of Donal,
continued to live in Java, later moving to the Good Samaritan Center in Selby.
She died Dec. 1996. Her daughter, Lois (Marvin) Wolf and husband live in Java.

Orville continued farming the home farm, until he retired in 1988. He continues
to live in the farm home, in which he was born, that was built in 1903 by his
father, Anton, and his uncle Joe Stangl.

A grand nephew, Richard Osterday, joined Orville in a farm partnership on the
Stangl Shorthorn Farm in 1984. Rick is the son of Richard and Elaine (Stangl)
Osterday, and grandson of Donal and Ella Stangl. Rick took over complete
management of the farm in 1988, and is gradually assuming ownership of the farm.
(See Family History)

The future of the Stangl Shorthorn farm looks bright in the hands of the fourth
generation on the farm. The fifth generation, Blane and Clay Osterday, show
great interest and energy about farm and ranch life for the future.

        Adolph Stangl
Adolph Stangl was born June 12, 1873, in Gross Eberharts, Austria, to Mr. and
Mrs. Moritz Stangl, where he grew to manhood. In 1898, he came to the U.S. on
the Kaiser Wilhelm, one of the larger ships on the ocean at that time. He
engaged in farming for his two brothers, Joe and Anton Stangl, for a few years,
and then he homesteaded and began farming on his own. On Nov. 7, 1902, he
married Magdeline Aman nee Merkel, at Bangor.

The couple farmed in the Spring Lake area, east of Java, until they retired to
the town of Java in the fall of 1918, where they built a new home.

(Photo:) Adolph and Magdaline Stangl

Magdeline Stangl had three children from her first husband, John Aman, who had
passed away: Amelia (Everett) Sebert; Julius Stangl, who lived at Java; and John
Stangl. One daughter, Mrs. Bertha Stulken, was born to Adolph and Magdeline

On Nov. 30, 1933, Magdeline Stangl died. Adolph lived alone in his home until
Nov. 9, 1935, when he married Louise Sauer. They continued to make their home in
Java until his death, Jan. 7, 1968. He had three grandchildren and 9
great-grandchildren at the time of his death.

        Julius Stangl
Julius Stangl was born Oct. 2, 1897 to Mr. and Mrs. John Aman, in a sod house
east of Java. His father died Nov. 21, 1898, when Julius was one year and two
months old. His mother married Adolph Stangl on Nov. 7, 1902, at Bangor, south
of Selby. They moved to the homestead and lived in a two-room claim shack.

In 1918, Julius and John, his brother, took over the farm home of their parents,
Adolph and Magdeline Stangl, who built a new home and moved to Java. The boys
did some batching for a few years and besides farming, also did some trapping,
buying their first car with money from furs and skins. They trapped and had
enough money left to drive the car for one year.

(Photo:) Julius and Isy Stangl

In 1921, there was a double wedding: Julius married Isy and John married Eunice
Whitney, sisters from Mobridge. They farmed together until 1923, when Julius
bought John's share of livestock and farm machinery. John and Eunice and their
son moved to Aberdeen, WA.

Julius and Isy farmed the home place for 24 years. They had no children. In the
fall of 1945, they sold their livestock and farm machinery and bought the Fred
Permann home in Java, and spent the winter months in OR, visiting friends and
relatives. When they came back, they moved into their home.

Isy (Whitney) Stangl died in June 1949. Julius lived alone for eight years, took
care of his yard and raised a lot of nice flowers, fruits and vegetables and
also worked as hired help on the farms of Reinhold Moser, Art and Herbert
Bieber.

In 1957, he married Hilda Diegel of Roscoe, at the home of his sister, Mr. and
Mrs. Everett Sebert. Julius passed away Sept. 6, 1974, and his wife, Hilda,
resides in Java.

(Photo:) The Julius and Hilda Stangl Family

Hilda has five children. Lloyd Diegel lives in Mitchell and has one son, Stacy,
and one daughter, Michelle. Lawrence and Janice (Fischer) Diegel live in
Aberdeen and have one son, Steve, and three daughters, Cindy, Lisa and Karla,
and five grandchildren. Phyllis and Al Hite also live in Aberdeen and have one
son, Les, two daughters, Carol and Tracy, and four grandchildren. Donna (Diegel)
and Carlyle Bieber live in Java and have two sons, Clyde and Kevin, and five
grandchildren. Calvin and Sandy (Diehl) Diegel live in Portsmouth, VA. Hilda
lived in her home in Java until Oct. 1992, when she sold the house and move into
an apartment in Java, where she continues to reside.

        Jacob and Katherina (Berg) Stiegelmeier
Jacob Stiegelmeier was born May 5, 1891, north of Java, to Jacob and Rosina
(Hausauer) Stiegelmeier, Sr. His father and mother were both born in Gluckstal,
South Russia, in 1862 and 1861, respectively. Jacob, Sr., passed away in 1927
and his wife, Rosina, passed away in 1938. Katherina Berg was born Aug. 6, 1898,
in Neudorf, South Russia, to Samuel and Rosina (Roth) Berg, who came to
McClusky, ND, when Katherina was 12 years old. Both of her parents were born in
Neudorf, South Russia.

Jacob and Katherina were married in 1919. Jacob attended Plainview Academy at
Redfield and was a teacher in ND, for two years. After he and Katie were
married, they farmed six miles NW of Java, living in the sod house on that farm.

Their children enjoyed fishing, swimming, and family picnics at Lake Hiddenwood,
which was just two miles west of the farm.

Katie and Jacob had four children, all of whom attended Edison Country School.
Wilmer graduated from Selby High School and married Rosina Bauman They had
Diana, Dawn, Mark and Paul. Milton graduated from Selby High School and married
Phyllis Bossert, and they had James, John and Jerome. Ellen graduated from Java
High School and married Harry Girard. They were the parents of Gary and Russell.
Harry Girard passed away and Ellen married Howard Bruett, who is also deceased.
DeLila graduated from Java High School, married Rinel Schneider, and they had
Rebecca and Pamela.

(Photos:) Jacob B. Stiegelmeier and Katie Stiegelmeier

In 1949, Jacob and Katie retired from farming and moved into Selby. Jacob passed
away June 20, 1967 at Bismarck and Katherina (Katie) passed away Dec. 15, 1988,
at Mobridge.

        Ben and Emma (Wolf) Stiegelmeier
Ben H. Stiegelmeier was born July 8, 1901, north of Java, to Jacob and Rosina
(Hausauer) Stiegelmeier, Sr. He attended rural grade school, graduated from Java
High School, attended NSC in Aberdeen, and taught in several rural grade
schools. Emma Wolf was born Nov. 6, 1904, to John and Rosina Wolf. She attended
Java school and graduated from Java High School with the class of 1924. She
attended a beautician school in Kansas City, KS, and upon graduation, worked as
a beautician for many years in KS, Aberdeen, and in Java.

Ben and Emma were married June 6, 1926. They made their first home in Ekalaka,
MT, where they operated a movie theater and soft-drink parlor. In 1927, they
returned to Java, where Emma owned and operated her beauty salon. Ben operated
the Plymouth-Dodge Garage, and farmed from 1928 until he retired, in 1981.

(Photo:) Ben and Emma Stiegelmeier

Ben and Emma were the parents of two daughters. Joy Lynne Tooley, residing at
Columbus, NE, is the mother of three sons, Patrick, Steve and Christopher
Tooley. Beverly married Wayne Schnaible and they are parents to a son, Perry,
and a daughter, Kelly Grieben. Beverly and Wayne reside 10 miles south of Java,
on their farm.

In addition to farming, Ben and J. Herman Fiedler owned and operated the Java
Theater in the 40's. In the 50's, Ben was co-owner of the Mobridge Commission
Co., a livestock sales barn. Ben served on many county, school, and town boards.
He was an avid sports fan and rarely missed any of the Java sporting events.
Both Ben and Emma thought that Java was always the best place to live. Ben
passed away Feb. 5, 1989, and Emma passed away on Mar. 26, 1996, both at the
Good Samaritan Center at Selby.

        Lanny and Karmen (Leber) Stiklestad

        Stuart and DeeAnn (Dearborn) Surma

Samuel Goetz was a descendent of the Gottlieb and Christina (Oster) Goetz family

        Henry A. and Ella (Adams) Taylor
Henry A. Taylor, born at Pittsfield, ME, on Oct. 12, 1863, attended school there
and graduated from college at Pittsfield. He came west and worked in Minneapolis
and later, in lumber camps in MN. In 1887, he came to Walworth County and filed
on a claim in the Adams Township NE of Java. He built a sod house and during
winter, taught school. He continued teaching for a number of years after he was
married. On Sept. 16, 1894, Henry married Ella Adams, who was born in West
Haven, VT on Dec. 18, 1877, the daughter of B.P. and Emma Adams. B.P. Adams
brought his family to Dakota Territory in 1886 and took up land in Walworth
County. Adams Township was named for him. The Adams family raised cattle, and
Ella and her brother, Elnathan, spent their time herding the cattle.

Henry was elected county auditor in 1897 and they moved to Bangor. When his term
expired, they moved back on the farm. Henry helped build the railroad that went
through Java, Selby, and on to Mobridge. He worked there all summer. He had a
team of horses that worked, too. The family built the first hotel in Java, The
Taylor Hotel. They lived in Java for a short time before they bought a farm 9
miles NE of Java. Henry was elected county auditor in 1911 and the family moved
to Selby. He was a charter member of the Masonic Lodge in Java. Henry and Ella
had two children, Frank and Nellie. Henry passed away Feb. 6, 1939 and he and
Ella are buried in Selby.

        Jacob J. and Bertha (Strobel) Teske
Jake was born at Evarts and moved to Eureka, with his parents, when he was a
child. Bertha was born at Eureka, where she attended school, as did Jake. Jake
went to work for the railroad when he was 13, and in 1924, became section
Foreman at Faulkton. Bertha and Jake were married at Eureka in 1925. They moved
to Java in 1928, and Jake was section Foreman for the remainder of his life.
Jake was a volunteer fireman and both were members of St. Paul Lutheran Church
in Java. Jake passed away in 1964; Bertha remained in Java until 1987, when she
moved to Sioux Falls, where she passed away in 1990. The Teskes had three
children. Clarence  was born in 1927 and died in infancy. Harvey was born in
1928, and Jeanette was born in 1934.

(Photo:) Bertha and Jacob Teske

Harvey was born, raised and educated in Java. He went to work on the Milwaukee
Railroad in 1943 as section laborer temporary (summers and holidays), and then
worked through the ranks as agent, telegrapher, train dispatcher and Chief
Dispatcher. He retired from the Milwaukee/Soo Line Railroad as Chief Dispatcher
at St. Paul, MN, in 1989, after a fulfilling career covering 46 years. He had
worked at various stations in MT, SD, ND and MN.

Harvey married Delores Bauer, a classmate, in 1948. Two daughters were born to
this union. Debby lives in Minneapolis and Lorri lives in Aberdeen and has three
children.

(Photo:) Delores and Harvey Teske

Delores passed away in 1968, and in 1972, Harvey married Marcella Schneider
Hough at Aberdeen. Marcella has a daughter, Lynette, who now lives in Maple
Grove and has two daughters. Harvey and Marcella live in New Hope, MN.

Jeanette graduated from Java High School in 1952 and was class Salutatorian. She
then went to school in Rapid City and later worked in Aberdeen, where she
married Virgil Munger in 1956. They moved to Sioux Falls in 1958, where Virgil
worked for the post office until his retirement. In 1990, they moved to
Larchwood, IA, where they presently reside. They are the parents of three
children, Kristi, Greg and Kevin, and have seven grandchildren.

        Martin Thorson
Martin Thorson, born in 1873, came to America in 1886, with his parents, George
and Emma Thorson, and two sisters, Turina and Ida. They came to Walworth County,
where his father filed claim on two quarters of land near the Spring Lake area.
They lived there until Martin became of age, then filed claim on a quarter of
land 10 miles SE of Java.

(Photo:) Mr. and Mrs. Martin Thorson

His sisters both passed away while quite young, during the flu epidemic.
Martin's father married Minnie Rathke in 1905, and they moved on his father's
farm. He was one of the directors of the Java Equity Exchange for a number of
years. He was also a school board member of the Ryan School, where four of his
children attended school. Five children were born to the Martin Thorsons, who
were Gladys, Loyd, Melvin, Ida, and Lorraine.

In 1911, a larger house was built on his land. They farmed for many years, as
Martin's greatest interest was grain farming and raising cattle and horses. In
1918, they bought a house in Java and in 1919, they returned to the farm. In
1920 the Thorsons moved to Compton, CA, when Martin's health indicated a need
for the change. Five years later, they moved to Riverside, where they bought an
orange grove and started raising oranges. Two more children, Dorothy and
Clinton, were born to them. Martin was a director of the Orange Packing House
Assn. for 25 years. In 1965, Martin passed away at the age of 88, and Mrs.
Thorson resided at Riverside with her two oldest sons until her death.
