        Edward Wagner
Edward Wagner was born and raised on a farm between Eureka, Bowdle and Java.
After he finished elementary school, he was able to attend high school, when the
government opened space at Java High School, for 50 cents a week. He became
interested in biology because he had a good teacher, whose face he can recall
but has forgotten his name. He also became interested in dentistry when his
father observed that, at $5 for a tooth filling, it was a good profession to
follow.

Edward was accepted at Walla Walla College, where he could work for four years
for all-school expenses. He went west and earned his bachelor's degree, after
which he attended WA State College (now University) and earned a Master's degree
in Zoology. After teaching at two senior colleges for four years in MA, and MI,
he earned his Doctor of Philosophy Degree at USC (Southern CA). He was given an
appointment at Loma Linda U, on a faculty position, mostly for research and
teaching medical students. After 40 years, he was given the status of Emeritus
Professor in microbiology. Since his work was in parasitology, he was able to
visit many foreign countries and he and his wife lived in Costa Rica and Africa,
for research work.

(Photo:) Edward and Ellen Wagner

Edward has fond memories of Java High School. He and a girl friend skipped
school to visit a farm, and got caught, and served 'time' for it. There were
nights a few of them went out for a 'walk', all harmless in the 30's. Baseball
and track were important events, but he doesn't recall earning any medals. He
doesn't recall having homework assignments, but does remember taking Latin,
which turned out to be valuable for him, as it helped in scientific terminology
in his future studies. He recalls the regional music contests in Mobridge, as
well.

Edward married Ellen Greenway of OR on Aug. 23, 1952. They have three children.

        Karl and Louisa (Naasz) Wahl
Karl Wahl was born Mar. 3, 1863 at Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, Romania, South
Russia. He was united in marriage to Louisa Wahl at Kloestitz, a village in
Romania, in 1889. Three months after their marriage, the young couple
accompanied other members of her family to America, to seek land and find a new
home. They spent eight days on ship to New York, three days on the train to
Eureka. On arrival there, they secured food supplies, a wagon, two oxen and a
cow, and settled on a prairie homestead. They lived in the open with a wagon box
turned over for protection, storing their food supplies, and sleeping at night,
until a sod house could be built. They used the wagon box for work during the
day. Three years later, they moved on their homestead located about six miles NW
of Java.

(Photo:) The Karl Wahl Family

They were baptized and confirmed in the Lutheran faith, attended church in the
little country church and later, St. Paul Lutheran Church in Java.

In 1926, they moved to Java and built a new home on the west side of Java. Karl
Wahl passed away Oct. 14, 1930 at the age of 67. Louisa continued to live in
Java until 1944, when she moved to Selby and lived for 22 years. She moved to
the Good Samaritan Center in 1966 and remained there until her death, Dec. 30,
1968, at the age of 99.

Twelve children were born to Karl and Louisa Wahl, Fred, Edward (died in 1968),
Emila (Alex) Adolph, George, Julius (died in 1921), Carl, Albert, Adam (died in
1964), Rose, (Ellis) Hoffman, Lydia (Bob) Hepper, Louise (John) Mutschler, and
Alvina (Larry) Ebert.

Fred married Caroline Keszler. Merle, their son, was born in their home in Java
in 1928. He grew up on the family farm 9 miles SW of Mound City. In 1950, he
married Hilda Schneider, who was born in 1927 to William and Emma (Werre)
Schneider on the farm that was homesteaded by her grandparents, north of Java.
After Merle and Hilda were married, they took over the family farm SW of Mound
City, where they lived and farmed for many years. Merle retired from farming and
went to work for the Corps of Engineers, at Mobridge. He met many people from
all over the U.S. that came to vacation and fish in Mobridge. Hilda and Merle
have one son, Eldon, who lives and works in Aberdeen. After Eldon was grown,
Hilda went to work at the Good Samaritan Center in Selby, where she continued
for 10 years. She then worked at the Mobridge Care Center for two years. When
the Fred Wahls retired, they moved to Mobridge.

(Photo:) Merle, Hilda and Eldon Wahl

        Frederich and Margaretha (Becker) Walz
Frederich Walz was born in Krien, South Russia, on Dec. 15, 1865, and came to
America in 1873, with his parents, Christian and Josephine (Beiler) Walz, who
settled around Freeman.

In 1885, he married Margaretha Becker, born in Russia in 1867, who came to
Freeman in 1883. They made their home on a farm NE of Freeman for a number of
years. In the spring of 1900, they and their three children, Pauline Walz Baer
(deceased), Christian (deceased), and Ferdinand, and Miss Magdalena Becker, a
sister of Mrs. Walz, came to Bowdle, which was the end of the railroad at the
time, by train, with all of their belongings. They moved to a farm 10 miles SE
of Java, which Frederich had purchased in the fall of 1899. Four more children
were born to this family. They are: Mrs. Elsie Gorne, Edward, Fred O. Walz, and
Theophil.

Frederich Walz was well known as a thresher. He owned one of the first Mogel
Kerosene threshing engines, which also pulled an eight-bottom plow. Frederich
was a stockholder of the Java Equity.

He died during the flu epidemic of 1918, and his daughter-in-law, Mrs. Christian
Walz (Pauline Miller), died the following day. Their funeral was held the same
day at Trinity Lutheran Cemetery.

(Photo:) The Frederich Walz Family

The mother, her five youngest children, and her sister, Miss Becker, continued
to farm until the children were old enough to go out on their own. Some of the
farmland is still owned and farmed by grandchildren.

Margaretha Becker Walz continued to live on the home place with her son, Fred,
until 1952, when her health failed. She spent some time with her other children,
and then spent her last remaining years at the Eureka Lutheran Rest Home. She
passed away in Jan. 1958, at the age of two days short of 91 years.

        Ferdinand and Emilie (Bieber) Walz
Ferdinand Walz was born in 1897, at Freeman, to Frederich and Margaretha
(Becker) Walz. Emilie Bieber was born in 1903 at Eureka. They both grew up in
Walworth County, south of Java, and were married in Nov. 1921. Their first home
was NW of Hoven, on the Herman Bonen farm. After one year, they moved south of
Java to what is known as the Herbert Bieber farm. Their three children, Leota,
Norwin and Orville, were born here.

(Photo:) Ferdinand, Emilie, Orville, Norwin and Leota Walz

On Feb. 16, 1926, the Axel Borg farm was bought. Two years later, they built a
home and moved to the new farm. Here is where the three children grew up. Leota
married Robert Elkins and they have one son. Norwin married Darlene Albrecht and
they have five sons. Orville, married to Delores Schuh, has three daughters, and
lives in Bowdle.

Ferdinand and his brother, Christ, owned a threshing rig and did a great deal of
threshing every fall. Ferdinand was quite active in church and community
affairs. He was a school board member of the Ryan School district for many
years, and was also a director of the Java Equity Exchange.

In the fall of 1953, they built a home in Bowdle. They are now deceased.

        Bob and Leota (Walz) Elkins
Leota Walz was born Apr. 27, 1923, the only girl and the oldest of three
children of Ferdinand and Emilie (Bieber) Walz. She attended country school and
graduated from Northwestern Lutheran Academy and from NSTC. After teaching for
eight years, three of which were in Java, she moved to Denver, CO, and worked in
the reservation office of United Airlines, until her marriage in 1964.

Since Leota was the oldest grandchild of her Bieber grandparents, she received
special treatment, especially from her teenage aunts. She also drove header box
and would be shocked into reality when the horses weren't in the right track and
she would hear her Grandpa's loud, shrill whistle. Leota's Grandfather Walz had
died before she was born, but he was very musical and passed this gift on to his
children and grandchildren. Before the Baer Church had an organ, he would be the
'fore singer'. Leota's dad was musical and played the violin, while her mother
played the organ. Even though her dad had only a third grade education, he could
figure out how to fix or build something electrical, mechanical, or in carpentry
work. As one of his pre-school grandsons said, "Grandpa can fix anything."

(Photo:) John, Leota and Bob Elkins

Leota married Bob Elkins Jan. 1, 1964, at Denver. They moved to a farm in ND,
where she still lives. Bob was born Apr. 24, 1922, the only boy and the oldest
of four children, to Silvert and Elsie Larson Elkins. He attended country school
and graduated from Taylor High School in ND. When Bob was eight, his father lost
an arm in a power take-off accident. Therefore, after high school, Bob helped
his father with the farming and ranching, later assuming the whole
responsibility. Bob's grandfather Elkins had a steam engine, which Bob's dad
would use to haul water, during spring breaking and the fall threshing, for the
whole pioneer area. His grandfather Larson was a Lutheran pastor, preaching in
English, Norwegian and German, for the immigrant pioneers in the Taylor area. He
also started many Lutheran churches within a 60-mile radius, traveling with a
horse and buggy and by train. Services were often during the week in the
outlying areas. Bob's mother was the church organist from the time she was 14
years old, until her own family was grown.

Bob and Leota had one child, John, who was born May 21, 1965. He attended school
in Taylor until his senior year, when Taylor and Richardton merged. After this,
he graduated from Phoenix Institute of Technology and the ND School of Science.
He worked five years at Channel 8 TV Station in Grand Forks, ND, and then as an
engineer for Western Geophysical on a seismograph boat.

Bob and Leota did small grain farming and, in the last years, were doing organic
farming. Originally, they raised Hereford cattle and later, mostly Simmental.
Hogs were raised in confinement. Bob loved to work with horses and died in Aug.
1995 in an accident, while mowing grass with his Suffolk team of horses.

        Norwin and Darlene (Albrecht) Walz
Norwin was born near Java on Mar. 9, 1925, to Ferdinand and Emilie (Bieber)
Walz. He attended rural school and graduated from Java High School. Darlene
Albrecht was born in Bowdle on Mar. 21, 1931. She attended rural school and
graduated from Bowdle High School.

They were united in marriage on June 2, 1953, at St. John's Evangelical Lutheran
Church in Bowdle. They moved to a farm eight miles south of Java, where they
still reside and run a grain and livestock operation.

Darlene and Norwin were blessed with five boys, Shawn, Sheilan, Gavin, Bryan and
Nolan. Darlene writes: There was never a dull moment on the farm. When we looked
out a window, we never knew what to expect. Maybe one was on the silo, windmill,
or walking across the top of the barn. One incident most people won't forget was
in 1958, when Norwin bought a new combine, parked it in the yard, and had to run
an errand in town. Sheilan, age two, climbed into the combine, which he started,
backed up and wrecked the gas pump, garage and combine! One day we got a horse
and Bryan wanted to go for a ride; the horse ran too fast for him, so he decided
to jump off. It took a few stitches to repair the injuries. Gavin was bitten by
our dog, which died the next day. Gavin had to get rabies shots. At times, we
felt we were at the doctor more than at home, either for stitches, broken bones,
or just plain illness.

Gavin and Bryan attended All State Chorus; Gavin and Nolan were Boys State
delegates. We took each day at a time, and have some very good memories of our
family.

Everyone in this area remembers the severe blizzard of 1966. We were very
fortunate. We, and the cattle, got through it fine. We still had the old coal
furnace that did not need electricity to run, and a kerosene stove, so we kept
warm and well fed. Another bad winter was 1977 and 1978. This was the first time
I was ever called for jury duty. One morning they called that I should come to
Selby for court. I told them it was impossible because the roads were blocked.
That didn't stop things. The snowplow started for our farm, followed by the
County Sheriff. Norwin and I got in the tractor and started from the farm, when
we met them down the road, where I got an escort with the Sheriff. This was a
fun ride in the police car. We had another bad winter 1996 and 1997. I really
don't know how many inches of snow we had, but it was enough to cover our
shelter belts and there was much damage done to the trees. There was also a
great livestock loss; we were fortunate not to lose any of our cattle.

(Photo:) The Norwin Walz Family

Norwin has been active in church affairs, served on the Java Equity Board
several years, a member of the Crop Improvement, received the 1968 State Tree
Farm Award, a member of the Walworth County Extension Board and the Selby Men's
Chorus. They organized in early 1975 and sang for the Java and the Selby 75th
Anniversary celebrations. The group performed at the lighting ceremony at Mt.
Rushmore in 1976, America's Bicentennial year, at Governor Janklow's
Inauguration in Jan. 1979, and at the National Association of Wheat Growers
Convention in Phoenix, AZ. The program was presented in many SD cities.

Darlene is active in church and ladies aid, Walco Extension Club and Walworth
County Extension, where she is county treasurer. She enjoys sewing, fancy work
and crafts.

Shawn was born in Aberdeen on Mar. 7, 1954. He attended school at Java for 12
years and graduated from Java High School in 1972. He then went to SDSU for two
and one-half years before he decided to take a break from school. He headed to
Houston, TX, where a friend from SD got him a construction job. This is where he
met Cathy Bynum and on June 4, 1977, they were married in Spring, TX. In Apr.
1978, they moved to Rapid City, where they presently reside. Shawn was in
various lines of sales work before he settled into the food service business. He
is currently a beverage specialist for Food Services of America. For the first
10 years of their marriage, Cathy was a homemaker, during which time they had
three children, Shawna, Dustin and Brandon. After the children were all in
school, Cathy went to work as a credit union employee, until she decided to
pursue her life-long dream of being an RN.

Sheilan was born May 25, 1956 and is the right-hand man on the farm.

Gavin was born Nov. 21, 1960, attended Java school and graduated from Java High
School in 1979. After high school, he attended SDSU, graduating with a BS in
Agricultural Engineering, in 1983. Gavin then found employment at Sperry New
Holland in Grand Island, NE, as a Manufacturing Process Engineer. In the fall of
1985, Gavin returned to SDSU to complete a BS in Mechanical Engineering. In the
spring of 1986, he traveled to Phoenix, AZ, to his new job as Mechanical
Component Design Engineer with AlliedSignal Engines. In Sept. 1991, Gavin went
to work for Chromalloy Arizona as a Repair Engineer, where he is today. He
married Lisa Pepperling on June 21, 1998. Lisa is originally from Omaha, NE and
works for the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office as a 911 dispatcher. Gavin is
living in Mesa, AZ, with his wife Lisa and stepson, Caleb, age 7.

Bryan was born June 14, 1963 and graduated from Java High School in 1981. He
graduated from SDSM&T with a Geological Engineering degree and worked, for a
short time, with A.G. Wassenaar, a geotechnical firm in Denver. He then joined
Foster-Wheeler Environmental, where he worked as an environmental engineer for
10 years. Recently, Bryan decided to change careers and join the fast-paced
industry of computers. Bryan is currently a software engineer for Parmin
Consulting Group, where he develops computer programs for the insurance
industry. Bryan married Suzanne Vannucci of San Carlos, CA, on Sept. 12, 1992.
They had a daughter, Bella Nicole, on May 9, 1996. Suzanne graduated from USF at
San Francisco, with a degree in Nursing, and worked as a Traveling Nurse for
several years before moving to CO. She has worked at St. Joseph's Hospital in
Denver for seven years, and is currently a member of the Cardiac Intensive Care
Unit.

Bryan, Suzanne, Bella and their Alaskan Malamute (Tua) live in the mountains of
Evergreen, CO, where they enjoy camping, snow skiing, mountain biking and rock
climbing. Bella is not far behind. She went camping for the first time when she
was two weeks old, skiing for the first time on an earlier birthday, rides in a
Burley trailer attached to her papa's mountain bike on many daring passes, and
loves to climb.

        Harvey and Sallie (Schlepp) Weisgram
Harvey was born to Frank and Lydia Weisgram at Java on Sept. 21, 1932. Frank,
who came from Austria with his parents when he was 14, was the town blacksmith
for many years. His shop was located next to their home, a block off of Main
Street. The familiar sound, from the blacksmith shop, of steel hammers striking
the anvil, which had echoed through the little town for many years, was silenced
when Frank passed away in Apr. 1972. Lydia passed away in 1990.

Sallie was born May 26, 1935, to Emanuel and Lydia Schlepp. She grew up on the
family farm, attended rural grade school and Java High School. Her parents,
after selling their farm in 1952, moved into Java and owned and operated
Schlepp's Cafe, famous for its delectable hamburgers and Lydia's 'mile high'
scrumptious pies. After several years, they sold the business and retired.
Emanuel passed away in 1977 and Lydia in 1988.

(Photo:) The Harvey and Sallie Weisgram Family

Upon graduation from Java High, Sallie attended a business college in Aberdeen,
and Harvey joined the U.S. Navy for four years. On Sept. 6, 1953, they were
married at Java. They lived in Boston a short time, while in the Navy; most of
Harvey's time was spent aboard a naval ship, which traveled to many European
countries. After his discharge, the couple lived in St. Louis, MO, where Harvey
attended a technical institute. After graduation, they settled in Mobridge,
where Harvey began employment with the Chevrolet dealership, where he was
employed for 39 years. Sallie and Harvey were active in the community. Harvey
served as a volunteer fireman and Assistant Fire Chief.

On June 19, 1962, a daughter, Lisa, was born. She graduated from Mobridge High
School, attended the U of Mary at Bismarck, and graduated with a four-year RN
Degree. She married Paul Nelson from Mobridge and they reside in Bismarck. Lisa
is employed at Bismarck/Burleigh County Nursing Services, and Paul is a computer
systems analyst with Pathology Consultants. They have two children, Kari and
Christopher.

Harvey retired in 1996 and the couple moved to Bismarck, where they are enjoying
their grandchildren's activities and growing years. Harvey still has ties to
Chevrolet, currently driving a courtesy car for Puklich Chevrolet and assisting
in the Service Manager's department.

        Tom and Susan (Darling) Weisgram
Tom Weisgram was born Feb. 16, 1940, to Frank and Lydia Weisgram of Java. He
attended all 12 grades at the Java school. After high school, Tom started
working for the Walworth County Highway Department, in various positions. He is
presently shop foreman. Tom served in the U.S. Army from Mar. 1963 to Feb. 1965,
when he spent some time serving in Hanau, Germany.

Tom married Susan Darling on Sept. 10, 1961. Susan is the daughter of Emery and
Nellie Darling, who were residents of Java for a few years. Emery was a truck
driver for Dan Dugan Trucking. Nellie and Emery are deceased.

Susan graduated from Java High School and worked as a nurse's aid in Mobridge
and Selby nursing homes. A victim of Multiple Sclerosis at an early age, Susan
has been a resident at Beverly Health Care in Mobridge.

Tom and Susan have one son, Patrick, born Jan. 13, 1966, at Hoven. Pat graduated
from Java High School in 1984. He married Sheri Eisenbeisz of Mobridge in June
1985. He attended Lake Area Vo-tech in Watertown for two years, studying diesel
mechanics and is presently a service manager for Butler Machinery in Aberdeen.
Sheri operates a day care center from her home. Pat and Sheri have a daughter,
Kelsey, and a son, Thomas.

        John and Louise (Schuh) Witlock Sr.
John Witlock, Sr., was born in Holland in 1884. He immigrated to the U.S. when
he was a young man. He farmed south of Java. In 1922, he married Louise Schuh,
who was born in 1899 at Tysplitz, South Russia and emigrated from Russia, with
her parents, when she was two years old.

After their marriage, the young couple moved on a farm south of Java. Many
hardships were endured by the couple and in 1931, they moved to the former
Gershin farm east of Java, where they farmed for several years. They lived on
various farms in the Java area while raising their four children and having them
receive an education.

Louise Witlock passed away in 1949, and shortly after her death, John, Sr.,
moved in with his brother-in-law, Guy and Min Schuch. John was employed as a
buyer for the Mobridge Livestock for many years. This gave him an opportunity to
visit with his friends and be in contact with the livestock business, which he
thoroughly enjoyed. Schlepp's Lunch at Java, was his favorite stopping place for
coffee and visiting. John spent several years with his daughters before moving
into the Good Samaritan Center at Selby, in 1968. John passed away in 1971.

(Photo:) John Witlock, Sr. Family. Anne, Casey, John, Jr., Helen, John, Sr. and
         Louise

The Witlock children were: Cornelius (Casey) married Evelyn Kleinemas. They have
a son and a daughter. John, Jr., married Anne Mueller and had six children,
David, Douglas, Becky, Denise and Deb, twins, and Jeanne. John is deceased. (See
Family History) Helen was a teacher and married Harold Nies. They had three
daughters, Patty, Bobbi and Cindy, all teachers. Harold is deceased and Helen
lives in Winner. Ann married Harold Schreter. They live south of Java and had
four children, Suzette, Bryce, Nancy and Tim. (See Family History)

        Rebecca (Becky) L. Witlock
Becky Witlock was born Aug. 30, 1953, to John and Anne (Mueller) Witlock, Jr.,
at Mobridge. She was baptized and confirmed at St. Paul Lutheran Church in Java.
She attended her first year of school at East Spring Valley School south of
Java. After attending the remaining 11 years of school at Java, Becky graduated
from Java High School in 1971. She graduated from Aberdeen School of Commerce in
1972 and worked in Pierre. She was later employed with WEB Water in Aberdeen for
seven years, and after in-house political turmoil, eleven jobs were terminated,
including Becky's. Later, she moved back to Java, where she now manages the Java
Super Valu Store owned by the Java Community Corporation.

Becky serves on the St. Paul Church Council, where she holds the Memorial Fund
treasurer position. She is president of the St. Paul Centennial committee and
serves on two of the Town of Java Centennial committees, as well. Becky is a
member of the Java Community Club and the Selby Women's Golf League. She is a
part-time painter, and bartender. She is a former Sunday school and Bible School
teacher and helped, a past member of the Selby women Jaycees and Selby Bowling
Association. Becky played the part of Calamity Jane in the 1983 Walworth County
Centennial celebration. She played for the Java and Selby Women's Softball teams
for 15 years and coached young girls' softball for six years. Her team had a
record of 8-2 during Becky's first year of coaching, and they won many First
Place trophies. In 1981, the Java Women's team took Second Place in the State
Championship. Becky recalls that it was a long trip home.

During her younger years, Becky was kept quite busy on the family farm. She
remembers spending a lot of time at her grandparents' farm, keeping busy in the
garden, washing her Grandpa's new car, combing his hair, washing windows or
playing games with her Grandma, one of which was Button-Button.

Becky has two brothers and three sisters, 13 nieces and nephews, and one great
niece, all of whom she spoils.

        George and Katherina (Gugel) Wolf Sr.
George Wolf, Sr., was born in 1833 in Marienberg, South Russia. He grew to
manhood in the southern area and was united in marriage to Katherina Gugel in
1858. George was appointed as a Judge for the South Russian Territory. He served
as judge for many years.

(Photo:) George Wolf, Sr.

George and Katherina had seven children, three sons and four daughters, who were
grown to adulthood before coming to America. George, Jr., married Margaretha
Schmidt; Matheus G. married Fredricka Jenner; John H. married Rosina Schmidt,
Eve married Fred Bickel, Rosina married David Schlepp, Sr., Elizabeth married
Jacob Oschner and Magdelina married Matheis Wolf.

George and Katherina migrated to the U.S. with other relatives in 1890, and
homesteaded in Walworth County, six miles NE of Java. In 1907, they bought a
home and moved to Java. Three years later, Katherina passed away and several
years later, George, Sr., remarried. George passed away in 1926, at the age of
93.

        Matheus G. and Fredericka (Jenner) Wolff
Matheus G. Wolff was born in Marienberg, South Russia, Sept. 21, 1866, son of
George and Kathryn (Gugel) Wolff. On Feb. 14, 1888, he was united in marriage
with Fredericka Jenner, who was born Oct. 5, 1865, the daughter of John and
Rosina (Hoffman) Jenner. He came to America on Apr. 24, 1890, with his wife and
daughter, and homesteaded three miles NE of Java. He was one of the early
settlers of Walworth County. They lived on this farm for 68 years, until his
death on July 31, 1958. Fredericka passed away in 1932. Calvin H. Wolff, son of
Henry H. and grandson of Matheus G., purchased the farm.

(Photo:) Matheus G. and Fredericka Wolff

To this union 10 children were born and all are deceased. Kathryn died in
infancy, Frieda married Jacob Sauer, John C., Henry H. married Martha Bender,
Emily married John M. Haux, Christ A. (died 1953) married Elizabeth Schuh, Lydia
(died 1955) married Henry C. Fiedler, Mary (died 1971) was married to Carl
Hepper, Jake passed away Feb. 21, 1973, and Rose passed away Apr. 26, 1973.

        Christ A. and Elizabeth (Schuh) Wolff
Christ Wolff, son of Matheus G. and Fredericka (Jenner) Wolff, was born July 11,
1890, three miles NE of Java, where he grew to manhood.

(Photo:) Christ and Elizabeth Wolff

On Jan. 15, 1915, he was united in marriage to Elizabeth Schuh, who was born
June 19, 1895, five and one-half miles NE of Java, to John and Fredricka
(Schlepp) Schuh, Sr. They farmed 9 miles NE of Java for about three years and
then moved six miles south of Java, where they farmed until 1921. They then
purchased land five miles east of McLaughlin, where they built their farm home.

Christ passed away on Dec. 24, 1953, and Elizabeth sold the farm and built a
home in McLaughlin, where she resided until her death on July 7, 1966. Two
daughters were born to this marriage. Hertha Overbeck and Lucille Smith. Christ
and Elizabeth had five grandchildren and three great-grandchildren at the time
of their deaths.

        Henry H. and Martha (Bender) Wolff

Bender, who was born Sept. 1, 1905, at the Sutley area north of Java, a daughter

        Calvin H. and Donna (Schreter) Wolff
Calvin H. Wolff was born on his parents' farm north of Java, on July 24, 1931,
son of Henry H. and Martha (Bender) Wolff. He began his schooling in a country
school. When he was 9 years old, his family moved into Java, where Calvin
continued his education and graduated from Java High School in 1949. Following
high school, he worked at different jobs, until he was drafted to serve in the
U.S. Army in Feb. 1952. He was stationed in Fulda, Germany, going over on the
ship and returning home on the ship, taking about 15 days to get to New York.
During the summer of 1954, Calvin helped build the cement Selby Equity elevator.

On Nov. 3, 1954, Calvin was united in marriage to Donna Schreter, daughter of
Henry E. and Magdalene (Bieber) Schreter. Donna was born Aug. 28, 1935, near
Swan Lake south of Java. She went to Theodore Country School for eight years,
and then to Java High School, graduating in 1953. After graduation, Donna
started working at the 1st National Bank in Mobridge, which is now the Norwest
Bank.

After their marriage, Calvin and Donna settled on the Henry H. Wolff farm NW of
Java. They had no running water or sewer. After buying the farm, remodeling
began in 1959. While living on the farm, they raised cattle and pigs, and
planted many crops. Calvin was very active in the community and served on a
variety of boards. Donna worked at the Registrar of Deeds office of Walworth
County, until a family was begun. Donna and Calvin had three sons, Patrick H.,
Mark A., and Jeffrey L.

(Photo:) Mark, Calvin, Donna, Pat and Jeff Wolff

Pat was born Mar. 25, 1957, graduated from Java High School in 1975, and

Heather was born Dec. 31, 1981 in Hoven. She is a graduate of Rapid City
Central High School; Kayla was born Oct. 7, 1987 in Mobridge. She attends
Southwest Middle School in Rapid City. They reside in Rapid City, where Pat
works for American Express Financial Advisors. Lore is an LPN and an aerobic
instructor.

Mark, born Aug. 22, 1959, graduated from Java High School in 1977. He continued

daughter of Leslie and Ramona Rau, in 1981. Three sons were born to this union,

Jeffrey was born Apr. 21, 1963 and graduated from Selby High School in 1981. He

Calvin and Donna enjoyed their children and seven grandchildren very much over

        George L. Wolf
George L. Wolf was born Dec. 7, 1877, in Marienberg, Russia, to George and
Katherine (Gugel) Wolf, Sr. He came to America with his family when he was 11
years old, and settled in the Java area. George L. married Margaret Schmidt in
1898. Two children, Emil (deceased) and Ida (Wolf) Wilson (deceased), were born
to them before Margaret Schmidt Wolf passed away in 1910.

On July 23, 1912, George married Lydia Schnaible, daughter of Karl and
Elizabetha (Oster). Lydia was born in Freeman on Oct. 20, 1889. They had four
children: Viola passed away in 1932; Irene married Edwin Buechler and lives in
Ipswich; Herman lived in Rapid City and is deceased; and Melvin lived in
Middleboro, MA, and is deceased.

George L. Wolf was in business in Java for many years, owning the Livery Stable.
He later built a farm located two miles north of Java, where he farmed for many
years. Lydia (Schnaible) Wolf passed away on Apr. 27, 1938. In 1942, George
moved into Java, where he was employed with the railroad. He passed away on Aug.
16, 1968, and is buried in the Lutheran cemetery at Java.

        John H. and Rosina (Schmidt) Wolf
John H. Wolf came to America with his parents, George and Katherina (Gugel)
Wolf, when he was 9 years old. A very large group came at that time. They
settled NE of Java, near the Matt G. Wolf place. John H. owned the farm that was
later known as the Arend Lakeman farm, one-and-a-quarter miles east of Java.

(Photos:) John H. Wolf and Rosina Wolf

Rosina Schmidt was a baby when she came to America with her parents in 1883.
They settled in the Artas area. John H. and Rosina were married at Java in 1902.
They moved into Java in about 1908.

Emma, was born to them in 1904, on the farm. Another daughter, Rose, was born
there two years later. Emma married Ben Stiegelmeier and had two daughters, and
Rose married Albert Bickel. Walter was born in Java in Mar. 1913.

John H. opened a tire shop north of the Bauer store in Java. Later, he moved on
the corner across the street, where he opened a garage and a bowling alley. He
had the Ford agency until the time of his death, Oct. 21, 1918. Ed Hughes was
the bookkeeper. The garage was sold to Philip Spiry and sons, of Java.

Java was a prosperous town in the early 1900's. John H. was the first Ford
dealer in the area west of Aberdeen. He was a great booster for the community.
At the time, Java had three garages, two banks, four grocery stores, two
lumberyards, a creamery and three of four cream buying stations, a newspaper, an
implement shop, a doctor and a dentist, a drug store, theatre, bowling alley,
blacksmith shop, livery stable, and a hotel. Rosina (Schmidt) Wolf operated a
hotel in the building that was on the corner north of the old post office. This
hotel was noted for its wonderful meals. Rosina passed away in July 1934.

        Matheis J. and Magdelina (Wolf) Wolf
Matheis J. Wolf was born in 1857, in South Russia. After he grew to manhood, he
was drafted into the Russian Army and served for six years. In 1883, Matheis was
united in marriage to Magdelina Wolf, daughter of George and Katherina (Gugel)
Wolf, in South Russia.

Six years later, Matheis, his wife and three children, along with a number of
friends and relatives, migrated to the U.S. In July 1889, they landed in New
York, and traveled to the Eureka area.

Matheis and his family homesteaded NE of Eureka, where they, and a few
neighbors, put up a sod house and barn. After six years of misfortunes and
drought, the family moved in with his mother, who was living on a farm NE of
Java. The Matheis Wolf family remained there a short time before moving on to a
farm six miles SE of Java, where they again built a sod house and barn, trying
to make their livelihood in farming.

(Photo:) Matheis and Magdalina Wolf

During the next 10 years, eight more children were born to the Wolf family,
which caused the family to lease a larger farm and put all the children to work.
They remained on this farm for three years, and then returned to the farm six
miles SE of Java. At this time, some of the older children had married and left
home.

After most of the children were gone from home, Matheis and Magdelina bought a
home in Java. In 1925, they retired and moved into Java, where they lived until
their deaths. Matheis passed away on Sept. 4, 1944 and Magdelina passed away on
Feb. 17, 1948.

        William and Katherina (Mayer) Wolf
William Wolf was born Mar. 8, 1900, on a farm six miles east of Java, where his
parents, Matheis and Magdelina, and family lived. William attended Alamo Country
School; after he finished school, he helped his father with the farming.

On Aug. 27, 1923, William was united in marriage to Katherina Mayer in the
Lutheran church at Java, where they were devout members. This young couple took
over his father's farm and farmed for many years.

(Photo:) William and Katharina Wolf

In 1935, the Depression and drought forced the family to sell the farm and move
to Java, where William was employed as a farmhand. In 1949, the Wolf family
moved to Bowdle, where he owned and operated the Wolf Dray Line.

Later, after selling his Dray Line, William was appointed as Chief of Police in
Bowdle, and held that position until 1965, when he retired. William and
Katherina are deceased.

Two children were born to William and Katherina. Their son Lloyd died at the age
of three.

Frances was born Jan. 7, 1925, in rural Java. She attended Alamo School for a
few years. The family moved to Minneapolis for a short time, and then lived in
Java, where Frances started going to school in the sixth grade. She graduated
from Java High School in 1943 and then worked at Schlepp's Drug until the fall
of that year. She went to Aberdeen and worked at the Cozy Cafe and later at the
White Way Cafe. Frances met Leonard Joachim and they were married on June 13,
1944, at Zion Lutheran Church in Aberdeen. They moved to Bowdle in Oct. 1944,
where Leonard and his father-in-law, Bill Wolf, were in partnership in the City
Dray Line for seven and one-half years. The business was sold in 1952. Leonard
then worked on a farm in the Bowdle area until Apr. 1952, when he went to work
at the Bowdle Creamery, where he was employed until Mar. 1983. Frances worked in
different cafes in Bowdle, including the Gold Nugget, employed in this capacity
for over 40 years. She also babysat. Frances and Leonard had one daughter, Judy,
who is deceased. Leonard Joachim passed away and Frances lives in Bowdle.

Frances has five grandchildren and 9 great-grandchildren.

        Friedrich (Fred) Wolf Sr.
Fred Wolf, Sr., was born Oct. 9, 1842, in Bergdorf, South Russia, to George and
Elizabetha (Amann) Wolf. He married Elisabetha Maeule on Oct. 13, 1864, in
Kassel, South Russia. She was born Nov. 16, 1843, at Bergdorf, to Martin Michael
and Katharina (Mittleider) Maeule. Fred and Elisabetha were the parents of
Magdalena, Friedrich (Fred), Jr. who married Justina Henke, Eva (Gottlieb)
Boehler, Christian married Rosina Schnaible, Amelie (John K.) Schlepp, and
Elisabeth (George) Sieler.

Elisabetha Maeule Wolf passed away in 1880 and Fred, Sr. married Eva Kurle on
Jan. 20, 1881 in Bergdorf, South Russia. Eva was born Sept. 1, 1860, at Bergdorf
to John and Eva (Braun) Kurle, who immigrated to the Java area. The children of
Fred and Eva: George married Katherine Himmerich; Jacob F. married Lydia Bauder;
Helena (Carl) Bauder; Magdalena (Anton) Dusel; Gottlieb J. married Karolina
Heer; Edward married Wilhelmine Spiry; John A. married Amalie Knopp; Henry F.
married Carolina Henne; and Dorothea (Emil) Spiry.

Fred, Eva and their family immigrated to the U.S. in 1890, and settled in the
Java area. Fred had been a teacher in Russia, and was a Walworth County
Commissioner until 1900. He passed away on Dec. 17, 1902, and Eva passed away on
Mar. 18, 1940, in the Eureka nursing home, at the age of 76.

        Fredrick and Justina (Henke) Wolf Jr.
Fredrick Wolf was born at Marienberg, South Russia, in Dec. 1868, to Friedrich
and Elizabetha (Maeule/Meile) Wolf.

He lost his mother in boyhood and his father married Eva Kurle. In 1890,
Fredrick, his father, mother and family, immigrated to the U.S., where they
settled NW of Java.

In 1896, Fredrick homesteaded a quarter of land northwest of Java, where he
lived until his death.

In 1897, Fredrick married Justina Henke, daughter of John and Rosina (Rollop)
Henke, of Fredonia, ND. She was born July 19,1877, in the Kulm area of South
Russia, and was four years old when her parents migrated to America.

Fredrick and Justina were the parents of six daughters, all born at home. They
attended nearby country schools and the Peace Lutheran Church north of Java. The
girls were: Karolina, who died in infancy; Rosina (Ed) Schnaible; Natalie
(Stadel) (Philip) Spiry; Justina (Ed) Schlepp; Elizabeth (John) Schlepp; and
Amelia (Christ) Schuh.

For many years the family lived in sod houses. The first one was very small with
only two rooms. Later, with the help of the oldest daughters, a larger one was
built. In 1917, they built a 9-room frame house, where they lived until
Fredrick's death in 1919. Justina moved to Java, where she built a new home. She
lived here until her death in 1956. She had married John Goetz in 1939. He
preceded her in death.

(Photo:) The Frederick Wolf, Jr. Family - 1918

Tom Schnaible, a great-grandson of Mr. and Mrs. Wolf, now farms the original
homestead land.

        Wolf-Keller Family History by Joan Wolf Carroll
My name is Joan Wolf Carroll. As a child I remember spending time with my
grandparents. My Grandpa Edward and Grandma Magdalena Keller lived across the
alley from our house some of the years, because we lived in the telephone
building on Main Street. We could run across the alley to watch Grandpa Ed work
in the garden. We could watch Grandma cooking on the kerosene stove; it looked
very fascinating but we were not allowed to touch it - with serious warnings
from both grandparents. Grandpa would let us pick up the angle worms he dug for
fishing, and put them in the tin coffee can. We loved the fresh cooked, tasty
fish with carrots and potatoes from the garden. Later I loved the green beans
too. Grandpa would bury all the table scraps and peelings in a hole he had dug
in the garden. I always wondered why the plants wanted those scraps.

We stayed with Grandpa Christ and Grandma Rose Wolf, too. I was scared of
Grandma because she spanked the boys for horsing around and not sleeping the
very first night we stayed there. We stayed in town when the weather was bad, so
we could go to school. (We had moved to the farm three miles from Java.) I liked
staying there so I could spend time with my friend Julia Schlepp, a neighbor
near Grandma's. I slept on a sofa in the kitchen and listed to that old clock
chime every hour. Grandma had the nicest flowers; today I have those Peony's at
my house and am so very thankful to have them. She divided and shared them with
many people in and around Java. Grandpa had animals. We helped him with the baby
chicks and we shelled corn by hand. Grandma made my favorite food, potato balls,
boiled in water, then fried in bacon grease and served with fried bread chunks.
She was a great German cook. I'll always remember her thin, floury, homemade
noodles drying on the old oil space heater.

Whenever someone had a birthday, Mom made homemade Angel Food Cake. I was in
charge of getting eggs from the hens. Sometimes the old clucks pecked my hands,
but we always had eggs for Angel Food Cake. Dad would make homemade ice cream
with the yolks. We had the aunts and uncles over. Dad's folks and his brothers
Carl and Gothart, and sister Lieta and their families would come. Mom's folks
and her brothers, Adolph (Jeff) and Ervin (Bud), and her sisters Emilie, Martha
and Helen and their families would join us, too. It was fun and a good way to
play with the little relatives, who were: Gerald and Jackie; Doris, Virginia and
Clifford; Merle and Marlin; Irene, Shirley and Darlene; Donna, Darryl and
Charlene; Dixie and Dennis; Alpha and Marjorie; Rosalyn (children Diane and
Doreen) and Dale. So many special memories! In time, some moved away, but I
still hear from Carl's wife, Liz, who lives in Lodi and is a friend of my first
grade teacher, Hilda (Bauman) Schaefer.

Our family is made of several Wolfs and Kellers, as Mom's mother came from a
family of Wolffs. Then she married a Keller. Their daughter, Hilda (my Mom)
married a Wolf, not related. Then brother Don kept the tradition going by
marrying a Keller. Their children's family tree was not believed by the school
teachers!!

My Mom told us she scared men away by saying she wanted eight children. In the
end, Irwin (Ervin) and Hilda (Keller) Wolf raised: Kenneth, Donald, Joan (Me),
Cynthia, Patty and Nathan. Those children have many more children: Kenneth and
Nancy (Tisdal) Wolf have Chad, Heidi and Andrea, who live in the Denver area;
Donald and Joanne (Keller) Wolf have Darcy, Douglas and Lei Ann, all living in
the Seattle area. Joan Wolf Carroll lives in Java and has a son, Jeffery, and
two adopted daughters, Rebecka Rose and Roberta Tutino. Cynthia and Charles
Burpee II of Enumclaw, WA, have twin sons, Shawn and Charlie. Patty lives in
Black Diamond, WA, married to Jim Johnston, who has a son, and Nathan has a son,
Chris.

Now we have a new generation of Wolf offspring. Ken has a grandchild, a girl
named Alexia. Don's grandchildren are: Darcy's girls, Stephanie Nicole and
Michelle Shyla; Douglas is not married; and Lei Ann has Zackary Liegh and Darren
Allan. Joan's grandchildren are: Becky's children, Ashley Rose and Cody.
Daughter Roberta's children: Christopher James, Jasmine Nicole and Dalton K.
Tutino. Cynthia, Patty and Nate are not yet grandparents!

The good Lord has given us many blessings and among them are our children,
grandchildren, in-laws, and many new people to love. We thank Him for our
health, which makes life meaningful!

        George H. and Katherine (Himrich) Wolf
George H. Wolf was born on Oct. 1881, and was the oldest son of Fredrich and Eva
(Kurle) Wolf. He had eight brothers and sisters, and five half brothers and
sisters.

His grandparents moved from southern Germany to the Colony of Bergdorf, located
a few miles from the seaport of Odessa on the Black Sea.

(Photo:) George H. and Katherine Wolf

George H. Wolf came to the U.S. with his parents in 1890, by 2nd class ship.
From New York, they came to Eureka, where his mother's sister (Mrs. Adam Merkel)
lived. A short time later, the Fredrich Wolf family filed a homestead claim and
built a sod house. Raising grain and livestock and milking was their livelihood.
In later years, the boys would cut ice, by hand, in a creek nearby and haul it
by horse to Java, where it was sold.

George's father, Fredrich had been a teacher in the old country, and served as
Walworth county commissioner for a few years, until 1900.

George and all his brothers built their homes in Walworth County. In 1904,
George married Katherine Himrich. This young couple settled on land three and
one-half miles west of Java, where George built a home and farmed for many
years. Three sons and three daughters were born to George and Katherine. The
Wolfs remained on the farm until the fall of 1917, when they bought a home and
moved to Java, where they remained until their deaths. George passed away on
Mar. 3, 1940, and Katherine passed away on Mar. 31, 1969.

The Wolf children were: Dorothea, born Jan. 7, 1905, unmarried, taught school
for a number of years and passed away Apr. 28, 1931. George J., born Nov. 29,
1912, unmarried, died May 18, 1938. Katherine was born Mar. 1906 and married
Albert Lenz. Susanna, born Nov. 28, 1915, married Alvin Spiry and had three
sons, Vaughn married Lou Pies and they have two children, Twyla and Arvyn, and
reside west of Java; Fredrick (deceased) married Marlene Schutts and had two
children, Pamela and Sandra; Roger married Shirley Mueller and they have three
children. Emil (deceased) married Alice McQuire and had one son, Bruce, and two
daughters, Sharon and Rebecca. Herman (deceased) married and had Dorothy,
Michael and Mark.

        Jacob F. and Lydia (Bauder) Wolf
Jacob F. Wolf was born Sept. 4, 1882, in Odessa, South Russia, to Fredrich and
Eva (Kurle) Wolf. He came to the U.S. with his parents in 1890. They homesteaded
near Java, where he attended school and grew to young manhood.

(Photo:) The Jacob F. Wolf Family

Lydia Bauder was born Apr. 17, 1889, near Scotland, SD. In 1900, her family
moved to Walworth County and settled on a farm SW of Java, where she attended
school and grew to young womanhood. On Oct. 18, 1908, Jacob and Lydia were
married in St. Paul Lutheran Church at Java, and they farmed two and one-half
miles west of Java. Four children were born to the union: Clara, Helen, Lydia
and Elmer.

In 1920, they purchased a new home in Java, to make it easier for the children
to attend school, but retained their farming interests until the time of their
deaths. Jacob passed away Dec. 19, 1957, and Lydia passed away Jan. 6, 1961.

The family began to be active members of the community and church. Jacob served
on the school board and elevator board, and the family acquired many good
neighbors and friends.

Clara graduated from Java High School in 1931. In 1932, she married Nick Noble.
They farmed near Java until 1941, and then moved to Lakeland, FL, where they
stayed for two years before moving to Camas, WA, where they permanently settled.
Nick died in 1969 and Clara is also deceased.

Helen graduated from Java High School in 1932. She trained in secretarial work
and was employed at the courthouse in Selby. In 1935, she married Henry Perman.
They made their home in Java, where he operated an implement business. Later
they moved to Selby, where her husband was elected County Auditor. He passed
away in 1959. Helen was then elected to that position and served in that office
for almost eight terms, when she died July 5, 1973. Three children were born to
this union.

Lydia graduated from Java High School in 1934. She attended a beauty school and
in 1935, opened a beauty shop in Java, and operated it for the next five years.
She married Cliff Shaver of St. Thomas, ND. They moved there to engage in
farming operations. They had six children.

Elmer attended school in Java and grew up to young manhood. He farmed the home
place and in the last two years of his life, operated the Recreational Parlor in
Java. He died in Nov. 1968.

        Henry F. and Carrie (Henne) Wolf
Henry F. Wolf, a lifetime resident of the Java area, was born Aug. 6, 1890, on a
farm four miles SW of Java, the son of Frederich and Eva (Kurle) Wolf. He had
five brothers and three sisters: George H., Jacob F., Gottlieb J., Edward, and
John A., Magdalena (Anton) Dusel, Dorothea (Emil) Spiry, and Helena (Carl)
Bauder. He also had several half brothers and sisters. Henry attended school in
the area and grew to young manhood on his parents' farm.

On July 23, 1916, Henry married Carolina (Carrie) Henne, daughter of Jacob and
Karolina (Schauer) Henne, Sr. The Rev. George Kirchdoerfer performed the
marriage. Carrie was born Feb. 26, 1899, in Neudorf, South Russia, attended
elementary school in Russia, and came to the U.S. with her family in 1911. They
settled in the Java area. Carrie had one brother, Jacob Henne, Jr., and six
sisters: Katie (Jacob) Goetz, Christina (David) Schlepp, Emma (Gotthart) Wolf,
Esther (Gotthilf) Schlepp, and two who died in infancy.

After their marriage, Henry and Carrie lived on a farm three and one-half miles
SW of Java, where they built a new home and farmed for many years. To Henry and
Carrie were born two daughters (one died in infancy) and two sons. The children
all received their elementary and high school education in Java, by commuting on
their own (no bus service in those days). The family remained on the farm until
1950, when they retired, built a new home in Java, and moved to town. The farm
was rented out until the youngest son, Marvin, returned from military service in
1952 to take over the farm. Henry and Carrie lived in their home in Java until
their deaths. Henry passed away at home, from a heart attack, on Mar. 20, 1959,
and Carrie passed away May 3, 1978.

(Photo:) Rueben, Lorraine, Marvin, Henry F. and Carrie Wolf

The Wolf children were Lorraine, Rueben and Marvin.

Lorraine graduated from Java High School in 1937. After graduation, she went to
Woodland, CA, where she was employed. She married Harold Fiechtner in 1938, at
Java. Harold had spent a year in a CCC camp in the Black Hills, near Nemo, and
had been employed in Aberdeen and in CA, prior to their marriage. After their
marriage, they returned to CA, where both were employed until 1939, when they
returned to SD to start farming five and one-half miles SW of Java. They have
retired, but are still living on the same place. They have one daughter, Sharon,
who graduated from Selby High School in 1958, and attended NSTC in Aberdeen and
Dillon Teacher's College in MT. She is married to Ken Mizerny. They live in
Aberdeen, where she is an elementary school teacher at Henry Neill School, and
Ken is employed with the SD Department of Labor. They have one son, Scott, who
is a graduate of Concordia College in Moorhead, MN, and is employed in
Minneapolis.

Rueben graduated from Java High School in 1940, and graduated from NSTC in
Aberdeen. On Aug. 15, 1948, he married Noma Misterek of Harrold, SD, where both
were teaching. During his high school years, Rueben received many essay,
declamatory, and art awards in district and state contests. He served in the
U.S. Navy during World War II. After his discharge, he was a teacher, teaching
speech and art in SD, NM, and CA schools. They had three sons: Marcus (deceased
in 1987), Michael, living in VA, and Martin in CA. Rueben passed away June 29,
1973, in Buena Park, CA.

Marvin received his education in Java, was stationed in El Paso and San Antonio,
TX, and in France, during his service in the military. After his release from
the military, he returned to farming. He married Lois Stangl June 14, 1953,
daughter of Donal and Ella Stangl of Java, and a Java High School graduate of
1949. She attended USD for two years and was a school teacher. They have two
daughters and five grandchildren. Laurel graduated from Java High School in
1978, received her BA in Computer Science from Augustana College in Sioux Falls
in May 1982, and her MA in mathematics education from NSU in Aberdeen in July
1988. She taught math and computer courses in Gettysburg High School for six
years, and in Hoven for one year. She married Conald Kaiser on Nov. 5, 1988.
They live on a dairy farm three miles east of Hoven. They have two daughters,
Sonja and Carrie, and one son, Erik. Eleanor attended Java school through the
eighth grade. The high school in Java had been discontinued, so she graduated
from Bowdle High School. She is married to George Mundorf of Naknek and
Anchorage, AK. They both received their Bachelor of Science Degrees in
Industrial Engineering from SDSM&T in Rapid City in May 1998. George was
commissioned as a 2nd Lt. in the U.S. Army, through ROTC. He received further
training at Fort Gordon, Augusta, GA, and is serving as Signal Officer for a
field artillery battalion in the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, KY.
They have two sons, Alexander and Christian, and the family is living in
Clarksville, TN.

        Julius and Ella (Goetz) Wolf
Henry and Rosina Wolf were married and had two children, George S. and Henry.

        Johannes and Marie (Banek) Wolff
Johannes Wolff was born Oct. 28, 1874 in Marienberg, South Russia, to Jacob and
Katherina (Maeule/Meile) Wolff. Katherina was the daughter of Martin Michael and
Katharina (Mittleider) Maeule. A daughter was also born to this union. When
Johannes was two years old, his mother passed away and their father remarried.
In the spring of 1889, the family came to the U.S. and settled in Walworth
County. They homesteaded 10 miles NE of Java. John was 15 years old, which made
him the sole farm hand, helping his father. John had one sister and eight half
brothers and sisters.

On Oct. 14, 1894, Johannes married Maria Banek, the daughter of Christoph and
Katherina (Meier) Banek, who lived five miles north of the Wolff farm. The Banek
family came to America from Freidenstahl, South Russia. They had a family of six
sons and one daughter.

(Photo:) The Johannes Wolff Family

Johannes and Maria settled on a farm four miles east of his parents, where they
raised a family of 9 children. The two oldest daughters passed away in the
spring of 1918, one in March and one in April; the older of the two was married
at the time of her death, and had a small son. The other children grew up on the
farm and later married, establishing homes near their parents' farm.

In 1934, Mr. Wolff became ill and went to Wichita, KS, seeking medical aid. On
May 4, 1934, Johannes passed away at the age of 60 years, leaving his wife,
Maria, and two children on the farm. In 1936, Maria sold her farm and moved to
Java with her two children, where she had purchased a home. In Oct. 1958, Maria
passed away at the age of 81.

The children of the Wolff family are: Gust married Martha Gross and had six
children; Lydia married Fred Gab and also had six children; Rosina married John
Jung, had no children, but fostered two that were John's brother's children.
Rosina's husband passed away in 1968; Reinholdt married Lea Zimmerman and had
five children; Arthur, unmarried, passed away in 1961; Maria married Alvin
Mittleider and had three children, two died in infancy; Hulda married Gehbardt
Pfitzer and they live at Java. They have one daughter, Lynda; Katherine and
Amelia are the two daughters who had passed away. Amelia was married to
Christoph Goetz and had one son, Robert.

        Fredrich W. Wosnuk
Fredrich W. Wosnuk was born in Russia, where he grew to manhood and was married.
The young couple, with their three children, came to the U.S., and settled in
the Dakota Territory. They homesteaded on a farm NW of Java, near the Schneider
and Kundert farms. Three children were born to this couple: Barbara, Theodore,
and Simon. Fredrich's wife passed away.

Martha (Fredrich's second wife) had one child, born in Russia, by a former
marriage. Her name was Annice, who married Philip H. Merkel, one of the first
blacksmiths in Java. This couple had seven children. Alma, one of the daughters,
lived in Java, and attended school until 1926, when she graduated. She married
Howard Johnson in 1928, and had a son, Jack Arthur. Jack and his wife, June, had
three children, Margret, Howard, and Karen. After Howard Johnson died in 1964,
Alma married, in 1974, Gerald R. Corson, youngest son of James and Kezia Corson,
who were among Java's earliest settlers.

Fredrich and Martha had eight children (one died in infancy). They were: Alec,
Susan, Pierre, Henry, John, Emma, and Cathryn, who married Dr. Philip Noble, son
of Philip and Grace Noble.

        Joseph S. and Helen (Ryan) Zarka
Joseph S. Zarka was born Feb. 12, 1890, at Oberward Burgaland, Austria. He lived
with his parents until the he was 12, when he set out to earn his own living,
herding cattle, but he wanted to take up a trade, so he decided to go to school
and take up the trade of a shoemaker. Joe later was enticed by the announcements
of the fruitful land being offered in America, so at the age of 16, he undertook
the long trip to the U.S., by himself. He came to the Java area and stayed with
his Uncle Ladis Bertha, who lived 10 miles south of Java. Joe worked for various
farmers until 1910, when he decided to go to Buffalo, Harding County, where he
filed claim and lived there until 1915, when he returned to the Java area and
stayed with the Barclay family, now the John Stefanich farm, and worked as a
farmhand.

(Photo:) Helen and Joe Zarka

On Mar. 5, 1918, Joe married Helen Belle Ryan, daughter of George W. and Mary
Anna (Zindel) Ryan. A month later Joe was drafted into the service of World War
I and was sent to Camp Sherman, OH. He was sent on to New York, before going
overseas, where he served in the Argonne-Meuse sector in France. He was in
battle for 32 days, when he was wounded and spent two weeks in the hospital in
Boataz, France, before he was sent back to the states, where he remained in the
hospital, until he was transferred to Camp Dodge, and then received his
discharge and returned home to Java. He rented land and farmed for many years.
Helen and Joe bought a farm in 1940, remaining there until 1947, when they
bought a home in Java.

Joe was very active in the American Legion, where he served as Commander for 18
years. He also served as District and County Commander, and later, State Vice
Commander. Joe was on the Walworth County Draft Board for 22 years, on the Java
City board and served as Mayor of Java for six years.

Helen, a teacher, was one of the charter members of the American Legion
Auxiliary, where she served as president for five years. They both were active
members of the Presbyterian Church. Helen passed away in 1972, and Joe passed
away in 1984 at the age of 94.

        George and Rosina (Grenz) Zeller
George Zeller was born June 3, 1867, in Bessarabia, South Russia. He came to
this country with his parents and brothers and sister in 1884. They spent their
first winter at the home of an uncle, Jacob Zeller, at Menno. George and a
brother and sister worked that winter for their board and room.

In the spring of 1885, the family settled in Campbell County, where they
homesteaded. Their first home, a rough hut, in the new country was typical of
the time. George said his mother cried when she saw her new home in a land where
there were no neighbors, no churches, and no schools. During the first year on
the homestead, they built a better home, and also soon had new neighbors.

George told of how oxen were used in threshing their first flax crops. The flax
was piled about three feet high and the oxen were led in a circle on the pile,
tramping the flax until the seed and straw were separated.

Since there were no churches or ministers in the newly settled territory, the
early pioneers conducted family worship with the father reading from his prayer
book. Later, ministers traveled from house to house. By 1888, the Hoffnungstahl
Church had been established eight miles west of Eureka, and only a few miles
from the Zeller home.

(Photo:) George and Rosina Zeller

On July 10, 1890, George Zeller married Rosina Grenz, the daughter of a pioneer
neighbor. Soon after, the young couple established their home 12 miles NE of
Java. Their first home was a sod house, with a blacksmith shop and barn attached
to it. The sod house was warm and was an improvement over some, for it had a
wood floor. The first year they farmed with their team of one horse and one cow.
Although the young couple lived less than 10 miles from their parents' homes,
the trip by horse and buggy was not often made, so the loneliness and privations
of the new home must have often reminded Mrs. Zeller of the hardships of her
first years in America.

The Samuel Grenz family had come to America in 1885. Rosina told of the shelter
that served while they were building their first house. A hole in the ground,
with an inverted wagon box over it, protected them from the elements and
animals. The teen-aged girl remembered the comforts they had left behind to make
the trip to America, and the first difficult years remained in her memory.

In 1899 a spacious frame house replaced the sod house. As other farm buildings
were built, the sod barn and blacksmith shop were torn down, but the sod house
remained in use as a "summer kitchen" for many years. The George Zeller family
moved to Java in 1908.

George Zeller bought a machine and implement shop from the Huether Brothers.
This became a family enterprise for their son, Gottlieb, was bookkeeper and
helped set up machinery, and their daughter, Rosie, served as clerk. In Jan.
1915, George bought the Java Branch of the Selby Implement Company. Buggies and
wagons were much in demand; they also sold threshing machines and tractors,
handling several lines of machinery including McCormick, John Deere, Deering,
Titan, Hart Parr, and Minneapolis. Several of the company names, such as Titan,
Hart Parr and Minneapolis have long since been forgotten on the farm scene. As a
forerunner to present-day diversification, George sold Eureka flour, getting the
flour in 50 and 100-pound sacks by the train car load. In 1916, he sold the
implement business to the Java Equity Exchange.

In Jan. 1912, George bought the Central Hotel from John J. Wolff. His daughters,
Lena and Rosie, operated the hotel for three years, until Mr. Zeller rented it
to the Campbells. He sold the Central Hotel in Nov. 1916.

In 1917, the family moved back to the farm. During 1918 and 1919, George Zeller
was state representative from Campbell County. Mr. and Mrs. Zeller and their
three youngest daughters moved to Eureka in 1925.

George Zeller was active in civic and community affairs. He served as county
commissioner in Campbell County, served on school boards, and was deacon in
church for many years.

After George died in 1942, Rosina moved to Java to be near the children residing
there. Again she became interested in the affairs of the community, whether it
was a school function or a quilting party, a hobby she pursued many years. She
passed away Nov. 1952.

Their children: Magdalena (Lena) Wolff, Agnes Linder, Martha Marquardt, Kathryn
Hamann, George L., Bertha Bieber, Rosina (Rosie) Spiry, Christine Schlepp, John,
Gottlieb, Elizabeth Schnaible, and Emma Keim.

        Gottlieb A. and Elizabeth (Bender) Zeller
Gottlieb A. Zeller, the oldest child of Rosina and George Zeller, was born Oct.
24, 1890, on a farm near Eureka. The family later moved to a farm 12 miles north
of Java, where they lived until Gottlieb was 18. At that time, they moved to
Java, and Gottlieb became bookkeeper at the Zeller Bros. Implement. During the
next several years, he also helped assemble machinery.

(Photo:) Mr. and Mrs. Gottlieb Zeller

Elizabeth Bender (Lizzie) was born May 9, 1893, near Sutley in Campbell County,
a daughter of Jacob and Elizabeth (Hauck) Bender. She attended rural school and
grew into womanhood on her parents' farm NE of Java.

On Nov. 14, 1912, Gottlieb and Elizabeth were married in the Reformed Church at
Sutley. They lived at the Zeller home in Java during the first winter. The
following spring, they moved to the Zeller farm. That fall, they returned to
Java. In 1916, they again took up farming on the Zeller farm.

In 1916, tragedy struck when their second daughter, Lydia, only a year and a
half old, strangled on a sunflower seed. Shortly after, they moved to a farm
near Leith, ND. Crop conditions there were unfavorable for the next several
years and they returned to Campbell County in Aug. 1921. During the move from
Leith back to the farm near Java, a wagonload of household goods caught fire and
only a few pieces were salvaged. Gottlieb and Lizzie and their little girls made
their home on the Jacob Bender farm until 1925, when they bought a farm, where
they lived for the next 22 years.

In addition to his farming activities while living in Campbell County, Gottlieb
was active in school, church and civic affairs. He served as county commissioner
and was an officer in the Ackerman School district for several years. He was a
board member of the Java Equity Exchange in the 1930's until 1941.

Gottlieb and Lizzie retired from farming in 1947, and moved to Java. He
continued his church activities, being an active Lutheran throughout his
lifetime. Lizzie was a long-time member of ALCW and also of the Java Garden Club
and Sewing club. She died very suddenly in Jan. 1959.

Gottlieb married Mrs. Carrie Geigle in 1960. He was interested in refinishing
furniture and in carpentry as a hobby, until his sudden illness that ended in
his death in Aug. 1965.

They had Agnes, born June 30, 1914, who married Sam L. Goehring, had two
children; Lillian, born Apr. 11, 1919, married Chris J. Pfitzer and they had
three children; Erwin was born July 5, 1925 and married Dalles Kurle. They had
two children; Betty was born Dec. 17, 1933, and married LeRoy Biel. They had two
children.

        John and Hazel (Walter) Zeller
John Zeller, son of George and Rosina Zeller, was born Feb. 16, 1904 at their
farm home 12 miles NE of Java. In 1908, the family moved to Java, where they
operated an implement business. Many of John's early memories were centered on
the implement shop. He assisted with the setting up of machinery by the time he
was 10 years old.

In 1917, the family returned to the farm. Here, John helped with the farm work.
They farmed entirely with horses. In those days, threshing often lasted until
late fall and it, along with corn picking and the preparation of the land, kept
farmers busy until long after the fall freeze.

Like most Dakota farmers prior to the 1920's, the Zellers hauled grain to town
by wagon. The hauling of grain was usually postponed until all the fall work was
done and these slow trips were often made on brisk, cold days. A wagon box would
hold approximately 50 bushels of wheat. Many farmers made the trip with two or
three wagon loads at once. They often met up with others hauling grain, so it
became a friendly convoy along the way. After snow was on the ground, sleighs
were used and the trip was much smoother. From the time they moved back to the
farm, John took part in the grain hauling. In 1925, his parents and three
youngest sisters moved to Eureka. John continued to farm.

He married Hazel Walter of Selby on Dec. 24, 1929. She continued teaching
through the spring of 1932, when rural teacher's salaries dropped below $85 per
month.

Mostly because they wanted to send their children to school in town, the Zellers
moved to Java in Oct. 1947. REA became available to their farm area within a
year or two after their move. Later, school consolidation meant the Java school
bus served their farm community. Also, the mail routes, which farmers of their
area had sought to bring closer to their homes, were changed to pass the Zeller
farm home, in contrast to the two and one-half miles they had to go to their
mail box.

(Photo:) John, Darrell, Hazel, Nancy and Sydney Ann Zeller

John continued grain farming for a time. He also became interested in carpentry,
a trade he followed for more than 25 years. He served on the school board while
in Campbell County and again after moving toJava. Recently, John served two
terms as Mayor of Java. Hazel helped organize the Java Garden Club in 1953. The
Altar Guild of St. Paul Lutheran Church became a reality because of her efforts
to establish a rotating flower committee for the church. She went back to
teaching a rural school for three terms. She also taught Sunday school for more
than 12 years. Hazel's interest in writing and gardening continued and in 1958,
she began her work on gladiolus. Through her hybridization program, she
developed and registered numerous gladioli, her main work being the development
of fragrant glads. In 1967, she organized Wonderful World of Glads, which is
sponsored by the North American Gladiolus Council. Hazel has been a nationally
accredited flower show judge and has served as flower show and flower show
schools chairman for the SD Federated Garden Clubs.

John and Hazel had three children: Nancy (Harry) Remien; Sydney Ann (Kenneth)
Seyer is deceased; and Darrell, who married Mary Ann Chapman.

        Ernest and Gloria (Schlepp) Zimmerman
Ernest was the youngest son of Jacob and Karolina (Grenz) Zimmerman. He was born
at Artas on Jan. 27, 1912. He attended school there. His father passed away when
Ernest was five years old. His mother remarried and Ernest lived with his
mother, stepfather, sisters, brothers and stepbrothers. A half-sister, Esther,
and a half-brother, Walter Aman, were then born. At the age of 12, Ernest
started working for farmers who needed help and gave him a home. He also worked
and lived with a sister and brother-in-law, Ted C. and Martha Biel, until he
entered the service of his country during World War II. After his discharge, he
again lived with the Ted C. Biels, until he met Gloria Schlepp and they were
married June 12, 1949. They made their first home on the John Brockel, Sr., farm
in Campbell County. Ernest continued to do some farming. He also worked for the
R.E.A., Rabenberg Implement, and Walworth County Highway Dept. He retired in
1975. After retiring, Ernest's health started failing and he passed away on Jan.
15, 1986, at the age of 73. He had two brothers, Edwin and Albert Zimmerman; a
half-brother, Walter Aman; four sisters, Martha Biel, Emma Kautz, Rose Wentz,
and Frieda Biel; a half-sister, Esther Bettger; four step brothers, Johnny,
Henry, Otto and Herman Aman; and two step sisters, Amelia Heisler and Alvina
Beck.

Gloria Mureen Schlepp and her twin brother, Clarence Richard, were born to
Samuel and Christina (Wolff) Schlepp on Apr. 21, 1928, on a farm one-half mile
south of Java. They attended the Java school, graduating from Java High School
in 1946. Clarence went into farming with his father until he entered the
service. After his discharge, he returned to farm with his father. Gloria went
to NSTC at Aberdeen in the summer of 1946. This was a period when there was a
shortage of teachers, so Gloria taught in a rural school in the fall of 1946.
She continued taking Extension and Correspondence courses, and attending summer
school before returning to NSTC for one semester, completing her requirements
for her Elementary teaching degree in 1971, with a minor in Art. She was able to
make use of her minor when she taught in the Glenham school system in 1990.
Gloria taught a total of 33 years in the rural schools, Java Public School, and
one year in the Glenham Elementary School. She retired from teaching in 1991.
Since retiring, she has spent her spare time volunteering at the Java Public
Library. She has worked in many areas of her church, including Ladies Aid and as
secretary of the Church Council. Gloria has spent much of her leisure time
traveling. She flew to Gainesville, GA, to meet her first grandchild, Alexander
Brad Zimmerman, the son of Brad and Carol Zimmerman, who was born on May 18,
1998.

(Photo:) Brad, Patanna, Gloria and Ernest Zimmerman

Ernest and Gloria had two children.

Brad Ernest Zimmerman was born in Mobridge on Feb. 27, 1953. He now lives in
Gainesville, GA, and is Controller at The Times newspaper. He attended school in
Java and graduated from Java High School in 1971. He furthered his education by
attending NSC in Aberdeen, and received a degree in Business Administration. He
also worked for Dakota Farmer, Aberdeen American News, and a newspaper in
Longmont, CO. He met and married Carol Murff of Gainesville. Brad and Carol were
married June 10, 1995. Carol is the daughter of Ruth and "Sug" Hamrick of
Gainesville. She was born Nov. 18, 1961 and graduated from North Hall High
School and the U of GA. Carol is Classified Advertising Manager of The Times.
Carol and Brad have a son, Alexander Brad, born May 18, 1998.

Patanna Caroline was born May 3, 1955, at Mobridge. She attended school in Java
and graduated from Java High School in 1973. She then attended NSTC and received
her Secondary Business Education Degree. Her first teaching job was in the
Cresbard High School. She has also taught in the Lyman County School in Presho,
and in the Faulkton High School. She also worked for the Foods and Nutrition
Dept. in Pierre. After teaching in the Faulkton school, she started working as a
Copy Editor at the Aberdeen American News in Aberdeen, where she is still
employed.

        The Zweigardt Family
The Zweigardt family, originally spelled Zweygardt, originated in the German
settlement of Hoffnungstal, Odessa, South Russia. The family has been traced as
far back as 1749.

The family settled in the Java area in the late 1880's. Gottfried Zweigardt was
born 1887, to Gottfried and Katharina (Fiechtner) Zweygardt, Sr. He had three
sisters. He married Magdalena Spiry on June 13, 1911, in Java. They had three
children, all born in the Java area. Gottfried was a musician as well as a
farmer. He played many musical instruments. Unfortunately, he died in the 1918
influenza epidemic, leaving Magdalena to raise three small children. About 1920
or 1921, Magdalena married Michael J. Aman and gave birth to two more children.
The children of Gottfried and Magdalena are:

Arnold, born Dec. 5, 1912, now resides in Spokane, WA. He married Emelie Keller,
originally from Java, on May 14, 1939. They had two children, Dixie Lee Bolinger
of Anderson Island, WA, and Dennis Arnold of Spokane, WA. They have four
grandchildren and three great-grandchildren. Emelie died July 21, 1997 in an
auto accident.

Laura Else was born Oct. 10, 1914 and lives in Sun City, CA. She has been a
resident of southern CA for many years.

Viola E. Fiechtner of Spokane, WA, was born Apr. 3, 1916. She married Walter
Fiechtner on June 23, 1936, in SD. They had four children: Ronald (deceased,
Marilyn, Marianne Angelo, and Larry, all of Spokane. They have two grandchildren
and four great-grandchildren.

The children of Michael Aman and Magdalena were:

Alice Anyan White, born Jan. 1, 1925, resides in Spokane, WA. She had three sons
by Thomas Anyan: Thomas, Michael (deceased), and Daryl of Spokane. She had one
son by Maurice White (deceased), William of Spokane. Alice has 10 grandchildren
and five great-grandchildren.

Melvin Roy, born Feb. 21, 1924, resides in Spokane. He married Maxine
Broemmeling of Genessee, ID, Sept. 25, 1949. They have three children, Kenneth
of Newman Lake, WA, Timothy of Spokane, and Jill of Seattle, WA. They have two
grandchildren and three step grandchildren.

Magdalena Spiry Zweigardt Aman died Feb. 7, 1982, at the age of 91. In this
Zweigardt line, Arnold's son Dennis Zweigardt, has only one son, Scott, to carry
on the Zweigardt name. He is not yet married.
