                   Churches & Organizations... Past & Present

(Photo:) A ruran sod church with a thatched roof, believed to be a Seventh Day
         Adventist Church that was north of Java. At far right is Jacob J. Aman.
         Other members of the Aman family are pictured, but not identified.
         Photo courtesy of Delila Biel

Religion played an important role in the lives of early settlers and still does
today in the community of Java. As the settlers staked out their claims they
broke the sod to plant grain; they built their sod homes for themselves and sod
shelters for their livestock, and they took time out every Sunday to worship
their God. As there were no churches, they would gather around their table and
hold a prayer meeting. As more people moved into the area they would meet in
someone's home or a schoolhouse and hold their prayer service. It took a few
years before there were enough people in the area to begin building houses of
worship. The first ones were constructed of sod as that was the only building
material they could afford. Around 1887 the first missionaries of various faiths
- Baptist, Reformed, Congregational Evangelical and Lutherans - began to
establish stations among the settlers and would hold services in homes of
settlers. The missionaries had their work cut out, as they had to cover a large
territory, which extended from Bowdle in the south to as far north as Wishek in
central North Dakota. As there were only a few ministers, the lay brothers would
conduct the service. The sermon was read from a prepared conduct of service or
from the Bible; songs were sung from memory.

Americans settlers would attend churches in Bangor or Mound City. The Germans
from Russia were not mixers and held their services among themselves and as the
number of families increased, they built their churches near the center of their
membership. The first church was built of sod and was shared by Reformed and
Evangelical. It is believed that this church was located on Grandma Sieler's
land in SE1/4 of Section 18, Blessing Township, Campbell County. Grandma Sieler
died in 1888 and was buried here. This church was struck by lightning and burned
sometime in the early 1890's. As new settlers filed their claims, new churches
were established. It is believed that the Reformed and Evangelical built
separate sod churches. Christ Rau donated land for a church and a cemetery on
SW1/4 of Section 23 of Blessing Township, Campbell County in 1894. This church
building and a barn were built of sod. This church was known as Odessa Reformed
Church or Sutley Reformed. In 1896 the Evangelical built a sod church on the
land donated by Peter Junker on NW1/4 of Section 30, Township 125 Range 74N of
Thompson Township. The outline of the building is still visible today.

ODESSA REFORMED CHURCH
The Reformed church had the largest membership of churches built in this area.
In 1884 the first group of Germans from Russia arrived and settled in Thompson
Township in Campbell County. They were the Buckenberger, Christina Kunz,
Koerner, Oswald and Schenkenberger families. In the spring of 1885, a large
number of Germans from Russia settled north of Salt Lake in Blessing Township in
Campbell County. Nearly all of these families were of the Reformed faith. They
were Jakob Geigle, Adam Leno, Adam, Philipp and Kaspar Sieler, Konrad Vollmer
and Heinrich Ottmer, Klingers and Schaeffer families. By 1889 the Jakob, Henry
and John Ackerman families along with Jakob and Peter Schneider, Andreas
Kundert, Gottlieb Boehler, Paul, Sr., Paul, Jr., Chris and Ludwig Huether, Jakob
Voremaier, Christian Rau, Frederick Biel, Johann Hochstetter, the Wilhelm Langs
and Becktolds, Jakob Bender and Gottlieb Bertsch, Karl Hauck, Sr. and Karl, Jr.,
the Karl Vollmers and Fredrick Wosnuks settled in what is now the eastern
portion of Valley, Blessing and Thompson Townships in SE Campbell County.

According to reports, the first Reformed church was a sod building, located on
Magdelena Sieler and her son Adam's land. She passed away in 1888 and was buried
near the church next to a large rock, which leads us to believe this church was
probably built before 1888. Verbal reports are that this church was shared by
Reformed and Evangelical. As this church was struck by lightning and burned,
Christian Rau donated land and a sod church was built near the present Leslie
Rau farm on the east side of Salt Lake.

The Odessa Reformed Church was served by a group from Artas; the group that
split away was served out of Eureka and this occurred sometime late 1890. This
church was built out of wood and was located one-half mile east of the Jakob
Geigle farm. The land was donated by Paul Huether, Jr., who lived on what is now
the Leroy Sandmaier farm. Some of families who belonged to this church were Paul
Sr., Paul Jr., Ludwig and Chris Huether and Jakob Dormaier and probably others.
This was a wooden building and when the Dormaiers and Huethers moved to
Washington state in the early 1900's, the building was purchased by the Odessa
group and moved onto the Rau site.

From 1884 to 1900, families moved into this area and filed claims, and by 1900
there was no land available to be homesteaded. Also, the need to expand the farm
and the period of poor crops caused settlers in this area to move to new sites.
The Adam Sieler family moved to Plevna, MT, Adam Leno to ND, Dormeier, Ottmer
and Huethers to WA, Klingers, Vollmer and Schaeffer to Tripp, SD, the Jakob
Schneider and Andreas Kundert families to Canada, Henry Ackerman and
Buckenberger families moved to Herreid. By 1916-20, most of pioneer members
retired to the town of Java. They were Gottlieb Bertsch, Karl Hauck, Jakob
Geigle, Jakob Bender, John Kundert and others. During the 20's the sons and
daughters were members of the church. The church split in 1929 and the majority
of members formed the Sutley Congregational Church.

The families who kept church open were Johannes and John Ackerman, Henry, John
and William Schneider, and Henry Kast. In 1936 the church was closed and the
building was sold. A number of pioneers and their offspring are buried in this
cemetery. The names that can be found here are Wilhelm Lang, Karl Becktol, Peter
Schneider, Adam Sieler, Konrad Vollmer, Johannes Ackerman, Jakob Ackerman,
Friedrick Biel, George Biel, Andreas Kunz, Christian Rau & Johann Hochstetter.

SUTLEY CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH
This church was formed in 1930 by Rev. Knaus of Eureka and was located on
Section 27, Township 125 (Blessing) Range 74N. The following families left the
Odessa Reformed Church to form the Congregational Church: Christ Rau, Ed F. Biel
Otto Kundert, Jacob Geigle, Sam Goehring, Edward Scmidt, Ted F. Biel, Ted C.
Biel, Fred C. Biel, Henry Brockel, John Kary, Mike Kary, Jacob Kary, and Ed G.
Biel.

The Bethesda Congregational Church, which was located about a mile north of the
Dennis Boschee farm in Walworth County, was moved to a new location in the
Sutley area, a half-mile south of the former Reformed Church. At that time the
membership of Bethesda was very small and those who voted to join were Henry
Delker, Johannes, Karl, Sr. and Karl, Jr. Wolf.

The Bethesda Church was organized in the 1890's and had a fairly large
membership. After 1900, many of the members moved to different states.

The first Sutley Congregational Church building was a wooden structure that was
purchased from Lutherans known as the Bauman Church east of Java. Shortly after
the building had been put on its foundation, it was destroyed by fire. From 1933
until 1940 the membership grew, and after World War II, the membership declined
when older members retired from farming and the number of farms were reduced.
The young people left the area.

Those who joined the, church during the 30's were Christ Gutjahr, Henry Boschee,
Albert Kary, Leo Biel, Albert Sieler, Fred Hochstetter, Eugene Rau, Jake
Pfeifle, Henry Schott, John Ackerman, John Holzwarth, Ted Meyer, Jacob
Holzwarth, Herbert Pfaff and Erwin Goehring.

After 1945, the sons and daughters joined the church. They were Alvin Kary,
Wilbur Kary, Roy Kundert, Floyd Biel, Virgil Biel, Hiram Biel, Andrew Munsch,
Wilmer Munsch, Herbert Rau, Victor Hirsch, Earl Biel and Wilmer Boschee.

In 1960 the Sutley Congregational Church united with the United Church of Christ
of Java. The building was sold and the membership purchased the old Java
Lutheran Church building.

Members who joined the United Church of Christ were Ted F. Biel, Mike Kary,
Wilbur Kary, Wilmer Boschee, Denis Boschee, Fred Biel, Albert Kary, Floyd Biel,
Erwin Goehring, Herbert Pfaff, Andrew Munsch, Victor Hirsch, Earl Biel, Herbert
Rau and Herbert Geigle.

For a brief period there was a Congregational Church located about three-and-a-
half miles north of Java. This membership was made up of Schlepps, Berreths and
Amans. According to an article in the Java Herald, a large confirmation class
was held around 1910. It is believed that the church closed when the Schlepp
family moved into Java and joined the Java Congregational Church.

SUTLEY EVANGELICAL CHURCH
The Sutley Evangelical Church was the first group believed to have shared a
church with the Reformed and in late 1887, built a sod structure on land located
in Section 30, Township 125, Range 74N. In 1896, the sod church was replaced
with a mud-brick church on a hill donated by Peter Junker. A cemetery was also
established. Evidence of a sod foundation is still visible and depressions in
the ground indicate a number of graves. It is believed that six children of
Ernst Freimark, who died in a period from Dec. 1894 to Feb. 1895, of typhus, are
buried here. They were John, Bertha (8), Katharina (7), Jacobine, Mathilda and
Frederick. The report stated that two more children were near death. When Peter
Junker moved to a farm on Section 21 of Thompson Township, the congregation
built a wooden church on land donated by Peter Junker, which was deeded Dec. 9,
1920 to the Zion Congregation of the Evangelical Association. Of interest is
that, on this same farm, Johann Eder and his wife Catherina had deeded land to
the Evangelical on Oct. 18, 1895.

Members and families were Peter Junker, Andreas Hirning, Gottlieb Freimark,
George and Fred Eberhardt, Christ Lutz, the Gust Rau family, George Raille,
Neumiller and Mittleider.

The church closed in 1958 and the membership transferred to the Eureka church.

WISENBURGER BAPTIST CHURCH of EUREKA
This church was located on Section 27, Thompson Township 125, Range 74N and
ground was donated by the Wisenburger family for the church and cemetery. The
church was established in the late 1890's and disbanded in the early 1930's. The
members of this church were Johannes Wolf, Christ Wolf, Fred Wolf, Gottlieb
Zimmerman, Valentine Kary and Simon Hirsch.

SEVEN-DAY ADVENTIST
This church was organized in the later 1890's. A building was erected and a
cemetery established on land deeded by Jakob and Margaretha Oswald, which was
Section 30, Thompson Township 125, Range 74N.

The members were Jakob Oswald, John Bauer, Kiesz, Adam Wagner, Jacob
Steiglemaier, William Moser, Jakob Aman, Peter Kast, Simon Bitts, Florian and
Peter Hartman, Ernest Krueger, Walter Brockel and Mrs. Philip Sieler.

The church building was moved to Java in 1940 and sold to the Church of God when
the members joined the Bowdle Advent Church.

LUTHERAN CHURCHES
Schnaible Lutheran Church was established by the Schnaible and Spiry families.
It was located about two and one-half miles north of Java. When Java was
founded, the members elected to establish what is now the St. Paul Lutheran
Church. [Freidensgeminde]

Helm Lutheran Church was located about five miles NW of Java and established by
the Helm families. John Job was the leader of this church prior to its closing.
It closed in the early 1940's and joined the Java congregation.

Bauman Lutheran Church was located NE of  Java Pioneer members were the Baumans,
Schuhs, Rosins. [Hoffnungstahl]

Neu Glueckstahl Church was located east of Java. Rev. Kirchdoerfer served as
pastor from 1902-1918. In 1946 the congregation disbanded and several members
joined St. Paul Lutheran Church in Java. [The same 15 people who started this
church also started St. John's in Bowdle]

Friedensthal Evangelical Lutheran Church was started when Gottlieb and Louisa
Knodle deeded land for the church building and cemetery in Section 125, Blessing
Township 125, Range 75N. On Feb. 12, 1901 a deed was issued to Hoffnungstal
Lutheran Church located west of Eureka, by Dave Fischer and Gust Metzger. The
pioneer families were Knodels, Paul Bauman, Bauers, Biebers, Fischers, Kiszlers,
Knotts, Metzgers, Oberlanders, Schicks, Holzworths, Benders and Zellers. This
church was closed in the late 1940's.

CATHOLIC CHURCH
A committee of John Kormendy, George Kormendy, Ladislaus Kormendy, Stephen Raba,
Frank Hagadus, Gaza Kormendy, Mike Zarka, and Ferdinand Alexander were appointed
to organize and choose lots for the purpose of erecting a new Catholic Church.

In May 1905, a building committee was selected and they purchased two lots south
of the C.F. Clement residence. Cornerstone ceremonies were held June 14, 1905,
and building got underway shortly thereafter. There were many volunteers who
helped faithfully and a year later, the new wooden structure was completed. On
Monday, May 14, 1906, the first mass was celebrated in the new church with the
Rev. Father Schell from Herreid, officiating. Rev. Father Schell served this
parish for four years and the congregation steadily attended it. In 1910 Father
Krause became the priest for this area, including the Selby and Bowdle
Congregations.

PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH
On Aug. 3, 1902, Sunday School Missionary, Isaac Perry, called a meeting at the
schoolhouse for the interest of organizing a Presbyterian Church. A few months
later, Rev. C.C. Todd of Aberdeen, pastor-at-large, assisted by Dr. Carson and
H. Grant, organized a Presbyterian Church. For three years, Rev. Todd and Rev.
Fischer, of Evarts, held part time services. The first members received into the
church were, Mr. and Mrs. Boyland, Mrs. J.C. Corson, Mrs. Consolver, Mrs. Grace
Noble and Mrs. Laura Harris.

In 1905, a student pastor, J.B. Foster of Delaware, supplied the church for the
summer and later became resident pastor, serving until 1908.

A lot and a cash donation of $1000 were received from a member, Wm. H. Payne,
toward a church building, and the wooden structure was built in 1905. The new
church was dedicated on Dec. 29, 1907, free of debt.

(Photo:) This was the Presbyterian Church in Java, with its beautiful steeple

The membership continued to grow; new members included Gerrit and Alice Noble.
The late Mr. Noble was elected and ordained as the first Elder of the church.
(Alice Noble was a resident of the Good Samaritan Center in Selby for a number
of years, until her death in Jan. 1974.)

Rev. Oltmans served this congregation for many years and later, neighboring
pastors conducted the services. In 1930, the church combined for a time with the
Reformed Church, to be able to pay salary of a resident pastor. This arrangement
was later terminated.

Misfortune struck this little congregation when, in 1936, the church burned to
the ground. Due to the Depression in the early thirties, when many members left
Java, it was not feasible to rebuild at this time. Later, the Aberdeen
Presbystery donated an unused building from Edmunds county to the Java
Congregation. This was dismantled, moved, and placed on the old foundation.
However, this building proved to be in poor condition and a weed fire damaged it
further. This compelled the congregation and Sunday School to continue their
services in the basement but later, the Seventh Day Advent Congregation shared
their church building.

The 50th Anniversary of the church was commemorated in Sept. of 1952, with a
dinner and special service, which was attended by former members. The
congregation never gave up hope, and with sufficient funds, undertook the
project of rebuilding. A fine modern church was built with much of the credit
for this achievement belonging to Rev. Leslie B. Lewis, who was pastor from 1951
to 1954, and gave so generously his advice, time and labor. Dedication services
were held on Nov. 29, 1953 with the Rev. Lewis in charge and Dr. Kann of
Aberdeen Presbyterian Church as main speaker.

Besides the Java Congregation, the Rev. Lewis also served the Roscoe and Pollock
churches. Later, Rev. E. Freeman took over the pastorate and served until 1959.
After 1959, Rev. Cedar and Rev. Rosendaal alternated their services for a few
years, until Rev. Rosendaal retired.

The membership dwindled with the younger people leaving the Java area and others
deceased, so with some reluctance the church had to be closed. The Rev. Cedar,
who served the Pollock Church for 25 years, continued as supply pastor until
Feb. 1969, when the Aberdeen-Huron Presbytery disbanded the Java Church.

PRESBYTERIAN LADIES AID
The women of Java and vicinity held a meeting at the home of Mrs. Gerrit Noble
on July 14, 1904, for the purpose of organizing a Ladies Aid Society. The Ladies
Aid Society was organized and raised funds to help furnish the new church. The
following ladies were elected as officers: President, Laura E. Harris; vice
president, Mrs. James Corson; secretary, Mrs. Philip Noble; treasurer, Mrs.
Jacob Stoller. Their meetings were held every two weeks, the members alternating
in hosting the bi-weekly meetings.

One fund-raiser was the church supper. When the Ladies had their regular meeting
at the church basement on Feb. 1, 1933, a supper was served at 5:30 p.m., with
the following menu: Roast pork, applesauce, mashed potatoes and gravy, corn,
pickles, buttered buns, pie and coffee. The ladies who were serving at this time
were: Mmes. W.C. Hicks, J.C. Schlepp, Kate Clement, Carl Jacobs, G.W. Hicks, and
Otto B. Wolff. Prices charged were 20 cents for adults and 10 cents for children
under 12 years was charged.

They also purchased the bell, which was later destroyed by the fire of 1936.
They financially assisted the church throughout the years. Among the early
members were: Mmes. Kate Clement, W.C. Hicks, H.J. Cook, Gerrit Noble, Peter
Noble, W.F. Dyer, Winkley, Eisentraut, Fiechtner, L.E. Harris, J. Stoller, W.F.
Ewald and H. Theilen.

JAVA UCC HISTORY
The Sutley Congregation was formed in 1929 and joined Selby to form the Selby-
Glenham-Sutley parish in 1930. The first services were held in the "Blessing
School House," with Rev. Knaus from Eureka holding the services there, until a
church from east of Sutley was moved. First Pastor, then Rev. Theodore Radach in
1930. In 1932 the church burned down and was replaced the following summer with
a church moved from southeast of Sutley. Rev. Radach left in 1933.

The Sutley Congregational Church was incorporated Dec. 1930. The trustees
signing the Articles of Incorporation were Sam Goehring, Theodore C. Biel, and
Mike Kary.

Rev. Christ Maedche became the next pastor. His work began Mar. 1, 1934 and he
served the parish until Nov. 1938. He organized the first Ladies Aid. During
Rev. Radach and Rev. Maedche all services were in the German language and
records were written in German.

Rev. Philip Reich served the church from 1939 through 1941. He started the
Christian Endeavor Youth Group. They met on Sunday nights, early enough so the
young group could make the movie at the "Grand Theater" at Java. The parents
also came to their meetings and went visiting the neighbors after the meeting.
We must say the attendance was nearly 100%. Rev. Reich also started the English
language services.

Rev. Elmer Bettenhausen served the parish from 1943-1945. The members remembered
him driving like mad. He was always late. Before the service, the church members
stood around and waited. They'd see a cloud of dust, and then hear the roar of
the engine, and here he would come, five minutes late! They debated whether or
not he could be related to the racecar driver.

Looking back at the treasurer's record in 1942, the three churches in the parish
paid the following toward the pastor's salary: Sutley, $81; Glenham, $49.50;
Selby, $90 for a grand total of $220.50 for the Quarter.

  1945-1946     Rev. Jacob Rath
  1947-1950     Rev. Ernest Sprenger
  1951          Student, Theodore Bader
  1952-1955     Rev. Jacob Rath
  1956          Student, Jonathan Knecht

For his ordination and first pastorate, Rev. Raymond Schatz came in Sept. 1956
and served until June 1962. He was an energetic, single young man who enjoyed
visiting in the homes of his parishioners, and helping them with the farm work.
During this time the Sutley Church was sold to Victor Hirsch and it still
remains on the property. Services were then held in the Java Presbyterian Church
until the old Lutheran Church was purchased on Mar. 25, 1960 for the sum of
$4,000. During this time a meeting of several denominations was held and an
association was formed, taking the name of United Church of Christ, and so it
became the Java UCC. Rev. Schatz made the wooden cross and candle holders.

Following Rev. Schatz's pastorate, supply pastors served. They were: Bob
Thompson, Luke Miller, and Rev. Ray Berry. Rev. Nein returned for a short time.

The summer of 1966 supply pastor, Steven O'Mally, came and started a
confirmation class, and Rev. Douglas Barrows came in the fall to complete the
work started that summer. Rev. Barrows stayed ten years, which is the longest
tenure in the church history. His home became a collection point for used
clothing, which was distributed to the needy, and is still being done. After
Rev. and Mrs. Barrows retired from ministry, they purchased a home in Java,
close to the church, where the congregation enjoyed their presence on Sunday
mornings. The two wooden candelabras were given to the church from the Barrows.

In May 1977, the Rev. Wayne Drueck came and served the parish for two and a half
years. Rev. Jeffrey Whitman, a newly ordained graduate, came in 1980-1985. Rev.
Jeff started the Offering Pledge system, which is still being used today.

  Rev. Jean Rosewell served the church in 1986
  Rev. Robert Alpers served 1987-1989
  Rev. Ralph Hoffman in 1989
  Rev. Sterling Wenzel in 1990
  Rev. George Fandt 1990-1992

In June 1992 a motion was made to close the church.

Highlights and Memories: Kenneth Biel went to Seminary after high school and
became the only ordained minister from the Sutley Congregational Church. He was
ordained in 1946; 1984, the Java UCC started a perpetual fund for maintenance of
the cemetery northwest of Java; Ted F. Biel, a dedicated Sunday School teacher,
taught as long as the Sutley church operated; during church services men used to
sit on the right side of the church and the women sat on the left side; on
Sunday morning Philip Goehring would ride a horse to church and light the stove;
after it was lit, he would send the horse home. He would stay until the family
came for church, going home with them. Later, the horse was sold to Eugene Rau,
and he did the same thing; Christmas programs were at least two hours long and
every child taking part would memorize their portion. There were long dialogs,
poems, and music. The church would be packed. Sacks and goodies were passed out
after the program and a gift exchange was held. The practice for this program
started before Thanksgiving and the program was always held Dec. 23; The Java
Church CYU would decorate the balcony at Christmas time. How beautiful the
church would look! Janet Biel started a youth choir in about 1970. For several
years their service of music was enjoyed every Sunday; Remembering Rev. Schatz's
saying on a Sunday morning, shortly before he left, that he didn't know of
another church that could say there were more people in church than there were
members; The Java UCC had one of the highest Mission Offerings per member in the
conference. In 1991 the mission offering was $1,464, and there were 37 members
at that time; Mike and Martha Kary were the janitors and they worked so hard.
Mrs. Kary always would want to wash the dishes whenever anything was going on in
church. Other dedicated janitors were Albert and Maggie Kary, and Dorothy Biel.

JAVA UCC LADIES AID HISTORY
The first records we can find of the Ladies Aid are from 1938. Although some
church records show that Rev. Maedke started the Ladies Aid during his ministry
from 1933 to 1938. The ladies met in the homes of the members for their first
meetings at night, and the entire family came. They also invited many guests and
their whole families also came. The furniture was moved out and replaced with
chairs and benches from the church.

In the record book of 1938, there were 18 members on roll call, four of which
were single girls. The girls in their late teens could join the Ladies Aid, and
what an honor that was! The president that year was Mrs. Henry Delker; vice
president was Mrs. Fred C. Biel; treasurer was Mrs. Christ Rau; and secretary
was Mrs. Jacob Geigle. Mrs. Leo Biel was also noted as secretary; she evidently
finished the term for Mrs. Geigle. On Jan. 14, the meeting was held at the home
of Mrs. Ted C. Biel with 12 members present and 16 visitors. (Imagine having 56
adults in your home for a Ladies Aid meeting, plus the children from all their
families!). While the ladies held their meeting, the men would visit, or if the
weather were nice, they would play softball. The men can remember someone
bringing a battery-powered radio and they listened to the Joe Louis and Max
Schmolling boxing match, with the power fading in and out.

After the ladies' meeting, the men would sing hymns. There was no piano or
organ, so there was no accompaniment, unless someone brought along a guitar,
accordion, or mandolin. Ted Mayer and John Ackerman could play these
instruments. Those men could really sing! The ladies were busy preparing a huge
lunch for everyone. They charged 10 cents for adults and high school students,
and 5 cents for grade students. At the end of the year, the two ladies who had
the most income during the year received a gift.

There were no minutes kept during the first years of meetings. They kept track
of whether the Pres. or the Vice Pres. conducted the meeting, the hymns that
were sung, how many members attended, at whose home it was held, the scripture
that was read, and the income for the month. The names of the visitors were
listed on a separate page in the record book. There were no minutes of the
annual meeting, only the results of the election of officers for the coming
year. The meeting was held at the church with no visitors present.

The programs were the highlight of the meeting. In 1942, they began writing the
minutes of the meeting each month. The program in one of the minutes read like
this: "A song was sung by two girls (a German hymn) followed by a poem by
Priscilla Biel, poems by Phyllis Brockel and Gladys Kary and Pearle Schott, poem
by Erna Kary, another poem by Norma Rau after which a song was sung by Mr. and
Mrs. Fred C. Wolff. More poems by Allegra Biel and Oliva Rau. Then the minutes
were read and business matters were taken up." The boys of the families also
took part in the singing, poems, and recitations for the program. Virgil and
Floyd Biel recalled that during the meeting, the young boys held boxing matches
in the basement. After Alvin Kary knocked out Floyd Biel at the Ed G. Biel home,
the parents put a stop to the boxing matches. We can see where the Ladies Aid
meeting each month served as an important social time for church members and
their families, and the whole community.

In the minutes of June 1941, the Ladies Aid had a picnic for the Sunday School
and they bought 10 gallons of ice cream and cones for $11.90. Virgil says he can
remember what a treat that was.

Later that year, Sept. 1941, the Ladies Aid bought two gasoline mantle lamps for
the church at a cost of $25.36. Bazaars were also held in the old dormitory
building on Java's Main Street. During the Second World War era, they donated
money to the War Fund, USO, and Red Cross. They were very dedicated to help the
war effort in any way possible.

At the Dec. meeting, 1944, the price for "meals" was raised to 20 cents for
adults, and also high school students, and 10 cents for grade students.

In 1946, the ladies purchased a new Communion Set and Collection Plates for the
church. They also decided to "reduce" the lunch to a drink, sandwich and one
side dish. However, the ladies say the lunches were always huge, and no one paid
much attention to the decision that was made at their Dec. meeting.

In June of 1947, Kenneth Biel attended the Ladies Aid meeting and presented a
program entitled "The Golden Rule". This was an especially happy and proud
occasion as Kenneth grew up in the community, attended the Sutley Church, and
went into the ministry.

In 1947, the members sent 17 Care packages to the needy in Germany (one of
clothing) and spent $100 on these Care packages. Other donations were a $25
scholarship to Yankton College, and $35 to Mission Fest. Many things were
purchased for the church, including hymnals and silverware, as well as gifts and
donations to the Eureka "Old People's Home" and for the "Feeble Minded" at
Redfield at Easter and Christmas.

In 1956, they began to rent the Legion Hall in Java for their Ladies Aid
meetings for those who wished. Claudia Pfaff was hostess in Oct. 1956 with 23
members present and 105 visitors! There were always more visitors at the
meetings than members; visitors enjoyed the hymn singing.

When a new young, single pastor, Rev. Raymond Schatz, came, the ladies purchased
a writing desk and it was given to him as a gift.

The last Java UCC Church was purchased in 1960 and they held their first meeting
in the church basement in June.

They purchased new hymnals for the church (75) at a cost of $2.52 each. The
flags were purchased in 1961. The piano was added in 1970 and folding tables
were also added.

For the chicken and ham suppers, each member had to bring four or five chickens,
four pies and salad. The suppers were held in the Legion Hall beginning in 1958.
Charges were $1.25 for adults, 75 cents for children seven to 12 years old, and
50 cents for children two to six years old. After purchasing the building in
1960, they had suppers in the church basement for a while, and then rented the
Legion Hall, where there was more space in the kitchen and more room for seating
the crowd. They had a German Smorgasbord in 1979. An article in the Mobridge
Tribune states that 200 pounds of flour was used, and they made over 1000 cheese
buttons. The church suppers were getting to be too much work for the members, so
they had pancake and sausage dinners for a few years. The last dinners served
were on Memorial Day in 1989. The church closed in June 1992.

Looking back, many missionaries were supported, many kits for World Service and
many other projects were supported. A lot of hard work was put into the meetings
at the members' homes, the bazaars, and suppers to earn money for the
organization. All sadly miss it.

The 1992 Membership was Katherine Barrows, Delila Biel, Dorothy Biel, Lorraine
Biel, Lillian Fandt, Allegra Hirsch, Esther Holzworth, Lorraine Kary, Elaine
Langston, Viola Munsch, Shirley Rau, Verda Schaffer, and Ella Stangl.

LUTHERAN CHURCH OF JAVA
A number of small churches had sprung up in the northeast part of the county
which were as follows:

Hoffnungstahl was built in 1887 by a membership of 22 families. Pastor Fredrick
Braun served this small congregation with the other three parishes. It later was
disbanded and joined St. Paul Lutheran Church of Java.

Friedens Lutheran Church, built in 1895, was located six miles NE of Java. It
had a membership of 18 families. Pastor Fredrick Braun and Pastor G.
Kirchdoerfer also served this Parish.

Neuglueckstal Church was built in 1901 and was located 9 miles east of Java.
Many members from the Hosmer Parish started this church and before too long, the
membership grew to 35 families. Pastor Attersburg from the Hosmer Parish served
this church.

The first St. Paul Lutheran Church was a one-room wooden structure built in
1897, on a hill near the Karl Schnaible farm. Charter members did most of the
work. In 1900, this congregation, together with Hoffnungstahl and Friedens
Church, formed the Java Parish. Rev. G. Schmidt served for a short time before
he was called back to Germany. Pastor Fredrick Braun took over and incorporated
the Java Parish. When the railroad was built and the city of Java begun, it was
decided to move this little church into Java. In 1901, the church was moved to
town on four horse-drawn wagons and placed on a lot. Later a parsonage was built
beside it. In 1902 Pastor Braun ended his ministry and Pastor George
Kirchdoerfer filled the vacancy.

The Parish grew with abundance; several Missionary meetings had to be held in
the Blinderman-Wolf Hall. Perceptive plans were being made to build a new
church. The previous structure was moved to the back of the lot and building
started immediately. In 1909, the 28x60 church was completed at a cost of $4800.
The old building was used for a schoolhouse. In 1932, it was necessary to expand
and a basement was placed under the church.

After 40 years of active ministry Pastor Kirchdoerfer retired on July 8, 1942.
The vacancies were filled with Pastor Westenberger in 1943, and Pastor E.H.
Haacke in 1950 until 1957. Membership had grown tremendously, which made it
possible for the congregation not to be vacant too long. Pastor A.H. Schmitt
filled the vacancy in 1958. Shortly after his arrival, new developments were
made and plans incepted immediately for a new church.

One year from groundbreaking services, May 10, 1959 to May 8, 1960, the
congregation was able to worship in the new church. Pastor Schmitt remained
until 1965. Membership was beginning to decrease as families were moving and
farmers were expanding. Pastor Parlow filled the vacancy and served for two
years. Neighboring Pastors served the congregation until Pastor Leon Schulz
filled the vacancy in 1968 to mid-1977.

In 1970, an acre of land was donated on the west side of the cemetery. Stained
glass windows were installed in the nave, narthex, and balcony in Feb. and
dedicated on Easter Sunday, Mar. 29, 1970. In 1973, the congregation of St. Paul
Lutheran Church burned the mortgage papers on Oct. 2, a day to celebrate.
Improvements were made at the cemetery in 1976, when volunteers put up a fence
on the north and west sides. The new Lutheran Book of Worship was adopted in
1978.

Pastor Waldemar Storm was installed in Sept. 1977 and stayed until 1984. Pastor
Julius Roehl served for three months, and then Pastor Loren Odland of Selby
consented to conduct services until Pastor Ralph Holmlund arrived in 1985 and
resigned early in 1992. Pastor Heskin of Trinity Lutheran Church of Mobridge
filled in from Jan. to Mar.; Pastor Brewer of St. John Lutheran Church of Selby
took care of the confirmation classes. Supply pastors served until Mar. 1, then
interim Pastor Ron Brugger from Huron served until June 1, when Pastor Anna
Peck, a graduate of Wartburg Seminary of Dubuque, IA, accepted the call. On Mar.
1, pastoral services were shared with Rural Bethany Lutheran Church and St. Paul
Lutheran of Java contract with Bethany Lutheran on June 2, 1992.

(Photo) Untitled

In Dec. of 1992, the church records were microfilmed. In 1993, a computer was
purchased, with Memorial Funds, for office use. A new Roger organ was purchased
in Oct. 1994 and the old organ was donated, in 1995, to St. Paul Lutheran Church
in Mound City.

In 1995: Andrea DeGroot-Nesdahl became bishop of the ELCA SD Synod; Pastor
Arthur Schmitt, former Java pastor, retired from the ministry in June; funeral
bulletins were provided; Roger Ehrich gave the church a hard cover book, "The
Lutheran Book of Java" in Aug; ceiling fans were installed in the church kitchen
in Oct.; and 41 surplus school desks were disposed in Nov.

In 1996: The St. Paul Lutheran Church Centennial Celebration was set for June
18, 2000; an area strategy meeting was held in Java with neighboring churches
attending. Bishop Andrea DeGroot-Nesdahl was the facilitator of the meeting in
June; a "Looking to the Future" dialogue was held in Sept.; and bees wax candles
were replaced with oil candles in Oct.

In 1997: A Centennial Church Committee was organized in Apr.; Oahe Special
Education Coop moved into St. Paul Lutheran in Aug.; and a new PA system was
installed in Nov.

In 1998: Pastor Anna M. Peck resigned in May. Rural Bethany Lutheran Church's
contract ceased with Pastor Peck's resignation; a new Sharp copy machine was
purchased in July; also in July, a straw vote was taken to determine whether
members wanted to call a pastor, offering a large increase in salary, or whether
they wanted to share a pastor with another congregation; and in Sept., the
Church Council decided to shut off the parsonage heat and winterize the
parsonage because of problems with its furnace.

In 1999: St. Paul Lutheran Church of Java negotiated with St. Paul Lutheran
Church of Bowdle to contract for a new pastor; a Reserve Parking sign was made
and placed for the pastor's parking; church pictures were taken for a new church
directory in Mar; the Church Council had a tiered flower stand made to display
flowers in the front of the church; and it was decided not to plant flowers
beside the church foundation, slope the area and replace the flowers with
plastic and rock. As of Jan. 1, 1999, there were 196 baptized members and 170
confirmed members.

LADIES AID SOCIETY/ALCW/WELCA
Mrs. George Kirchdoerfer, Mrs. Christ Schnaible, Mrs. Christ Wolf, and Mrs.
Jacob Fiechtner organized the American Lutheran Church Women of St. Paul
Lutheran church of Java, originally known as the Ladies Aid Society, in the
summer of 1905, under the leadership of Pastor George Kirchdoerfer, at the
Lutheran parsonage. Having no public meeting place, the Aid met in private homes
for many years, until the basement under the church was completed. Through the
years, many fund-raising projects were carried out by this organization, the
proceeds of which were contributed to the many charities of the church, besides
helping financially with improvements of the church interior.

In 1946, the first edition of the Aid's cookbook was published, containing
recipes of the members. On Feb. 1, 1951, the pastor's wife, Mrs. E.H. Haacke,
introduced the work of the Women's Missionary Federation and at that meeting,
the Ladies Aid voted to become affiliated with the WMF, and the English language
was used at the meetings. Results of that bonded effort were very gratifying,
supporting the eight departments of the WMF besides assisting with the needs of
the local church and congregation. At that time there were 63 members.

The WMF held their first meeting in the new church on May 10, 1960. Besides
donating a substantial sum to the building fund, the Society fully equipped the
new kitchen and also purchased four sets of paraments. It had a membership of
110, one of which, charter member Mrs. Christ Wolf, was still with the
organization .

In Dec. 1960, the name of the Society was changed again, this time to the
American Lutheran Church Women (ALCW), as the auxiliary of the American Lutheran
Church adopted this name.

In 1961, the members were divided into five working groups, each group taking
its turn in working for church functions and funerals.

It was decided in 1963 to publish a second edition of the ALCW cookbook, with
recipes added by members of the then-present Society. Two thousand cookbooks
were published and sold.

Bible study groups were started in Jan. 1965. There were five groups in 1975,
four meeting in their classrooms, with a different group each month remaining in
the social room with the honorary members. In 1975, there were 171 members in
this organization, which met as a group on the first Weds. evening of each
month. This group continued to contribute much to the congregation and various
charities and Missions. The last charter member, Rosina (Christ) Wolf, passed
away Dec. 28, 1972 at the age of 87.

Officers of the organization in 1975 were: President, Priscilla (Ervin) Mueller;
vice president, Anne (John) Witlock; secretary, Violet (Erven) Aman; treasurer,
Lila (Fred C.) Bieber; education secretary was Mary Ann (Wilbur) Krause; and
stewardship secretary, Florence (Merle) Noess.

Honorary members were: Mmes. Eddie Anderson, Lydia Bauer, Fred Bauman, Henry
Bender, William Frank, Ed Gill, John Goetz, Ed Goetz, Jacob J. Haux, Margaretha
Haux, Jacob Himmerich, Marie Hofer, Adolph C. Horst, John Kapfenstein, Emanuel
Keller, I.C. Krause, Rudolph Kurle, David Lemley, Jake Nehlich, Ed Naasz,
Margaret Naasz, Eva Ochszner, Christina Oster, Fred Permann, Lydia Pfaff, Julius
Pfitzer, Linda Pregitzer, Reinhold Sackman, Frieda Sauer, William Sauer, John
Schadler, David Schlepp, Emanuel Schlepp, Michael Schmierer, Ed Schnaible, Henry
Schreter, Adolph Schuh, C.F. (Rosie) Spiry, Jacob Sonnenfeld, Philip F.
(Theresa) Spiry, Philip H. (Natalie) Spiry, Sam Spiry, Adolph Stangl, Ben
Stiegelmeier, Jacob Teske, Frank Weisgram, Carrie Wolf, Edward Wolf, William
(Bill) Wolf, Henry H. Wolff, and Gottlieb (Carrie) Zeller.

Women of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of America, which was known as American
Lutheran Church Women of St. Paul Lutheran Church of Java, is still a very
important part of the church.

The women now have three working groups that work for funeral and other events
held in the church. They have an annual church supper, bazaar, and a soup
supper, with proceeds going toward helping in the church, wherever it is most
needed. A Third Addition to the cookbook was made in 1976.

The WELCA give gifts to the Good Samaritan Center at Selby during Christmas and
also have a Birthday Party at the Center in Nov. of every year.

Edythe Schefner, Carol Fiedler, and Donna Bieber, WELCA women of St. Paul
Lutheran Church, have held offices for the Northern Plains Conference.

The women make quilts and put together health kits, school kits, layettes,
sewing kits and mid-wife kits. These are then sent to Lutheran World Relief,
although some of the quilts are kept in the church to be used for local families
who have had a crisis in their home. A quilt is also given to each local
graduating senior. WELCA also makes Easter and Christmas baskets for the elderly
and the shut-in.

In 1993, the Katherine Goetz family gave a memorial to go toward the purchase of
table cloths for the social hall; in 1996, Marge Fiedler made three different
sets of center pieces for the tables, which are used during different seasons.

The group still meets on the first Weds., of  each month. There are 42 active
members and many absentee and honorary members. Officers are President, Betty
Sandmeier, Vice President, Viola Goetz, Secretary, Gloria Zimmerman, and
Treasurer, Pam Seyer.

ALTAR GUILD
The Altar Guild of St. Paul Lutheran Church started in Jan. 1960, under the
leadership of Pastor Arthur Schmitt. There were 22 charter members; three are
still members and they are Lila Bieber, Lorraine Fiechtner, and Hilda Stangl.
The first officers were President, Mrs. Arthur Schmitt, Vice President, Mrs.
John Zeller, and Secretary/Treasurer, Mrs. Henry H. Wolf.

Present officers are President Lorraine Fiechtner, Vice President Betty
Schnaible, and Secretary-Treasurer Florence Noess. Other members are Lila
Bieber, Irene Fiedler, Violet Goetz, Anna Mueller, Clara Nehlich, Loretta
Schnaible, Magdalena Schreter, Dorothy Schneider, and Hilda Stangl.

The Altar Guild members take care of the chancel area. They set up and help with
the Communion ware, take care of the flowers and candles, put up the Christmas
window decorations, the Advent wreath, and the porcelain Nativity Set on the
inside.

Over the years, they have taken care of the choir robes. They have made or
purchased Christmas tree skirts, Chrismons for the trees, and purchased lights
for the tree. Other purchases have been a pall, pottery vases, usher badges,
anchor bar for the altar to hold the linens, paraments for different seasons of
the church, guest books, banners, baptism napkins, pacifer cloths, and Communion
ware bags. The Altar Guild usually buys the wine and wafers for Communion.
Members have taken care of the outside flowers and evergreens.

The church janitor, Mrs. Bob Goetz, now takes care of the altar linens by
laundering them, and changes the paraments as needed for the church year.

Many changes have taken place over the years, but the purpose of the Altar Guild
is still to beautify the services and keep everything in order. The women have a
free-will offering at each meeting, to help purchase what is needed. Many
Memorial gifts have also been given, which helps to buy the flowers.

Rev. George Kirchdoerfer
In 1923, Rev. George Kirchdoerfer of the Java St. Paul Lutheran Church (St.
Paul's, at that time) wrote an article in the Java Herald. In it, he wrote about
the little church three miles north of Java. When he came to Java, he wrote,
there was a small parsonage consisting of two rooms. One was used for the
kitchen and the other for parlor, study room, bedroom, etc. He was a single man
then and had plenty of room and was satisfied. In 1903, the parochy sold the old
parsonage and built a new one, which was again enlarged in 1915 by the addition
of a second story.

He wrote that in 1902, all the people were poor but they were satisfied and
happy, the minister also. He had to drive nearly every day and felt very proud
as he drove over the prairies of his adopted country. Once, when he drove to his
congregation in the country, he could not find the right road and got lost.
After an hours' ride, he saw a little town ahead of him but did not know the
town. A little later, he found that this town was Java and that he had made a
round trip. Although he got lost at times during a snowstorm, he always managed
to find his way home. He wrote that he had never once missed a service on
account of sickness.

In 1900 to 1923, Rev. Kirchdoerfer had baptized 913 children, performed 259
marriages, buried 233 people, and confirmed 525 boys and girls.


                   READING, 'RITING, & 'RITHMATIC

THE COUNTRY SCHOOL
Children were taught at home during the homesteading days. Sometimes beginner's
books were brought with the household goods, sometimes the family Bible was
used. A slab of smoothed wood was used as a slate and a piece of charred wood
served as pencils. Although people living near a town were able to purchase
slates and pencils, most had to make do with what they had.

As the area grew, the families got together to hold school in a home, or they
built a small structure for a school, "four walls with the future inside it."
Children walked to the school, often by the age of four and up to age 18, or
with a wagon, buggy, or on  horseback.

Regular schools were established after the organization of districts, and a
County Superintendent was elected. There were no grades in the early years; a
student was in the First Reader, Second Reader, Third Reader, and so on. When a
pupil completed the Eighth Reader, he/she could attend an "Institute" and write
an exam to receive a "second grade" certificate. Some were fortunate to attend a
college, where they would receive the "first grade" certificate.

Many of the rural schools held three-month terms in the fall, followed by three
months in the spring. In many instances, there would be a different teacher for
each term. With the interruptions of terms, the teachers had to be conscientious
and hard working, instructing the pupils to read and write, and often, to speak
the English language.

Northern Normal Industrial School held a six-week teachers training course.
After completing this, the prospective teacher would write a state exam and
receive a teachers certificate before they got a contract. They rode horseback
to school, round trip, and during bad weather, would board with families. Wages
were so small that many teachers lived with their students' families, each
family taking a turn. The homes were small and crowded, and the teacher had no
privacy.

The rural schoolteacher was faced with a big job, where the position of janitor
was included in the regular work. The one-room building contained a coal-burning
stove with a jacket around it, which caused the heat to circulate. The teacher
was responsible for starting the fire, washing off the black boards, sweeping
the floors, along with other "chores" as needed. Extra buildings included two
outhouses, and a barn for the horses. Pupils brought their own lunches, usually
in a gallon syrup pail, and water. There were two 15-minute recesses and an hour
for lunch, at noon. Games were played, such as Fox and Geese, London Bridge,
Pom-pom-pull-away, prisoner's base and ball. The 3 R's were taught out of books
sent out by the County Superintendent of Schools, such as the Dick and Jane
Series and the Strayer-Upton math books.

As times improved, wages were increased and living conditions were better. Good
schoolhouses were built with more adequate heating systems. By the Thirties, WPA
workers replaced many of the buildings, and most schools were held for 9 months,
with a good course of study.

Teachers became scarce during World War II, and in many instances wages went up
to $125 a month. This situation continued for a few years, until grain and stock
prices fell. Terms were cut to 8 months during the Depression and many teachers
taught for $45 a month.

There were 24 districts in Walworth County in the heyday, each district
supporting one or more schools. As consolidation of rural schools with the
larger city schools took place, the rural districts faded away. Some of the
districts were Blue Blanket, Glenn, Swan Creek, Swan Lake, Hiddenwood, Spring
Valley, Highland, Adams, Spring Lake, Ryan and Theodore. Schools mentioned in
these districts are Washington, East Swan Creek, West and East Spring Valley,
Spring Lake, Sunnyside, East and West Ryan, and Irving. The East Spring Valley
School was located near the Henry Mueller farm and was later moved along the
road now known as Highway 12, and the West Spring Lake School was moved to the
Kalman Kormendy farm. The Glenn School was used for church services, where Rev.
George Kirchdoerfer held many services. It was known as the Perman School and
was later sold to the Ervin Muellers and moved to their farm. In 1927, Lauretta
Clifford and Lena Mertz taught in the Spring Valley District; Olive Overby,
Christine Carlson, Edward Kunz and Natholia Kindsfater taught in the Spring Lake
District; Mary Wolf, Mrs. Alice Noble and Rose Wolf were teachers in the
Highland District; Mrs. Grace Noble taught in the Ryan District; Mrs. Florence
Moser and Bessie Lawrence taught in the Adams District; and Donald Ingalls
taught in the Glenn District.

(Photo:) The Kundert School. That's the Town Board president in front!

Highland District #16, organized in June 1889, included Holmes, Sunshine, Edison
and Hawthorne schools. The 1906 graduating class consisted of Elizabeth, Emma
and Linda Boehler, Carl and Jacob Flemmer, Henry, Jacob and Katherine Haux,
Philip Jesser, Ed and Gottlieb Hirsch, August, John, Katherine, Mary and Rosie
Lutz, Jacob, Matilda, and Theresa Ochszner, Barbara, John and Olga Schlepp,
Gottlieb and Magdalena Schock, Doradena, Edward and John Wolf. Frances W. Cape
was the teacher. At some time, a vote was taken to close Highland and move the
students to school in Java. The people voted No; shortly thereafter, the school
building burned down. Blue Blanket District #8, organized in Mar. 1885, included
Lindberg, Monroe, Blue Blanket and Mark Twain schools.

Other rural schools mentioned are Ackerman,  Alamo, Bender, Bertsch, Blessing,
Buckenberger, Delker, Edison, Erbe, Garfield, Heizer, Helms, Hindemith/Norbeck,
Irving, Kundert, and Meyer. Some of the rural teachers were Lila Arndt, Delores
Bauer, Frances Bender, Hilda Bender, Delila Aman Biel, Lieta Boehler Haux,
Gerhardt and Eileen Fiedler, Olive Frazier, Agnes Gehrki Manders, Sam Goehring,
Robert and Frieda (Goetz) Haux, Myrtle Green, Oscar Kapfenstein, Gus Kundert,
Aaron and Ruth Lakeman, Viola Mittleider, Gerald Pfitzer, Ethel Ryan, Helen
Ryan, Gloria Schlepp, Dean Schnaible, Freida Schuh, Loretta Schuh, DeLila
Stiegelmeier Schneider, Helen Witlock, Lois Wolf and Hazel Zeller.

THE JAVA PUBLIC SCHOOL
Most of the records of the first years of the school's history have been lost or
misplaced. The school history begins in 1901, when the first term was held in a
building that had been moved from south of town. There were 23 registered
students and the first teacher was Mrs. Philip Noble, who was paid $35 a month.

Among the first students were Arie Cook, Alice Corson, Grace Corson, Emma
Fiechtner, Bertha Hall, Elizabeth Hughes, Ethel Sammons, Elsie Sorwied, Archie
Stewart, and Ida and Nettie Stoller. The pupils ranged in age from five to
eighteen years. James Corson, Philip Noble and Volney Varnum were on the Board
of Education.

(Photo:) Java Schoolhouse 1903 to 1921

In 1903, a two-story frame building was built two blocks east of Main street,
where it remained until 1921. O.I. O'Reilley taught the advanced grades and
Lisle Pratton, the primary grades. In 1907, more classroom space was required,
so an addition was built to the south side of the old structure. Two years of
high school were added. Freeman Chute was the principal. There were only three
high school students, Elizabeth Hughes, Bertha Hall and Freda Hein. In 1909,
Wendell Nies was Superintendent (he married Freda Hein in 1914); Helen B. Ryan
(Mrs. Joseph Zarka) completed the courses in that year. Henry Cook and Vina
Varnum completed the high school courses in 1914. George Hicks and Philip Noble
were sophomores and Frances Stangl (Mrs. Raymond Lee) a freshman. Betty Hughes,
teacher, also taught the seventh and eighth grades. In 1919, with A.G. Savage as
principal, Fritz Clement was listed as the first graduate of Java High School.

The enrollment of the school continued to increase and, in 1920, the school was
remodeled. Later, in an effort to meet the growing demand for more space, a
small two-room structure was put up and used for the primary classes. The 1903
building was becoming a fire hazard, and school superintendent E.C. Giffen was
one of the leading promoters for the construction of a new building. The people
of Java began to make plans for the erection of a new, fireproof building, and
on Mar. 29, 1921, the issuance of bonds in the amount of $60,000 was approved
for construction of a new brick building. When the votes were counted on the
issue to proceed with the bonds, 232 Java residents had voted, with 170 in favor
of the new school, and 62 against. The community voted in Apr. 1921, on two
locations for the school, with 97 favoring the south edge of Main Street, and 31
voting for a site north of the railroad tracks.

Fred R. Comb Co. was the contractor for construction ($49,175), and A.B.
Donaldson for plumbing and heating ($12,385). Carl W. Clement did the electrical
work. The new building was completed in Dec. of 1921 and was 126' long, 66'
wide, with a full basement and two stories. The building housed a gymnasium,
which was one of the larger ones in the area at that time and had balcony
seating for about 200 people. A stage with a dressing room on each side was
built on the opposite side. Classes were moved to the new building in Jan. 1922,
and school opened on Sept. 11, with 48 high school students and 9 instructors,
including Superintendent Giffen. The old wooden school building was purchased
and demolished in 1923, parts of it used in construction of barns, hog houses,
etc.

In the fall of 1961, Java approved a bond issue for $160,000 for the completion
of a new 720-seat school auditorium and other improvements, which included
facilities for band and other musical events.

High school enrollment dropped to 27 in the 1984-85 school year, less than the
state requirement of 35 for continued state aid. On Oct. 24, 1984 a meeting was
held to discuss the school's options to continue operation by raising taxes,
contract out high school students to neighboring schools, or close the school
and merge with other districts. A mailing to the district voters showed that 147
wanted the school kept open, 97 wanted the upper grades contracted with the
grade school kept open, and 21 wanted the school closed.

With the enrollment below the state minimum of 35, $85,000 in state aid would no
longer be available to the district. Cost to taxpayers and adequacy of the
curriculum were the primary questions raised. An election was held Jan. 22, 1985
to decide whether to continue operating the high school, or to contract the
upper four grades to other schools. Out of 417 registered voters in the
district, 335 voted, with 183 favoring closing the high school, 152 favoring
continuing. The vote brought about the closing of the high school on July 1,
1985, with the students going to neighboring schools on contract, and the grade
school continuing to operate.

(Photo:) Unsigned

The final graduation was held May 18, 1985, with Gust Kundert, JHS graduate, as
speaker. Final day for students of Java High School was May 23. At that time 13
students planned to go to Selby, 11 to Bowdle and two to Eureka. In the 65 plus
years of existence, there were over 900 graduates of Java High School; those of
the last graduating class were Kevin Ackerman, Patricia Aman, Diane Carlson, Jon
Dobson, Doug Frank, Traci Sandmeier, Sandy Schreter and Charlene Wolff. There
were six high school instructors in the final year.

The Java School District was reorganized into the Selby Area School District on
July 1, 1990. Falling enrollment brought about the vote for reorganization of
the Selby, Glenham and Java School Districts. Members of the last eighth grade
class to graduate from Java were Tricia Bieber, Tina Boschee, Brian Gill, Jesse
Miklos,  Julie Raba, Chris Rivett and Don Ruzsa.

Java Public School Superintendents or administrators, and yearly events follow:

John Bibelheimer, 1904.

Freeman Chute, Principal, 1907.

Wendell Nies, 1909. Elva Dye, head teacher, assumed administrator duties to
1910.

Erma C. Brown, head teacher, 1910-11.

E.H. Noteboom, 1914-15, Co-Superintendent. Katherine Cook taught at Wolff School
NE of Java. [Walworth County had 2,198 children between the ages of 6 and 20,
and 1,490, or 67.8% of them attended school.]

There were no recorded Superintendents in 1915-1919. Night school was offered in
1919-20, ages 16-21 could attend; E.C. Giffen was the teacher.

E.C. Giffen, 1920-22, was the originator of the Play Day activities for grade
children and was responsible for the first boys' and girls' basketball teams. He
later became state superintendent of public instruction. Java was placed on a
three-year accredited list, and Latin was taught, in 1920. 1921 high school
students published a newspaper, "High School Pep", done in hand set type.
Students did the writing and typesetting at the schoolhouse. The four-page
bi-weekly paper included news stories, advertising, and an occasional photo. The
first music performances, instrumental solos, vocal solos, duets and trios, were
held in the school in 1922; Emma Oswald was music director.

E.H. Halverson, 1923-24. Miss Marie Banse (Hicks) and M.C. Munson were members
of the high school staff.

M.C. Munson, 1925-26. Typing was introduced into the classroom, when four
typewriters were purchased.

G.B. Shimmon, 1926-27-28. During his tenure much work was done in landscaping of
the school grounds. The Java Maroons were admitted to the Hickory Stick
Basketball Conference and won their first Hickory Stick conference title under
the tutelage of Bert Popowski; the girls' team resumed their winning ways again.

A.E. Sullivan, 1929-30-31. It was during his first year that Java High School
students participated in the dedication ceremonies at Mobridge for the famous
Indian Bird Woman, Sakajawea and historical data of the school was sealed in a
steel box. In 1929 an all-school program replaced the usual carnival. Among
those taking part were Vivian Bauer, Ervin Kunz, Gust Kundert, Leota Krause,
Arend Lakeman and Walter Wolf. Directors were Erna Kunz, Ida Roberts and A.E.
Sullivan. In 1930 the Java Maroons won their first and only district title by
defeating Selby 15-14. Frank Heezen was the coach. In the spring of 1930 the
first speaking contest and debates were held in the school. Merton Bender went
to the state extemporaneous speaking contest at Vermillion, after winning the
district event. Debaters included Gust Kundert and Arend Lakeman. Plays and
operettas were also presented, with the entire school taking part in some of the
programs. In 1931 the janitor's job at the school became so popular that there
were 15 applicants for the job. Bids ranged from $50 to $80 a month and Fred
Pregitzer was the lucky man at $70.

Frank Heezen, 1932-1936. In 1933 Coach Roy Stewart organized the first "J" Club.
Members included those lettering in major athletics, declam winners,
cheerleaders and editor of the Maroon and Gold News. The 13 charter members were
Edgar Aman, Arthur Boehler, Ben Buckenberger, Herbert Fiechtner, Ida Klein,
Fritz Krause, Otto Kundert, Adeline Lutz, Alvin Oltmans, Herbert Sauer, Walter
Sauer, Harold Spiry, and Lydia Wolf.

Ephraim Renz, 1937-38. High school enrollment was 102, up from 92 the previous
year; 45 were staying in the dormitories. In 1938 the first annual, "The Pilot",
was published. In the early years, the annuals were a "home job" that consisted
of mimeographed pages with the individual photos glued in place. Aaron Wagner
was editor-in-chief of that first effort. In later years, the annual became a
printed hard cover bound book, and renamed "The Panther".

Dale Summers, 1939-43, left the teaching profession to become a lieutenant in
the U.S. Navy. In 1939 students were charged $1.75 per week for board and room
to stay in the dormitories. Enrollment was 92 in high school, with a good
percentage being tuition students. There were 17 girls and 35 boys staying in
the dormitories. In Dec. 1939 Rueben Wolf won two state titles, one in the WNAX
Radio Essay contest at Yankton, and taking first in the dramatic division of the
state declamation league contest at Howard. In 1940 Della Bauer was selected as
one of six students in the state to read an essay on WNAX Radio, Yankton. Also
in 1940, the Java music department received a trophy awarded by the State High
School Music Assn., for groups receiving a superior rating in Mobridge contest.
In May that year four boys in the music department went to St. Paul, MN, to
compete in the National Regional Music Contest, as a quartet. They were Ernest
Flemmer, Emanuel Stickel, and Ervin and Roman Walz. Their director was Leonard
Stehr. 103 students were enrolled in high school in the fall of 1942, probably a
record. That year the school was selected as the local site for signing up for
gas and other ration during World War II. Basic rationing limited driving to 240
miles a month, and speed limit was 35 mph. School time was also changed to "war
time" hours, 10 a.m. to 12 noon, and 1:15 p.m. to 4:15 p.m. In Oct. 1942, I.R.
Krause held a meeting about starting a school band; 40 students were interested.

Harold F. Spiry (JHS Class of 1933), 1944-1952. There were 76 students in high
school and 82 in the grades. In 1946 the area to the west of the school building
was improved and made into a city park. That year the school session opened
Sept. 3, although there was talk of postponing the school opening because of a
statewide polio epidemic. In May of 1948, Marilyn Jacobs was named Duchess at
Northern Day at Aberdeen, selected from 51 contestants. The following year
Kenneth Goetz and Kathleen Schlepp were chosen Duke and Duchess at Northern,
winning in a field of 47 high schools competing. Bonita Moser and Archie Aman
were chosen as the Duke and Duchess candidates for 1952, to represent Java at
Northern Day in Aberdeen. Marie Doerr and Jeanne Boehler attended the Duchess.
Gilbert Schlepp was part-time band instructor. Under his direction, many
Division I ratings were earned at music contests. During the 1940's, the school
owned one bus that was used to transport students to out-of-town sporting
events; driver, Gehbardt Pfitzer.

H.A. Peterson, 1953-54. A "pep band" was organized in 1953 under full time
director Clark E. Newman.

Harold Larson, 1955-56.

D.J. Leighty, 1957-58.

Vern Cowley, 1958-61, superintendent and coach in 1958; during his second term,
Java school reorganization was approved by a 303-75 vote, and areas to the
south, and to the north in Campbell County, became a part of the Java school
system. A bus route was started north of Java in 1958, which brought students to
school. In the 1960's, a complete route was begun to gather farm students for
school in town. Cowley gave up coaching in 1960 and devoted his time to school
administration, while Kenneth Nesland took over the coaching duties.

Charles Singh, 1961-63. The Band Mothers bought new uniforms in 1962, which were
used by the band at Gypsy Day in Aberdeen, and for other events. Four school
buses were purchased at a cost of about $6,000 in 1962.

Gerald Nelson, 1963-65. The new auditorium was dedicated Jan. 26, 1964. Eight-
week session kindergarten was operated for a number of years in the mid 1960's.
Classes were held in the school and for a time, in St. Paul Lutheran Church.
Gloria (Schlepp) Zimmerman and Irene Goetz were teachers during that time.

N.M. Fisher, 1965, stayed for only one term.

Stanley B. Raabe, 1966-75. Java High School Band participated in the largest and
most colorful parade in the history of Gypsy Days. They won top honors in Class
C field and in parade competition. In 1974, the Java music groups, band, mixed
chorus, and boys and girls glee clubs all took Division I ratings. Steve Serr
was the band director and Harold Spiry directed the vocal groups. Earlier that
year, students earned 11 Division I ratings for solos and small ensembles.

Dean Stryker, 1976-77.

Orville Creighton, 1978-80. A kindergarten class was organized, authorized in
Mar. 1980. That first year, a five-week session was held with Betty (Marvin)
Pfitzer as teacher. On Mar. 27, 1978, Eileen (Reuben) Schmierer was presented
with a plaque from the PTO for 30 years of teaching and serving as elementary
principal in the school system. In 1978, Java was represented for the first time
in All State Chorus. Attending were Nancy Schreter, Charlene Goetz, Gavin Walz
and Scott Sauer. In 1979, Charlene Goetz, Bonnie Stangl, Donovan Stefanich and
Scott Sauer attended All State Chorus. Richard Goetz and Bryan Walz were
nominated to the 1980 McDonald's All-American High School Band.

B.J. Wasko, 1981-1990. Janette Grenz taught the kindergarten class of nine
pupils in 1982. Two Commodore 64 computers were purchased. In 1983, a mini-bus
was added to the system to transport football players to practice at Bowdle.
Joan O'Toole was the 1984 kindergarten teacher and in 1985, kindergarten was
taught for a full semester for the first time with a certified teacher, who was
Marie Hirning of Eureka. Transportation dropped to three routes: Jerome Lee's
route had 19 students and traveled about 90 miles a day; Dean Moser, captain of
School Transportation, had 22 students and drove about 96 miles; Tom Mikos had
the shortest trip with 14 students on the north route, traveling about 60 miles
a day. The Java High School Band raised $5,000 and attended the three-day World
of Music Festival at Edina, MN. They brought home a trophy and plaque. Eileen
Schmierer retired at the end of the 1985 school term.
