School Music
Gilbert Schlepp, a JHS graduate, served as part-time band instructor in the
1950's, winning many Division I ratings at music contests.

A new band was organized in the 1952-54 school year, with Clark E. Newman as
director. High school and elementary students performed in the band; the uniform
was a gold sweater and black pants. It was a great moment of pride when a band
member would earn a "letter" to be placed on their sweater! Quartets, soloists,
ensembles and accompanists performed at music contests, which included marching
in the Gypsy Day parade. Mrs. Marguerite Newman often drove the younger band
members to the contests, singing all the way.

In 1974, Java music groups all took Division I ratings in band, mixed chorus,
girls glee club, and boys glee club. Band director was Steve Serr and vocal
director Harold Spiry. Earlier that year, students earned 11 Division I ratings
for solos and small ensembles.

(Photo:) Java School Band 1953-54. Clark Newman, director, is standing at the
         back in the middle

In 1975 soloists and groups, including the band, earned 15 Division I ratings.
Colleen Frank was chosen for All State Band in 1975 and 1976.

In 1978 Java was represented for the first time in All State Chorus. Attending
were Nancy Schreter, Charlene Goetz, Gavin Walz and Scott Sauer. In 1979
Charlene Goetz, Bonnie Stangl, Donovan Stefanich and Scott Sauer went to All
State Chorus.

As its final project in 1985, the Java High School Band raised about $5,000 and
attended the three-day "World of Music" Festivals at Edina, MN. They brought
home a trophy and plaque. Members were Kristi Aberle, Patricia Aman, Lynelle
Bieber, Mark Bieber, Heidi Fiedler, Lisa Fiedler, Doug Frank, Jeff Helm, Jimmy
Krause, Wendy Lutz, Vicki Miller, Danette Rau, Traci Sandmeier, Kim Sauer, Cindy
Schneider, Paul Schreter, Sandy Schreter, Tim Schreter, Lynette Stefanich, Kim
Wasko, Scott Witlock, Nolan Walz, Chad Wolf, Charlene Wolf, David Wolf, and
Sandy Wolf, and Mrs. Nanette Jordan, director.

School Sports
Before the new building was completed in 1921, boys' and girls' basketball games
were played in the old Grand Theatre building, where the first indoor boys' and
girls' basketball teams were born. Games were often followed by a dance or
lunch. A group of high school girls formed a club, "We Seven", and served lunch
to the ball players. Fritz Clement coached the first boys' team and Genevieve
Fargen of Flandreau coached the first girls' team. The teams played towns as far
away as Cresbard and Faulkton. First games played in the new gym were Saturday,
Jan. 22, 1922, when the boys' and girls' teams took on Cresbard.

The girls' team was excellent. Typical was their win over Faulkton, 36-2. The
team went undefeated for many years, winning 71 of 73 games played, for a total
of 1846 points against their opponents' 406.

In 1922 and 1924, the Java High School Girls Basketball Team won the State
Championship. In 1922 they were challenged by a Carthage team and played the
game at Aberdeen Normal (NSU), winning 32-2. In 1924, they entered the state
girls tournament at Mitchell, breezed through Mt. Vernon, Chamberlain,
Harrisburg and Plankinton. They met Lake Andes in the finals, Java winning 20-16
in overtime. Playing on the Championship team were Hildegarde Aman, Lieta
Boehler, Eunice Campbell, Gretchen Clement, Tillie Dufloth, Agnes Gehrki, Mary
Krause, Erna Kunz, Alma Merkel, and Elizabeth Noble. Their coach was Helen
Hanson.

(Photo:) South Dakota State Champions 1924. Back: Eunice Campbell, Lieta
         Boehler, Agnes Gherki, Erna Kunz, Alma Merkel. Mid: Coach Helen Hanson,
         Tillie Dufloth, Mr. Halverson. Front: Toots Noble, Gretchen Clement,
         Hildegard Aman, Mary Krause

Again in 1926-27, the girls' squad had an incredible season with 13 wins and no
losses, with a total of 499 points to their opponents' 75! A noteworthy game was
that with Roscoe, Java scored 73 and Roscoe, 0. Bert Popowski coached the team
consisting of Lydia (Lieta) Boehler as Captain, Frieda Blinderman, Bessie Ewald,
Emma Hartman, Elizabeth Krause, Geraldine Krause, Annette Spiry, Nettie Spiry,
and Emma Stangl.


To the Java High School Girls' Basketball Team
(J.W. Stout, Stickney, South Dakota)

Hail to thee! Girls' Basketball team of Java!
How I rejoice that so well you have done!
Thirteen straight games and each one a victory;
Scoring a ration of seven to one.
Six splendid seasons your team undefeated,
You've made the seventh one better than all;
Not even "close" is your nearest opponent,
You've showed them all how to play basketball.

Led by Miss Boehler, the "Last of Mohicans,"
One of the very best guards in the state
Your march has been a succession of triumphs
Truly she captained a team just as great,
Miss Bessie Ewald has been her side partner
And has well copied her prowess and skill;
Often they've kept their opponents from scoring,
Helping their teammates climbing the hill.

Those Spiry girls surely do well at center;
Eyes that can see and hands quick to serve;
Hartman and Blinderman play fine at forward;
Making their shots "counters" that seldom swerve.
Here's to the substitutes able and willing,
Krause's at forward and Stangl at guard;
Not for a moment, did one of them falter,
What tho the playing was ever so hard.

What of the coach who has taught them such playing
Meet Bert Popowski-but that's not enough
He is a player himself with a record
I'll "bet my hat" that boy "knows his stuff."
Play on Fair Java and may you keep winning
And, when they mention the teams of real worth
To, from the east or the west they may hail them
I'll speak for JAVA, the "STAR OF THE NORTH!"

(NOTE: We refer to Miss Boehler as the "Last of
Mohicans" because she is the last of that splendid little
team that "won out grandly at the finish" of the Mitchell
tourney of 1924.)

Girls' basketball was discontinued in the mid 1930's because the state thought
it was too strenuous for them! It was resumed in 1975, with play in the
Yellowstone Trail Conference and participation in a statewide organization. In
1979, the girls' team was conference co-champions. In 1983, the Java Panthers
girls' basketball team was the YTC Champion, with Mark Schumacher as coach. The
championship team consisted of Patricia Aman, Lori Biel, Berta Carroll, Heidi
Fiedler, Lisa Fiedler, Wendy Lutz, Traci Sandmeier, Sandy Schreter, Vicky
Schreter, and Kim Wasco. Student manager was Charlene Wolf; cheerleaders were
Dinal Carlson, Wendy Hofer, Vickie Miller, Cindy Schneider, and Missy Seibel.

(Photo:) The Ever-Victorious 1926-27 Squad. Back: Bessie Ewald, Annette Spiry,
         Emma Hartman, Frieda Blinderman, Emma Stangl. Front: Sup't. George
         Shimmon, Geraldie Krause, Captain Lydia (Lieta) Boehler, Elizabeth
         Krause, and Coach Bert Popowski

The boys finally had a winning basketball team in 1930, winning the district
tournament and placing second in the regional. This was never repeated in the
school's history. Frank Heezen was the coach of the winning team, which
consisted of Art Boehler, Emil Boehler, Leon Kast, Herbert Kirchdoerfer, Erin
Kunz, Edward Schlepp, Albert Wolf, and Walt B. Wolf.

In 1957, the boys won the YTC tournament for the first time. They won the
conference championship in 1969, and placed second in the conference and
district tournaments.

The Java Panthers boys' basketball team won the title of YTC Champions in 1970.
Playing on the winning team, coached by Dan Besonan, were Steve Biel, Tom
Goehring, Myron Grenz, Dwight Helm, Steve Kary, Terry Kary, Randy Pfitzer,
Marlow Schaffer, Rodney Schaffer, Doug Schlepp, Jerry Schneider, and Shawn Walz.
Student managers were Clyde Frank and Brad Zimmerman. Doug Schlepp was chosen as
the first man on the second squad of the class "B" All State team.

In 1974, the Panthers took the YTC tournament championship in a double overtime
from Bowdle. Bill Reidburn was the coach. In 1976 and 1977 season, the Panthers
were runners-up in the YTC tournament.

Sometime in 1912-1913, a football team was organized, but the surrounding
schools had no teams with which to compete. Five football games were played in
1948, the first actual year of football. Coach Lee Bell saw his team win only
one game that year, but in the following year, they were undefeated, winning the
6-man Hiddenwood Football Conference Championship with six wins and no losses.
On the first football team were Archie Aman, Earl Anderson, LeRoy Biel, Elmer
Boschee, Curtis Frank, Kenny Goetz, Marlin Hochstetter, Marvin Hochstetter,
Richard Kary, Adrian Kast, Jerald Pfitzer, Robert Pfitzer, Wallace Spiry and
Calvin Wolff.

In 1974, the Panthers, now a 9-man team, took the YTC title with an undefeated
season. They won their second YTC title with an 8-0 season in 1976. Because of
declining enrollment, football was dropped in 1979, resumed in 1980, when they
played a 6-game schedule in a 6-man team. This continued in 1981, and football
discontinued for the 1982 season. Java joined Bowdle to play football in 1983
and 1984.

(Photo:) 1930 District Champions. Back: Sup't. Sullivan, Emil Boehler, Art
         Boehler, Edward Schlepp, Herbert Kirchdoerfer, Coach Frank Heezen.
         Front: Ervin Kunz, Albert Wolf, Leon Kast, and Walt B. Wolf

In 1974, Pat Wolff went to the state track tournament and took second place in
low hurdles. In 1975, five boys went to the state track meet, after winning the
YTC and the regional meets. Dan Biel, Darrell Grenz, Glenn Neumiller, Doug
Schneider, and Pat Wolff attended. Valerie Jacobs, Kathy Ketterling, Peg
Ketterling and Chloe Krause also went to the state meet and placed fourth in the
state. Mark Melcher was an outstanding track star from Java High, attending the
State Track Meet three times and taking first place at the State "B" Cross
Country Track Meet in 1977 and 1978. In 1979, Richard Fiedler won the state meet
at Chamberlain, making 22 out of 25 free throws. He was 12 years old!

Beyond the 3 R's
Dormitories were started in 1934 to bring students from outside the city area.
The girls' dorm was in the Campbell Hotel on the east side of Main Street, and
the boys were in a room on the first floor on the west side of the school
building. There were 16 boys and 12 girls in the dorms in the first year. Boys
were housed in the Gershin home on Main Street, until the room in the school
building was finished. Dormitory cooks were secured from the relief rolls in
Java. The dorms were closed in 1944.

Carnivals were held in the old school gymnasium. Each high school class selected
a Queen and Marshall candidate prior to the carnival. Ballot boxes for the
candidates were placed at a decorated booth, and the student body would place
their votes in these. The winning candidates were crowned at a separate
ceremony. The high school students would set up numerous fun booths, a favorite
of the children being the Fish Pond, where all sorts of prizes could be
"caught." Many an allowance was spent on the tickets to play the games at each
booth.

A high school carnival was held in March of 1923, raising $216. In April of
1923, while the old school building was being torn down, plans were being made
to build a tennis court at the new school site. In connection with the schools
close that year, the freshman class held a wiener roast at Haux's grove, with
faculty members as their guests. The school picnic was held at Hiddenwood Creek.
Baccalaureate, Senior Class Night, a gymnastic exhibition and Commencement were
also held in the closing days.

Homecoming royalty was selected from the Senior Class and would reign over the
Homecoming activities in the fall. Coronation was held in the school gymnasium
after a program, followed by the lighting of a bonfire. Whitewashing of the
streets would take place after the bonfire and in the morning of the next day, a
parade would be held. There were decorated floats, the school band and horses in
the parade; all members of the student body of Java High School would
participate. The last Homecoming King and Queen were Doug Frank and Traci
Sandmeier, who are now married. Tom Goehring and Barb Schnaible were Homecoming
King and Queen in 1972, and they are also married.

The Sweetheart Ball, held around Feb. 14, began in 1968, and became a Java High
School tradition. The sophomore class planned and hosted the event. Sweetheart
Royalty included:

OAHE SPECIAL EDUCATION COOPERATIVE
The Oahe Special Education Cooperative service unit is located in north-central
SD and currently serves eight member school districts. All or large portions of
Campbell, Edmunds, McPherson, Potter, Walworth, and a small portion of Corson
Counties make up the present service area. The coop offices are located in Java,
which is centrally located based on the present membership.

For the past year, the total enrollment in the eight member districts was 1,645
students. During the past school year, the cooperative served 203 students in
the various special education programs. This number has been fairly constant for
the past several years.

At present, the Oahe Coop has 20 employees including 16 certified and 4 non-
certified people. The 15 certified staff members include the director, a school
psychologist, a pre-school coordinator, a deaf interpreter, seven special
education teachers, and five speech therapists. The four non-certified personnel
include the business manager, two pre-school aides, and a custodian.

A variety of services are currently provided to the member schools. Services
that are provided directly include pre-school disabled, special education
instruction, speech therapy instruction, and psychological evaluations. The coop
also coordinates physical therapy and occupational therapy services for the
members through Children's Care Hospital and School, based in Rapid City.

The Java Dormitories by George K. Nies, Class of '41
Certainly one of the most important eras in the history of the Java Schools was
during the years when the school provided dormitories.

During the years of the Great Depression you could get room and board for $1.75
a week. My father would give me $2.00, and I had the choice of spending 15 cents
for the Sunday night movies, and two quarter pound Power House chocolate bars,
or save the money for something else.

I would save the money and buy six sugary cinnamon rolls for 20 cents and then
sell them for a nickel to the rich kids. When I had saved enough I spent 80
cents for 24 bars of candy at the Eisenbeisz Pool Hall and sold the candy for a
nickel a bar to high school kids. They would interrupt the class I was in, and I
would go to the dorm in the high school and bring up candy. Even some of the
teachers bought candy from me.

The dormitories attracted all kinds of kids from outlying areas, Kluckmans and
Vojtas from Mound City, Simons and Wendlings from Hoven, Reuers, Boschees,
Permans and Bamesbergers from Lowry, Ballinskys from Akaska, Eberhardts from
Eureka, Alvin Schmidt from Herreid, and Schillings and Baers from Bowdle. I
don't think we had anyone from Selby.

Coaches Roy Stewart and Dutch Manders (who was dean of the boys' dormitory) were
in their heyday with a dozen basketball players all over six feet.

The boys stayed in the dorm at the school, but had to walk down to the girls'
dorm for all their meals. I think I got permanently bent by facing a howling
blizzard for the three-quarter mile walks before breakfast.

I remember Alfred Eberhardt, who was about half the size of his brother, Gideon,
wearing a long overcoat and farmer type overshoes. Alfred grabbed a hold of a
truck going north toward the girls' dorm one cold day and was almost airborne as
the truck picked up speed. Those big overshoes were making tracks twenty feet
apart as Alfred hung on for dear life.

Katie Pfaff and Frieda Sauer were the cooks, and I can still remember the taste
of the corn bread swimming in butter and syrup. And the best halupsie (pigs in
blankets) that I ever ate.

After lights out at night, the dorm became a war zone. If you didn't hide your
sneakers someone would pick them up and hurl them away in the dark.

World War II And The Java School by Freida Schuh
[Excerpts from the Java Herald, May 25, 1990]

The 1942-43 Java faculty was made up of seven women and one man. Mr. Dale
Summers served, not only as administrator, but he coached all sports and was
instructor for shop, and social sciences. There were close to 100 students in
high school and 70 in elementary grades. One janitor took care of the building
and grounds and also stoked the coal burning furnace. During the severest cold
weather, he often spent the night at the schoolhouse. Teachers and students went
home for lunch or brought their own. Teachers would take turns on noon duty.

The downstairs west rooms served as a boys' dormitory with Mr. Henry Hauck as
Dean. The girls' dormitory was on Main Street in the old hotel building. Mrs.
Martin Gehrki was their Dean. All dormitory students ate all meals in a dining
room in the girls' dorm. The cooks were Clara (Fiedler) Nehlich and Hulda (Wolf)
Pfitzer. They cooked and baked on wood burning ranges. Mr. Gottlieb Fiechtner
was the janitor and carried the fuel as well as groceries. The only convenience
was cold running water, which was heated on the stove for dishwashing. Imagine
cooking three meals a day, five days a week for 50 growing young people at a
salary of $45 a month!

The day after the U.S. declared war on Japan and Germany, in December 1941, all
tires were frozen. That meant that no dealer could sell or trade any of the
stock that they had on hand.

Commodity rationing began in the fall of 1942. In order to reach every family in
the area, the two-day registration for coupon books was held in the school gym
with teachers serving as registrars. The students enjoyed a two-day vacation. We
set up tables and were kept busy the first day. The second day we had time on
our hands and we would sing old songs while I.R. Krause, the band instructor,
played the piano. Sugar was the first food to be rationed and we soon learned
how to use honey and corn syrup instead. Other things that we rationed were
canned goods, soap products and shortening. In the spring of 1943, even shoes
were rationed. The shoe coupon was "B.29", and since one of the U.S. Air Force
bombing planes was the B29, we called our new shoes "bombers."

Ladies hose were very hard to get. We could wear uncomfortable cotton or rayon
"service weight." The rayon ones were easy to snag and would run if snagged.
Silk stockings were no longer available and nylons were just coming on the
market at over $3 a pair. They were very hard to find.

One of the teachers was from Moline, IL, and for Christmas, she gave each of the
teachers a pair of "full fashioned" nylons, in the latest color. Her mother ran
a ladies shop and had sent them to her to share with her fellow workers. She
also sent sugar coupons, which the teacher would share with us occasionally.

People were asked to gather and sell scrap metal to be used in making war
material. Old stoves, engines and parts of farm machinery were all loaded on
railroad cars and shipped out. The elementary grades had a contest with four
piles of old junk. The seventh and eighth grade room was ahead until the last
day, when one of the parents dumped two old cook stoves on the fifth and sixth
grade pile. The coveted prize was a picture for their room.

Pupils were also encouraged to buy savings stamps at 25 cents each. When the
savings stamp book was full, it could be traded in for a U.S. Savings Bond that
would be worth $25 in 10 years.

Mr. Summers, our wonderful, kind-hearted superintendent, was in the Army Reserve
and was called to active duty when school closed in the spring. One senior boy
quit school during the winter and "joined up." Several others enlisted or were
drafted soon after.

Senior Class Poem

We'll be leaving old Java High quite soon
We are going to leave it to stay.
The tie that binds will be cut in two
On Graduation Day.

We've lived and learned and played together
Now the time has come to part
May the mem'ry of these last few days,
Be imbedded in each heart.

We're graduates, no matter how
Our high school life was led
The important thing on the program now
Is facing the life ahead.

We've studied hard these last few years
We've tried to do our best
Each new task came as part of the game
To be carried on with zest.

Let us hope that we keep the good work up
In our struggles with toils and strife
And the spirit used in our school days gone
Be taken up in life.

Of the days of our high school life, old pals,
But few are remaining yet.
And when they are gone and we out into life
Let us hope that we don't forget.

By Leo A. Nies, Himself, Esquire
May, 1929

The Junior Class of Java High School presented The Death Bird, by Robert St.
Clair, in the High School Auditorium on Mar. 23, 1944 at 8 o'clock.

Synopsis of Scenes: The entire action takes place in the living room of the
suburban home of Nelson Thoreau.

Act I: An autumn night. Act II: Directly afterwards. Act III: The following
evening.

Stage Managers: Clifford Naasz, Wilmer Schuh, Merle Wolf. Prompters: Loraine
Delker, Elsie Hochstetter. Cast of Characters: Prof. Nelson Thoreau, a famous
magician, Harold Lutz; Margaret Caldwell, his fiance, Ardelle Jacobs; Phillip
Caldwell, her brother, Clayton Perman; Ada Reed, Thoreau's cousin, Patty Krause;
Elvira Reed, her niece, Velna Kulm; Swami Rama, an East Indian mystic, Calvin
Aman; Idabelle James, a female detective, LaRayne Job; Jack Stevens, a newspaper
reporter, Oscar Kapfenstein; Lili De Vere, a dancer, Ardella Schlepp; Boru, an
African servant, Herbert Geigle. Directed by Miss Van Buskirk. Entertainment:
Band, directed by Mr. Krause; Girls Trio, directed by Miss Raynes; Boys Quartet,
directed by Mrs. Hauck.


                   A Century of Java Organizations

Throughout the years of Java's existence, many organizations have been
established and later, discontinued. There is not a large amount of information
about the early organizations, yet they must be noted to give a complete history
about the town and the people living in and around Java over the past 100 years.

The Farmers' Alliance/Farmers' Union
Henry L. Loucks of Clear Lake organized the Farmers' Alliance in the fall of
1884. The Alliance engaged in many activities in the interests of its members.
It established farmers' elevators and other co-operative enterprises and
furnished fire and hail insurance to its members. Most of its business
undertakings were unsuccessful. In 1890, the Alliance organized a political
party known as the Populist or People's party. The election of 1896 finally
brought victory to the Farmers' Alliance in SD. The Populists joined with the
Democrats and dissatisfied Republicans and nominated Andrew E. Lee of Vermillion
for the governorship. In the national election the contest lay between William
McKinley of OH, the Republican candidate, and William J. Brian of NE, who was
nominated by both the Democrats and Populists. Bryan campaigned actively in SD
to help the Populist ticket. McKinley was elected. The election was a close one
in SD. Lee, the Populist candidate, won the governorship by a margin of 319
votes. Bryan carried the state over McKinley by about 200 votes. The Populists
succeeded also in winning most of the state offices and electing a majority of
the legislature. Interest was turned to the Farmers' Union after it was
organized in SD in 1916. The Farmers' Union was similar to the Farmers' Alliance
in many ways, also engaged in a number of co-operative enterprises whereby its
members could buy supplies at lower prices and ship their crops directly to
market. It promoted educational work among its members, and had a legislative
program designed to serve the needs of the entire state of SD. In the Diaries of
George W. Ryan, it was noted that he was a member of the Java Farmers' Alliance
and of the Java Farmers' Union. No other members were mentioned in his notes,
although he wrote about the meetings and his attendance.

Knights of the Maccabees
The Knights of the Maccabees was a fraternal insurance group of a type extremely
popular in the U.S. in the late 1800's, when many commercial insurance companies
refused insurance to all but the well heeled. In 1896, it had 182,000 members,
and included an extremely large number of farm workers. The Maccabees began in
Ontario in 1878 but completely reorganized, in MI, in 1881. Originally it
operated on an assessment basis: whenever a member died, each living member was
assessed 10 cents to go into a pot to provide the widow $1000. After
reorganization, it became much more sophisticated, collecting monthly
assessments based on payouts. By the 1890's it provided not only death benefits
but also sick benefits of $4 to $10 per week; total and permanent disability
benefits of $50, $200, or $300 annually (depending upon the size of the
assessment); $175 to $2000 for  loss of hands, eyes, feet, etc; funeral
benefits, and so on. Acceptable members were "All white persons of sound bodily
health and good moral character, socially acceptable, between 18 and 52 years of
age." Coal miners, "aeronauts" and other dangerous professions excluded.
Manufacturers, sellers, and "drinkers of likker" also excluded.

Groups like the Maccabees, Foresters, and Woodmen provided these benefits, along
with social meetings and other gatherings. Each had its own ritual legend. The
Maccabees had the story of Mattathias Maccabee and his sons, the leaders of the
Jewish revolt against Syrian desecration of the Temple.

C.K. Hair of Aberdeen, the state commander of KOTM assisted by J.V. Arnold and
L.E. Smith of Ipswich, Dr. Beil S.J. Hoffman, J.D. Stewart, John Bibelheimer,
Clarence and Ben Clark of Selby, instituted a new tent of that order in Java on
the night of Feb. 16, 1904. The following officers were installed: Post
Commander, G.P. Vick; Commander, C.F. Clement; Lt. Commander, Henry Thielen;
Recordkeeper, W.L. McCafferty; Finance-Keeper, Jacob Stoller; Chaplain, John
Hofmeyer; Physician, Sigmund Rosenthal; Sergeant, C. Huether; Master-at-Arms,
Joseph Bosch; 1st Master of Guards, Kurt Eisentraut; 2nd Master of Guards, C.C.
Gross; Sentinel, Daniel Reide; and Picket, J. Eberhart.

Java Commercial League
The businessmen of Java held a meeting on the night of Apr. 18, 1905, for the
purpose of organizing a businessmen's club. Every businessman became a member
except one. On Thurs. night, Apr. 20, 1905, a board of directors was chosen,
which included John Hofmeyer, W.C. Hicks, Fred Krause, Henry Thielen, and Christ
Wolf. On Apr. 29, another meeting was held at the C.F. Clement home and the
following officers were elected: President, Kurt Eisentraut; 1st Vice President,
H.J. Cook; 2nd Vice President, Jacob Stoller; Recording Secretary, Christ
Huether; Corresponding Secretary, C.F. Clement; and Treasurer, S. Rosenthal. The
club had a membership of 52, with meetings held the first Tuesday of every
month.

The Java Literary Society
During Feb. of 1906, a large number of Java citizens met at the schoolhouse to
organize a Literary Society. Kurt Eisentraut presided and C.F. Clement was
selected as secretary. The organization was effected and different committees
appointed. A debate was held upon the question "Resolved that ancient times are
greater than modern times." E.E. Reber, L. O'Reilly and E.W. Sackett took the
affirmative; A.I. O'Reilly, J. Stratton and Art McCafferty, the negative. The
negative was chosen with H.J. Cook, Mrs. H.L. Hughes and C.F. Clement as judges.

On Mar. 3, 1906, another meeting was held to adopt a constitution and by-laws,
allowing persons of good moral character, regardless of age, to become a member.
Each became a member upon paying a fee of 10 cents, and monthly dues of 10
cents. Sixty-five members enrolled at this time. A permanent organization was
effected by the election of the following officers: President C.F. Clement; vice
president, Arend Lakeman; secretary, L. Pratton; and treasurer, Mabel Smith. At
the Mar. 17th meeting, 16 more members were added, bringing the total to 81.

Lady Maccabees
The Ladies of the Maccabees were organized in mid-1800 and not at first
recognized by the Knights. Persistence paid off, and according to Albert C.
Stevens, (in 1896), "Its successful career has surprised many, even among its
well wishers, and has shown that women may safely be entrusted with the conduct
and management of many of the broader business affairs of life."

In Mar. of 1910, Hattie L. Westmeier of Bath came to Java to organize a local
lodge of the Lady Maccabees. She got 20 of the best ladies in town to join. Dr.
Beil of Selby examined them, and all passed examinations successfully.

The ladies were: Mary Anderson, Mary Beckman, Julia Borchert, Maria
Buckenberger, Beatrice Chittick, Kate Clement, Emma Click, Tina Gehrki, Lillian
Heerwald, Magdalena Hepper, Emily Hicks, Ethel Hicks, Ellen Hofmeyer, Grace
Lehmann, Myrtle Roberts, Ethel Ryan, Helen Ryan, Bertha Schlepp, Johanna Schott,
Nora Schott, Cora Stuart, and Ella Taylor. Mrs. S.N. Hereford of Aberdeen, Lady
State Commander, installed the following officers: Post Commander, Grace
Lehmann; Commander, Johanne Schott; Lt. Commander, Tina Gehrki; Record Keeper,
Emily Hicks; Finance Auditor, Kate Clement; Chaplain, Julia Borchert; Sergeant,
Nora Schott; Mistress-at-Arms, Mary Beckman; Sentinel, Ella Taylor; Picket,
Ellen Hofmeyer; Capt. of the Guards, Myrtle Roberts; Platoon No. 1, Ethel Hicks;
Platoon No. 2, Lillian Heerwald; Pianist, Bertha Schlepp.

Chatauqua Reading Circle
Sometime during Sept. 1911, a number of ladies organized a Chatauqua Reading
Circle: Mrs. R.M. Hennings, president; Mrs. E.B. Adams, vice president; and Miss
Bernice Gordon, secretary. Nothing more is known about this club.

Masonic Lodge
Local Masons tried to organize a lodge at Java as far back as 1908. Several
previous attempts to organize a lodge were made, but always without success. In
Apr. of 1913, the local Masons rented the Helm Hall and had it remodeled. In
Nov. of 1914, the Java Masonic Lodge was formally instituted with Dr. Sigmond
Rosenthal installed as Worshipful Master. Other officers installed were Philip
Noble, E.H. Noteboom, Jacob Helm, H.J. Cook, W.E. Cole, Fred Krause, I.C.
Pratton, H.A. Taylor, and H.L. Hughes.

Camp Fire Girls Society
In Nov. 1913, the girls of Java High School organized a Camp Fire Girls Society.
This organization was under the leadership of Mrs. Fred Bauer.

Eastern Star Chapter No. 123
The Java Chapter of the Eastern Star was organized on July 24, 1916, the
Mobridge Chapter helping institute the Chapter. The ceremonies took place in the
Masonic Lodge rooms of Java, which were tastefully decorated with flowers and
greens by the local Star members. Worthy Grand Patron Dr. B. Hart of Blunt,
assisted by Mrs. Hart, held the meeting. Otto Doherr of Selby acted as Grand
Secretary, reading and presenting the Charter. Miss Rose Schmidt of Selby acted
as Worthy Matron, and Mrs. A. Beil, also of Selby, as Grand Marshal.

Officers elected were: Worthy Matron, Johanna Schott; Worthy Patron, Jacob J.
Wolff; Associate Matron, Sarah B. Hughes; Secretary, Grace Noble; Treasurer,
W.C. Hicks; Conductress, Pearl Hennings; Associate Conductress, Emily T. Hicks;
Chaplain, Clara Barclay; Marshal, Richard Bellis; Organist, Vina Varnum. Star
Points were: Ada, Alice Noble; Ruth, Louise Bohle; Esther, Emilie Eisentraut;
Martha, Kate Clement; and Electa, Carrie Noteboom; Warden, Emma Wolff; and
Sentinel, H.J. Cook. In Dec. 1938, the Java Chapter surrendered its Charter and
consolidated with the Hope Chapter of Selby, with 17 members coming into the
Hope Chapter at this time.

Junior Red Cross
On Sept. 20, 1917, a Junior Red Cross was organized in Java. Tillie Dufloth and
Helen Aman were the organizers. Members were Helen Aman, chairman; Tillie
Dufloth, secretary; and Lorraine Schott, treasurer. Other members were Gretchen
Clement, Leota Schott, Elizabeth Noble, Agnes and Elizabeth Gehrki.

Girl Hiker's Club
The Girl Hiker's club made their first hike on Sept. 27, 1921, to Haux Grove.
They gathered wood and soon had a fire blazing. Supper was spread, roasted
wieners forming a large part of the menu. Jokes were laughingly exchanged and
snatches of songs could be heard. Occasionally a picture was snapped when the
opportunity presented itself. At dusk a meeting was held for the purpose of
electing officers, who were: Chairman, Rozella Hunter, and treasurer, Pearl
Forbes. Other members were: Gretta Finch, Grethel Finch, Genevieve Fargen, Rose
Rissky, Freya Clement and Eunice Campbell. The plan was to increase the hike two
miles each trip in order to gradually become accustomed to the strain.

Embroidery Club
A new club was organized at the "Dove Cote" on Nov. 23, 1922. The club was
christened "Embroidery Club" and each lady member arrived with her fancy work.
The club members were Mrs. W.C. Hicks, Mrs. G.W. Hicks, Mrs. E.C. Giffen, Mrs.
R.M. Hennings, Miss Pearl Forbes, Rozella Hunter, Rita Ryan, Freya Clement and
Genevieve Fargen.

Four-H Clubs
The Smith-Lever Act of 1914 provided for a national program of clubs, and
authorized the federal government to give money to the states to help organize
them. By 1924, the name 4-H Club was generally accepted and enrollment grew
steadily during both World Wars. A green four-leaf clover with a white H on each
leaf, the emblem for the boys and girls clubs, stands for the four key words:
head, heart, hands, and health. Members learn to do by doing and follow
objectives, which prepare them in all ways for their future as adults. When boys
and girls become members, they make this pledge:

"I pledge My Head to clearer thinking, My Heart to greater loyalty, My Hands to
larger service, My Health to better living, for my club, my community, and my
country."

It is not known exactly when 4-H appeared in the Java area, but a 1931 issue of
the Java Herald showed Mrs. August Doerr as the leader of the Flying Needle 4-H
club. Members were Freda Jesser, Elsie Naasz, Lydia Wolf, Violet Wolf, Susie
Wolf, Verna Lutz, Margaret Eisenbeisz, Lucy Krause, and Alvina Wahl.

Other 4-H clubs, those who organized them, and in which year are: 1939, Happy
Eight, Mrs. Christ Sauer; 1940, Jolly Helpers, Mrs. Jacob Haux; 1941, Alamo
Beeves, Jacob Oster, and Horseshoe Luckies, Christ Sauer; 1942, Glen-Go-Getters,
Metha Walz; 1943, Victory 4-H, Albert Aman; 1949, Spring Lake Lads and Lassies,
Orville Stangl; 1951, C Club, Mrs. Jake Schlepp; 1952, Nimble Fingers, Mrs. Otto
Schnaible; 1957, Happy Juniors, Mrs. Erwin Sonnenfeld; 1968, Four Leaf Clovers,
Sharon VanderMartin; and in 1970, Java Go Getters, Dean Moser. Lynelle Bieber, a
4-H member, organized Country Bumpkins and Becky Witlock, another 4-H member,
organized Spring Valley Handicrafters.

According to an early issue of the Java Herald, in 1964, Alma Sonnenfeld helped
organize Horseshoe Trailers. Floyd Oster was the leader. Members: Dennis
Boschee, Randy Pfitzer, Steve and Terry Kary, Roger and Paul Darling, Marlow and
Rodney Schaffer, Tommy Goehring and Lyle Oster.

In 1956, Mrs. Herman Fiedler was the leader of Nimble Fingers. Margaret
Hochstetter was president, Madeline Mueller, vice president, June Bieber,
secretary , Marion Fiedler, treasurer, and Carolyn Fiedler, reporter. In 1964,
Diane Fiedler received a trophy for top achievement in 4-H work and her sister,
Carolyn, won second place.

Junior Leader, Rebecca Schneider, of Happy Juniors 4-H Club, was selected to
attend National 4-H Congress in Chicago in 1973. Another 4-H Club noted in 1973
was the Busy Bees.

Grandmothers Club
In Oct. 1934, the Birthday Club met with Mrs. Mae Campbell and Mrs. H.J. Cook as
hostesses at the Cook home for a Sunday one o'clock dinner. It was decided to
organize a club to be known as Grandmother's Club. Meetings were to be held
every third Saturday afternoon of the month and lunches to be served.

The following officers of the club were elected: Mrs. Kate Clement, chairman;
Mrs. Gerrit Noble, vice chairman; and Mrs. H.J. Cook, secretary. Those present
were Mrs. B.S. Stowell of Selby, Mesdames: Peter Noble, W.C. Hicks, Philip
Noble, Kate Clement and the hostesses.

Thimble Club
Two clubs, the East Side and the West Side Sewing Club, were social clubs, the
members of which would meet once a month to share their handiwork projects.
Later the clubs merged into one and it was named the Thimble Club. Their float
won a 1st price in the Java 1975 Diamond Jubilee parade. Members of the West
Side Sewing Club in 1950 were Eva Bauer, Margaretha Eisenbeisz, Lydia Frank,
Mrs. Ed Goetz, Mrs. Fred Krause, Tillie Naasz, Amelia Pfitzer, Katie Sackman,
Freda Sauer, Barbara Schadler, Mrs. Dave Schlepp, Christina Schlepp, Louise
Stangl, Martha Wolff and Lizzie Zeller.

Members of the Thimble Club in 1975 were  Martha Bender, Irene Fiedler, Lydia
Frank, Maggie Kary, Nettie Kast, Louise Keller, Anna Mueller, Martha Naasz,
Martha Schmierer, Hertha Spiry, Hilda Stangl, and Martha Wolff.

Chamber Of Commerce
Minutes of the Java Chamber of Commerce, the official organization of the City
of Java, were recorded from the years 1947-1958. On Jan. 20, 1947, a meeting was
held for the purpose of organizing a Chamber of Commerce. Temporary chairman at
that time was J.S. Pfitzer. A.C. Schlepp presented literature from the various
Chambers of Commerce, and the benefits of such an organization were discussed.
Everyone present was in favor of organizing an official commercial organization
such as a Chamber of Commerce. It was suggested that a committee of five be
appointed (together with the temporary chairman) to draw up a set of by-laws and
a rate schedule for the different classes of membership. Others serving on this
committee were G.W. Hicks, Frank Weisgram, Reinhold Moser, Ben Stiegelmeier, and
Leon Kast. A.C. Schlepp, temporary secretary, signed the minutes of this first
meeting.

On Mar. 11, 1947, a special meeting was held to elect officers for the newly
formed organization. Officers were: President, Chris Pfitzer; vice president,
J.S. Pfitzer; secretary, A.C. Schlepp; and treasurer, Art Eisenbeisz. It was
moved to adopt the third Monday of each month as the regular meeting night.

The following businesses were members of the first Chamber of Commerce: Class A:
Eisenbeisz and Son and the Java Equity Exchange; Class B: Bauer and Sons, C.L.
Hicks Exchange, Elmer's Market, Gill Hardware, Job Cafe, Kary Store, Java
Herald, Schlepp Drug Store, Grand Theatre, Sterling Oil Company, Central Lumber
Company, McCabe Elevator, and Bagley Elevator; Class C: Spiry Garage, Pfitzer
Garage, Schuh Repair Shop and Weisgram Blacksmith; Class D: Individual members
to include carpenters, clerks, postmaster, mail carriers, railroad men,
teachers, farmers and laborers.

The Chamber of Commerce became the Java Community Club, after over 20 years of
existence. Serving as president of the Chamber throughout the years following
1947 were: E.R. Kary, A.C. Schlepp, J.S. Pfitzer, Elmer Biel, Ervin Wolf, G.W.
Hicks, Gilbert Schlepp, Marvin Pfitzer, Ray Pfaff, and Floyd Biel. Those who
held the vice president position were Leon Kast, Elmer Biel, E.R. Kary, A.C.
Schlepp, Chris J. Pfitzer, G.W. Hicks, G.A. Zeller, Marvin Pfitzer, Floyd Biel,
Orville Jensen, and Bob Pfitzer. Secretaries were J.S. Pfitzer, Ben
Stiegelmeier, G.A. Zeller, A.C. Schlepp, C.J. Pfitzer, Gottlieb Zeller, Reuben
Schmierer, Leon Kast, Elmer Schlepp, Eddie Anderson, Francis Jensen, Clifton
Schnaible, and Marvin Wolf. Chamber treasurers were Art Eisenbeisz, Ole Naasz,
Reuben Schmierer, Gerhardt Fiedler, C.L. Hicks, and Pastor Paul Parlow.

Sew and So Extension Club
On Nov. 12, 1948, Mrs. Jake Rabenberg and Mrs. Merl Masteller of Selby organized
the Sew and So Extension Club in Java. Twelve members joined the club at this
time, who were: Eileen Schmierer, president; Susie Spiry, vice president;
Lillian Pfitzer, secretary-treasurer; Phyllis Bell, Marge Boehler, Rosie
Eisenbeisz, Viola Fiedler, Margie Mueller, Elizabeth Scott (Mrs. Otto
Schnaible), and Mrs. John Woodruff. Other members noted were Henrietta Bieber,
Lila Bieber, and LaRayne Schlepp.

During 1949-50, seven new members joined the club. The first annual picnic was
held at Lake Hiddenwood. The club also sponsored a 4-H club, the Nimble Fingers,
for a number of years. In 1955, the club started a cookie and candy exchange at
Christmas, and also started entertaining their husbands with an annual party.
The club entered exhibits at the Mobridge Northern Show of Progress in 1956-57,
and received a plaque for the most entries. The club joined with the Home Arts
Club to participate in the March of Dimes drive. In that same year, a set of by-
laws was drawn and adopted.

In 1958, the club hosted the Walworth County Spring Tea, which was held at the
Java school. They received permanent possession of a plaque from the Northern
Show of Progress at Mobridge, in 1959. The club won 2nd place on a booth,
"Plaster Plus", at the 1966 Walworth County Christmas Fair.

At a club meeting in June 1968, 11 members had quite an experience. They were
forced to take shelter in a root cellar, while a tornado roared above. Every
member survived and the home received little damage. Mrs. Herbert Fiechtner, a
member, received statewide attention in 1970, when the Aberdeen American News
named her Farm Wife of the week. In Apr. 1968, the club hosted the International
Festival and Tasting Tea held at the Java school auditorium.

At the 1974 Walworth County Spring Tea in Mobridge, four members received their
25-year pins. These charter members were: Lila Bieber, Viola Fiedler, Betty
(Otto) Schnaible and Susie Spiry.

1975 members were Lila Bieber, Henrietta Bieber, Kathy Fiechtner, Viola Fiedler,
Priscilla Mueller, Betty Pfitzer, Helen Pfitzer, Joyce Pfitzer, LaRayne Schlepp,
Betty Schnaible, Loretta Schnaible, Mrs. Walt Simons, Alma Sonnenfeld, Susie
Spiry, Ann Witlock and Vivian Witlock.

Home Arts Club
The Home Arts Club continues to be an active organization in the community after
50 years of organization (since 1948). In the past 25 years, several members
have held County Offices: Marge Fiedler and Dorothy Schneider as County
President; Dolores Schreter as secretary; Verda Schaffer as treasurer. In 1982,
Marge Fiedler served as District President. Several members were awarded their
25-year pins from the Walworth County Homemakers. They are Emma Fiedler, Anna
Mueller, Violet Goetz, Verda Schaffer, Lorraine Biel, Hazel Zeller and Dorothy
Schneider.

On Apr. 16, 1989, the club celebrated their 40th Anniversary with an Open House
Tea held at the school gym. Many past members and guests were present.

The club adopted a Special Child (Jay Schaffer) at the Dept. of Human Services
in Custer, and remembered him with gifts on his birthday and special occasions.

During the 1986 All-School Reunion, the club set up a large quilt display in the
Lutheran church basement, with a Kuchen Kitchen for those wishing to eat a bite.

In Sept. 1989, a Style Show and luncheon entitled "Turn of the Century Review"
by Marilyn Niewoehnor from Rugby, ND, was held at the school. The proceeds went
to the Java Centennial Fund to help promote the State Centennial that was held
that year.

(Photo:) Home Arts Club. Back: Lorraine Biel, Verda Schaffer, Dolores Schreter,
         Donna Bieber, Sharon Bieber, Marjorie Fiedler, Front: Janice Wolf,
         Marva Ferguson, Dorothy Schneider

The club members did many things together as a group, such as: Holiday booths at
the County Holiday Fair; planted a Centennial Tree at City Park, along with
several other trees over the years; put outdoor restroom facilities at the park;
favors and gifts for the residents of Selby's Good Samaritan Center; mini-
workshops; went to Pierre to see the Capitol adorned with Christmas trees, and
held a soup supper to raise money for playground equipment (wings and Eagles
Perch), picnic tables, etc. at City Park.

In Nov. 1992, the club voted to become a Social Club, as the state cut out a lot
of projects for the County and not much was offered. They are still active
within the community, and do things that interest them, such as attending plays
at the Aberdeen Community Theatre and NSC, Homemakers schools, preparing a
foreign supper and a silly supper for the members, craft projects, floats for
the town celebrations and they serve lunches at auction sales to support their
projects.

Emma Fiedler was the only charter member until 1993, when she moved to Jackson,
MN. Currently, there are 9 members: Lorraine Biel, Donna Bieber, Sharon Bieber,
Marge Fiedler, Marva Ferguson, Verda Schaffer, Dorothy Schneider, Verda Schaffer
and Janice Wolf.

Walco Club
Walco Club, a Walworth County Extension Club, was organized in 1950, with Mrs.
Jake Rabenberg of Selby assisting. Charter members still active include Mrs. Art
Bieber and Mrs. Norman Schumacher.

(Photo:) Walco Club. Back: Darlene Walz, Millie Bieber, Mardella Bieber,
         Caroline Lee, Carol Fiedler. Front: Joanne Bieber, Beulah Schumacher,
         Wanda Moser

Ever-extending education is the goal of Extension, using the sociability of a
club's atmosphere to benefit in subject matter and in leadership skills.
Community service involvement through volunteerism benefits the young and old.

Officers and project leaders rotate so all members may experience leadership.
They learn about nutrition, clothing, home management, citizenship, child
development, home furnishings, health, safety, international, recreation,
consumer education, money management, leisure activities, and more. The program
is flexible, responding to new interests and needs.

Children are counted as the most important of crops. Walco has served and
assisted 4-H clubs in Achievement days, sponsored the Spring Lake Lads and
Lassies 4-H club, and awarded shears to the 4-H Junior Dress Review winner.
Walco has sponsored a "Fun" activity, such as a fishpond, at the Bowdle Mother's
Club Halloween party for community children. Entertainment and treats are
provided annually to the Bowdle Nursing Home residents. Less fortunate persons,
such as those at the Redfield State School, are remembered with cards and gifts.
Contributions are made to the Memorial Art Center, Crippled Children's Hospital,
Agricultural Heritage Museum, and other worthy projects.

Social meetings include hosting a Christmas dinner part, entertaining husbands
at a Valentine's party or theatre, and family picnics in July. Educational tours
have included Sica Hollow, Dakotah Factory at Webster, and places of interest in
Aberdeen, such as the School for the Visually Handicapped.

Present members who continue to learn and serve are Millie Bieber, Beulah
Schumacher, Carol Fiedler, Wanda Moser, and Darlene Walz.

Java Garden Club
In the early summer of 1953, the Home Arts Extension Club was instrumental in
starting the Java Garden Club. Three members of the Mobridge Garden Club helped
organize the Java Garden Club. Not all members of the Home Arts Extension Club
became members of the Garden Club. Among the original members were Eva Bauer,
Letha Bieber, Lila Bieber, Emma Fiedler, Tina Gehrki, Marie Hicks, Mary Hirsch,
Rose Jacobs, Nettie Kast, Rosie Spiry, Emma Stiegelmeier, Maggie Vaggen, Janice
Wolf, Lois Wolf, Martha Wolff, Hazel Zeller, and Lizzie Zeller.

(Photo:) Java Garden Club. Back: Loretta Schnaible, Viola Goetz. Mid: Hilda
         Stangl, Betty Schnaible, Lorraine Fiechtner, Alma Sonnenfeld, Lila
         Bieber. Front: Carol Fiedler, Clara Nehlich, Nettie Kast, Violet Goetz

Since 1967, the club has created a spot of beauty on Main Street on the lot
north of the Legion Hall. In 1972, the club secured title to the lot with the
help of Henry H. Wolff, when it was sold for taxes. Every summer there is a
continuous display of blooms, beginning with tulips, followed in season by iris,
peonies, day lilies and roses. Every year a large circular bed of annuals is
planted, usually petunias. The members take turns caring for the garden plot.
Ornamental crab apple trees and Blue Spruce trees have been planted. A white
fence with the plaques identifying this as a Garden Club project, and
recognizing members, who have passed away, makes for an attractive background.
The members of the Garden Club purchased a picnic table for the city park, in
1956. There are presently 11 members of the club. They are: Lila Bieber and
Nettie Kast, both charter members, Lorraine Fiechtner, Betty Schnaible, Carol
Fiedler, Viola Goetz, Violet Goetz, Clara Nehlich, Loretta Schnaible, Alma
Sonnenfeld and Hilda Stangl.

The Garden Club year follows almost a fixed pattern: flower show and tea in
June, July or Aug.; a family picnic, usually in July; a tour of area
greenhouses; and a Christmas party in early Dec. or late Nov.

Almost from the beginning, the members have enjoyed having and being Secret
Sisters. They observe anniversaries, birthdays, and Christmas, and any other
occasion they wish. Their identities are revealed at the Christmas party, and
new names are drawn for the coming year. For a number of years, each Java Garden
Club member has given a Christmas gift for a resident of the Selby Good
Samaritan Center. In addition, they have participated in benevolences of many
kinds.

Java PTA-PTO
A group of parents, teachers and clergy organized the Java unit of the Parent-
Teacher Association on Oct. 5, 1955, in the high school auditorium. The purpose
was educational and members of the association were devoted to the welfare of
the children.

The meeting was called to order under the supervision of Mrs. Norman Anderson of
Lowry, the District 11 PTA. president, sister-in-law of Eddie Anderson. She
explained the purpose of the meeting and discussed the work of the Parent-
Teacher Association. Officers were elected, who were Mrs. Carl Jacobs,
president, Eddie Anderson, vice president, Mrs. Emory Darling, secretary, and
Mrs. Ervin Wolf, treasurer. The second Monday of each month was selected as the
meeting night. The meetings opened with group singing, reading of the Objects of
the PTA, and the Pledge of Allegiance to the Flag.

Many projects were undertaken to provide funds to purchase items such as
photocopier, basketball uniforms, film projector, library books, tape recorder
and public address system, to name a few.

The annual PTA Convention for District 11 was held in the Java school auditorium
in 1963 and the spring PTA Conference was held there in Apr. 1968. In Oct. 1970,
the Association voted to leave the state and national PTA and become the local
Parent-Teacher Organization.

Officers in 1975 were Sandy Jacobs, president, Donna Bieber, vice president,
Lucille Melcher, secretary and Helen Sauer, treasurer. The Java PTO,
discontinued in 1981, served their intended purpose to realize a deeper
understanding and appreciation of the work that goes on between parents and
teachers for the students.

Java Band Mothers
Started in Feb. 1961, the Java Band Mothers Club, consisting of 40 members, was
busy. They donated food and time, and with the wonderful support and cooperation
of all the people in the community, were able to make a generous donation toward
the purchase of 40 new uniforms for the Java School Band.

The club had various means of raising funds, such as sponsoring carnivals,
serving meals, holding food sales, organizing a Town vs. Country basketball
game, having a post office auction, card parties and selling community
calendars. They sponsored two to three students a year to attend the
International Music Camp at the Peace Gardens, and were able to purchase a
variety of new musical instruments through the years.

The first officers were Mrs. Ed Anderson, president, Lorraine Biel, vice
president and Anna Mueller, secretary-treasurer. Gerald Cutshaw was the advisor.
There were 39 band mothers in 1975. This club is no longer active.

Java Community Club
In 1968, the Java Chamber of Commerce changed its name to the Java Community
Club. The Community Club holds a membership drive in Jan. of each year, usually
having an evening meal at the local cafe. Anyone who joins at this time is
invited to a free steak feed at the Feb. meeting.

The purpose of the Community Club is to benefit the entire community. They have
held several benefits for local families, donated to the local Fire Dept., the
ambulance service, Hiddenwood Project, and have purchased park equipment. The
Club has sponsored many softball and baseball teams, and purchased uniforms for
the teams in the past. The Java Community Club helped purchase and install a
picnic shelter at the City Park, with part of the money coming from the Gold
Committee and from a memorial from the Ray Langston family. Members of the Club
have participated in the sponsored events such as Santa Claus Day, the 1985
Easter Egg Hunt, a gun safety course, dances for teens and adults, and a CPR
course in 1982 through 1985. They have donated turkeys for the Christmas
Giveaway. Over the last several years, they have helped pay for swimming lessons
for the local youth.

At the annual membership drive in 1990, the Community Club voted to look for
someone to take over the operation of the Java Cafe after owners Paul and Sandy
Jacobs announced that they would be closing. A committee was appointed to look
into the matter. They were Blackie (Harlan) Krause, Ray Langston, Merle Noess,
Ted Schneider, Calvin Wolff, and Holly Wolforth. When the Java Community Cafe
Corporation was developed, the Community Club donated $1000 to assist in the
purchase of the cafe.

Member Virgil Biel announced that he would join with another committee to make
an informational brochure on Java. This brochure would contain photos of
available houses in town and information about the community and would be
distributed at trade shows to help promote the town and fill vacant houses.

The main fund-raising event, the Hog Roast, is held each year at the Java Legion
Hall on the first day of pheasant hunting season. The event's popularity has
grown and is well attended by hunters from many different states. The hog is
donated and is roasted and served by Community Club members.

Past officers have been Floyd Biel, Steve Biel, Ron Fiedler, Earl Frank, Brian
Gill, Clifford Grenz, Roger Hirsch, Harlan Krause, Merlyn Melcher, E.J. Monthye,
Bob Pfitzer, Marvin Pfitzer, Clifton Schnaible, Dennis Schneider, Ted Schneider,
Jeral Schreter, Marvin Wolf, and Calvin Wolff. Present officers are Todd Biel,
president, Dwight Helm, vice president, LeRoy Sandmeier, secretary, and Steve
Biel, treasurer.

Java Community Club Improvement Corporation
The first meeting of the Java Community Club Improvement Corporation was held
Feb. 23, 1976. At this organizational meeting, five directors were elected, who
were Steve Biel, president; Merlyn Melcher, treasurer; Donna Bieber, secretary;
and Erna Schlepp and Wes Frank as directors.

On Mar. 9, 1976, the Corporation and the Jubilee Commitee held a joint meeting.
At this time, it was decided to transfer Jubilee funds to the Corporation funds.

Plans to clear the title on the lots to build a low-rent apartment unit were
made. Jack VonWald, attorney, was the legal adviser. Blueprints and specks were
obtained from Otto Heupel of Eureka, who gave an estimate of $60,000 for a
38'x76' building.

The directors met with Bob Bothwell, County Supervisor, on May 1976, to help
prepare a loan application. In June 1976, the board went to Eureka and met with
Don Heupel. A new bid of $55,083.56 was given and a motion was made and seconded
to accept this bid.

The directors, Bob Bothwell, and Don Heupel met with FHA in Selby on Sept. 23,
1976. At this time, the construction contract was reviewed and signed.
Construction was to begin Oct. 1997, and the building ready for occupancy on May
1, 1977. The apartments were ready on Apr. 17, 1977 and an Open House was held
from 2-4 p.m., with about 275 people attending. Four female renters, Ella
Buckenberger, Pauline Eiseman, Katie Schneider and Ella Stangl, moved into the
apartments in May 1977.

In July 1979, a second low-rent unit in Java was considered. A survey was taken
and plans were placed on hold until July 21, 1981, when Don Heupel, contractor,
attended the Corporation meeting. He stated that construction on a second unit
could begin Aug. 2 and be completed by Dec. 2. Construction began on Aug. 21,
1981. An Open House for this second unit was held Dec. 18, 1981, with about 55
people attending. Three women, Ida Goetz, Emma Wolf, and Natalie Spiry took
occupancy on Dec. 26, 1981. Lydia Krause moved into an apartment in Jan. 1982.

The Sunrise Apartments are on the east, and the Sunset Apartments are on the
west. The eight apartments were occupied as of July 1999.

There are approximately 40 Corporation members, many of whom have served as
officers and directors. Present officers are: Merlyn Melcher, president, Violet
Goetz, vice president, LaMoyle Aman, secretary, Delores Schreter, treasurer,
Irene Fiedler, member-at-large.

KITT Club
On Mar. 25, 1985, 12 interested and energetic women attended an organizational
meeting at the home of Joan O'Toole in Java. In attendance were Lois Aberle,
Gloria Aesoph, Deb Biel, Kathy Fiechtner, Carol Gill, Judy Grenz, Linda Hirsch,
Joan O'Toole, Mona Rau, Danon Schneider, Jeanne Schneider, and Viv Witlock.

Discussion was held and it was decided to name the women's club the KITT Club,
an acronym for Keeping In Touch Together. Members of the club wanted an
organization that would be involved in community activities, good for families,
couples and children. They wanted to provide memory-creating fun activities for
the children of the Java community.

Officers elected were Jeanne Schneider, president, Joan O'Toole, vice president,
Danon Schneider, secretary, and Lois Aberle, treasurer.

The first project of KITT was an Easter Egg Hunt scheduled for Apr. 6 at 2 p.m.
at City Park. All members donated a dozen eggs and dyed them on Apr. 3, at the
home of Jeanne Schneider. Carol Gill donated the dye and was responsible for a
decorated box for a drawing. Viv Witlock brought her pickup, out of which prizes
were given; Deb Biel was school publicity chairman; Jeanne Schneider was the
Easter Bunny and Judy Grenz portrayed a Clown. Jeanne and Carol purchased prizes
with money provided by the Java Community Club. Members arrived early at the
park to hide the eggs. The weather was cool and windy but 72 eager children came
to participate. The Clown gave out balloons, which impressed the children. Prize
winners were: Pre-school, Derek Noess; Kindergarten-First grade, Sarah Miller;
Second thru Fourth grade, Arvyn Spiry; Fifth through Sixth grade, Michael
Hirsch, and the Grand Prize was won by Tricia Murray. All members celebrated the
success of the event, and plans for future endeavors were made.

Others to join were Lou Aman, Marjorie Fiedler, Sandy Osterday, Linda Raba,
Faith Rau, and Pam Salzer. During its existence, KITT Club held a Sexual Abuse
Clinic, Halloween parties at the school gymnasium, where many prizes were
awarded and a lunch was served, a Babysitting Clinic, CPR training, and Easter
Egg hunts and breakfasts. They hosted a highly successful and fun five by five
softball tournament, and held a big 4th of July picnic at City park. The members
sold concessions at school sports activities and auction sales to earn money
that financed the variety of activities. They also made Java Community
Calendars, a project involving the school children. Each class was assigned a
month or two and the children drew their interpretation of that month. KITT
judged the drawings and selected those to be used in the calendars. The members
also put together an annual for the school. They took pictures of the children
with Santa Claus and donated these to the parents. KITT Club was designated as
Boosters for the Java's SD Centennial Celebration and dressed as clowns, carried
balloons, and traveled throughout the area, announcing the event. They marched
in the Java SD Centennial Parade, and then sold concessions at City Park. KITT
also had a concession stand at the Selby SD Centennial and All-School Reunion
activity.

On a social level, the women of KITT entertained their husbands with Valentine's
and Christmas meals, celebrated birthdays, went on tours, planted trees, and
thoroughly enjoyed their time together. As time passed, many of the members
moved away, and the Java school closed. KITT Club, though short-lived, reached
its goals before it discontinued. The memories remain.

Senior Citizens of Java
The Senior Citizens of Java was formed in Oct. 1989. Burton Sheffner was elected
president, Gus Schaffer, vice president, and Loretta Schnaible, secretary-

The purpose of the organization was to promote fellowship and entertainment for

Community Cafe Corporation
When Paul and Sandy Jacobs, previous owners of the Java Cafe, made plans to
close the business and relocate, there was no interest in the purchase of the
business. A small town without a cafe just didn't seem right, so a group of
concerned people of Java and the community formed the Community Cafe
Corporation. Shares were sold with the purpose of acquiring sufficient funds to
purchase the Java Cafe and keep it opened. Officers elected were Ted Schneider,
chairman, LeRoy Sandmeier, vice-chairman, Donna Bieber, secretary, Merlyn
Melcher, treasurer and Delila Biel, member-at-large. The building was repaired
and made ready for business, operating as the Java Community Cafe.

1991 board of directors were Ted Schneider, president, LeRoy Sandmeier,
secretary, Calvin Wolff, board member, Wilbur Kary, treasurer and Delila Biel,
vice president. Dorothy Schneider was manager, employees were Delores Schreter,
Bea Miklos, Donna Wolff, Betty Sandmeier, Jodi Fiedler, Jody Aberle and Lori
Allbee.

When the Nelsons purchased the cafe, the Corp. was dissolved; some shareholders
invested in the Store Corp.

Gold Committee
A group of five people, including Donna Bieber, coordinator, Florence Noess, Gus
Schaffer, Rueben Boehler and Cornelius Schnaible, met in 1993 for the purpose of
seeing Java become a Gold Community. Efforts were fruitful and in Mar. 1994, the
Gold Committee came into existence.

The committee was responsible for starting a recycling project and working on
City Park improvements. The Ray Langston family gave a memorial of $500 to the
community to help put up a shelter at the park. Many projects were held to raise
sufficient money, and organizations also donated to the project. The Gold
Committee also received a grant and in the summer of 1997, some park equipment
was placed into the park. In 1998, the Java Community Club and the Gold
Committee purchased a sturdy shelter and placed it in the picnic area of City
Park.

Some of the other goals are still in progress, such as helping with repair on
the Legion Hall, town beautification, more park improvements, and helping with
the Java Centennial.

At the present time, the committee consists of Coordinator Donna Bieber,
Florence Noess, Gus Schaffer, Cornelius Schnaible, and Dwight Helm.

Java American Legion
The Java Legion Post was organized on Nov. 18, 1946 at a meeting held in the old
City Hall with 35 or 40 veterans in attendance. It was decided to name the post
the LaVerne Bauer Post, No. 275 of the American Legion in honor of Flight
Officer LaVerne Bauer, only son of Mr. and Mrs. John Bauer, Jr., who died in a
plane crash over China on Oct. 22, 1944.

Anton Mueller was named as the first Commander; other officers elected at this
organizational meeting were: Gerhardt Fiedler, vice commander; Gilbert Schlepp,
adjutant; Wes Frank, sergeant at arms; G.W. Hicks, finance officer; Othmer (Ole)
Naasz, historian and Elmer Biel, chaplain. A group of businessmen had purchased
the old City Hall building sometime before and turned it over to the new Post to
be used as a Legion Hall. Several years later, this building was sold to Fred
Permann Plumbing and Heating.

Late in Sept. 1949, ground was broken for a basement for a new Legion Hall on
the lot south of the former Grand Theatre building.

Due to lack of finances, it was decided to finish the basement and use it as the
hall until a structure could be built above it. This dream became a reality when
the Grand Theatre building was purchased and lumber from it was used for the new
hall, which was finished Sept. 1961. A Grand Opening dance was held on Sept. 8
with music furnished by Mike Dosch of Bismarck, and his electric organ and
Gerhardt Bauman of Hosmer, and his accordion.

Java American Legion Auxiliary
In the spring of 1948 LaVerne Bauer Post No. 275 of the American Legion at Java,
authorized the organization of an American Legion Auxiliary unit. Post Adjutant,
Gilbert Schlepp and Post Commander, Joe Zarka conducted the meeting. Mrs. Bertha
Stowell, District 14 President, presided and assisted with the organization. The
following were elected as officers: President, Helen (Joe) Zarka; first vice
president, Mrs. Marvin Gross; 2nd vice president, Mrs. Carl Hepper; secretary,
LaRayne (Gilbert) Schlepp; treasurer, Miss Gloria Schlepp; historian, Mrs.
Gerhardt Fiedler; chaplain, Mrs. Edward Goetz; sergeant at arms, Mrs. Emanuel
Schlepp; executive committee, Clara (Jake) Nehlich, Clara (Elmer) Biel, and
Susie (Alvin) Spiry. Other charter members were: Mrs. Fred Bauer, Marge (Rueben)
Boehler, Mrs. William Frank, Mrs. G.W. Hicks, Mrs. Alex Krause, Mrs. Andy
Mueller, Mrs. Christ Naasz, Mrs. Adolph Pfaff, Linda (Fred) Pregitzer, Lillian
(Chris) Pfitzer, Helen (Harold) Pfitzer, Christina (Sam) Schlepp, Mrs. Art
Schumacher and Mrs. Merle Wolf.

The main purpose of the Auxiliary is to help care for veterans and their
families, especially those hospitalized. Christmas gifts and money are sent to
the Hot Springs Veterans hospital, also all monthly showers called for by the
state department are donated. Gift Shop articles, which are made by hospitalized
veterans, are ordered each year and sold locally. A Poppy Poster contest and an
Americanism Essay contest is held each year and cash prizes are given to the
winners. Poppies are made by disabled veterans and every year the Auxiliary
sponsors a poppy drive.

On Memorial Day the graves of deceased members of the Legion and Auxiliary are
decorated with flags and wreaths. After the Memorial Day program the Auxiliary
has served a dinner at the Legion Hall. Other means of raising funds are card
parties, and serving lunches at dances and turkey raffles. The Auxiliary has
sponsored a Girls State Candidate every year since 1949.

Our Veterans of Military Service

The Civil War broke out shortly after SD was opened to settlement. The settlers
at once formed two volunteer companies of cavalry, but their activities were
confined to the home front. The outbreak of an Indian war in 1862 required the
presence of soldiers on the Dakota frontier. The population at the time was so
small that the Territory's quota of troops for the Civil War was filled by the
two volunteer companies.

The Spanish-American War broke out between the U.S. and Spain in Apr. 1898. A
regiment of 12 troops of cavalry, known as "Grigsby's Cowboys", was organized.
Five of the troops were from South Dakota. A National Guard regiment from SD,
commander Col. A.B. Frost, arrived at Manila in Aug., shortly after the war was
ended. Trouble with the natives developed and the soldiers remained in the
islands for a whole year.

World War I broke out in Europe during the summer of 1914. Within three years,
the U.S. was involved in the conflict. President Wilson appealed to the
Americans not to take sides, but there were strong feelings of sympathy for
England and her allies, and when Germany began to interfere with American trade,
public opinion became more and more anti-German. Sen. King proposed barring
German language papers from circulation, revoking the charter of the German-
American alliance. Suspicion grew in Walworth County, which resulted in rigid
laws and orders pertaining to the display of the American flag, the wearing of
patriotic buttons, and the banning of German speech and newspapers. German
measles and German fried potatoes became Liberty measles and American fries. The
German State Bank of Java became the American State Bank. More than 32,000 SD
men served in World War I; nearly 22,000 were called to service under the
selective service law. In July 1917, names of 70 young men of Walworth County
were drawn. The lists of names on the honor rolls contained many names of German
origin, and there was scarcely a family that didn't have a loved one in the
armed services.

On the Home Front, women organized Red Cross societies or sewing circles and
engaged in welfare activities. Libraries collected books for the soldier's use,
and campaigns or drives were organized to raise money for such organizations as
the Red Cross to help them in welfare work and recreational facilities in army
camps. In the government's effort to raise money, the sale of Liberty Bonds was
developed. The people of SD invested over one hundred nine million dollars in
such bonds. By July 19, 1917, the Java Red Cross Auxiliary collected newspapers
for money for the Red Cross; contributions totaled $252.25 at that time.
Production of food and war materials was speeded up, and the work of the farmer
played a large part toward winning the war. An appeal for more wheat brought
about production from 45-million bushels in 1917 to 62-million bushels in 1918
in SD alone. Thousands of acres of grazing land were put under cultivation and
the rains arrived at the right time. Economy was good during 1916-17, with
livestock, dairy, poultry, and grain prices reaching a new high. In Nov. 1918,
an armistice was agreed and peace treaties were signed at Versailles in 1919.

Selective Service, or Draft, law was passed nationally in 1940, with local
boards serving each county. All men from the ages of 21-35 were given the choice
of enlisting before their draft number was called. L.Rueben Boehler was the
clerk of Local Board #19 located in Selby, from 1947 to 1955.

World War II came to the U.S. on Dec. 11, 1941, when the Japanese attacked Pearl
Harbor. "We interrupt this broadcast to bring you a news flash. The Japs, at
dawn this morning, attacked Pearl Harbor. No details are as yet available." The
U.S. was formally at war at 3:10 p.m. (EST) Monday, when Pres. Roosevelt signed
the resolution, which declared war on Japan. Those who were exempt from active
service went into war work, farmers increased production, and crops were
enormous. Livestock and dairy prices doubled and tripled, as did the production
of these commodities. A drive was instituted for the mobilization of 'woman
power' and women went to work in all possible jobs. It was the time of Rosie The
Riveter, preservation of food, gasoline shortages, tire and tube rationing, a
scarcity of electrical equipment and tools, a lack of new cars and trucks,
machine rationing, and a labor shortage brought on with the high percentage of
young and middle-aged men in the service or war work. Food sellers were urged to
stock up on canned goods, farmers were urged to check on their fuel and mileage
allotments, ever-constant reminders of rationing for processed foods, sugar,
fuel oil, shoes, etc. were noted in the local paper, which was then the Walworth
County Record. Colored stamps were purchased for different products. There were
almost 30 billion ration stamps in the 150 million copies of War Ration Book
Two, or more than all the postage stamps produced by the Government since 1931.
Two hammermills were allotted to Walworth County and furnished to Earl Erbe and
Mike and Leo Arbach, who showed a great need for such a machine and agreed to
let their outfits do all the custom work possible in the community.

Red Cross workers became active again, with production of sewed and knitted
items for Red Cross kits; Mrs. G.W. Hicks was the production chairman for Java.
Some of the sewed articles the local chapters made from Mar. 1, 1942 to Jan. 5,
1943, included 69 ditty bags, 103 bedside bags, 400 Red Cross kits filled for
soldiers and marines embarking for foreign duty. Knitted items included 32
sleeveless sweaters for navy, 38 helmets, 29 turtleneck sweaters, 25 watch caps,
40 army sweaters, and 40 mufflers.

Commander in Chief, Pres. Franklin Delano Roosevelt died Apr. 12, 1945. Pres.
Harry S. Truman became the new Commander in Chief. World War II ended Aug. 14,
1945.

The Korean War began June 25, 1950, and was the first war in history in which
troops of a world organization acted as "police" to fight an aggressor nation.
The UN charter, signed by the major nations of the world in 1945, had outlawed
all such aggression. So the UN asked member countries to aid South Korea. On
June 30, Pres. Truman ordered U.S. ground troops to the aid of South Korea, and
great numbers of U.S. troops and equipment were rushed to the aid. Major U.S.
forces, plus token forces from its allies, landed under the overall command of
Gen. Douglas MacArthur.

The Korean War was one of the bloodiest in history. In the 37 months of
fighting, both sides used most of the modern machines of war, except atomic
weapons. Total casualties were estimated at 4 million. The Truman agreement was
signed July 27, 1953, with all fighting ending at 10 p.m.

The Vietnam War began, for the U.S., on Feb. 28, 1961 and ended May 6, 1975.
"Ask not what your country can do for you, but what you can do for your
country," the infamous speech of JFK, inspired the generation to service in
warfare of survival, with orders only to advise and assist. It was a monotonous
war of firefights, ambushes, booby traps and snipers, blood sucking leeches, mud
during monsoon rains, mosquitoes and an invisible enemy. It was guerilla warfare
with nothing familiar. Television cameras brought the war into our homes while
we watched our boys fight in places that we could not pronounce, but that would
become legendary.

In 1983, following a military coup, U.S. forces invaded the island of Grenada.
Troops were withdrawn in 1985 after a democratic government was reestablished.
In 1982, Israel launched a full-scale attack on Palestinian bases in Lebanon. As
a UN peacekeeping force, U.S. and European troops were deployed in Beirut in
1983 and met by terrorist attacks. Multinational forces left in 1984. In 1989
Noriega, self-declared President of Panama, declared war on the U.S. and in Dec.
20, 1989, 25,000 U.S. troops invaded Panama. Noriega was captured in Jan. 1990
and brought to the U.S. for trial. On Aug. 7, 1990, Operation Desert Shield
began a mass deployment of coalition forces to protect Saudi oil reserves. Iraqi
president Saddam Hussein ignored the UN Security Council's ultimatum for
withdrawal and Gen. Normal Schwarzkopf launched Operation Desert Storm. On Feb.
24, 1991, the ground war was launched, and Kuwait was liberated two days later.
A ceasefire was declared on Feb. 28; Saddam Hussein has remained in power.

Unfortunately, a complete list of Java service men and women is not available,
nor are many of the dates of service. The following includes names taken from
Separation Records, Family Histories and the LaVerne Bauer American Legion Post
#265. Veterans noted have been placed in the time frames of the various wars,
conflicts and peacekeeping missions according to available information. It does
not mean that those listed actually served in the arenas of conflict, but were
indeed prepared to participate if required. There are those within the list who
proudly served during times of peace, and there are those for whom no
information about their dates of service was available. At best, the list
provides an indication of the loyalty of our Java area servicemen and women.
Within these pages, they are rightfully honored.

Most of the photographs were taken from the pictures displayed in the Java
American Legion Hall. Stuart Surma of Java was kind enough to reproduce them for
this book, with the assistance of Gus Schaffer.
