Germans From Russia Heritage Society
Die Deutsche Freiheit Chapter "Preserving our Heritage and Enriching our Lives"
by Rosina Bauman Stiegelmeier

On Nov. 14, 1982 the area chapter of Germans from Russia Heritage Society was
organized at a meeting held in the Legion Hall in Java. Charter members
numbering more than 60 from Java, Selby, Bowdle, Roscoe, Onaka, Aberdeen,
Hosmer, Eureka, Artas, Mound City, Glenham, Mobridge, including all the rural
areas, signed a petition to become affiliated with the International Society of
Germans from Russia headquartered at Bismarck, ND. The name selected for this
local chapter was "Die Deutsche Freiheit."

Preserving the "Heritage and Ethnicity" of our ancestors who emigrated from the
Odessa area of South Russia to America and claimed a Homestead in this area
during the late 1800's through early 1900's, became the primary reason for
organizing the local chapter. This was the second of five chapters located in
South Dakota; the other four being at Menno, Aberdeen, Pierre and Rapid City.
All but the chapter at Menno were organized later than 1982.

The story of our ancestors and pioneers in the Dakotas takes one back to 1773-
1804 and Southern Germany from whence most ancestral families in this area
originated. Invited by Katherine The Great and Russian Czar Alexander, the
German farmers and artisans made the journey to South Russia via the Danube
River and also overland, traveling in groups of 25 to 100 families. Their route
lay through the countries of Austria, Czechoslovakia, Moravia, Galacia, and was
a hard, laborious trip that lasted six months and longer with many casualties on
the way.

The Russian Government extended privileges in the form of a manifesto to these
Germans as incentives to come into this area of Russia where they would change
the barren land into a beautiful and productive country. For this they were
promised freedom to maintain their German language, freedom to worship,
exemption from military service, exempt from taxes for five years, several
hectares of land, and a monetary loan at low interest with an easy repayment
schedule.

Our people were hard working, industrious, religious, and successful. They
developed and built villages, "Dorf", built schools and churches, reared large
families, and, after a century these people who had proven themselves as a God-
fearing, productive class of people, became the envy of the Russian Government.
Soon the Czar's promises were broken, sons were drafted into the Russian Army
and burdensome taxes were levied. In addition, the bright future they once
envisioned began to fade.

It was then they looked to America with hope, even though they would have to
start over again. The "Homestead Act" was promoted rather vigorously to the
European countries and with railroads being built Westward into the Dakotas,
they too, were inviting people to come and develop the prairies. Thus came the
immigrants in large numbers to claim a 160-acre homestead. According to the
census taken in 1920 more than 50 percent of the population in the Dakotas were
Germans from Russia.

More than twenty chapters from the following states belong to the International
Society of Germans from Russia Heritage Society headquartered in Bismarck, ND.
They are South Dakota, North Dakota, Minnesota, California, Ohio, Washington,
plus the Canadian Provinces of Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan. Every
state in the United States is represented by the 2100 individual and family
members who belong to the Society. The Society was originally founded in Jan. of
1971 and functions as a non-profit, non-denominational, non-political
organization. Its goals are educational and social and holds as its purpose the
bringing together of people who have an interest in discovering and preserving
the rich and varied elements of their heritage, handed down through the years.
The motto of the Germans from Russia Heritage Society is "Preserving our
Heritage and Enriching our Lives".

The first board of directors of Die Deutsche Freiheit Chapter was: LeRoy Bender,
President; Marvin Wolf, V. President; Normal Hettich, Secretary-Treasurer; Gust
Kundert and Phonia Diedtrich, Directors; and LeRoy Bender, Chapter
Representative.

Some chapter activities include:

A German worship service has been held each year since 1990 in one of the area
churches.

Served the Schmeckfest at Eureka for five consecutive years beginning in 1989.

Co-hosted the International GRHS convention at Pierre in 1994.

Participate in the annual convention of the SD Association of Germans from
Russia.

The Eureka German Singers entertained at programs, nursing homes, worship
services, etc.

Have speakers and programs at our meetings, which promote understanding of
German heritage.

Had prizewinning parade entries and scrapbooks.

Members and guests enjoy a potluck supper at the November meeting each year.

The Charter was presented to Die Deutsche Freiheit Chapter during the
International Convention held at Bismarck, ND, in July 1983.

History as I Remember... by Fred G. and Rosina Bauman.
Excerpts from Footprints, 1975

About 200 years ago, after the Turks had left the Ukraine territory in South
Russia by the Black Sea, this large country was in need for many willing workers
to come and settle and build up this land. The Russian czar and his wife,
Katherine the Great, called on the people in Germany to come to South Russia and
settle this great land, the Ukraine. She was a smart wife to him.

Then our ancestors from Wuerttenberg, Germany followed this call, left their
homes in Germany and started on this long and dangerous journey, in large hand-
powered boats. They took their belongings with them. They traveled on the Danube
river and overland routes to the Kherson state or territory and established a
village called Hoffnungstal (in English, Hope Valley), about 75 miles from
Odessa. As an inducement, the Czar had promised them freedom of religion and
military service, and I was told, a small loan. These people nearly all got poor
after this hard journey; some got sick, and some even died on their way to
Russia.

But they worked hard, cultivated the land, planted fruit trees and vineyards,
and built up this country, also, later paid taxes. Their village was growing
fast; in later years, they built a very large Lutheran church in the center of
the village, also large schools, and a courthouse. They elected their own
village government officials as follows: a Schulz (mayor), and an assistant
Schulz (assistant mayor).  A Bittel was the village messenger (as there were no
telephones), a judge, a police, and a secretary.

The fine for minor offenses usually was from 5 to 25 hard lashes with a stiff
twisted rope, or with a willow rod on the person's seat. Sometime the judge gave
jail sentences. A major crime was punished by district or federal courts.

Their church services were mostly in German. Their schools were half the time,
the German religious language, and half the time in the Russian language. The
children were required to attend school the sixth and up to including the
fourteenth years. Then they were confirmed and became members of their church.
The village was laid out something like our towns, with wide streets with each
family place about as big as a city block, and was surrounded by a four-foot
high nice straight stone wall, as most farmers in later years owned a few work
oxen or horses, a few milk cows, chickens and geese. They kept their livestock
on their places in the village, which was called a dorf. In the summer time,
boys or men were hired to take all their cattle to the pasture every morning,
and bring them home every evening. A boy even had to drive their geese out to
pasture and bring them home evenings.

Their grain fields were a few miles from the village, as well as their melon
patches. They planted usually in one place together some distance from the
village. When the melons got ripe, they hired a watchman to guard the melons so
nobody would steal them.

In about 1870, the Russian government required the able-bodied 21 year-old boys
to serve in the army. Each man or boy could draw a number; those who drew a
lucky number did not serve in the army. My mother's oldest brother was one of
the first who had to serve to help fight against the Turks. He was a medical man
and so was required to give first aid to the wounded Russian soldiers behind the
battle lines. The Turks were driven back again.


                   SAFETY & SERVICES

TOWN MARSHALL
The first Town Marshal in the town of Java was Jacob Schafer, who was appointed
in 1903. Jacob Pleinis, Sr. served for several years, after moving into town in
1924, and Felix Knittel had also served in this capacity. Ed Goetz was City
Police Office and resigned in 1948. In 1949, Christ R. Hochstetter was appointed
at $100 a month for the first month, and $125 thereafter. He remained in this
position for seven years. Julius Pfitzer was City Police Officer for a number of
years. Bob Goetz served as Chief of Police for 21 years, followed by Mike
Darling. The town of Java had no City Cop for a number of years, until Ed Allbee
was appointed in 1999 as Night Watchman.

JAVA VOLUNTEER FIRE DEPARTMENT
The Java Fire Department was organized on Mar. 1, 1905 with six members on Hose
Co. 1, and three members on Engine Co. No. 1. On Mar. 6, 1916 the Hook and
Ladder Co. 1 was used and four new members were added to the department. In June
of 1922, the hand-drawn Chemical Engine No. 1 was used, adding four more new
firemen.

The Java Fire Department of Jan. 1911

Secretary - Ed Aman

                 Schafer.

The Department was reorganized in Nov. of 1939, at that time 10 new members were
added. In Dec. 1939, the fire fighting equipment was improved when the city
purchased a Model B Ford truck for $125 from Spiry & Sons. The vehicle, a milk
truck from Minneapolis, was transformed into a fire truck, with Frank Weisgram
doing all the welding and other firemen assisting. The Chemical and fire hose
equipment were mounted on the vehicle. The fire department then had a fire truck
second to none, in comparison to the other cities of equal size.

In the spring of 1957, a new truck was purchased from Luverne Fire Apparatus
Company.

The department not only fought fires but also performed other accomplishments
for the Java Community. During the year of 1925, the department purchased
restaurant equipment from an Aberdeen concern. Bill Moser, Sr., hauled it to
Java and put it in a building owned by Jacob Helm. Arend Lakeman, Sr., purchased
that building and operated a leading cafe for many years.

On Friday evening, Mar. 27, 1936, the fire fighters presented a play "Colored
Minstrel" at the Java High School auditorium. Frank Heezen directed the play and
I.R. Krause the music. This was a great success, which was enjoyed by the
citizens of Java and surrounding areas.

The annual fish fry between Java and Mobridge departments began in 1938 and
continued until around 1995. This was a joyous and good-fellowship affair,
creating companionship.

Firemen in 1974 were: Russell Bender, Mike Darling, Robert Goetz, Arlo Fiedler,
Gerhardt Fiedler, Oliver Goetz, Raymond Goetz, Clifford Grenz, Ron Ketterling,
Merlyn Melcher, Julius Pfitzer, Robert Pfitzer, Fred Walther, James Wilhelm,
Julius Wolf, and Marvin Wolf.

Honorary Members: Harold Fiedler, Edward Goetz, Louis Horst, Sam Spiry, and
Berthold Schnaible.

Present Firemen are: Ed Allbee, Heath and Larry Bermel, Dan Biel, Ralph Bond,
Arlo Fiedler, Jerry Goetz, Leslie Noess, Alan Schaefer, Jerry Schreter, and
Marvin Wolf. Dwight Helm serves as Assistant Chief and Gary Fiedler as
Secretary-Treasurer.

The local firemen attend a fire school every year, adding to their proficiency.
Meetings are held every month, where films are shown to keep the firemen updated
on procedures. The equipment is checked during these meetings.

Telephone lines were installed in 1977 in a few business places and in a few
firemen's homes to handle fire calls.

Two CBs were installed in the fire trucks in 1978.

Fundraisers by the Volunteer Fire Department have been annual dances, sausage
feeds and serving the evening meals at the annual Java Kuchen Festivals.

In 1974, an annual Steak Fry was begun as an appreciation for the firemen and
their families.

The fire hall was moved to the "Band Building" at the south end of Main Street
in 1994. The Firemen donated many personal hours to remodel the building.

JAVA FIRE DISTRICT
The Java Fire District was organized in the spring of 1994. Officers elected
were Ted Schneider, president; Les Rau, vice president; Steve Biel, secretary-
treasurer; and Arnold Lutz and Norwin Walz members-at-large. The District,
funded by taxes, was organized for the purpose of providing fire protection for
residents of Campbell and Walworth Counties who reside within the district.

In 1996, the Board purchased a used Chevrolet pickup with fire fighting
equipment, with the aid of a Rural Development loan. Additional clothing and
equipment has been purchased for the Fire District. Expenses for local firemen
to attend annual training schools to further their education have also been
paid. A very successful fund-raiser in the form of a pancake and sausage feed
was held Feb. 6, 1999.

The 1999 Board consists of Roger Hirsch, president, Robert Seyer, vice
president, Christine Schaefer, secretary-treasurer, and Cornelius Schnaible and
Dan Schneider, members-at-large.

EMERGENCY MEDICAL SERVICES
Emergency Medical Services is a system of care for victims of sudden and serious
illness and injury.

Ambulances in the early 1960's were often called Horizontal Taxi Cabs. They were
designed to carry patients in a horizontal position, but did not allow for
attendants to perform CPR. Morticians ran many ambulances.

In June 1962, the Ray Mile Funeral Home in Mobridge gave Selby their first
ambulance, the first one of three hearses. In May 1964 McGlurie Funeral Service
replaced it; the old one was traded in. In 1968, a Cadillac replaced the second
ambulance and in 1974, a Ford was purchased. In 1992, the Selby Volunteer
Ambulance received a $20,000 grant from SD 1st EMS Improvement Grant Program,
for a new ambulance. The State awarded Selby Ambulance $20,000 matching grant
fund and the Walworth County Commissioners agreed to aid the Selby Ambulance
Service with $25,500 in funding to replace the 1977 model with a 1992 model. The
Selby Ambulance Service contributed the remaining $16,754. The City of Selby
purchased a radio in Dec. 1992.

In 1966, most Ambulance attendants had little or no medical training. The
training that they did get was through the Red Cross. In 1969, the Emergency
Medical Technician came into being with a training course of 81 hours. The EMT
Ambulance was trained for basic life support procedures and administering CPR.

The Selby Fire Department and the Selby Ambulance purchased the Jaws of Life in
Feb. 1993, with a cost of $6,850. This replaces the use of crow and pry bars.

The Selby Ambulance purchased an AED (Automated Electronic Defibrillator) in
June 1996. This was purchased through grants and donations. The machine is used
mainly for heart attack victims to stabilize the electrical impulses of the
heart.

In the fall of 1987, 13 individuals from the Selby area participated in a three-
month training course for Emergency Medical Technician. There are three active
charter members, who are LaMoyle Aman, Josie Holder and Roger Walker. In 1991, a
class for EMT's was held, gaining eight new members, Patti and Roger Bauman,
Rick Eisemann, Rosalyn Manharth, LaDean Moak, Myron Moos, Becky Ruzsa, and Alan
Schorg. There are now 11 EMT's serving the Selby and surrounding area. Their
purpose as EMT's is to serve the community and surrounding area and give the
best care possible, personal and professional. The use of 911 came into the area
in 1996 and is very effective.

Most of the area EMT's have held an office. Officers at this time are: President
Roger Walker, Vice president LaDean Moak, Secretary LaMoyle Aman, and Treasurer
Rosalyn Manharth.

JAVA POST OFFICE
Early in July 1975, members of SD's Congressional Delegation announced that the
U.S. Postal Service was seeking bids for a new postal facility in the Town of
Java, SD. Initially, the facility was to contain 1404 net square feet in its
interior, and its location was to be within a block of the existing post office
building. Interested persons with desirable locations were to contact the
Postmaster. The Postal Service would lease the building for a period of 10
years, plus four renewal options, each of a five-year duration.

About the middle of Oct. 1975, the Postal Service awarded a contract of Rath,
Inc. of Eureka, to build a structure containing a net interior of 1276 square
feet. At about the same time, a first class mail service improvement program was
put into effect. Under this program, first class mail was to receive service
that was equal to, or surpass, the service of airmail.

Early in Feb. 1976, a problem arose when an order stopping construction of the
new post office building, was issued. One of SD's Congressional Delegations
protested the work stoppage order to the Postmaster General. At this time the
Java Post Office was serving 122 rural patrons and 127 town box holders.

Locally, petitions were circulated, protesting the work stoppage as well as the
possibility of eventual closure of the post office. A District Postal Manager
was contacted, and a meeting with the contractor was held, as well as with town
officials and postal patrons. It was learned that many post offices were being
considered for reorganization rather than closure, and this hastened the order
to stop construction.

About the 20th of Feb. 1976, word had been received that Java would not lose its
post office, and that construction would soon resume on the new building. It was
learned from the District Postal Manager that the opposition to the work
stoppage was more than was anticipated. He also added that, even though the
building would be completed, the postal service was still desirous of
implementing some economy in the post office.

On Sept. 10, 1976, an Open House was held at the new Java Post Office. Area
people were invited to view the facility and to partake of refreshments. Local
efforts in circulating petitions, which gather over 375 signatures as well as
outright opposition by the patrons and their Congressional Delegation, proved
successful so that Java was able to retain their postal service.

SOUTH DAKOTA PUBLIC BROADCASTING SERVICE
In early July 1975, it became known that a new transmitter, plus an antenna, was
to be located near Lowry. The 1975 Legislature provided for funding of this
facility, and the new station, when completed would be connected with the other
six existing Public Broadcasting Service Stations, through microwave.

The station was scheduled to provide a complete public service program was well
as five hours per day of instructional TV for elementary and secondary
education. The station, to be received on Channel 11, was assigned the call
letters KQSD, and would transmit to Campbell, Dewey, Edmunds, Faulk, McPherson,
Potter, Sully, and Walworth counties, and the northern portions of Hand, Hughes
and Stanley counties.

By early Oct., the tower had arrived at the sit and Allied Construction Co., of
Wichita Falls, TX, began construction. Unfavorable windy conditions hampered
construction of the tower during the early stages and continued to be a major
factor in delaying the construction progress. The height of the tower was a 325
feet in early Dec., and by mid-Dec., was at 660 feet. Windy and cold weather
conditions kept construction off schedule.

The transmitter for the station was housed in a steel building near the base of
the 750-foot tower, and technicians had busied themselves with the wiring
installation, and by mid-Dec., had completed the work on the broadcasting
station. After the tower was completed, an 80-foot antenna was added on top. By
early Mar., wintry weather again hampered the final preparations. As soon as
weather conditions permitted, the work was completed and a regular program
schedule was begun, providing additional TV to viewers in Java and surrounding
areas.

5-COUNTY TRANSLATOR DISTRICT
Shortly after the 1979 new year, word was received that the proposed 5-county
translator district had been given approval. According to officials of the
district, a contract had been given to the EMCEE Corporation to begin
construction of the necessary facilities to bring TV from the three major
networks on SD channels. A transmission tower and relay towers would be
utilized, with the existing tower near Lowry, and would be a part of the system.

At first, it was hoped that work could be completed in four or five months.
During the early stages, windy weather conditions hampered progress. Other
problems also arose, which required negotiation and by mid-Aug., it was apparent
that the construction phase would require additional time. Work progressed
slowly and in early Oct., a defective part had to be replaced. By the end of
Oct., most of the equipment had been received.

As work continued and the equipment installed, additional negotiations were
necessary. Testing and adjusting the signals of all three channels were
completed by mid-Dec. Call signs for the translators at the Lower tower site
were as follows:

Channel 56: CBS, K56AX, signal originated at Reliance, SD. KPLO.

Channel 62: ABC, K62AV, signal originated at Mitchell. KXON.

Channel 68: NBC, K68BM, signal originated at Presho. KRPY.

Call sign for the Roscoe site, Channel 59, ABC, K59BL, signal originated from
Aberdeen Cable Co.

Various degrees of success in reception was noted in the area, some receiving
good pictures without the UHF antennas, others having better reception with
antennas. With the antennas and receiver sets properly tuned and adjusted,
reception was generally very good, offering Java and the surrounding area a
higher quality of TV reception.

SENIOR CITIZENS NUTRITION PROGRAM
Ron Dolin from the Greater Missouri Development Association of Lemmon met with
the members of the Java Legion and Auxiliary in the fall of 1980. Arrangements
were made to serve meals at the Java Legion Hall, using the kitchen facilities
in the building. Iris Neumiller was hired as the coordinator, and the first
meals were brought Jan. 6, 1981.

Initially, the meals were cooked at Herreid, with Green Thumb workers Art and
Freida Zimmerman, of Herried, transporting them. Iris was coordinator until
1983, when Viola (Ray) Goetz took the position.

A tragic accident occurred in Aug. 1984 while Art and Freida Zimmerman were
delivering the meals from Herried. Art was killed at the scene and Freida passed
away several months later. Clarence Bauer then delivered the meals.

After another meeting with Ron Dolin, Sept. 1984, it was decided that the Java
Legion Hall kitchen would be used for cooking the noon meals for Java and Selby.
The kitchen was remodeled and Delila Biel was hired as cook in Nov. 1984.
Priscilla Mueller was hired to help cook until the Selby Senior Citizens
building was completed in 1986. Verda Schaffer served as substitute cook. Butch
Wolf and later, Virgil Biel, transported the meals.

After Delila retired in Aug. 1993, Dolores Schreter became the cook and Verda
Schaffer continued serving as substitute cook. In 1996, the Lemmon office was
closed and Java became part of Area IV at Aberdeen.

Leon and Nettie Kast were instrumental in getting the nutrition program started
in Java, and served as volunteers. Leon was chosen to represent Java as its
delegate to the council meetings. He retired from that position in 1988 and Gus
Schaffer became the delegate and served on the board until 1998. The first board
members of the Java Nutrition Site, in 1987, were Burton Sheffner, Marvin Wolf,
John Zeller, Nettie Kast and Verda Schaffer.

Gus Schaffer has been delivering meals to the shut-ins since around 1986. This
home delivery program provides nutritional home cooked meals to adults who are
confined to their homes.

JAVA PUBLIC LIBRARY
The Java Public Library became a reality in the spring of 1987, through the
efforts of a group of volunteers, under the auspices of the Java Arts Council.

Books and videos were acquired by numerous donations. The original Board
consisted of Warren Aman, Lary Dobson, Carol Fiedler, LaRayne Schlepp and Gloria
Zimmerman. The members rolled up their sleeves and, with the consent of the city
council, cleaned up the main portion of City Hall on 1st Avenue. They
constructed shelves and stocked them with the books. Margaret (Roy) Berreth was
hired as part-time Librarian.

For a time, the Board held weekly Bingo sessions to augment their meager funds,
but due to poor attendance, this was discontinued.

All work done at the Library is on a voluntary basis, supplied mainly by the
members of the present Board, who are Carol Fiedler, Oscar Fiedler, Jr., Yvonne
Helm, LaRayne Schlepp and Gloria Zimmerman. Gloria and LaRayne serve as
Librarians.

"Hopefully, the year 2000 will find the Library going strong, serving the
community of Java with an abundance of good reading material well into the next
century."

The following piece originally appeared in the South Dakota Magazine, Yankton,
SD, Jan-Feb 1992. The Java Centennial History Book Committee has express
permission to publish "The Great Java Stakeout" (unedited) from author,
Copyright holder and Java High School graduate (Class of  1954) Marvin C.
Hoffer. Thanks, Marv!

THE GREAT JAVA STAKEOUT

The Northern Plains of South Dakota are generally a quiet part of the planet,
but long about 1953, or so, there was a flurry of small town robberies that had
that touch of professionalism about them. Numerous little towns were "hit" by
what appeared to be a better-than-average gang who easily robbed feed stores,
hotels, and any business that they chose to, in the black of night. Word quickly
spread among the small farming villages and towns (that is a village with a
mayor) that a slick bunch of thieves were rampaging through the Dakotas and
"knocking over", or was it "knocking off", every mattress, cigar box, safe, and
till around. No evidence, no observations. "They sure know what they are doing!"
Local sheriff and town marshals had no clues, except a smelly cigar butt, and
matchbook from a restaurant in London. England, that is.

It was rumored that "The Gang", as it was known by, was driving a high-powered
auto, with plenty of speed, as they eased into a sleeping town where the only
thing awake at 2 a.m. is a calico tomcat serenading his true love on the back
fence. They always seemed to know what to rob, and when. Was this an inside job?
Is somebody getting a percentage?

Java, S.D., the Coffee Town, sits almost on top of the Continental Divide, east
of the Missouri River and west of the Mississippi. The Divide is all of 3200
feet elevation - doesn't quite give you a nosebleed as you mosey over the top.
In fact, the only evidence of the Divide is that the Milwaukee Railroad had to
put on extra steam engines at Aberdeen to pull

the grade west, then dive into the Missouri River Valley at Mobridge. Java, and
its residents, all 400 or so, were certain it was only a matter of time till The
Gang hit a safe, or two, on a moonless night. Fearful business, this robbery
stuff.

The Town Marshal was Fritz Stetterhock, and his son Edgar, or "Turk", as he was
better known as, was his genuine deputy. Turk was a Navy veteran, and a boxer of
note who thought some form of resistance and vigilance was necessary to stave
off The Gang,

His father, the Marshall, tended the town during daylight. Both kept trained
eyeballs to the East. They definitely weren't looking for the Wise Men. It was
rumored that The Gang roared out of the Twin Cities. Minisoda, that is. Everyone
knew that St. Paul and Minneapolis harbored thieves and renegades. Even has a
house of ill-repute, where lutefisk, lefse, and day old krumkakka are served hot
off the smorgasbord. Sinful part of Minisoda. There is even something about St.
Paul in the Old Testament. Makes sense now that I look back on it - yep, The
Gang came from the Twin Cities alright. Sometimes you have to look reality
smack-dab in the eye, and ignore it.

Turk got the short end of the law stick by inheriting the night shift. Long
about early summer Turk enlisted a cadre of unfit, daring, but willing, young
men from the Plains, who were plumb fed-up with talking about The Gang while
shooting pool at the Biezemann Pool Hall, for a nickel a game. My brother Al and
I were among the trusty, undeputized, marshals-to-be. Must have been about six
of us. Local gossip had it that as a group we were 2-3 bales short of a full
load. But then, the gossipers were not volunteering! Turk gave us his latest
theory how to capture thieves, and positioned most of us at what he believed
were strategic locations, although he didn't use those big words.

On such safe, but strategic location, was atop the Red Owl Store on Main Street.
We reached this lofty spot by way of a rickety ladder with three rungs missing
propped against the rear of the store, then shuffled across slippery wooden
shingles like hogs on thin ice to ease-up against the rear of the false store
front. From there, even a weak-eyed fellow could see clean up northwest to the
Lutheran Cemetery and points beyond into Nort Dakota, as well as hear any
approaching vehicles on the crunchy gravel streets and roads from all corners of
the globe. A Command Post, if I every saw one. The only thing higher and more
commanding was the silver city water tower, 100 feet short, with a single light
bulb at the pinnacle that only Hank Gramwiesz, the town blacksmith, was brave
enough to change now and then.

Turk stationed a few brazen junior mounties around the Main Street in the belief
that The Gang surely would "hit one of the stores in the Java Business District
this night". Doubt that any store owners realized that their business was in a
district. Almost had a ring of immorality about it. The rest of the trusty,
undeputized marshals-in-the-making were drinking orange soda pop, straight, and
coffee laced with milk down in the American Legion Hall basement, also on Main.
Sort of a weak reserve force. This was the genuine Command Post, the Big One, in
that it had a live telephone. Turk, nor anyone else, ever informed any of us
who, or where, we should call, or why, in the event of a robbery, or even the
hint of one. Was comforting to known that we had a telephone at our fingertips
though. Modern, well organized? This was 1953, mind you.

Roll call for these duties was always done by "nick name". Never the pedigreed
title they hung around your neck at birthing time. So we answered to Stiffle,
Satch, Gator, Boone, Turk, Polio, Squirt, etc. Each name had great social value,
and was descriptive of real or avowed attributes. Parents were informed that
their young, brave sons were performing great public service. Parents didn't
think much about it, figuring it would all blow over like a prairie
thunderstorm. Java slept on...

Was long about a Friday eve when Turk positioned his dubious sidekicks on top
the Red Owl, "Gator" (my younger brother) on the front porch of a private home
on Main, and Turk "laid low" near the Equity Service Station and grain elevators
at the north end of Main. He had his father's genuine, 38 caliber revolver,
rumored to work, and a big 6-cell flashlight. The warmth of the early summer
afternoon had turned to a cool, but comfortable, evening with only a two dozen
fat mosquitoes per deputy. It was as dark as the inside of an Angus bull that
night, but the Main Street lights shown bravely like candles in a Dakota
blizzard. I recall that there was always more dark than light.

Stiffle, Satch, and Boone (that's me) hunkered down on the roof of the Red Owl
listening for evil to strike this sleepy little Germanic town. The Lord Mayor,
Samuel Spitzer, also the Legion Commander, had sanctioned this escapade, in the
belief that it was better than sleeping through a big robbery. The proverbial
Scout motto "Be prepared" came into play here. We made little noise, shown no
lights, nor did anything that might tip off the thousand and one thieves we
thought might be within earshot of our lofty perch. We tried to read each
other's lips in the dark instead of whispering, but we could have communicated
better by sending messages in Mandarin Chinese. Each of us had this spontaneous
urge to trip fantastic to the outhouse when someone (?) started climbing the
wobbly ladder at the back of the Red Owl. Fear, raw, gut-wrenching fear, came
over us like a dark shroud. It was about 25 feet to the concrete sidewalk below,
so jumping was not an option, although Stiffle appeared committed to that route
in that he had one leg dangling over the edge. Turk puffed from the ladder, "Ya
guys see anyting?" After we had our basic body functions under control, more or
less, we all agreed that we had not, and mumbled "nuttin." Never mentioned to
Turk that fear can blind a man sure as putting him in a black sack.

Then we saw the lights! Car lights! Sneaking, we were sure, into town by way of
the northwest passage up by the cemetery, about a strong half-mile from out
Observation Post. Turk scrunched down behind the store's false front as we said,
"How can day be comin' from the Vest, da Twin Cities are east of Jafa?"
Sometimes our German heritage oozed into our speech and "v" became "f". We now
were positive that Java was on The List for this night's robberies. It was a
shade more certain than a hunch. By now the car with weak, pitifully weak,
headlights clattered across the old railroad tracks at the north end of town,
making tons of noise on the dry gravel street. What robbers would leave their
lights on and make that much racket unless they were heavily armed, and mighty
sure of themselves? Bladders began to rhythmically, then frantically, urge their
keepers to ease the situation, but we all lay petrified on the roof in utter
certainty that "this was the Big One!" This law enforcement business had a
desperate side to it. We must have been standing too long in the sun to hire-on
for this duty!

No one had any idea how we could get to the telephone across the street at the
Command Post and alert Washington, D.C. that is. The White House, any outhouse,
or anyone about our impending doom. Panic set upon all of us. Swift and
absolute! Surface evidence of panic was uncontrolled twitching, spastic legs and
arms, holding your breath for fifteen minutes, and drooling out of both sides of
one's mouth at the same time. There was an implication of level-headidness about
this handicap.

Slowly the car eased up the hill (Java is built on a glaciated prairie pinnacle)
and drove on south. Turk blurted "That's Ollie Swenson!" Sure enough it was
Ollie. Heck, we knew it was Ollie all along. We weren't slow, but weren't swift
either. Could tell by how the left headlight shone straight into the ground, and
the right beacon was weaker than the left.

Turk left his trusty band of spooked non-deputies and headed for the Equity, his
favorite outpost at the rear of the Service Station. He had barely walked across
the street and disappeared into the dark side of night, when a long black car,
without lights, slithered quietly out of the side street down by the G&L Store.
It happened so fast, that we thought it must be Ollie looping around for another
tour of Main at midnight, but the lights weren't on so we weren't positive. The
powerful engine, with all eight cylinders purring, and the shape of it nixed
that thought. Fast! My left leg began quaking with spasms and my mouth got so
dry that I couldn't spit. Wasn't fear, mind you --- just intense concern. Made
things pucker-up that had never puckered-up before.

The sleek black auto stopped near the Equity Service Station, about 100 feet
from where Turk, our "Night Marshall", was hunkered-down behind the waste oil
barrels. His revolver was cached in its leather pocket around his girth. Turk
was a bit pugnacious, brave, bold maybe. He let loose with his best commanding
voice into the dark pit of night "Whatja ya guys want round here? Huh?" All this
while shining his trusty 6-cell flashlight at the car from behind the oil
barrels. From the black car came the bright orange blast of a pistol aimed at
Turk's weak light. The bullet tore a big hunk out of the pitch black night, as
Turk dropped his light, and burrowed deep into the dirt. He was petrified on his
knees like a Muslim in deep prayer, deeper the better.

The car threw up a rooster tail of gravel as it roared up Main and south out of
town at speeds we estimated from our perch atop the Red Owl Store at over 100
miles per hour, give or take 60 or so. Gator was hunkered-down low behind the
enclosed front porch of the private home on north Main as the action roared by.
Best I can recall, after almost 40 winters, is that he was armed with a -22 cal.
Special rifle. For the life of me I can't imagine today (1991) why he, at about
15 years young, would have a rifle for such an escapade, but so was the life
style way back when. In any event, he touched-off a few rounds of ammunition at
The Gang in their iron chariot because "it was the right thing to do" in the dim
light of the circumstances. Adrenaline flowed by the gallon, and we didn't even
know what the stuff was that made our eyes spin in different directions at once,
and made us feel twelve feet tall. This entire shoot-out at the Not-Okey Correl
was without a script, and you played out the scene as it rolled by. No retakes,
just "live". This was in the days before the boob tube. Here was a young sprout
that hadn't shaved yet, decked-out in a pair of Osh-By-Gosh bib overalls, and a
pair of hand-me-down shoes, doing law-and-order battle with experienced outlaws.
A parents nightmare. Serious stuff!!

Quiet descended on our world like hot gravy over cold mashed potatoes after The
Gang in its souped-up escape machine roared south at the speed of light. We
conjured-up numerous scenarios as to how Turk had fared in the face of withering
fire in the battle zone. It must have been hours later, so it seemed, when Satch
braved the trip down the ladder with Stiffle and me sneaking along behind.
Stiffle mumbled something about his wet left pant leg. My legs had a terrible
case of the shakes, and reacted to my forceful commands on the steep ladder like
two hunks of overdone spaghetti.

We hunkered mighty close to the protective dark recesses of historic buildings
as we slithered down to where we expected to find Turk in a pool of dark blood,
next to the waste oil barrels, behind the Equity Service Station. We found Turk.
He was on his knees checking his revolver to see how many shots he had fired. He
was fully alive, and kicking, no holes in his hide. Hadn't fired a shot. He was
absolutely positive that he had blasted all six rounds in the heat of battle,
but couldn't recall reloading. Stress will do that to a man, you know. The mind
fogs over, and turns to cold mush. Eyes glaze like frost on a window pane, and
you can't recall your middle name, or even if you had one.

Well, we all stumbled knock-kneed like a gaggle of drunks to the Legion Hall
Command Post to hold a "post-battle discussion". More to brag and recite lies,
then truth. Turk was the Hero of the Decade for routing The Gang who were going
to steal Java blind that night. We all had a hand in the action, and no-one was
injured. Pure, undiluted luck, with a bucket of stupidity thrown in. You would
think we all just stumbled down the gangway. Huh?

The Gang apparently henceforth and evermore eased into Minisoda to harass, those
"Norvegians" with their barns full of ripe lutefisk and their fields full of
purple rune stones. But we were dead wrong! Now for the rest of the story. We
learned after daylight crept out of the East like molasses on a winter day, that
the local "Mounties" had captured The Gang south of Java on old highway #12, the
Yellowstone Trail. Their trusty and souped-up black chariot was snorting much
steam like Old Unfaithful because Gator had luckily (?) pumped a couple of shots
into the power plant radiator, and they came to an inglorious and untimely halt
a long way from their Twin Cities hangout.

The "news" inflated various skinny hairless chests like a Holstein udder that
hadn't been milked for three days. Apparently The Gang was employed for some
years making license plates at the S.D. penitentiary in Sioux Falls. Or they may
have "gotten-off light" for good behavior. At ages I estimate to be about
mid-70s, or more now, they are swatting mosquitoes on the front porch somewhere
in nortern Minisoda, while munching on leftover beer cheese on stale lefse.
Crime maybe doesn't pay?

The sound of genuine gunfire, roaring engine, and gut-wrenching fear race across
my memory like an old movie, when I recall that wild night, way back when, of
the Great Java Would-Be Robbery.


                   SPECIAL EVENTS & OBSERVATIONS

"DAYS OF 1883"
A unique celebration, depicting the days of the opening of this section of the
state when the first sod of soil was turned, was planned for Aug. 28 and 29,
1932, by the people of Java and the surrounding area. A ballgame, parade with
floats representing the days of 1883, a display of relics and other articles
used in those days, an open-air program, band concerts, programs, and dances at
the various halls were planned. The biggest event planned was a rodeo, held at
the ballpark.

Chairmen were William Kunz and Fritz Clement, and A.C. Schlepp was elected
secretary. The Finance Committee consisted of Jacob Helm and J.F. Perman. I.R.
Krause, C.F. Spiry and L.L. Helm were serving on the Program Committee. The
Street Sport Committee included F. Clement, John Lutz and Reinhold Baker, while
Arend Lakeman, Ed Gill and Adolph Pfaff worked on the Parade. Jacob Helm was in
charge of the Speaker Committee and F. Clement, John Schadler and August Doerr
were on the Advertising Committee. Bill Hepper, in charge of the Rodeo, secured
the services of several professionals to compete in the Aug. 29th rodeo. L.L.
Helm headed the Baseball Committee, William Kunz and C.F. Spiry were in charge
of the Relic Committee, and serving on the Music Committee were I.R. Krause and
A.C. Schlepp.

(Photo:) John Haux drove the team with Gov. Green and Joe Parmley as riders in
         the 1883 Celebration parade

People in nearby districts were appointed to gather relics and help line up
floats for the parade. From the Highland District: J.C. Schlepp, I.C. Krause and
C.M. Haux; Adams District: Christ H. Wolff and Ed Merkel; Spring Lake District:
E.E. Erbe and Donal Stangl; Spring Valley District: Glen Powell and Fred Seyer;
Ryan District: Fred Bieber and Andrew Bauer; and John Kary and Mr. Geigle from
the Ackerman District.

Among the rodeo participants were the McMacken brothers, Joe and Francis, of
Trail City, who were famous for their ability with bronco riding and
bulldogging. They took part in rodeos at Madison Square Garden in New York, and
many other large rodeos all over the U.S. They brought with them wild broncos
and trick horses for an exhibition.

The two-day celebration was touted as one of the most successful celebrations
ever staged in Java or nearby cities. The big event began on Sunday with a ball
game between Mobridge and Java, with Mobridge winning 1-0 after nine innings of
"real fast baseball." Festivities began Monday morning with a mammoth parade,
which featured old time costumes, vehicles from the by-gone days when this
country was founded. Three prizes were awarded for the best floats; the ox-drawn
cart by John Haux taking first; the sod shanty of John Bauer and Wm. Jesser,
second; and Arend Lakeman and J.C. Schlepp's paper covered shack took third.

Mayor Wm. Kunz gave an address on Main Street, immediately after the parade, to
begin the open-air program. His address was followed by short talks about their
experiences in the old days by the following pioneers: B.P. Adams and H.P. Hall
of Mobridge, John Erbe of Bowdle, G.W. Ryan of Java, Arne Strand of SW of Java,
and Geo. Zeller of Eureka. Nettie Kunz, Freda Jesser, Vivian Bauer and Mrs. A.W.
Spiry sang several songs in costume, and Vivian Bauer also gave a solo. The
comic number hugely enjoyed by the crowd, by the six minstrels included Ed,
Wilfred and Ervin Kunz, Henry Hauck, Levi Krause and Arthur Buckenberger.

The "Hungry German Five" in costume, consisting of I.R. Krause, Sam E. Spiry,
J.C. Schlepp, Rueben Schlaht and A.C. Schlepp, furnished music during the day.

The rodeo was probably the most outstanding event, with about 2000 people in
attendance. They watched the McMacken brothers, a group of riders from Lowry and
several outside riders who showed their riding and bulldogging skills. Gov.
Warren E. Green and Joe Parmley spoke to a large crowd after the rodeo.

Various street sports, and dancing in the evening, rounded out one of the
biggest days ever held in Java. The Art B. Thomas carnival shows were on the
midway.

At the Herald office, 295 pioneers registered and obtained ribbons.

Violet Neumiller Aman said: "Days of 1883 were held more years than just one.
The McMacken Brothers of Trail City and the Crawfords from Lowry organized the
Rodeo and, I believe, provided the stock or animals for the Rodeo. J. McMacken
was married to Grace Noble, daughter of Philip Noble. He had surgery and was not
supposed to ride that day, and when he got off the bull or horse, he collapsed
and died. Hepper bought five big steers from my dad, Christ Neumiller, for $100,
to use in the Rodeo."

(Photo:) Costumes were the order of the day at Days of 1883

JAVA GOLDEN JUBILEE
The people of Java and surrounding areas celebrated Fifty Years of progress on
June 14 and 15, 1950. Wednesday, June 14, was designated as Farmers and Old
Timers Day with a morning parade beginning the festivities. An introductory
program, with speakers and musicians, followed the parade. After the noon meal,
Ipswich played Java in a baseball game at the ballpark. The Johnny Steen Rodeo
was held north of town and then the kids, up to age 14, were entertained with
street sports. The Java Band gave an evening concert, shows were held at the
Grand Theatre, and Paul Opsahl, Pres. of the State Farmers Union, gave a speech.
Free Stage Acts were performed with Glen Burklund, concertina artist, Marguerite
Burklund, soloist, and Kenneth Spencer, internationally known ventriloquist. The
Golden West Carnival was on the Midway, and dancing took place at night.

(Photo:) 1950 Jubilee Parade. Albert Bender and Reuben Schmierer in buggy,
         Marvin Gross is standing

After the parade on Thurs. morning, Good Neighbors Day, the Mobridge Band gave a
concert. Again, street sports were held, this time for kids of all ages, and
Java's Little German Band provided music. Joe Robbie, then Democratic candidate
for Governor, gave a speech, followed by a baseball game between Eureka and
Java. The Honorable Gov. George T. Mickelson gave a speech before the Whisker
Judging Contest. In the evening, the Mobridge Band held a concert, which was
followed by a speech from the secretary of the Aberdeen Chamber of Commerce,
Geo. Bassingwaite. The Burklunds and Mr. Spencer again performed on stage, and
the celebration ended with good dancing to good music.

(Photo:) Kary float "Living in the early days" in 1950 Jubilee Parade

Members of the executive committee in charge of Java's Golden Jubilee
celebration were Joe Zarka, Elmer Biel, Harold Spiry, J.J. Lutz, Reinhold Moser
and Gottlieb Zeller. A.C. Schlepp was chairman of the executive committee, John
Zeller was chairman of the finance committee, Marvin Gross was sports committee
chairman and C.L. Hicks, a member of the finance committee.

(Photo:) On 1950 Parade float are Betty (Zeller) Biel under trellis, Bonita
         (Moser) Spiry and Shirley (Bieber) Kast at front

JAVA DIAMOND JUBILEE
In anticipation of the Java Diamond Jubilee to be held Thursday, Friday and
Saturday, June 12, 13 and 14, 1975, the town was buzzing, or not buzzing if one
was a Brother of the Brush. Committees were formed, chairmen appointed, and
activities planned. Marvin Wolf was named the General Chairman on the Executive
Committee, accompanied by Wes Frank, vice chairman, Emma (Herman) Fiedler,
second vice chairman, Nettie (Leon) Kast, secretary and Oscar Schnaible,
treasurer.

(Photo:) Java's Diamond Jubilee Parade

Other committees were: Advertising, Merlyn Melcher, chairman, John Zeller,
Julius Pfitzer and Henry H. Wolff; Publicity: Mrs. Marvin Pfitzer, chairman,
Mrs. Otto Schnaible and Gloria (Ernest) Zimmerman; Pictures and Antiques: Maggie
(Albert) Kary, chairman, LeRoy Bender, Martha (Henry H.) Wolff, and Mr. and Mrs.
Julius Stangl; Street Sports: Floyd Biel, chairman, Calvin Wolff and Ted
Schneider; Historical: Erna (Elmer) Schlepp, chairman, Lillian (Christ) Pfitzer,
Harold Spiry, Eileen (Rueben) Schmierer, LeRoy Bender, and Fritz, Ida and Bruce
Clement; Carnival: Robert Pfitzer, chairman, Marvin Pfitzer and Merlyn Melcher
(Chuck's Enterprises of Sioux Falls was secured for the event.); Parade: Elmer
Schlepp, chairman, Sandy and Paul Jacobs, Bradley Bender, and Mr. and Mrs. Mike
Darling (Two parades were held.); Dances: Java Legion arranged for all dances;
Sod House: Elmer Schlepp, chairman; Souvenir Committee: Frances (Gary) Naasz,
chairman, Mr. and Mrs. Fred C. Bieber, Mr. and Mrs. Harold Fiechtner, and Mr.
and Mrs. Gerhardt Fiedler; and Evening Program Committee: Freida (Ellsworth)
Schuh, chairman, Cornelius and Loretta Schnaible, Ellsworth Schuh, Mr. and Mrs.
Don Sauer, and Ann and Harold Schreter.

The Java Brothers of the Brush held "Kangaroo Court" Friday night following the
Herreid-Java game. Harlan "Blackie" Krause was accused of shaving; he pled not
guilty. Christ Pfitzer had introduced the case to the court. Harold Schreter was
the attorney for Brothers; Defense Attorney Bob Seyer was asleep on the job.
Arresting officers were Dick Biel and Joel Fiechtner. Tried by a jury of six
members of the Brothers of the Brush, Blackie was found guilty, fined 50 cents,
and sentenced to sit perfectly still through the Java-McLaughlin basketball
game Tuesday.

Harold and Chris Pfitzer were tried for starting their beards too early, and
both pled not guilty. The venerable judge, referred to as "your ornery", was
Harvey Rau; bailiff was Bob Pfitzer. After a fine job of interrogating the
prisoners by Attorney Schreter, and a rather weak case presented by Defense
Attorney Seyer, the jury found both guilty. The sentence? 50 cents each in
fines, and they were to sweep the floor at half-time of a basketball game the
next week. The Brothers of the Brush stated it might be necessary to hold
further trials at a later date. "Better be good boys, the Brothers are
watching!"

(Photo:) Java's 75th Birthday Parade

During "Kangaroo Court" held by the Java Sisters of the Swish, Marjorie Fiedler
pled for mercy from Judge Dorothy Schneider. Bailiff was Joyce Pfitzer. Erna
Schlepp and Lorraine Biel, partners in crime, escaped the grasp of Police
officials, Helen Sauer and Donna Bieber. An all-points bulletin was issued and
the fugitives were captured, taking refuge in the Schlepp's Cafe. Lorraine had
to wear a fake beard for wearing a "Brothers of the Brush" pin at a church
meeting, and Erna had to wear a large sign stating: I was a naughty "Sister of
the Swish" for losing her membership pin. Wife of football coach Walt Simons was
found guilty for going to work several times without wearing her membership pin.
She also had to wear the Naughty sign, for a week. Delores Schreter was found
guilty of showing off her Jubilee dress by wearing it on a day not designated by
the committee. She had to wear overalls to work at the Java school lunchroom.

Irene Fiedler was tried for wearing her dress too short, showing off her ankles.
Defense Attorney Mary Anne Krause tried to prove to the jury that their own
female members did indeed wear dresses shorter than Irene, but to no avail.
Irene had to wear overshoes the remainder of that evening. The Jury? Calvin
Aman, MaeNerva Bender, Diane Simons, Delores Schreter, Harlan Krause, Jeral
Schreter, Hilda Stangl and Anna Mueller.

Booster Trips provided excellent advertising and fun. The Boosters visited
Bowdle, Hosmer, Eureka, Ashley, Linton, Zeeland, Strasburg, Long Lake, Herreid
and Mound City. The next trip found them in Hoven, Gettysburg, Lowry and Akaska,
Selby, Glenham and Mobridge.

The Jubilee Book, Footprints, arrived in early June. The book contained over 200
pages and over 200 photos. This hard cover book sold for $8 back then. All
copies were sold.

(Photo:) Horseless Carriage in 1975 Jubilee Parade

Parade entries were judged during the first parade and awards given out the
second day. Trophies were presented to:

Jubilee Cup: Thimble Club, depicting early furnishings

Pioneer Cup: Merlyn Thorstenson, Selby, horse drawn header and box

Floats: 1st, Vivian's Beauty Shop, old and modern beautician equipment; 2nd,
Sew & So Extension Club, old and modern methods of washing clothes ; 3rd, Home
Arts, revolving birthday cake.

Horse Drawn: 1st, Covered wagon, Eureka; 2nd, Selmer Anderson, Cresbard, buggy;
Rueben Neumiller, buggy, 3rd.

Old Cars: Clarence Berg, Stockton, CA, 1929 Model A Ford, 1st; Bud Bader,
Mobridge, Model A Ford, 2nd; 3rd, Arlyn Erbe, Java, Model T Ford.

Junior Division: 1st, Pat Weisgram, Java, wagon and dog; 2nd, Deb Prasek, Selby,
funny bike; 3rd, Kevin Ackerman, Java, three-wheel bike and covered wagon.

Miscellaneous: 1st, Rueben Neumiller, horseless carriage driven by stationary
engine; 2nd, Jubilee Band by PTO group; and 3rd, Old Prospector from Mobridge,
with burro and pack.

Emcee Helmuth Beck acknowledged each float as a winner as it passed the
reviewing stand on the second day. Les Helm served as the other parade
announcer. The parades all started on time and went off like clockwork, thanks
to careful previous planning. Elmer Schlepp was parade chairman. Even the
weather cooperated, even though the wind was going at it a bit strong. Selby had
two good days and then there were thundershowers on Saturday, but they came
before the parade started in Selby, while at Java, they held off until after the
parade.

(Photo:) Happy 75th Birthday, Java!

Gerald and Alma (Merkel) Corson of Houston, TX, received plaques as the oldest
pioneer couple traveling the farthest for the Jubilee. Alice Kundert, SD State
Auditor, placed the Pioneer Crown on the head of Loy Miklos Sr., 90, at a
Pioneer program Friday morning. Pioneer Queen was Mrs. Louise Stangl, 92, both
long time residents of the Java area. Mr. and Mrs. Jake Haux were honored with a
plaque for being the longest married Pioneer couple (59 years) at the Jubilee.
Mr. and Mrs. Julius Krueger of Yakima, WA, were also recognized for their
marriage of 56 years. Mr. and Mrs. Clarence Berg of Stockton, CA, were given
recognition for driving a 1929 Model A touring car all the way from CA to Java.
Mrs. Edwin Aman was recognized as traveling the farthest, from Lodi, CA.

Entertainment consisted of music by The Family Tree, composed of Jon, Bernie and
Jeff Stulken, and Pat Stulken Russell, children of Hubert Stulken of Selby;
Janice Bender Wolf and her son played two selections on banjo and guitar; Debra
Sauer, age 8, daughter of Don Sauer, played piano; Tammy and Ivy Pfitzer, Scott
Sauer and Sue Bender presented several musical numbers on drum, guitar, organ
and tambourine; Paul Raba played several violin selections, accompanied by
Margaret Mertz; Rural Route Delivery, made up of Kathy and Mr. Friend, Angie
Marin, and Ole Neuman, Mobridge violinist, performed country music. Ricky Goetz,
drummer, joined them; Irene Raba sang and played the guitar; and the Selby
Jubilee Mens Chorus, which included men from Selby, Lowry, Java and Glenham,
performed under the direction of Micki Frankenstein.

Mobridge Jaycee members measured the beards for the Longest Beard, giving 1st
place to Harold Pfitzer and 2nd place to Albert Aman. Finalists in the Most
Handsome Beard were Glenn Hirsch, Ted Schneider, Albert Kary, Bob Pfitzer, and
Bob Machan. Jim Wilhelm received 1st, Albert Kary, 2nd, and Bob Machan, 3rd.
Henry Bender took top honors for the best-looking moustache. The stubble award,
Trying the Hardest, went to Harold Schreter.

Winners in the Sisters of the Swish Style Show were Cynthia Krause and Mrs.
Charles Pfitzer for the Oldest Original; Hazel Zeller, Natalie Spiry and
Priscilla Mueller for Duplicate of Original; Anna Mueller and five daughters,
Marjorie Fiedler and two daughters, and Shirley Rau and a daughter were winners
in the Mother-Daughter division; Four Generations winner went to Mrs. Adolph
Stangl and family, Ida Lutz and family and Katie Schneider and family; Jubilee
Dresses, ages 7 and under, went to Jodi Fiedler, Jami Fiechtner and Joyce Spiry.
In the 8-13 age group, Lori Biel, Lori Spiry and Tami Grenz took honors. In the

awards. In the adult division, Marjorie Fiedler, Alma Sonnenfeld and Ronette
Rader were winners.

An estimated 8,000 people attended the Jubilee, which ended with religious
services in the two churches.

Java and area residents commenced the celebration of Statehood on June 17-18,

wagon pulled by Belgian horses, was honored with 1st place in the Horse and

2nd and the Bank of Hoven won 3rd.

At the Kuchen Kitchen and Quilt Show, Java's famous Kuchen was so successful
that serving had to stop by 3 p.m. Saturday because there was no more remaining;
the ladies had to go back to their freezers for more, and that still wasn't
sufficient. A beautiful quilt display, sponsored by the Home Arts Club, was also

the Legion Hall.

KUCHEN FESTIVAL
Webster's dictionary describes kuchen as "a kind of German coffee cake made of
yeast dough and often frosted or filled with raisins, nuts, etc."

Rosina Baumann, who was born in Russia in 1902, said that kuchens were made with
a topping of sugar, butter, flour and cinnamon. It was called "rivela" in a
German cookbook. Kuchen, considered a delicacy, was expected at the table during
Christmas, Easter, and special family occasions. Each family passed the recipe
down through the generations, and the Germans from Russia brought their recipes
to the U.S. when they homesteaded in the 1800's. Every cook has a special
ingredient they like to use. Choices include cherry, cheese, prune, rhubarb or
sugar.

One day while Florence and Merle Noess, then owners of Java Super Valu, and Bea
Miklos, a store employee, were talking about how nice it would be to have a
customer appreciation day.

After a couple of meetings and two weeks of planning, the day was set. July 14,
1990, was the first of 10 years of a Kuchen Festival, sponsored by the Java
business community.

The kuchen was baked by members of the Java Senior Citizens and was the main
feature and free coffee was served all day. Visitors enjoyed a craft fair,
German dinner at the cafe, a softball game for the kids, a local talent show on
Main Street, square dancing, a greased pig contest, and a Tug o' War between
city and country men. Selby area men gave a Black Powder demonstration at City
Park, and a steak supper was enjoyed at the Community Cafe, with Kermit Kluz
providing music. The evening was topped off with Bingo in the school lunchroom,
sponsored by the Java Library Board, and dancing on Main to  music played by a
disc jockey.

The Java businesses all donated money to get the event started. Each year the
Festival has grown. Without the faithful people who donated Kuchen over the past
10 years, the event would not have been successful. It has taken many long
volunteer hours to keep the "Java" hot and projects continuing.

Dorothy Schneider, manager of the Java Community Cafe in 1990, had asked
Florence how meals to prepare for. Florence figured about 150. The noon meal
topped out a 250! No one went away hungry and all enjoyed the German dishes. A
year or so later, 500 people were served.

"It has been a lot of hard work by all who have helped in any way, with a very
rewarding feeling at the end of the day of a job well done," Florence said.

The third Saturday in June was the day set aside for the following 9 years as
"Java Kuchen Festival Day". The Java Centennial will continue the celebration
for the year 2000.

MEMORIAL DAY
Originally, Memorial Day, or Decoration Day, honored men who had died in the
Civil War. It now honors members of the American armed forces who gave their
lives for their country. Since the end of World War I, Memorial Day has also
been Poppy Day; the sales from the small, red artificial poppies help disabled
veterans.

In 1929, exercises for the annual observation of Memorial Day were held at the
high school auditorium. Chairman G.W. Ryan, and Assistant Chairman Kate Clement
arranged the committees who would be in charge of the various parts of the
program. The following committees were appointed: Program, Kate Clement,
Chairman, A.C. Schlepp, Agnes Gehrki, Mrs. Philip Noble; Decorating Graves, G.W.
Hicks, Chairman, J.E. Spiry, E.B. Moser; Seating Audience, Wm. Kunz, Chairman,
Martin Gehrki, C.F. Spiry, Philip Noble, John Bauer, Jr., John Schlaht; Flowers,
Mrs. F. Clement, Chairman, Myrtle Ewald, Mrs. P.H. Spiry, Mrs. C.L. Hicks, Mrs.
Jacob Helm; Decoration and Loyal Emblem for Hall, Mrs. Martin Gehrki, Chairman,
Mrs. Wm. Jesser, Evelyn Bauer, Mrs. W.C. Hicks, Mrs. John Schlaht, Mrs. G.W.
Hicks; Procuring Speaker, Wm. Kunz, Chairman, Arend Lakeman, P.H. Spiry, Fred E.
Bauer; Printing Programs, F. Clement.

The 1929 observation began at 2:30 p.m. and included the music of the Java
Municipal Band, a violin solo by Gladys Wolff, accompanied at the piano by Laura
Noble, a piano duet by Anges Gehrki and Vivian Bauer, and Flag Drill by a group
of girls under the direction of Grace Noble and Agnes Gehrki. Attorney Paul O.
Urban of Timber Lake gave the address in the "American language" and a part in
German. Geraldine Krause gave a reading, Annette and Nettie Spiry and Ida Kast
and Mae Aman performed a vocal quartette, Vivian Bauer sang a solo, with Agnes
Gehrki at the piano, and Hon. G.W. Ryan gave the Remarks.

Of interest is that, in 1931, the Memorial exercises included a parade of the
Selby American Legion Post members, their firing squad, and the Java Band, from
the schoolhouse to the depot. They proceeded to the cemetery NW of Java, where
short memorial services were held and a volley was fired over the grave of Henry
Spiry, who died while in service during World War I. Taps concluded this
service. The afternoon program included band music and singing, music from a
mixed chorus, a reading by Laura Noble, and an instrumental piece from trio A.C.
Schlepp and son, Gilbert, playing cornets, with Lenora Schlepp on the saxophone.
Then a flag drill by a group of boys and girls who deposited bouquets of flowers
near a tablet bearing the names of the Java community boys who had served in the
World War. Cecelia Krause and Elizabeth Noble directed the drill, and Vivian
Bauer accompanied on the piano. Laura Noble, Vivian Bauer and Clara Lange also
provided music. It was said that a large crowd represented the surrounding
communities at this exercise.

Java's observation of Memorial Day continued, and in 1948, the Legion Color
Guard performed the Advancement of Colors, Rev. L.A. Westenberger gave the
Invocation, Gilbert G. Schlepp (adjutant) directed the band, readings were given
by Marilyn Jacobs and Delores Schnaible, the Boys' Quartet, consisting of Harold
Schreter, Oscar Kapfenstein, Norwin and Orville Walz, gave a vocal selection,
Irene Kraft sang a solo, the Brass Ensemble performed a selection, and a group
of children, under the direction of Nettie (Henry T.) Hauck, did the flag drill.
The Legion Color Guard closed the program with the Retirement of Colors.

The Java Legion and Legion Auxiliary continue the observation of Memorial Day
with a program and cemetery services.

INDEPENDENCE DAY
Always a big celebration in the town of Java, the Fourth of July stands out in
the memories of those old enough to have participated in the event in one way or
another. Committees were appointed in May 1927, after the Commercial Club
decided that as long as a celebration was going to be held, it was not going to
be any half-hearted affair, but the real thing. The Finance Com-mittee reported
that sufficient funds had been raised to sanction the venture.

(Photo:) 1948 4th of July Parade. Dennis "Uncle Sam" Pfitzer, Gary Goetz on
         tricycle

Committee members for the "grand old-fashioned celebration" were: General
Arrangement and Program, I.R. Krause, Arend Lakeman and Wm. Kunz; Music, A.C.
Schlepp; Advertising, F. Clement and Jacob Helm; Parade, G.W. Hicks and Ed Gill;
Decorating, Mrs. M. Gehrki, Mrs. Kate Clement, Mrs. W.C. Hicks, Mrs. F.E. Bauer
and Mrs. J.S. Pfitzer; Street Sports, C.F. Spiry, L.A. Gershin and Ed Gill;
Fireworks, Fred Bauer, Fred Krause and Wm. Jesser.

In the Forties, family picnics were a standard part of the day. The children,
excited to be in the big parade, would decorate their bicycles with red, white
and blue crepe paper and streamers. Dressing in costume was also a part of the
excitement. The music of the marching bands generated an excitement among the
crowd, and it was so much fun to see the many entries. Potato salad, watermelon,
and fried chicken were consumed in quantities; families visited, children played
in the park. At night, of course, parents brought out the Sparklers, the advent
of things to come. Children waved the shining Sparklers in the night sky,
creating patterns that seemingly echoed. While this was taking place, several
businessmen of the area were busy getting the display ready for the Big Show.
Cars would line up around the baseball field, people sat on the hoods of their
cars, everyone waiting for the moment when the fireworks would begin. Colorful
lights flashed in the sky, the crowd oohed and aahed, and hoped for more. The
annual Java celebration of freedom in America was indeed a "grand old-fashioned"
event. Children were tucked into bed and adults joined with one another to dance
until dawn. What a day!

VETERANS DAY
Commemorates the courage and patriotism of all the men and women who have served
in the U.S. armed services. It is celebrated on Nov. 11. Many other countries,
such as Canada, Great Britain, and France, celebrate Nov. 11 as Armistice Day to
commemorate the end of fighting in World War I on Nov. 11, 1918.

Veterans Day celebrations in the U.S. include parades and speeches. Special
services are held at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Arlington National
Cemetery, Arlington, VA. In 1919, Pres. Woodrow Wilson proclaimed Nov. 11 as
Armistice Day to remind Americans of the tragedies of war. In 1954, Congress
established Veterans Day to honor all American veterans.

In 1948, at the Java High School Auditorium, Java and area people recognized
Veterans Day at a program. Commander Joseph S. Zarka, the High School Band,
directed by Gilbert Schlepp, vocalist Irene Kraft, address by attorney Pat
Morrison, Mobridge, and mixed chorus selections, directed by H.F. Spiry,
completed the program.

SNOW QUEEN CONTEST
The Java Chamber of Commerce conducted Snow Queen Contests in Java, beginning in
1948. The first contest included Bettie Aman, Delila Aman, Allegra Biel,
Priscilla Biel, Betty Freimark, Erna Goetz, Agnes Schlepp, Gloria Schlepp, and
Ann Witlock as contestants.

Business places in Java issued a ballot with every $1 purchase made, and on the
ballot could be written the name of any one of the young ladies competing. The
contest committee notified the five young ladies having the highest number of
votes. Judges from Aberdeen came to Java when the Coronation Ball was held. The
judges interviewed the candidates and the winner was selected on the basis of
personality and beauty. Delila Ama was the first Snow Queen of Java.

MUSIC
The Java Band held a business meeting on Mon. night, Oct. 5, 1903. It was
decided to hold Mon. and Fri. night rehearsals per week and to hire an
instructor, H.C. Buechler, for $30 a month.

The Java Orchestra organized Nov. 4, 1903, with members: Edward Rose, violin;
I.R. Krause, cornet; Henry Thielen, clarinet or cello; and C.F. Clement, piano.
Ed Rose was the leader, I.R. Krause was secretary, and Henry Thielen was the
treasurer. A Whitney piano was purchased from the John McArthur and Son Music in
Aberdeen.

The Java Cornet Band held its annual election of officers on Mon. Dec. 7, 1903.
Officers elected were: S. Rosenthal, president; Joseph Bosch, vice president;
C.F. Clement, secretary; Henry Thielen, treasurer; Jacob Schaffer, marshal; and
Jacob Stoller, Christ Huether and John Hofmeyer, trustees. The meeting showed
much enthusiasm and indicated that the band would be running smoothly again.

The Java Musical Culture Club was organized in Feb. 1906, at the home of C.F.
Clement. The musical society consisted of Mrs. K. Eisentraut and Mrs. C.F.
Clement as sopranos, Mrs. W.C. Hicks and Mrs. A.D. Mashek as altos, A.E. Rose as
tenor and K. Eisentraut and John Hofmeyer sang bass. C.F. Clement was their
director.

The Java Quartet was organized on Mon., Apr. 12, 1909 and consisted of W.L.
Sacket, first tenor, A.E. Rose, second tenor, Carl F. Clement, first bass and
John Hofmeyer, second bass. Another male quartet was noted in Dec. 1911 with
C.F. Clement as the director and Messrs. Spiry, Doerr, Krause and Bauder as
singers.

The Java Municipal Band purchased new uniforms of white caps and duck trousers
in 1928. Paid by the City of Java, they held weekly open-air concerts in the
bandstand in front of the Gill Implement shop. A.C. Schlepp was director in
1931.

Java's State Baseball
The summer of 1975 was warm and dry, but lots of activity was going on in Java.
Java High School played host to an all-school reunion, the city was celebrating
its 75th Jubilee, and the American Legion Baseball Team was having an
unforgettable season, which ended in winning the State B. Championship.

The team had a great regular season, managed by Floyd Biel and coached by
Clifton Schnaible. The team took a 17 win and 4 loss into the District
Tournament. The District was a 10-team single elimination event, held in Groton,
where Java played Groton for the championship, defeating Groton 10-9.

Next was the Regional Tournament held at Eureka. This was a 4-team, double
elimination event. Java won the first game against Lemmon, 21-2. They then lost
to Redfield, which meant they would have to play a well-rested Redfield team.
They won both games, 28-3 and 17-9. This brought Java to the State "B" 4-team
double elimination event held in Mobridge.

In the State "B" Tournament, Java played Lake Andes and Spearfish, winning both
games. This led to a double-headed on Sunday, playing Colton. Java lost the
first game to Colton, 3-2. In the Championship game on Sunday night, Java bats
were hot and they won 28-10. The 28 runs were a state record for a Championship
game. Glen Neumiller, Hugh Neumiller and Pat Wolff were the leading hitters in
the Championship game.

The next week, Java had to take on the Rapid City Post 22 for the overall State
Championship, and the right to represent the State in the National Regional
Tournament. The games were played in Milbank, as this was the 50th Anniversary
of the American Legion Baseball and Milbank is the birthplace of American Legion
Baseball.

The Rapid City team proved to be too much for Java, as they won both games 10-0.

The Legion team just kept on a great tradition of Java Baseball that had begun
in the early 1900's with the town. Java's team was always known as a tough team
to beat and had many notable players throughout the State.

(Photo:) 1975 American Legion State B Champions. Back: Manager, Floyd Biel, Dan
         Biel, Steve hendricks, Pat Wolff, Darrell Grenz, Paul Schnaible, Doug
         Schneider, Glen Neumiller, Bryce Schreter and Clifton Schnaible. Front:
         Batboys Billie Krause and Scott Sauer; Dan Schneider, Hugh Neumiller,
         Mark Wolff and Scott Schneider

The 1945 Amateur team placed 2nd in the State Tournament. In 1971, the Teener
team was undefeated before losing in the Regional tournament. IN 1973, the
Teener team placed 7th in the State Tournament. For many years, Java had a good
program freom Little League on up through American Legion Baseball.

George Hicks, Jeff Pfitzer, Floyd Biel, Clif Schnaible, and Snip Schnaible were
all long-time Java players. Joe Mueller was one of the best pitchers in the
State (in 1949, Joe placed on the All-Tournament first team). The Wolf brothers,
Hank, Jake and John, and Reine Moser also contributed to the State Tournaments
for other towns. Later, Steve Biel, Dan Biel, Doug Schlepp, Steve Kary and Craig
Pfitzer played with other teams for State Championship.

Java has three people who were elected to the SD Amateur Baseball Hall of Fame,
with their histories and plaques on display at Lake Norden, SD. They are Julius
Pfitzer (1960), George Hicks (1962), and Floyd Biel (1992).

                   A Place Called Home

A PIONEER TELLS OF EARLY DAYS by Fred G. Bauman
When I and my parents came to Walworth County in the year 1893, from the Ukraine
near Odessa in South Russia, there were many prairie chickens around here. They
were very beautiful birds about the size of a tame chicken, and they had very
good meat, and did no damage to farmers' crops. They were catching grasshoppers
and other insects and found food in fields after crops were harvested and on
straw piles.

I can still remember how they played with each other on a calm evening. The
rooster acted like a turkey gobbler, and sang "Doodle-Doo-Doo", and the hens
played catch and ran around and cackled. This could be heard sometimes a mile
away. They stayed with us till about 1920 or even longer. But when the pheasants
came, they drove our prairie chickens away; they even destroyed their nests.

About 1895 to 1897, our first one-room schools were built here on the prairie.
Four schools to each township. The teachers' salaries that time were $25 to $30
a month. The children most of the time walked to school sometimes 3 miles or
more, and some teachers walked sometimes up to 5 miles. There were no roads,
only some wagon trails. We and nearly all pioneers broke up the sod with ox or
horses.

My father bought 2 big oxen and paid $400 for them. They weighed about 1800
pounds each. They worked without bridle or lines, just by word. They were
faithful workers as long as the weather was not hot. Some Sundays we hitched
both oxen on our stone-boat and drove to Grandfather's farm 6 miles away. They
were my mother's parents and they were born in Hoffnungsthal, South Russia in
1830. This was the same village where I was born in 1892.

In later years, farmers used mostly horses (as they could go faster than oxen)
to plow their fields with walking plows; then seeded the wheat by hand and
worked it into the ground with a drag. To harvest they used a header on which 4
horses were hitched behind the 12-foot wide cutting bar; to push the header, the
operator had to stand behind the horses, on a platform supported by one wheel to
guide the header. A wagon, with a big header-box on it and pulled by 2 horses,
had to drive beside the header, and the header elevated the grain up on this
box. From this box we pitched the grain by hand and stacked it in big stacks to
cure and dry.

We and some of our neighbors then bought a threshing machine together, which was
powered only by horses. The machine was moved with 4 horses between the wheat
stacks. Then we pulled the horse-power in place about 40 feet from the thresher
and drove poles into the ground to hold it in place. A flexible rod ran from the
horsepower to the thresher to drive the thresher. Then we hitched 4 horses
around on the horsepower in pairs; one pair behind the other to get the power to
drive the thresher. The thresh-machine had no self-feeder, only 2 platforms high
up in front of the machine. A man had to stand between the platforms and feed
the grain into the machine, which was pitched on the platforms by 2 men. The
threshed grain came out on the underside of the machine and poured into a bushel
basket. When one basket was full, then a man pulled it away and replaced it with
an empty basket, counted the bushels, and loaded it on a wagon.

In later years, we had steam threshers. They were much bigger machines with long
self-feeders where 3 or more men could pitch the grain on; also a straw blower
to blow the straw on big piles, and the threshed grain ran on the double-box
wagon from a big spout. The big steam engine pulled the big 10-inch wide
flywheel, and a 150-foot long endless 10-inch wide heavy belt from engine to
pulley on the thresher. The steam engine required 2000 to 3000 gallons of water
a day to make enough steam. It burned straw, or in later years sometimes coal.

The fireman had to get up by 4 a.m. to get the engine steamed up by about 5 a.m.
When he had steam, then he pulled the whistle, and he whistled and whistled,
waited a few minutes and whistled again to show that he had enough steam to
thresh and thus called the crew to come.

The housewife or cook had to get up by 3 or 4 a.m. to have breakfast ready on
time. This was all hard labor. There was only very little oil pumped up from
Mother Earth those days, only for kerosene and lubricating oil. There was no
electricity yet, only kerosene lamps and lanterns. And for fuel to heat the
house, we used cow chips, flax straw, corncobs or wood. Everybody drove with
horses; later we got buggies, and even top buggies.

In later years we got better machines. To plow we got two-bottom gang plows
where the farmer could sit on the plow. This plow required 5 horses to pull it.
Then we got seeding machines to seed our fields; and later we got 10-foot wide
grain drills to drill seed into the ground. Also grain and corn binders, which
made grain into bundles. Then it was shocked by hand to dry. When it was dry, it
was hauled to the thresher.

Years later we got small tractors. They ran on steel wheels and pulled two-
bottom and later three-bottom plows. All this was a big improvement over our
early day farming.

In early days when I was 9, I had to walk behind a one-bottom hand plow with 2
horses hitched on it, hold the plow, control the horses, and walk about 20 miles
a day.

In the later 1930's and 1940's the grain combines took over most of the hard
work to harvest our grain. But in this part of the country, we had nothing to
harvest in 1934 and 1936 through 1939. Drought, grasshoppers, and Mormon
crickets left nothing to harvest, not even feed or grass for cattle. Farmers and
everybody got very poor.

President Roosevelt came to Aberdeen, and looked conditions over and gave all
the help he could. As soon as he was elected, he froze all the banks and pushed
our Depositor Guarantee Law through Congress. And from this time on, to my
knowledge, nobody lost any more money in a bank as deposits are insured up to
$20,000 in each bank.

About 1909, we saw some automobiles, but when our horses or cattle saw a car
come near, they got so scared that they ran away over the hills.

About 1912, Mr. Parmley of Ipswich, started a drive to build a highway and
called it the Yellowstone Trail, now Hwy 12. At first they built a dirt grade,
but when it rained much, then the cars cut deep tracks into the wet dirt road,
and cars couldn't go on. Then later they hauled gravel on this highway. The
gravel packed on the road and made a very big improvement.

By this time there were many cars in use, and Henry Ford built the Model T
