touring car about 1909. These cars sold for about $400 or less. By this time
people had a little money; then they began to buy cars.

John H. Wolf (the father of Emma (Ben) Stiegelmeier) had the first Ford garage
in Java at that time, and he sold the Model T cars nearly as fast as he could
ship them in. The Model T touring cars had no self-starters so people had to
crank the cars to start them. The touring cars had tops with side-curtains; the
curtains could be removed, and also the top laid down.

There was also much fun when our old pioneers got Model T cars as they were so
used to horses. When they drove with their horses and wanted to stop they
hollered "Whoa!" And their horses stopped. But when they drove with their cars
and hollered "Whoa", their cars did not stop. Then the farmers sometimes got
excited and forgot how to stop the car. One farmer drove with his Model T and
forgot how to stop it. He then got more excited because he couldn't stop. There
was a haystack near, so he drove right against this haystack; and then his car
stopped. Another old pioneer farmer also forgot how to stop his car. He drove to
the pasture and circled around there till all his gas was used up. Then his car
stopped.

One farm family, with their team of horses, came to their church every Sunday
early and on time. Then they bought a new Model T car and next Sunday they
wanted to come to church with their nice new car. But when next Sunday came and
they wanted to get to church on time, they couldn't get their new car started.
They cranked and cranked till they were all played out, and till it was too late
to go to church. They then called a mechanic that same afternoon and found out
they didn't have their car switched on. For many pioneers it was a hard job to
change over from their horses to cars.

I bought my new Ford car in 1919, but by this time the price was up to $750 as
there was inflation in our country on account of the war. Everything went up in
price; land prices went as high as $100 per acre. And many people said they were
sure that land prices would stay that high or go even higher and this would be a
good investment. But later in 1929 the recession started; many people lost their
money and others lost their jobs. The stock market crashed; banks were forced to
close and depositors lost their money. And by 1934, land was almost worthless.
Wages and everything came down very low.

In 1932, we had a good crop, but we received only 20 to 30 cents per bushel for
our best wheat, 3 cents for corn, one cent per pound for our nice 100-pound
pigs. I fattened my calves, and when they were about 18 months old, I sold them.
They weighed about 1000 pounds each, and they were nice and fat. I received only
$28 for each steer.

Then in the year 1934, we received no snow and no rain, and the wind was blowing
up to 40 and 50 miles nearly every day, and started our fields to blow. Big dust
clouds went up in the air everywhere; and farmers were unable to stop it.
Farmers seeded most of their crops with hopes that it might rain later; but no
rain came all summer. It was so dry that not even a stalk of grass would grow.
Then farmers were forced to get rid of most of their cattle and got very little
for them. Baled hay was then shipped in, but much of this hay was of poor
quality and high in price. Farmers were forced to take feed and seed loans.
Everybody became very poor, farmers had no income, only expenses. People wanted
to work, but there were no jobs.

One good thing was our government had started the W.P.A. work a year or two
before; then every poor person who was able to work was required to do some work
to earn a living. Farmers built roads with their horses; townspeople came with
their shovels and helped. The men in Java also dug ditches by hand to lay water
pipes. Then by 1938 and 1939 Java got running water, and by 1947 and 1948, Java
got sewer systems.

In 1935 we got rain, but then a new strain of rust came and shriveled our wheat
badly. And on top of this, the farmers east of Java were hailed out. All the
windows on our house were knocked in by the big hail stones. In 1936, no snow
and no rain and dust storms all summer and a total crop failure. In 1937 almost
a total crop failure,  the grasshoppers ate up everything that looked green.
1938, a little rain, but grasshoppers again destroyed almost everything. Then in
1938, the Mormon crickets came by the billions; they were very big fat fellows,
all colors. Our garden vegetables were eaten by the 'hoppers, except the onions
and garlic, which the 'hoppers didn't like; but then the Mormon crickets came,
they also ate up the onions and garlic. 1939, we thought we would get a little
crop, but the big grasshoppers and Mormon crickets destroyed it.

Our government in 1938 and 1939 furnished to the farmers poisoned bran to spread
on the wheat fields. Then I and my neighbor built a poison spreader and I spread
the poison on my best wheat field, and I killed the 'hoppers by the millions,
but for every one I killed about 50 others came to his funeral, and they did not
go home any more, and this field was eaten up the very first.

I had a 25-acre field of corn. On July 4, I walked through this corn, it was
about knee high. I had hopes this corn might help out for feed for my livestock,
but while I was in the field, millions of 'hoppers came flying high. And when
they saw this green field they came down and by evening not one stalk was left
standing; it was all destroyed.

Then I had another field prepared to plant sugar cane on. I went to do this
field with my corn planter, and also about 100 pounds of cane seed in a grain
sack. I left the sack with the cane seed by the end of this field and started to
plant. When my planter boxes were empty, I drove over to my sack to fill up my
planter boxes again, but when I came to the sack, the Mormon crickets had eaten
my grain sack, and my cane seed was spread around into the dry grass and weeds.
And I had no more clean cane seed.

By this time, the farmers had had no income for over 7 years, only expenses, and
worked for nothing. Nobody cared to own land any more, as the land produced
nothing. People could pay no taxes, and values of most everything came down.
Teachers' salaries came down to about $45 in some rural schools.

Then, thanks to God, in 1940 we got rain and crops again, and conditions
gradually became normal again. [Excerpt from The Java Herald, June 13, 1975]

REMEMBRANCE by Fred G. and Rosina Bauman
I was born in Hoffnungstal in Kherson in 1892, and in 1893, I came to the U.S.
with my parents, Friederich and Christiana (nee Fiechtner) Bauman. We came on a
small ship, and it took 31 days to make the trip. We landed by New York, then
went by train to Bridgewater, SD, as my uncle Gottlieb Fiechtner, Sr., came to
Bridgewater a few years before. But that same year we, and also uncle Gottlieb
Fiechtner, Sr., came to Walworth County, as there was a little rough and stony
land left here for a homestead.

When we came here, Bowdle was at the end of the Milwaukee railroad. All the
farmers as far west as the Missouri river had to travel by team to Bowdle or
Eureka, to haul their grain and get their groceries. They traveled across
country, as there were no fences and no roads those early days.

My father then took up a 160-acre homestead five miles east from where Java is
now located, and uncle Gottlieb took a 160-acre homestead four miles east.
Gottlieb Fiechtner's wife's brothers, Philip Spiry, Sr., and his brothers, Fred
and Karl came out a few years before we did, and they were living about three
miles north from where Java is now.

We built a sod house called semljanka in Russia, and a sod barn, and we got a
well. Nearly all the pioneers were poor and had a hard start to build up this
country. Bangor, five miles south of where Selby is now located, was the county
seat.

The next year my father bought two oxen which weighed about 1800 pounds each;
and they worked without bridle or lines, just by saying the words, "Gee, or
haah, or hoh!"  We also bought one horse and one milk cow. With the two oxen,
the horse and the cow hitched on the breaking plow, we broke up some sod and
seeded some flax.

Later the same year, my mother was raking hay with one ox called Jim. I was
sitting on the frame of the rake, and mother was sitting on the seat. Jim worked
faithfully as long as the weather was cool, but by 10:30, it got hot. There was
a small lake about 300 feet away; then Jim looked towards this water, and turned
around and walked right into the four-foot deep water with the rake and mother
and me on the rake. Jim enjoyed it very much in the water for about six hours;
and he did not care how hungry and thirsty mother and I were. We pleaded with
him. "Jim, please take us home." Then about four p.m., Jim looked back at us and
felt sorry for us, listened to us and was good enough to walk out of the water,
and take us home.

About two days later my father hauled this hay home with both oxen on the
hayrack on a hot day again. He had a very big load of hay and was sitting on top
of his high load; and he drove past this pond of water. Then Jim and Charlie,
the oxen, turned around and took him, with his big load of hay, into the deep
water. Father had to wait almost six hours until Jim and Charlie were good and
ready, and pulled the load home.

Sometime later, David Blinderman started a grocery store on the prairie about
five miles north of Java. John Hofmeyer started a grocery store at the little
trading post called Rosella. Also a trading post and post office were started
about 12 to 14 miles NW of Java, near the Christ Rau, Sr., farm. This was called
Sutley. All this was a great help to the pioneer farmers who would travel by
teams those days.

In the year 1899, the Milwaukee Railroad started an extension of their road to
the west of the Missouri river. By 1900, three new towns were started: Java,
Selby, and Evarts, west by the Missouri.

Java was growing very fast. Henry Thielen and Joe Bosch started the first
grocery store about one block east of Main Street. David Blinderman moved his
grocery store to Java from the country to west Main Street. Bauer, Hoff &
Stoller moved a building from Eureka, enlarged it, and started a grocery, dry
goods and hardware store where the Christ Pfitzer Paint store is now. The post
office was in the Bauer store and run by Stoller's daughter. Mr. Jacob Stoller
also moved his home from Eureka, and built an addition to it. The home is now
owned by Amelia Wolf. The firm of Bauer, Hoff, & Stoller also built a large
grain elevator at an early date. John Hofmeyer from Rosella built a very large
two-story building on the corner on Main Street, north of the present barber
shop, and started a grocery, dry goods, and hardware. The second story of this
building was used for a dance hall. Cook and Arend Lakeman built a big building
on the corner of east Main Street and sold groceries and hardware. Now Java had
five grocery stores in its first years, also two lumber yards. Fred Diegel built
a hotel on the corner of east Main Street, north of the post office. Later he
sold it to George Zeller. He also built a large livery barn east of his hotel,
which was later operated by George L. Wolf. He did livery work with his Model T
in later years. A second hotel was built on east Main and later sold to my
uncle, Jacob Fiechtner, then to Bill Campbell and later, it was used for a high
school girls' dormitory.

A medical doctor, Sigmond Rosenthal, moved from Eureka, and located on east Main
Street. He practiced medicine for nearly 20 years in Java. Later R.M. Hennings
started a drug store on west Main Street, there were two implement dealers, two
blacksmiths, and later two banks: The American State Bank, owned by Philip
Spiry, Sr., and sons, and The First State Bank, owned by Mr. Hicks and Jacob
Helm. An attorney, son of an early pioneer farmer, Mr. Adams, located on east
Main Street. (Adams Township is named after Mr. Adams).

In 1897 about 12 farm families organized to build a church on the prairie, five
miles east and one mile north of Java. These poor pioneers, including my
parents, donated all the work. They called it the Hoffnungstal Church, because
half the members came from the village of Hoffnungstal in Kherson, and the other
half, from Hoffnungstal in the state of Bessarabia in South Russia. The Rev.
Ottersberg from Hosmer, served us until 1900, coming to us by team 23 miles. He
could not come every Sunday; then the deacon read the sermon from the book,
which was written by a minister in Germany and contained a nice sermon for every
Sunday. My father or John Schuh, Sr., read the sermon most of the time. In 1900,
the Karl Schnaible and Spiry small church was moved to Java, and located where
the Congregational is.

In that same year, our Hoffnungstal congregation, the small Java church, and the
Peace congregation (about eight miles north of Java) joined together and called
a minister, Rev. Fred Braun, a young single man, who served us one and a half
years. Rev. George Kirchdoerfer, a young, single pastor from Germany, served us
40 years. A year after he came, he got married and they raised four children.
For a time he served six congregations: The St. Paul Lutheran in Java, our
Hoffnungstal church; the Buechler church, eight or 9 miles east from Java; the
Bauder and Perman congregations, which had met in a school about 12 miles SE
from Java; the Peace congregations, eight miles NW of Java and Lowry. He had to
travel by team and could serve only one church on one Sunday. The other churches
had services with the deacon reading the sermon from the sermon book.

Our Hoffnungstal church had no organ; in later years I took my violin and led
the singing. I taught the children and the older people many new songs. Later
our congregation bought an organ, which I played for the church.

About 1909, the Java congregation moved the small church from its place and used
it for a schoolhouse. They built a larger church in its place, which is now the
Congregational church. About 1930, we sold our Hoffnungstal Church to the Sutley
Congregation, and we joined the St. Paul Lutheran Church in Java. About 1931,
this church was raised and a full basement was built under the church. Later we
sold it to the Congregational people. Then we built the large church, which we
still use. [Excerpts taken from Footprints, 1975]

Remembrances of Early Day Java by Gertie Banik Goodmanson
In the fall of 1899, our father, John Banik, moved our two-room house from
Bowdle to Java, near what was later to become Main Street. He built a small
blacksmith shop nearby. Then he sent for his family. Our mother, Katie Banik,
was visiting her parents with their three small children, Gertie, Anna and
Elsie.

At that time there was no depot in Java. There was only a junction, about a mile
north of Java, and a spur had been run in. When Katie and the children arrived,
they got off the train. It backed out and Katie looked around. It was all
prairie! She turned around and looked up the hill. At the bottom of the hill she
saw a grain elevator (Ewald's), and a small building a ways away (Thielen's
Lumber Yard). On top of the hill, she saw a larger building (Hofmeyer's Store),
and a ways away and across from Hofmeyer's she saw the little two-room house she
recognized. Near by was a smaller building. (John's shop).

John came running down the hill and gathered up his family. They trudged up the
hill. From up there Kate saw two houses, (Thielen's and Ewald's). Katie was on
the verge of crying. "Is this where we're going to live? " she asked. "It will
build up," John said, "You'll see. There are a lot of farmers around and no
blacksmith. You'll see. This will be a town." She went inside. One room of the
house held two beds, a cradle for Elsie, a dresser, a sewing machine and a
wardrobe. The other room served as a kitchen and living room. A range to cook on
and to heat the house, a table and chairs.

Two years later a boy was born, Albert. He died of convulsions and was buried in
the Adventist cemetery, south of Bowdle. There was no Adventist Church near Java
then; later, one was built in Sutley, about 9 miles north of Java.

As John had promised, the town began to grow. In 1902, John moved the house
closer to what was later to become Main Street. He sold his shop to John
Weisgram and built a larger one on front of the house.

His business had grown so much he needed to enlarge. He and Simon Bitzer went
into partnership. Simon did carpentry work. He made wheels, spokes, sled
runners, etc. John did the blacksmithing. John bought a large engine on which
was attached a huge flywheel. On this flywheel was a wide leather belt, which
extended across the room to run other pieces of machinery.

One day we will never forget. Somehow my father's clothes got caught in the
flywheel. He grabbed a bar and hung on for dear life. The powerful wheel tore
most of his clothes from his body. When Simon finally got the engine stopped,
all my father had left of his clothes was a strip of heavy underwear over his
shoulder and part of one leg. His flesh was torn, mangled and bleeding. If he
hadn't been so strong, he would surely have been killed.

John brought the first car to Java, a small red Franklin. He taught Gertie, who
was about 10, to run the car and they drove up one street and down another to
show that even a child could run it.

He sold an International to Fred Dufloth and Mrs. Dufloth came, raging "It goes
too fast! You'll get him killed!" But Fred drove it and never did tip over.

John began selling threshing machines about the countryside. He sold many rigs
and began operating a rig himself. He hired men on header boxes to haul sheaves
from the field, men to pitch them into the separator, men to sack the grain as
it came from a huge spout and men and wagons to haul it away. Then there was a
waterman, a fireman for the steam engine. John was the engineer.

Hofmeyer's Store was the only store for miles around for a long time. In it one
could find almost every necessity from thread to harnesses. There were bolts of
cloth, even laces, on shelves and showcases. Men's overalls and jackets, shirts,
shoes for men and women, underwear, etc., groceries lined the opposite wall.
Flour, sugar, candy in large glass bowls, spices, salt in cloth sacks, etc.
There was no such thing as canned foods. You canned your own.

I, Gertie, remember running across to the store for a penny's worth of candy.
Those days are gone forever.

Some flour stood about in 50-pound sacks, as well as the sugar. Also Hofmeyer
kept some in bins from which one could buy smaller amounts.

In the back were farm tools, rakes, hoes, spades, etc. hanging from the wall, or
standing in racks. Hand tools, etc. from hammers to nails and screws. Harnesses
hung from the wall, bridles, even a saddle or two. One could smell the leather
throughout the store. Hofmeyer's was Java's "Trading Post", in the early days.

The town began to grow and grow fast. In 1902 Cook and Lakeman built a store
kitty corner from Hofmeyers, (Later owned by John Wolf ) . Their homes were
either built or moved in. John Bauer built a store across the street from
Hofmeyer's. Bauer's had the first postoffice in Java.

Halls moved a large building in across the Main Street from Hofmeyers and made a
hotel out of it. Later, Fred Diegel bought it and Halls built across Main street
from our place, and later installed a telephone office on the first floor. Mae
Campbell bought Diegel's hotel and later had the building moved down to the foot
of the hill in the next block. This she ran as a hotel for many years.

John Banik built onto his blacksmith shop. Also, he added two more rooms to the
house. In the NW corner of the implement shop, John built a room downstairs and
a large room above it. In the downstairs, with only a dirt floor, Dr. McCaw
started the first dental office in Java. He later built across the street and
had his office there. Years later, Dr. McCaw was killed when the car he was
riding in plunged off the high cut bank of the Missouri near Mobridge.

Carl Clement built a building on Main Street and started the first newspaper in
the vicinity. His home was established at the NE outskirts, across from what
would later be the grade and high school. A saloon was built next to Bauer's
store. Dave and John Blinderman built a small store near the railroad tracks,
with living quarters in the rear. He later moved next door to the saloon.

Mr. Winkley started a meat market next to Mae Campbell's hotel. In those days
you got liver and kidneys for free!

Homes were built or moved in and trees planted. Grandma Harris' small   house
was moved in next door to John Banik's implement shop. She held the first school
in town. Who will ever forget Grandma Harris. She was nurse and teacher for all
of us then. When illness struck, she was called. There was no doctor then. It
was much later that Dr. Rosenthal came to town. John Banik and Simon dissolved
partnership and Dr. Rosenthal's family moved into the Bitzer house. Dr.
Rosenthal also started a drugstore on Main Street, across the street from Mae
Campbell.

A firehall was built a bit east and next door to our place. A large fire bell
was installed and whoever discovered a fire ran to pull the rope to the bell.
Every man was a fireman in those days. Later Java bought a fire engine.

Behind it was a small jail, which was built for the unruly and behind that, next
to the alley, a tall windmill had gone in, which supplied the town with water.
At the huge, round trough the city's stock was watered.

A lot of homes had cisterns, but we carried every drop we used from this well.
In the evening, before washday, we carried water to fill two barrels. Lye
softened it during the night. Maybe this windmill is still standing, though many
changes have taken place in the years gone by.

A Lutheran church was built, with the parsonage behind it, on the street behind
Hofmeyer's store. Rev. Kirchdoerfer taught many of Java's children during summer
vacation to read and write German.

On the hill farther west, a Presbyterian church went up. There most of us
children went to Christmas programs and received a small sack of goodies.

Fourth of July was a great day then. A big parade, fireworks, firecrackers
popping all day and night. Dancing all day and far into the morning. A decorated
haywagon was loaded with the youngsters of Java and they rode in the parade,
waving their small flags. By then we had a Java band and they marched and played
rollicking marches. As I remember it, August Schlepp was the leader of the band.

Willis Banik was born on the 4th of July, and is well celebrated to this day. It
is a day I'll never forget. Relatives had poured in and they slept on the
floors, in wagons and wherever there was room. I was not allowed to ride in the
parade. Dr. Rosenthal was there and soon there was a new baby in the house. That
was Willis. Allie, Harry and Elmer came along later.

John tore down the old house and built a new two-story house on the same
location. John now sold cars, threshing machines, tractors and farm machinery.

The family grew up, were married and moved away. At this time, Gertie
(Goodmanson) has one son, two grandsons and 8 great grandchildren; Anna (Storrs)
has no children; Elsie (Reiswig) has two children, and two grandchildren; Willis
lives in Lodi, and has no children; Allie became an ophthalmologist and author
of several books. He has one daughter and two granddaughters; Harry has four
sons and one daughter and four grandchildren. He lives at Mobridge; Elmer lives
in Rapid City. He has no children.

Our father, John Banik passed away in Oct. 1936. He was buried at Aberdeen. Our
mother, Katie, resided for many years at Wakpala. She passed away in Mar. 1971,
at Mobridge. She was buried in the Mobridge cemetery. She lived to the ripe old
age of 93.

Many changes have taken place in Java, but the wonderful memories we have will
always be with us. For there we spent the happiest days of our lives. [From
Footprints, 1975, and edited]

Pete Frazier, SHREWD HORSETRADER by Freida Schuh
At the turn of the century, Pete Frazier was working as a cowhand in the Evarts
and Lebeau area. Later he moved to Mobridge, where he owned a livery stable.
Each spring, Pete would bring in a herd of wild horses from west of the Missouri
river. These horses would be broken to ride or to work, then when he was certain
that all the horses were well trained he would tie them together and head east
to Java, where he spent several weeks trading and turning the horses into cash.

He was well known throughout the Java area for his knowledge of horseflesh. He
never deliberately cheated anyone, but if someone would out-smart him in a
trade, he would not be satisfied until he evened the score.

His daughter, Freida, now Mrs. Ellsworth Schuh, often helped him get started
away from Mobridge. The horses all wore halters, which were tied to the tail of
the horse in front. They traveled in 2 rows. Between 30 and 40 horses were moved
in this manner. Pete took the lead and one of his hired hands would follow. The
horses were allowed to rest, graze and drink only once on the 30 mile drive.

Pete always spoke well of the Java people. He said that the German women were
the world's best cooks, and no doubt his praise and compliments earned him many
an invitation to a meal.

He spoke German well enough to carry on a conversation. He also spoke Sioux
Indian fluently and was often called on when an interpreter was needed. He died
of a heart attack when he was 64 years old. Only a week before his death, he had
trailed a small herd of horses from southeast of Java to Mobridge. [From
Footprints, 1975]

[The following article was collected and edited for the Dakota Freie Presse by
F. W. Sallet, and appeared in that newspaper on July 8, 1909.  The letter was
translated by LaVern J. Rippley, St. Olaf College, and was printed in The
Heritage Review, the offical publication of the Germans from Russia Heritage
Society at Bismarck, ND. The following was copied from that publication.]

Walworth County, South Dakota JAVA by Jacob Aman
On Apr. 27, 1889 I arrived with my wife at Eureka. My home colony was Landau in
the district of Odessa; my wife's was Klein-Neudorf. When we arrived there,
Eureka was the chief target of German-Russian immigration. We met no
acquaintances but found many good people who were glad to help their fellow
countrymen in any way they could. I came to America to acquire land, so my first
question was where could I get it. We were told that there should be good land
about 20 to 24 miles southwest of Eureka and so we set out immediately with
Schumacher's black horses. At that time it was rare for a farmer to have horses.
Most had only oxen. We met a man who for a dollar was willing to seek out a
claim for us. A gentle valley cut through the land that we examined and we liked
that very much. However, we had no knowledge of the endless prairie and thus
accepted what our leader pointed out. He showed us only land that was not
rolling and thus we believed that the hilly land around us would always remain
open pasture and hay land. But in a few years all the land had been taken, for
the most part, by German-Russians. The hilly land is just as good as ours. All
the land here is undulating, has about two to three feet of black soil, and is
underlain with yellow clay.

Among those who homesteaded land here with me some 20 years ago I would mention
the following: Jacob J. Aman, Jacob Stiegelmeier, Peter Hartman, Jr., F.
Hartman, Wilhelm Moser, Jakob Wolf, John Fiechtner ["Pioneer Footprints, Diamond
Jubilee, Java, SD 1900-1975" lists the homesteader as Gottlieb Fiechtner], Karl
Krause and Johannas Krause.

I used to be a Russian soldier but got tired of it. Although I had a good
position I decided to emigrate to America, for my father and brothers were also
going to America. Since I departed for America straight from the military I had
no time to earn money for the trip. So I took a portion of my father's money and
set out. I arrived in America as good as broke. There was no way to make any
money here. I asked myself what I should do with my land? I could not get rid of
it, not even for a minimal price, because at that time we were paying the same
price for a claim, as we had to pay for a team of horses. Now I'm happy that
nobody bought the land.

I had to endure some hard times. Only those who have experienced a similar
situation, trying to get established on the wild prairie without money, earnings
and without any help can understand how we had to live at the outset.

But the bad times had their good side. People pulled together and became better
friends. Worship services had to be conducted in the small sod houses in which
we ourselves lived and our prayers were more earnest than they are today. Men
and animals became so used to living with each other that when a farmer drove to
church on Sunday, his cow wanted to come along and on occasion it happened that
a pig or a dog followed the wagon to church.

It took a year before I could get a cat, two years to get a dog. On the wide-
open prairies there was nothing but buffalo paths, worn down four or five
inches, and the bones of destroyed buffaloes, some antelope, and occasionally a
rabbit. Because the prairie burned so often, there was very little wildlife.
Today there are plenty of rabbits and prairie dogs. Back then each farmer had
two or three horses, about the same number of cows, and there was enough
government land where he could make hay. But there was not always enough hay for
the few animals we had. Now-a-days every farmer has 10 or 15 horses and more, as
well as about 25 to 40 head of cattle and still there is enough hay to feed his
animals. Today each farmer has two, three or four quarters of land and some 200
to 300 acres under plow and even then enough hay, proof that it rains more now
than 20 years ago. Back then we also planted corn but we rarely got a crop. You
ought to see our corn fields today. We harvest about 40 bushes per acre. This
year once again we will have a good corn crop. The same holds true for
everything we plant. In the initial years I planted trees twice. They grew well
at first but then died off. Today I have trees on my land that are 40 to 50 feet
tall. At first we drove to church on Sundays with a team of oxen. Church was
conducted in some farm house. Now we drive our two beautiful horses hitched to a
nice buggy to a large, beautiful church in which there are still plenty of empty
pews. The reason for that, however, is not a lack of rain but discord among
people. Nearly everybody has a different faith and there are so many different
sects. There ought to be but one religion even as there is only one baptism. But
I do not want to start preaching; everyone has the freedom to believe as he
wishes.

[The following article, taken from The Java Herald, 1923 Special Edition, has
been edited. On Apr. 12, 1885, Philip Spiry, Sr., and his brother Fred arrived
in Menno, SD, where they worked. Their parents and sister, Barbara, and brother,
Carl, joined Fred and Philip in Menno. Philip Spiry, Sr. was the president of
the American State Bank of Java in 1923]

AN INTERESTING STORY by Philip Spiry Sr.
In the spring of 1889 we decided to go north and file on land. Fred and I had
two ponies, two cows, two steers and two heifers. The second year I purchased
the two cows and the other four were the increase. The two horses we bought on
time as well as a wagon and some machinery. In Freeman we got a small car and
loaded it with our stuff and Carl and his father-in-law did the same thing, also
Carl Schnaible and Fred Jesser; and we came to Eureka. From there we took our
folks and the stuff to the farm of Henry Aman, located about four miles NE of
Eureka.

After arriving at Henry Aman's place we started out to look for some land to
file on, but after driving all over the country we could find no land that
suited us. We then heard that there was plenty of land vacant in Walworth
County, and they were looking for German-Russian settlers, especially in the
part that is known as the "Blueblanket Valley". So we started out for this
county. We stopped at Sutley, Campbell County, and there they told us that
Walworth County was about three miles south of that place. After having lunch
there we again set out. The first farm we struck was that of H.R. de Maligon. As
he could speak the German language he told us that all of the land south of him
was unoccupied and that we could file on what we wanted.

Mr. de Maligon went along with us to look over the land. At that time he had a
sod shanty for a house and his nearest neighbor was Mr. Winkley whose land laid
along Hiddenwood creek. Mr. Van der Vorm was located on the farm now occupied by
Jacob Haux and Roper Bosch was on the farm now owned by Gottlieb Boehler while a
little further south were the Lakeman and Noble farms. We noticed that these
folks all had very deep wells and as we did not have money to put down such
wells we decided to locate along the creek where the water was more shallow.
Fred Jesser was the first one to pick his land and then Carl Schnaible. Philip
Aman and my brother Carl got into a scrape over some land as they both wanted to
file on a piece of land right along the creek, so finally Mr. Aman said he would
leave us and file on land in McPherson County where his brother was. Brother
Carl was the next to file and last Fred and I filed on the farms we now own.

The next day we went to Bangor and made out our filing papers. A few days later
Mr. Aman returned from McPherson County as he could not find any land there and
filed on a quarter just east of us.

The next thing on the program was to put up our buildings, but as Fred and I had
only about $8, the people told us that we could buy Missouri lumber for a dollar
a load. So the next trip was to the Missouri after this lumber. We went to Mound
City and then west to John Hills' place, where we purchased our first load,
which cost us $1. We then returned and unloaded and went over to Henry Aman's
farm, where our folks were staying. As this was too far for us to go we took
them to Sam Grenz's place, which was about 8 miles west of Eureka. We then went
back to our land and broke sod and put up our first house at a cost of about
$3.50, without the labor, and then went and got father and mother. I tell you we
felt as rich as Rockerfeller when we harvested our first crop, which was 18
bushels of flax. We had two hogs but nothing to feed them, but they managed to
rustle enough for themselves and when fall came we tried to butcher them, but,
Good Night! they had feet like deer and could run like them; and we could not
catch them. Finally Fred took his gun and shot them. We then had some fine pork.

The next year they stormed Walworth County and it was settled east of us and all
around us, so we decided that we needed a post office. I got signers and sent in
an application for a post office, which we named "Spiry Postoffice". Dave
Blinderman moved from Sutley on the quarter now occupied by John Hochstetter and
was appointed postmaster. After that we were very happy in our little sod house
and having a post office.

In 1900 when the railroad was built to Evarts they put up a little shack where
the stockyards are now and Henry Theilen started a little store. This was the
first building and business in Java. When the railroad company found out that
there was a demand for lots around the little store, they platted out the town
and began to sell through, agent, J.C. Corson.

Then things began to boom. Bauer, Hoff & Stoller came down from Eureka and
started a general store and warehouse, then John Hofmeyer began to build and
Fred and I put an Implement shop up where the Equity Exchange now is. This was
the beginning of Java.

After this, many other business places started, Carl F. Clement came down from
Eureka and started to publish the German Herold and later the English Herald.
Then came the Taylor hotel and many others.

In 1903 I was elected County Treasurer. I held this office for two terms. I was
in office through the county seat fight. George Ryan was county auditor, Bill
Hoffman, register of deeds; E.G. Powell, clerk of courts; John Koch, sheriff and
W.B. Burr, states attorney. But we did not have as pleasant a time as the boys
now have, in that old box of a court house. Everyone had to be their own janitor
but still we couldn't keep warm enough to keep the ink from freezing.

In  1906 when my term expired, I moved to Java and organized the German State
Bank, with three stockholders: John Bieber, brother Fred and myself and have
been there ever since. I shall close, but, in closing I wish to say that I hope
our young people will not have to undergo the hardships we old fellows had to,
even to the many times that we were forced, by grim necessity, to celebrate the
Fourth of July without a cent of money in our pockets.

Bauer & Sons Tell of Their Experiences in Java
In the fall of 1900 we moved with our household effects from our farm near
Eureka and commenced the construction of a store building. This was the south
part of our present building, and we hauled our lumber from Selby as there was
no lumberyard here at that time. There were no other buildings here except John
Hofmeyer, who was beginning his store also.  There were three of us who formed
the partnership known as Bauer, Hoff & Stoller, and we commenced business about
Christmas time in the winter of 1900. Henry Thielen had small store but he quit
business shortly after we started. In the spring of 1900 John Erbe started a
lumberyard here so that after that the people could buy their lumber right at
home. There were only one or two residences here at that time and no streets or
sidewalks.

In the year of 1901 the town of Java grew rapidly. Many new businesses were
started up. Among these were Lakeman Cook & Co., John Blinderman, Dr. Rosenthal,
who moved down from Evarts, McCafferty's bank and many others. It seemed as
though the town grew up over night. In 1903 this bank, which had been purchased
by Buechler, failed and the First State Bank was started. Many people lost
considerable money when this bank broke as there was no depositors' guaranty
fund in those days. In this year also came the Java Herald and several other
businesses. In the summer of 1903 they built a new school house, which was
considered a big one in those days.

In 1905 we built an addition to our store on the south side as our business was
getting to be so big. Those were great days, during the boom, and there has
never been a time in all our history when business was better except perhaps
during the war boom. In 1908 Hoff left the partnership and we continued the
business ourselves. Hoff went back to Eureka, his original home. The town
continued to grow and it was during this year that we voted to have a fire
engine and other municipal improvements of which the town was much in need.

Things continued to go along smoothly, business being good although the boom was
beginning to die out. The past eight years had seen many changes in the town and
surrounding country as both were building up very rapidly. Many settlers had
made their homes around Java and were beginning to substitute their sod houses
with large frame buildings.

In 1915 Jacob Stoller dissolved partnership and since that time we have operated
the store alone. We saw another big boom in Java from 1918 to 1921, when many
beautiful homes were built and new business enterprises launched, but the times
will never again be like they were back in the earlier years of our town and
community. Our city is becoming more and more modern as the years roll by, but
we still look back with pleasure upon those pioneer days when the country was
new and sparsely settled, but we are very contented to live in the present where
we have our electric lights, movies and various other amusements. [The article,
taken from The Java Herald, 1923 Special Edition, has been edited.]

Memories of the Jacob Stiegelmeier Family
[Written by Emma and Ben Stiegelmeier for Footprints, 1975]
The Hartmans, Amans, Mosers and Stiegelmeiers left South Russia in the early
1880's. Their homes were Bergdorf, Odessa and Gluckstal, on the Black Sea. They
were on the road to Brehmerhafen, Germany about 15 days, then on to America.
They arrived at Eureka in late Sept. 1880. They met a man, Mr. Biebelheimer, who
located them about 20 miles SW of Eureka, which was the Sutley area. Sutley was
also their postoffice. Those must have been the times.

Jacob and Rosina Stiegelmeier lived under a wagon box 3-1/2 ft. wide, 2-1/2 ft.
high and 10 ft. long, with my two sisters, Eva and Rosie, the first winter.
Their basic food was flour and salt. For meat it was prairie chickens and
rabbits mostly. My dad walked to Ipswich, pulling a small sled, to get supplies
for the family. The trip usually took three days. He would walk behind a sled or
wagon coming from Winona, which was about six miles west of now Pollock, on the
Missouri river.

Every settler had a single-shot 12 gauge shotgun. That gun was a must when they
left the Eureka area because of the Indian scare. Although at that time the
Indian scare was a thing of the past, the settlers were wary because of the
stories they had heard.

I asked my mother one time what impressed her most about America and she told me
that seeing the Statue of Liberty upon arrival in New York was so awesome that
many people, including her, cried like children. One thing she said was sad:
When our group had to part from others in New York, because so many people did
not pass the eye checkup tests and had  to be held back. Fortunately everyone in
this group had good eyes and was passed on through the lines and on they went to
South Dakota. The second year, my dad and neighbors built sod houses and living
was better.

The four worst stories that were told, were the time in 1905 a bull killed Peter
Hartman, grandfather of Pete Hartman now living in Bowdle. The massacre of the
minister, his wife and four children at Winona. Supposedly this crime was
committed by Indians. Hal Tracy from Pollock told me that several old timers on
their deathbed admitted that they were the killers, not the Indians. The tornado
in 1902 left the settlers with bare ground, not even the sod houses withstood
that storm. After that they used rock with the clay sod to withstand the storms.
They held. The fourth and worst event the folks talked about was where in North
Dakota a lawman killed the Wolf family, all but a small child. He was arrested
and convicted of the crime and was sent to prison for life.

Some of those things were gruesome, but the prairie fires my folks talked about
weren't too pleasant either! About every 4th year, the fires would take
everything and generally came from the southeast and burned all the way to the
Missouri river. The people had to work hard plowing fire guards to save grass.

We were a happy bunch. We didn't mix too much with people 8-10 miles away
because travel was either on foot or horseback. For pastime in winter evenings,
we would sit around the kitchen table, eat apples and chew Russian peanuts and,
of course, the big boys would tell stories of how strong and brave they were. I
wasn't so big and my job was not to tell the tall tales; instead, I listened.

The group were Sabbath (Saturday) keepers. The church was about 11 miles NE of
Java near the Jacob Oswald farm.

In my early days the 4th of July was the big day of the year, going to Java,
because Java nearly always celebrated with a parade, ball game, foot races, sack
races, 3-legged races, dances, etc. One thing sad was we had to be home at
sundown, to milk cows and feed calves. When the 4th of July was on Saturday we
had to stay at home.

I feel that I was always happiest in the Java community when I was young. I
traveled extensively but for some reason I was always glad to be back home. The
people have been really good to us, and if I made some small contribution to the
Java people and community around, I surely got paid four-fold for it, and to all
young people coming up in line to build and prosper I would gladly say: "May the
sun shine softly upon your faces, may the wind be always at your back, and may
the rains fall gently upon your crops." Thank you. Emma and Ben Stiegelmeier.

The following two stories are the work of former Java resident Marv Hoffer, who
holds the Copyright and has given permission for them to be printed in
Centennial Memories.

STALE POPCORN AND 15-CENT MOVIES
Copyright by Marv Hoffer January 25, 1990 Lewistown, MT
It was long about the mid-50s when main street boiled with excited activity on
Saturday night, the Big Night on the Northern Plains of South Dakota. Cars,
dust, farm folks, stray dogs, and kids walking the Loop. Up one side of Main,
down the other. The grocery, hardware, bank, drugstore, creamery, pool hall, gas
station and barbershop were "open" late into the night. Farm folks and town
folks gossiped, laughed, sold eggs and cream, played pinochle, and watched the
crowed drift by.

Saturday night. The Show Hall was open for business! Hard, sweat-soaked work for
the big folks and chores plus 'rithmatic and writin' for the kids all week
whetted their appetite for entertainment, and a change of pace. All work and no
play dulls the edge of life. The show, or movies, opened minds to great change,
new perspectives, and a chance to see what the rest of the world was doing. A
time to peer over the fence of our worldly neighbors out in Hollywood, Africa,
Europe, Cape Fear and hidden places beyond. We had only a limited understanding
of how massive, complicated and grand our planet was. Sheltered in our little
niche? Yep, most of us, and we liked it that way.

No television existed in that part of the world, and radio couldn't compete with
a genuine show in color, black-white for that matter. I was about 16 and
fortunate to be hired by the Frank brothers, Wes and Art, who were the proud (?)
owners of the Java Theater. They had purchased that institution from Ben
Steiglemeier and Herman Fiedler some short years previous. The Show Hall. Lordy,
that sounds as though it had a cathedral ceiling, massive purple stage curtains,
and a flashing marquee out front. It did, only if you closed your eyes and
imagined it so to be. But it didn't matter. Saturday night in Java, A little
farming town on the Dakota Plains.......the place to be. It was Home Town. Held
in the highest esteem by the 600 or so souls in town and the scattered farming
families in the Northern Great Plains. They sure don't make towns like that
anymore.

My job was what today's hard-core business types would call "multi-faceted."
Translated: jack-of-all-trades, master of a few. Some time during mid-day I
hustled down to the Show Hall basement to fire-up the old monster furnace and
stuff its innards with black coal, then hope that it could defrost the upstairs
so a person could take off his heavy sheepskin storm coat. Out with the big
broom to sweep the stale popcorn from the last showing on the previous Wednesday
night. Oh yes! We had three full nights of shows in Java, Wednesday, Saturday
and Sunday. It must have been hard for people to find their mouths in the dark.
There was more popcorn on the floor than I could sweep.

The Show Hall was a narrow, long building with about enough seats for 150 souls,
give or take 50 or so. Memories are not that strong on mathematics. The seats
were the folding wooden type that pinched a hand so that you remembered it two
weeks later. Each seat bottom had about five pounds or more of "juicy fruit,
spearmint" gum stuck to it, in thick layers and chunks turned to concrete. Must
have been at least 30 years accumulation. I never tried to dislodge it - would
take weeks and all for naught. More plastered on each show. Without a bed post
handy, the seat bottom was the next best thing.

The Milwaukee Road steamed and snorted into Java twice a day to bring a
cornucopia of passengers, take on the mail, load eight and ten-gallon cans full
of a week's accumulation of sweet (?) cream, and unload mail and film cases
which contained the acetate rolls for the show that evening. It was my job to
meet the evening train belching hot steam and acrid coal smoke, then haul the
two-three heavy steel film cans to the "upper and inner sanctum", or projection
booth, on the second story at the rear of the Hall. Adolph Horst ran the Dray
Line for years, so there was a time that he and his team of horses pulled his
dray wagon from the depot to the Show Hall with the very heavy reel cases. Made
my skinny legs buckle to lug those cans up the narrow and steep stairs to the
projectors. There were times during the winter when the steam engine had to buck
blizzards and travel mighty slow on cold steel which made it nip-an-tuck just
before show time.

Art and Wes Frank taught me the basics, more or less, of film projection on
equipment that predated the Big One, WWII. Carbon-arc lamps sent the image down
the old Show Hall to drop it on the ancient stage screen of light canvas
stretched on a 2x4 frame. This was a very basic theater. The floor did not slant
from rear to screen as today's theaters do.

The movie projection concept was simple, yet mixed with equal portions of black
magic, smoke and mirrors. A large carbon-arc rod lightly kissed a smaller
diameter carbon-arc rod by turning a couple of handles within the guts of the
projectors. The juice at 220 volts A.C. snapped them to life as they briefly
touched into an intense blue-white light that would blind a man without the
tinted green window on the projector. The reaction and heat was similar to some
passionate kisses I have seen on screen. Remember those? Fumes erupted from the
projector that would choke a good horse, but most of these were vented up a pipe
into the Class I Dakota airshed. There they mixed with the local stockyard
aromas, municipal waste treatment wetland south of town, and other Class I
additives.

The whole ritual involved considerable polished motion to load the rolls of film
into the projector. Show Time!! First came the news reels, RKO and others, to
tell we who lived in a sheltered part of the globe about the world well beyond
the city limits, followed by a couple of short cartoons which everyone hooted
and stomped about, young, old, and ancient. Folks paid good money to see the
show, so expected to have it all, news, cartoons, and the main feature. Cost a
solid 15 cents for kids under 14 or so, and 35 cents for adults. That would be
any male man enough to show more than peach fuzz on his chin. Inflation took its
toll, and the price for kids sky rocketed to two-bits and 50 cents for big
folks. Inflation ruined many great institutions.

The nightly show was usually about 2-4 reels long. Or if you measured it the
times Mom had to take 2-4 kids to the bathroom, about 27 trips. Which meant that
she saw the first half of the RKO Newsreel - something about mountain climbing
in Tibet, and the last ten minutes of the movie where the hero rides off into
the sunrise after a night of battle and intrigue. Ah, the responsibilities of
motherhood. Dads were not noted for "tending the kids" while the show was on.
Right?

(Photo:) Delila Aman at the Grand Theatre

There were two carbon-arc projectors, side by side, both angled from the booth
onto the screen way down the far end of the building, through the haze, eleven
overwintering moths, and two boxelder bugs looking for each other in the dark.
Each was loaded with a reel of acetate film plus a take-up reel. As the show was
projected onto the screen from projector #1, I enjoyed the movie during its
first showing, and started the second projector carbon-arc lamp as the "switch"
came nearer. The whole process was nothing short of magic to most folks. To me
it was a combination of cold steel nerves, butter fingers, and watery eyes from
the projector smoke.

If you watch old movies you will see in the upper right hand corner of the
screen a "blip", or small dark circle. That signals switch over time to the next
reel. The trick was to be on your toes for the first blip, then quickly start
the second projector and shut down the first in one clean, masterful motion. It
required graceful motion and synchronization - and I was blessed with neither.
Most of the time it worked, some times there was a long string of numbers and
bright light followed by stomping of feet and hollering from the courteous
crowd. It always awakened the "nappers", and brought the passionate couples into
an appropriate posture. Some folks even started wandering out the back door exit
thinking the show was over.

The greatest reactions came when I goofed during such famous shows as Quo Vadis,
during those moist love or battle scenes. When the crowd got into the substance
of the movie, they were as though in a trance. To be snapped out of that
hypnotic involvement by a fumbling projectionist was a cardinal sin. No
tolerance for error allowed by the Saturday night crowd.

On occasions, more often than I wanted, the film would tear so it no longer was
taken up by the rear reel. Instead, I simply opened the reel door and let her
spew onto the projection booth floor like 600 pounds of rattlesnakes out of a
gunny sack. The old acetate film was very flammable, and with those carbon-arc
lamps throwing enough sparks and heat to melt lead, it makes me squirm even
today, some 39 years later.

Make the switch to the second machine, then begin the art of quick hand-splicing
film on the old work bench at the back of the booth. Spin it onto the rewind
reel and into the film can for the next show. Never did have any of that film
ignite on me, but Lordy, Lordy, had it done so in that metal-incased booth, I
would have been barbecued like German sausage on a spit.

My projection profession lasted only a couple of years as I recall, then they
gave me a diploma down at the high school and I headed for a military base to
put my time in as a GI for God, Country, Mom, and Apple Pie, not necessarily in
that order.

The Java Theater, or Show Hall, served the town well as a civic gathering place,
for politicians to flop their lips and spew unkept promises, a few magicians,
talent contests to select best looking lass for the Snow Queen Contest, wild
wedding dances, and even roller skating where everyone looked like a hog on ice.
But that is another story, or two.

It was the practice to show the same film on Saturday, Sunday, and the following
Wednesday evening. Cost of film rentals required at least a fair profit return.
The boob tube came onto the scene and the greater ability and willingness of
folks to travel to other parts of the globe made the profit margin too slim for
the Theater to continue. It was closed, with great regret. An era passed, and
15-cent movies were only a fond recollection to the privileged few who lived
those historical years. Eventually the building was salvaged for its lumber,
especially the hard wood flooring it contained. Stained with shoes of every walk
of life, bubble gum, soda pop, and burns from tobacco users.

The hallowed halls of the old Theater was the place where young boys and girls
could gently and shyly hold hands in the dark thinking great passionate
thoughts. Some of those materialized as they grew into young men and women,
married, then longed for the times when they used to hold hands in the dark at
the show. We often hold dearest that which we no longer have, and regret not
loving and enjoying it when we had it.

A farm family could bring in 12 dozen fresh eggs with a little chicken manure on
them plus a 10-gallon can of cream and get enough cash to pay for everyone's
show ticket, under $2.00, and still have enough for three sacks of groceries, a
beer, Hamms, for Dad, and a soda pop for Mom and each of the kids. Quite an
evening. Thanks to 57 chickens and 11 milk cows back on the farm who clucked and
mooed as they paid for their bed and breakfast.

Yep, times have changed, and I'm a bit sorry they have. Those were simpler
times, good times in life, never to be repeated. I'm grateful for having enjoyed
those days and learned a trade I never used again. But then, I wouldn't care to
sweep stale popcorn and be a "professional projectionist" for the rest of my
life. Would you? Maybe?

SUNRISE DANCE, A HARVEST TIME TRADITION
Copyright By Marvin C. Hoffer January 17, 1992 Lewistown, MT
Dakota Spring ripened into Summer heat. Fall was marching close behind. Corn
ears filled with golden nuggets. Billowing oceans of wheat, oats, barley, and
hay drooped plump heads as days became shorter. Harvest. Work began before
daylight, lasted long after sunset. Days of haste, before the long, Dakota
Winter cloaked this land in its fierce mantle. Everyone worked, long, hard, with
purpose. Life depended on it. Harvest was the fulfillment of the entire year's
efforts, investments, hopes and survival. Then, with strenuous labor and buckets
of sweat, harvest was complete.

Sunrise Dance! Time for celebration, happiness, relaxation. The Harvest Festival
Dance of tradition. Across the glaciated Dakota Plains, in old opera houses,
Legion halls, and on the open prairie, Harvest Festival dances were performed by
thousands of men and women who earned these simple pleasures. A celebration of
thanksgiving and survival.

Wherever three or more musicians were gathered, there was a rollicking band for
a Sunrise Dance. Farmers who only that evening had crawled off a combine, or
green John Deere tractor, scrubbed with abrasive Lava soap to shine their
calloused hands and sun-browned faces in great anticipation of a long night of
Sunrise Dance. Musically educated, or not. They came also from the blacksmith
shop, corn field, butcher shop, halls of education, but not "men of the cloth."
Never did know a clergyman who played in a dance band, although many were gifted
musicians. Their music was to celebrate the harvest of souls before God. Like
birds of a feather musicians spawned small mixed groups of foot-stomping prairie
musicians. Saxophones, drums, electric organ, an accordion from the Olde
Country, a guitar now and then, and not much else, except talent and a love for
music. Music, olde-time music was the laxative that made it happen.

Long about 9 or 10 pm, when the fall day warmth turned to comfortable cool,
these intrepid merrymakers laid their ears to their instruments and "tuned"
them. Eventually mellow sounds came forth. Foot-stompin' music that brought back
memories to older minds like sunrise bursting on a summer morn. We all were
younger. Once.

Ma put on her "special occasions", colorful dress and her red, low heel shoes,
then said "Oscar, lets go to the dance." Pa had been waiting for at least a half
hour in the blue, 1949 Ford pickup. Cows had been milked, supper eaten, kids put
up for the night, with the oldest in charge, more or less. Off to town, 18 miles
distant, across prairie lit by a full moon. So large, so close, you could almost
see the boats sailing on the canals. Ma sat extra close to Pa thinking amorous
thoughts--must have been that old moon. There's something romantic about
thundering down a prairie trail at 35 mph in an old beater pickup under a full
moon. Pa had problems maneuvering the floor shift with her sitting so close, but
voiced no complaints. Just kept on chewing on his mustache, and dodging
potholes.

Cost $1.00 a head to get into the Sunrise Dance. By time they parked the Ford
and Pa combed his unruly, black mop once more, the Happy Hustlers were pumping
away on the first of 5-6 hours of music, Dakota style! Peppermint schnapps had
been passed around the band to lubricate tonsils, fingers, and spirits. Away we
go! Polkas, waltzes, two-steps, and schottische were blasted out to the crowd of
160 strong, excluding a few who sat along the walls gathering ammunition for the
forthcoming week's gossip. "Look at that woman dancing with..."  "Now who is
he dancing with!!??" "Did you know...?"

Now and then a band member got his tonsils sufficiently loosened to belt out a
vocal to accompany a waltz. Some could sing, others.....well, they should have
continued practicing while milking cows. Dances were played in sets of 3-4
selections. Someone always was quick with the dance floor lubricant, sprinkling
it on between sets. A robust woman and her equally endowed mate could flit about
the slick floor to a polka beat in whirls that made me dizzy watching, never
missing a lick, never failing. Light as goose down. Grace, intense enjoyment,
punctuated by a beller and a holler now and then, to let the world know that
this is the Sunrise Dance. A time to enjoy. The Festival of Harvest.

Long about 1-2 a.m. heat generated by the whirling dancers in the hall was
billowing out doors like smoke. Erie under the full moon, but no-one noticed.
Sweat poured from every pore of the overheated body. It was a sweet success
sweat--born of hard work, and enjoyment. An ancient German proverb states:
"Arebit makes das lieben siese"-"Work makes life sweet". Sweet it was, be it in
the field, or on the dance floor.

Women flounced to and fro the powder room to freshen-up. Men waited impatiently
to prance and strut their stuff with their women of the night. Children danced
with children, women danced with women, men danced with women, women danced with
children. No class distinctions here. Don't recall seeing men dancing with men.
Must have been an Olde German tradition.

The band was hired for 4-5 hours, but as they signaled their "last" dance, the
crowd passed a brown hat, and peppermint schnapps to the band. That refreshed
the music makers for at least 1-2 more hours. The building was bursting with
folks bent on dancing every dance, laughter, a constant roar of voices. Like ten
thousand geese gabbling just before they leave for the morning grain fields.
Those were good times. If you stepped into the chill night to gather your senses
and cool your body, you could see a faint pink glow of a rising sun in the
distant East.

The crowd nurtured the dance till the band pumped-out the absolute last strain
long about 4 am. Then the overheated, dog-tired crowd of Sunrise Dancers drifted
to the door and journeyed home on gravel trails that wandered among wheat
fields, prairie, and sloughs. Five, black and white pussy cats with vertical
plumes marched in single order across the road. Pa slowed to let them pass in
the breaking daylight. Ma was dreaming of dancing, and didn't notice.

Some of us gathered shotguns, goose hunting gear, and a bit of grub then drove
120 miles east on the Yellowstone Trail to meet the first flights of snows and
blues at Sand Lake Refuge. We had danced the night away with some of the
sweetest blossoms on the Prairie, but now were anxious to shoot a few, plump
geese, and sleeping blissfully in a warm blind for 2-3 hrs. It has been a good
year.

SATURDAY NIGHT IN TOWN by Herbert Geigle
In the early days, usually the head of family did the shopping for the entire
family. The women and children stayed at home. Only occasionally would they be
permitted to go to town. Starting in the mid-1920s, it became the practice in
small Dakota towns for the entire family to go to town to do the shopping and
socialize on Saturday night. This was possible because of the family car. All
week family members planned for Saturday night, and whenever one got up on
Saturday morning, they knew what to expect. At the breakfast table, the father
encouraged everyone to work a little bit harder and faster to finish work early
in the day. Mothers and daughters prepared all of the baking and most of the
meal preparation for Sunday dinner.

The Saturday evening chores would be finished early, especially if we shipped
our cream in either 5, 8 or 10-gallon cans, destination to the creameries in
eastern South Dakota or Minnesota. Tags would be fastened to the cans' handle
and another to its lid, naming the sender and designation. The local train would
stop in Java around 6 p.m. daily except Sunday and pick up cans of cream. The
next day except Sundays, the train (it was called The Local) would arrive in
Java between 9 and 10 a.m. and drop off freight and empty cream cans; they would
be lined up next to the depot for the farmers to claim at their leisure. About 3
to 4 days later, a check would be received in the mail. If we planned on selling
the cream to a local buyer, we arrived in town later. We would bathe and dress
and then load the case of eggs and can of cream into the car and take off for
Java.

(Photo:) Cream station, 1909

The cream station was the first stop in town, where we would unload the can of
cream. The cream buyer would weigh the filled cans, take a sample of cream to
test for butterfat content and quality of the cream. Sweet cream was preferred
and brought a much higher price. After the sample was taken, the cream from the
farmer's can would be emptied into the creamery's can and the farmer's cans were
then washed and weighed. The net weight of the cream based upon its butterfat
content was calculated and either a check was written or cash paid to the
farmer. These tasks were completed in about thirty minutes after the cream was
delivered. Depending upon the finances of the family, the cream money was either
picked up as soon as it was ready or when they picked up their cream cans just
before the family returned home later that night. Different creameries would set
up buying stations in Java. During early years, Java had a large number of
buyers, but in the 30's, John Schlaht was the most successful dealer. He
purchased cream, eggs, live poultry and hides for the Bowdle creamery. He and
his wife retired and Mike Kary took over and enlarged by adding iron junk. After
Kary, Art Freimark took over and was followed by Christ Pfitzer. This station
was located on the south side of today's cafe. Mrs. Ted Spiry had her station
next to the old post office, and she, too, was successful. When the farmers went
into the milking business, they sold their milk direct to the cheese factory.
Others discontinued milking and went into the feeder business. Egg production no
longer was profitable and there was no need for cream and egg buyers.

The next stop was to sell the eggs. Most grocery stores bought the farmer's eggs
and when the wife completed her shopping, the egg credit would be applied
against the price of groceries. The purchased groceries were packed into the
farmer's own wooden egg crate as paper sacks were not very common and were quite
expensive for the merchants. Each egg crate had the farmer's name on it; some
were decorated and some were painted in different colors. Egg crates were
constructed in either fifteen or thirty dozen two-compartment capacities. This
meant there were five layers in each compartment with three-dozen eggs in each
layer. After the eggs were counted (sometimes candled to see if some
unscrupulous farm family put bad eggs in with the good fresh eggs), and removed
from the farmer's case, the farmer's fillers and flats, to keep the eggs
separated to prevent breaking, were folded and placed back in the case. The
people of Java had a choice where to buy their groceries. There was Gershin's,
Hepper's Market, Phil Spiry Meat Market, Bauer & Sons, and Lange's Store. I
remember Louie Gershin would give candy with each order, and at Hepper's Meat
Market, Bill Hepper would hand out a wiener and believe me, that was a treat!
When Mr. Gershin retired and moved back to Minneapolis, Emanuel and Gertrude
Kary took over the store. I worked for them on Saturday and Saturday night
during my high school days. This was my first job and I enjoyed the grocery
business. Helen Helm was a clerk and Ida Gearhart was senior clerk. Mr. Kary
sold his business to Gilbert and LaRayne Schlepp and they named it G & L. They
closed the store due to a lack of business. Hepper's Meat Market was operated by
Karl and sons Bob and Bill, and when Karl died, Ed Hirsch took over the
operation and then sold it to Elmer Biel. He did custom butchering and made a
lot of sausage.

Elmer, Marvin Gross, Fred Schott and myself did the butchering and made
different kinds of sausage. We would have to hand-mix the ground meat and put
all kinds of seasoning in the mixture to make the "perfect sausage". The mixture
would be put into casings and then cooked or smoked. Once a week, we would make
bratwuerst, liver-wuerst and beef baloney. Elmer sold this business to Marvin
Pfitzer and later, his brother took over. Spiry's meat marked was located where
the Java City Liquor building now stands. The market burned in the mid-30's, and
in the same fire, half of Bauer & Sons was destroyed. This building was in the
now vacant lot south of City Liquor. The bank building that was destroyed in the
same fire is now where Marin-Biel Insurance is located. Bauer & Sons lost the
dry goods section of their store. Under the management of Evelyn Bauer and her
brothers, John and Fred, they were able to continue with the store. The business
continued until Evelyn's death. The Lange's store was under the management of
Mrs. Lange and continued until the early 1940's. Mrs. Lange passed away and the
store closed.

The money received from the cream and eggs bought the necessities for the
family, plus spending money for candy, soda pop, popcorn, ice cream, and tickets
to the movie. Cream and egg money also paid for clothes, equipment, repairs and
parts, tobacco and always salted-and-roasted-in-the-shell sunflower seeds.

On Saturday nights, the ladies went to the grocery and dry goods stores and
visited with acquaintances and relatives. The narrow aisles would be so full of
people standing and visiting that, at times, it would be a real problem for
people to do their shopping and for clerks to get around in the store to fill
orders. In those days, when the lady of the house did her grocery shopping, she
could not grab a cart, fill it, and then head to the checkout. Depending on the
merchants, small town grocers relaxed and let the customers pick up and carry
items to the counter and the clerk wrote down the items in the order book.
Usually, the customer went to the counter where the clerks and cash register
would be found. When a clerk asked if he could help, the customer read off the
items on the grocery list. The clerk wrote these items down in the order book
and, after the clerk had the shopper's complete order written down, went around
the store picking those items off the shelves, carrying them to the counter and
entering the prices in the order book. It was possible, and even encouraged, for
the shopper to wander around the store to look over the merchandise and the
prices, but not to remove items from the shelves.

This increased sales because the shopper always remembered a few items she had
not included on her list and, of course, she was sometimes tempted to try some
new product. When the order was complete, the clerk totaled the grocery amount
and applied the egg money. The farm wife always got a carbon copy of her order
so she could check the prices and totals. The last chore for the clerk was to
pack the groceries in the egg crate and either place it off to the side in the
store, or carry it to the farmer's car. There was never a worry that someone
would ever steal from someone's purchased and paid for groceries while sitting
in the store. Each store had a bench inside and in front of the store for the
ladies to sit and wait for their husbands.

Father Made His Rounds: The men did their business at the Schuh or Spiry garage,
Ed Gill's Hardware, or got their hair cut at August Schlepp's barber shop. They
would chat at Central Lumber with Fred Helm, or stop in to chat with Ludwig Helm
or C.L. Hicks to cash a check or check on their insurance; buy gas and oil or
have their car serviced at Hochstetter's Sterling station or at the Equity
Service, and probably order bulk gas from John Lutz or Gerhardt Fiedler. They
would stop to see whether their plow shares were sharpened at Frank Weisgram's
Blacksmith shop, or stop in at Perman's Implement. They socialized with
acquaintances at these places of business, and, after finishing, they headed for
the Speidel Recreation Parlor or Eisenbeisz Billiards and Pool Hall. Maybe they
would have a beer or two, purchase a packet or two of sunflower seeds, spitting
the shells on the floor or sidewalk, and visit. At Eisenbeisz's, both pool
tables would be occupied and four tables of cards would be played, Pinochle,
Buck Euchre, and one table would be reserved for Poker. Eisenbeisz also had an
on-sale license, so the "hard stuff" could be sold. This was pretty much a male
reserve and very few women came into this establishment, except to get money or
remind the 'old man' that it was time to go home.

When both husband and wife had finished shopping or visiting, they sometimes
went to the Lakeman Cafe or A.C. Schlepp Confectionery for a frosty or an ice
cream sundae, or to the Job sister's cafe, operated by Minnie and Tillie, who
later sold to Claudia Pfaff. The Kary furniture store became Schlepp's Cafe,
operated by Slippery and his family. Later, his nephew Elmer and his wife, Erna,
took over the operation. The farmer and his wife would have something to eat, or
a cup of Java before rounding up the youngsters and heading for home.

The Youngsters Also Had Things To Do: The older boys and girls paraded (walking,
not cruising) up and down Main Street, visiting with their friends and both
sexes looking each other over, but not letting on that they were doing so. Many
an important decision was made about each other on this Main Street promenades,
and the decision to treat a girl to a five-cent ice cream cone was one not to be
taken lightly, in those days. Many youngster would go to the movie operated by
Eddie Perman, and later by Fiedler and Stiegelmeier, and then by the Frank
brothers, which cost about 10 or 15 cents for admission. I remember my first
movie in color was "Gone With the Wind", in 1939.

Can you imagine that there used to be parking problems on Main Street in the
30's? Parking was on both sides of Main from the lumber yard down to Schlepp's
residence, and from the Equity service station down to the Schnaible residence.
Also, some of the side streets were utilized. In front of each cream station, a
No Parking sign would appear, so patrons could unload their cream. By the mid-
fifties, this era ended and a new one began.

NEW LAND and MEMORIES by Ruben Aman
The Homestead: In Jan. 1889, Jakob J. Aman entered the U.S. Land Office in
Aberdeen and filed papers to acquire his land in what was then the Dakota
Territory. The Dakota Territory was established by an act of Congress in 1861
and covered all of North and South Dakota and much of Montana and Wyoming. It is
interesting to note that the U.S. acquired the Dakota Territory in 1803 through
the Louisiana Land Purchase.

The Railroad: In those days, homesteads were moving west toward the Missouri
River. By 1880, two railroads had been constructed through the Dakota Territory
west of the Missouri River. I have been unable to locate records on when Java
Junction was constructed and made available to homesteaders of the area.
However, I do remember my father telling me, when I was a very young boy, that
the spur track was called Java Junction. The railroad workers named it Java
Junction. That name came about when, upon their arrival in the area, they would
stop and have a coffee break.

In Nov. 1889, North and South Dakota became the 39th and 40th state of the U.S.
I believe the Java Depot building had been constructed because the surrounding
area of Java Junction was developing. Java became a town in the year of 1900.
Our heritage is an incredible story and we should all be honored to participate
in this wonderful celebration about our favorite town, Java.

Arriving At Their New Land: In my mind's eye, I have tried to understand and
envision what it might have been like when our grandparents arrived at their new
land in their new country. It was wintertime and I know that it was very cold.
They had no house to live in. Some unanswered questions I have are: Where did
they get water to drink and bathe? What did they eat? How did they survive the
harsh elements? Did they have any money? If they did, where could they buy
supplies? How would they travel for their supplies?

During the winter they could not plant a garden. It would be another three
months before they could plant anything. One can only imagine about the
neighboring family, the Stiegelmeiers, a half-mile away. I'm sure they joined
one another in hunting wildlife for meat and hides, and collected melted snow or
ice from lakes for water. By Apr. of 1889, they may have found dandelion and
pigweed growing on the creek banks for greens to eat and then they could look
forward to planting gardens by late Mar. or Apr. We can all certainly admire
their courage to survive this environment, not only the Amans but all the
homesteaders of that time period in the Dakota Territory.

The Sioux Indians: The Sioux Indians were west of the Missouri River by about 20
or so miles away. I'm unaware if the Aman or other pioneers had any safety
concerns about them but I pause to think of how they might have handled fishing
the river when they were so close by.

I was raised on this same homestead. I remember Indian relics all around us on
the untilled prairie land. I observed many rectangular layouts of cobblestone
and circular patterns with perhaps a diameter of 10-12 feet. We found arrowheads
along the creek beds and lakes. Most of us can remember the prairie and recall
the untilled land that now is our crop land and think what it would be like to
arrive in that environment at a young age, having a new bride, no money, a few
supplies, and only the "will to work". It truly amazes me!

The First House: Our grandparents in 1889 did start to build their home. It was
made of stone and sod with dirt floors and they would bear and raise five of
their six offspring in that sod house. Only their youngest daughter, Ida, would
be born in the new house. I remember my father telling me the sod house had an
attached chicken house and a room for a cow. This old sod house is now a pile of
stone and more stones over the years have since been added from the tilled
cropland. Yes, I can remember picking up rocks with a team and wagon. I should
note that between 1889 (year of the homestead) to 1897 there was a serious
drought in the territory of what is now known as South Dakota. How could these
pioneers survive? Not only my forefathers, all of our forefathers, yours and
mine, the real pioneers of SD! I am very proud of them. They were rough and
hearty people.

The New Home: In 1903, times were much better. Our grandfather built a new
house, barn, granary and other out buildings. Inside each building, in a type of
German script lettering my grandfather painted, with white paint, Jakob J. Aman,
1903. The letters were about 12 inches high.

(Photo:) This is the new (1903) home of Jakob J. and Elizabeth Aman. L-R: Jakob
         J. Aman, Ida, Elizabeth, Esther, Jakob, John, Edwin, and Albert Aman.

Memories: I have a lot of fond memories about my youth and growing up on the
farm with my brothers and sisters. I remember winters could be quite cold. I
especially remember my mother's large wood and coal cooking stove which we used
a lot for heat in the winter, as well as for all the cooking my mother did for
the family. My mother was an unusually talented cook. I remember the fine meals
and bread she would prepare on that cast iron wood burning stove. In the
winters, we kids would sit at the dining table looking out the window seeing
