nothing but white snow sometimes covering everything. Snowdrifts would reach as
high as the roof. It was impossible to travel or visit Java so we were
frequently isolated in our farmhouse for long periods of time. Of course, one
day is a long time when you are a youngster.

I remember our country school, Sunshine School, that was located about three
miles away. It was a country school where grades kindergarten through the eighth
grade were taught in one room. I recall three rows of school desks with a wood
bench in front of the teacher's desk where she would call grade students for
class sitting on the bench before her. Our school had a potbelly wood stove back
in the corner for heat during the winter months.

I recall going to school in a one-horse buggy with my sister in sometimes very
snowy weather. One day we were going to school in a near blizzard. Our horse,
Silver, got too close to a telephone pole and detached the buggy from its
harness leaving us behind. Silver continued all the way to the school and
entered the barn where the horses were kept for the kids that came to school by
way of horseback or buggy. I do recall that discipline, respect and honor were
very prevalent when we were growing up. These principles were taught to us in
the home, as well as school.

I remember the rhythmic sound of the steam engine in the Powerhouse in Java. You
could hear it all the way out to our farm. I remember hearing the train passing
Java and blowing its lonely whistle. I wanted to rush to see it go by, however,
it was many miles away but it was easily heard at our farm. The water tower in
Java could be seen from afar. It was always one of the first indications we had,
as kids, in visualizing how much further we had to travel. I remember the
granary elevators. My father would take me with him to the elevators in our 1926
Chevrolet truck. My father would dump our grain into the elevator and I would
wonder as a boy: Where in the world does all this grain go? I saw other farmers
dumping their grain, too, and was always amazed how big that hole was in the
ground because we could never quite fill it up. I remember the Fred Helm lumber
store and frequent visits my father would make there to visit with his friends.
I recall, especially on Saturday nights, seeing my father sit at a huge table
surrounded by perhaps ten men swapping stories and always chewing on sunflower
seeds. The shells on the floor appeared to be inches deep!

I recall going to the depot often to deliver cream cans full of cream for the
market. We would deposit six or eight cream cans and then pick up our empty
return cans from the previous trip for the next round. I am told by my cousin,
Delila Biel, that Janice Bender Wolf is working to make the Java Depot a
historical site. God bless her. I want to donate. How about you?

All the ladies in the area visited Carl Hepper's Market. I recall my mother
shopping and boxing her supplies and remembering rows of boxes selected and
prepared for and by the ladies. The boxes would sit on the floor until each of
the families would be ready to depart for their farm. While my mother was
shopping at Hepper's Market, we kids would be enjoying the evening on the
streets of Java with our friends and relatives. The railroad workers were in
town on some Saturday nights, too. These men were very generous. They would line
us kids up and play the game "leeny meeny miny moe" and the kid they ended up
with landed an ice cream cone. The kid that ended up last in the game was never
supposed to get an ice cream cone. However, when the game was over the railroad
men always saw to it that the last child received an ice cream cone also. During
the depression, my mother and father handed me 10 cents for us four younger
children to spend on treats in town. It seemed like a lot of money then and it
bought candy for all four of us. Not much but enough.

I remember Frank Weisram's blacksmith shop where my father would go for
repairing certain damaged equipment items. I remember our country church, north
of our farm, and our family attending every week. This church was located north
of our ranch in Campbell County and was moved to Java some years later. I don't
recall the year of the move. But what remains there now is a cemetery. Many of
our relatives including our grandfather and grandmother, our father, and other
members of the Aman family are buried there.

The biggest event in my childhood and that of our family was to go to town
Saturday nights. We were Seventh Day Adventists and could not do our chores
until sundown on Saturday. I remember all of us kids hustling to do our chores,
milking cows, feeding chickens, taking care of animals with quick dispatch and
discipline. The responsibility for our chores was strictly managed by our
father. Not to do them would mean the lost privilege of going to town on
Saturday night.

(Photo:) This picture was done some time around 1903. My Dad was about 8 or 9
         years old at the time and he told me he remembered a man sitting in the
         field just east of our farm, creating the picture.

Our entertainment was limited to the radio. Some of my old favorites are: Lum
and Abner, Amos and Andy, Henry Aldridge. If Lulu Bell and Scotty were on from
the Grand Ole Opry, my mother would pull rank. The only other entertainment that
I recall would be to visit our aunts and uncles at their farms. I remember going
to my Uncle Jake's home often for dinner and visiting with my cousins. On the
Sabbath, quite often, my Aunt Ida and her two boys, Eugene and Orville, would
come to our farm and stay for dinner and  relaxation.

I remember our neighboring farms: the Reinhold Moser's, the Newmiller's, the
Hartman's, the Krause's, the Oswald's, and the Biel's. I'll always remember how
well kept the William Oswald horses were. They would shine in the sunlight. His
boys knew how to carry their horses, I'll bet.

More On Our Homestead: This land is still owned by a member of the Aman family.
My father lost his life in a thrashing accident in October of 1942. My older
brother, Edwin, and I (Ruben) tried to work the farm the following year. We were
too young and it became obvious that we couldn't manage the challenge. Our
family, with our mother, decided we should sell our farm. We did, in fact, sell
our farm to our Uncle Jake, our father's oldest brother, who left it to (as I
remember) his oldest son, Albert. When Albert passed away, he left it to his
younger brother, Calvin Aman. Yes, our grandfather's homestead of 1889 is still
in our Aman family. That's one hundred and eleven years ago January 23, 2000. 1
feel a great comfort in that and hope my cousin, Calvin, will again someday pass
it on to another part of the Aman family. Our farmhouse, barn and buildings are
all gone now, but the land, the original Aman homestead, will always be there
... no one can ever change that.

There is a saying that you can take the boy away from the farm but you can't
take the farm away from the boy. At quiet times, in my mind's eye, I frequently
visit our farm. I can still hear the music the wind made blowing through our
cottonwood trees. In the evening, in the barn, I can see our horse teams in
their stalls feeding. I always liked to listen to horses feeding - is that
strange? No! I can see and hear our milk cows at milking time feeding on their
gallon of oats and, yes, I can smell the fresh milk and see the calves and barn
kittens gathering for their share of the skim milk.

I revisit the time we had a Russian farmhand, Mr. Blinus. A storm in the mid
1930's destroyed our windmill. We kids had to pump water by hand for the
livestock. Mr. Blinus made a game out of this chore. He had us take turns
pumping while teaching us how to count in Russian, one through five. I can still
count in Russian: o'deen,  dwaut, dreet, cha'dary, beite (not sure of correct
spelling though). Funny how there are things you never forget. Of course, the
fun was over when the horses and cattle came to drink and we had to start over
again.

I always see my parents working in the garden near the windmill. My mother would
can much of the garden vegetables every year - hundreds of jars I remember.

I see my parents walking in a wheat field nearing harvest time. I see them in a
lush field; it looks like the best harvest ever. How is that I see such a
beautiful picture when the 1930's to 1940's were really tough times.

I can see our family table - the smell of mother cooking our supper. I can hear
us kids as our father taught us to say grace before supper. I can smell the
kerosene lamps burning. Most of all, I can feel my mother's gentle hands, her
unconditional love, and her warm hugs on a cold night at bedtime. Yes, these are
good memories - suppose they are like the farm - you can't take them away from
the boy.

My best wishes to all our families and friends that have known and loved Java,
the greatest town in the U.S.A.

I'm Ruben Aman, a Java boy.

P.S. I want to thank my niece, Laurie Aman, for her help in putting these
thoughts in type. She was a big help.

Remember the Winter Of...
Jan. 12, 1888: Severe blizzard that began early in the morning, paralyzing the
whole territory. Many lives and livestock were lost. Tunnels were dug from
houses to wells and barns.

Jan.1949: Snow covered a nearly bare ground and strong winds piled the snow.
According to the newspaper, the blizzard of 1888 was short-lived, lasting around
12 hours. The first of the '49 blizzards lasted nearly four days. Other severe
SD weather conditions in Jan. took place in 1873, 1912, 1916 to 1919, 1929-30
and 1936-37.

Jan. 3, 1950: On the anniversary of the terrible 1949 blizzard, the weatherman
had another. Electric power failed and left many without heat. Some families
depended on their old coal furnace and many went to the basements, where laundry
and oil stoves kept them warm. Many of the homes had no mail delivery for three
weeks, some had no phones. It was estimated that 40 inches of snow had fallen
since Dec. 15. Another snowstorm hit for three days in March. Northwestern Bell
Telephone reported 1,000 wire breaks and 69 poles down.

1955: The worst blizzard in recent years occurred, two died.

Mar. 2, 3, 4, 1966: The wind increased, causing a full-blown blizzard. As the
storm progressed, electricity came to a halt and the only form of communication
was from transistor radios. The snow drifts in the country covered trees and
buried equipment, as well as low houses and sheds. The Red Cross Unit brought a
weasel in to help people who had called for food, fuel, and medical help. This
blizzard claimed 10 lives and an estimated 95,000 head of livestock. Around
Java, 16 people were reported injured.

1977: Reported as the worst blizzard in 10 years.

Jan. 1997: One blizzard after another created havoc. Several feet of snow had
already accumulated on the ground, when a 50 m.p.h. howled and a light snowfall
added to the lack of visibility. Snow banks became deeper, wind chills were down
to 80 below, grocery and meat suppliers were unable to travel and supplies ran
short. Roofs collapsed from the heavy snow, schools were not in session, and
roads were blocked. Java people couldn't get out of town and the rural community
couldn't get in to town. Many ranchers were cut off from their herds, and many
got disoriented while trying to check on the livestock. President Clinton
approved Gov. Janklow's request for a disaster declaration in the state, which
provided emergency services.

(Photo:) Joe Zarka to the southeast of his house after the 1966 Blizzard

(Photo:) At the southwest corner of Java after the 1997 Blizzard

(Photo:) "And ve vas chust Shtuck!" Underpass after Blizzard of 1997

(Photo:) A different kind of blizzard in 1988. Those tumbleweeds didn't "drift
         along!"

Hessel Dyk, Pioneer of Java, Passes Away
Funeral services were held in Java, Weds., Dec. 29, 1948, for Hessel Dyk, about
88, who passed away at an Aberdeen hospital on Fri., Dec. 24, after an illness
of a few days duration. He had been staying at the Fairview Rest Home for a
number of years, due to the infirmities of old age.

Hessel Dyk was one of the early pioneers who homesteaded near the present site
of Java, and after the town was started made his home in Java until a few years
ago. He disposed of his land, SE of the town, and had not been actively farming
for many years.

He was born in Holland and his mother passed away when he was seven years of
age. After his father's remarriage, he left home and came to this country to
make his home. He was never married, and his only known near relatives are a
nephew in this country and a niece in Holland. When the Java Herald was
established in Java in 1903, he worked in the print shop for a number of years
as a pressman. One of the colorful old pioneers of this end of the county, he
was known by most of the older residents.

He attended the Presbyterian Church in Java for many years. Funeral services
were held in the S.D. Adventist Church in Java at 2 p.m., with Rev. Ford of the
Presbyterian Church of Pollock, officiating. Interment was made in the Java

[Hessel Dyk's remembrances, following, were taken from the Java Herald, Sept. 7,
1923, and his obituary also from the Herald.]

TALES OF EARLY JAVA by Hessel Dyk
In the spring of 1889, finding I could not get enough work to keep me as busy as
I wished to be, I left my old home in Holland and sailed for the U.S., going
directly to Grand Rapids, MI, where I had a cousin living. I stayed with this
cousin for about 10 days after which I proceeded to Bowdle. At this time I was
taken to the home of a friend of mine, by the name of Van der Vorm, whose farm
was located east of the present Haux' Grove. I stayed here a short time and then
hired out for the summer to some folks by the name of Roper Bosch, I received
the top wages for my work, which were at that time $18 a month. To a boy just
over from the old country, I thought I was getting lots of money, and I was for
those days. I worked for these people for two years and managed to save up quite
a little money. I had in the meantime taken up land, my pre-emption being the
quarter upon which John Pregitzer is now living.

(Photo:) Hessel Dyk

After leaving Roper Bosch, I batched it for a year with a man by the name of
John Hegert and farmed my quarter at the same time. Our shack was located a
little NW of the Garret Noble farm. Later on finding that it would cost me $200
to prove up on this quarter, and realizing that the land was so cheap I let it
go back to the government. Later, however, I took up my homestead which is
located about two miles south of Java.

I farmed with two oxen and two horses. I had a fine buggy which was considered
"some class" in those days. I believe that a good buggy in those early times was
considered more than an automobile is today, for they were by no means common.
Our crops were fair, but we had to haul every bit of our grain to Bowdle and
when you consider our motive power was oxen, you will imagine that this was
anything but a pleasant job.

My first impression of SD was anything but pleasant. All I could see for miles
and miles was prairie, with no towns and only a few houses and farms to break
the monotony. I thought to myself that I would get out of here as soon as I
could, but being broke I had to go to work and earn the necessary money. During
the time required to earn this money, however, I grew to like the country, a
fact that is self-evident, because I am still here, and intend to remain here
until I pass out.

When one steps into a steam heated train or a fine automobile, a matter of a few
hundred miles doesn't worry one, but I can recall how, way back in Feb. 1895,
Roper Bosch and I drove to Andover to visit some friends. It was an awful trip
and on the way back we drove from Aberdeen to Bowdle against a stiff NW wind,
with the thermometer registering around 20 below zero. Talk about your pleasant
trips, it took us two days to make Andover and the same coming back.

In the fall of 1900, things being kind of dead here I went back to Michigan to
visit my cousin, where I remained until the following spring. During my absence
the railroad had been extended to Evarts and upon my arrival here everything was
a hustle and a bustle. The town of Java had seemed to spring up overnight and I
decided that I would live in town and farm at the same time. I have done this
ever since and the past 20 years have seen Java grow from nothing to a fair
sized and prosperous little city.

In the earlier days of the town, things were sort of wild with gambling houses
wide open. It was not until a few years later when the town had established a
stable form of government, that things quieted down somewhat. I had never seen a
place grow like Java did the first five years of its existence. It seemed like
we would go to bed at night and wake up the next morning to find that three or
four new buildings had gone up overnight.

Shortly after the Java Herald was started and for many years afterwards, I used
to help them print and fold the papers. I can recall how many times we used to
work all night to get the English and German papers out. It was tedious work,
printing all those papers on the old hand press and them fold them afterwards.
When we used the old hand press we had to roll them off by hand, ink by hand, a
very slow and tiresome Job. It was always a big relief to all of us when the
paper was out and in the postoffice.

I have lived in Java ever since it was started and in the U.S. for 34 years, and
my residence in this country and town has been very pleasant. When I left
Holland I had to break all my home ties, but I have never regretted coming, to
become a citizen of the best and biggest nation in the world, and I am perfectly
contented to live in SD and Java until my time on this world is up. The early
days were hard ones, but those hardships make these days of comparative luxury
more pleasant.
